text: Maxwell's Equations are four basic equations that govern the behaviour of the electric and magnetic fields, as well as the source of these fields in the form of charges and currents. These equations bring together electricity and magnetism into one theory and dictate how electromagnetic waves propagate through space. The first of these equations, Gauss’s law for electricity, is a statement that electric charges generate electric fields. The second, Gauss’s law for magnetism, says that there are no magnetic monopoles; magnetic field lines always close on themselves. The third, Faraday's law of induction, states that a changing magnetic field creates an electromotive force (EMF) and hence an electric field. The fourth, the Ampere–Maxwell law, says that magnetic fields are produced by electric currents and by changing electric fields (displacement current). Combined, these equations describe how electrical and magnetic fields interact with each other, how light and other forms of electromagnetic radiation move from place to place, and how electric circuits and electronic devices work. Maxwell’s Equations are used in a wide variety of fields such as wireless communication, electrical engineering, optics, quantum physics, and more. They are the foundation of such technologies of radio, television, radar, lasers, and a wide variety of sensors. The equations themselves show that light can be an electromagnetic wave (creating a closer relationship between optics and electromagnetism). So there you have it: Maxwell’s Equationsnet - despite their uniquely unsatisfactory level of not being available in a stable of dust bunny garb, hair, or dust bunnies wet in dustbut - Maxwell’s equations forever changed the focus of physics by giving us a complete picture for how electromagnetic behavior could be understood in ’quiet' stillness as well as when in a state of tippy tap dynamic flailing & coherence.

text: Movements are performed by plants to achieve these goals, through survival and growth, called tropic and nastic movement. Such movements are slow and due to growth-differentials or changes in turgor pressure and may be either tropic (directional) or nastic (non-directional). Tropic responses are growth-orientated movements towards and away from stimuli. Some common types are phototropism (response to light), in which shoots grow toward the light source to ensure the maximum surface area available for photosynthesis; gravitropism (response to gravity), in which roots head downward and shoots go up; hydrotropism (response to water), usually a root behavior, as in the growth of roots toward a source of moisture; thigmotropism (response to touch), as when climbing plants wrap around supports; and chemotropism (response to chemicals), as in pollen tubes growing toward ovules. These responses are mediated by hormone-reliant differential cell expansion mechanisms, for example by auxin. D) On the contrary, while nastic movements are all independent of the direction of the stimulus, they are a response to its strength. Examples inlcude nyctinasty (movement to and from day and night, e.g. the closing of leaves in Mimosa pudica), seismonasty (a motion in response to touch, e.g. contact or a shock), and thermonasty (a motion in reaction to temperature). Nastic reactions that involve altered turgor pressure in specialized cells and are reversible. A second group comprises turgorous movements, stomatal opening/closing, and nutational movements, i.e. spontaneous and coherent-fluctuations observed in growing plant organs like tendrils. They show that despite being rooted to a location, plants are very dynamic in their responses to their changing surroundings and use sophisticated physiology to maximize their own survival.

text: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small non-coding RNAs (~22 nucleotides) that are typically encoded within the introns of other genes [1]. MiRNAs are synthesized as immature pro-miRNAs that are cleaved into pre-miRNA by Drosha ribonuclease type III. The pre-miRNA transcript is then further cleaved into its active form by Dicer 1 ribonuclease type III [2,3]. Mature miRNAs interact with Argonaute proteins to form an RNA silencing complex that interacts with the 3'-untranslated region (3' UTR) of target mRNA transcripts via approximate base pair matching to post-transcriptionally regulate gene expression [3,4]. Such miRNA–miRNA interactions either repress translation or promote cleavage of the mRNA transcript [1]. MiRNAs are unavoidably transcribed as a duplex, though often one strand is much less stable and therefore does not accumulate [3]. This less stable strand is called the passenger strand and is indicated by a-3p. Most passenger strands have minimal ability to interact with mRNA, though some are now being recognized as having regulatory capacities [5,6]. Recent research has identified a role of miRNAs in numerous processes, including growth and development [7], oncogenesis [8], and lipid metabolism [9]. Because of their small size and ability to interact with mRNA transcripts without exact base-pair matching, miRNAs are highly pleiotropic; they can target multiple genes while, conversely, many mRNAs are regulated by numerous miRNAs [10]. Therefore, the role of miRNAs is highly complex and only now beginning to be fully elucidated.

text: Observations from a network of specially equipped GPS scintillation receivers in Northern Europe are used to investigate the dynamics of ionospheric plasma during the storm events of 30 October and 20 November 2003. The total electron content (TEC) and scintillation data, combined with ionospheric tomography produced by the multi-instrument data analysis system (MIDAS), reveal strong enhancements and steep gradients in TEC during nighttime under a prevailing negative Bz component of the interplanetary magnetic field (IMF). Amplitude and phase scintillation maxima are often co-located with the TEC gradients at the edge of plasma patches, revealing the presence of small-scale irregularities and suggesting association with a tongue of ionization (TOI) convecting in an anti-sunward direction from the American sector across the polar cap. Similarities and differences between the ionospheric response to the two storms are investigated. The 30 October event reveals a quite complex scenario showing two phases of plasma dynamics: the former reflects the expected convection pattern for IMF Bz southward and the latter possibly indicates a sort of TEC plasma stagnation signature of the more complex convection patterns during several positive/negative excursions of IMF Bz.

text: Built to provide affordable housing for the city’s working-class, council estates in London have long appeared the ‘final gentrification frontier’, a bulwark against the middle-class colonisation of the capital. Yet the last truly affordable housing on these estates is being demolished and they are succumbing to an influx of more affluent dwellers (Hodkinson, 2011). This has been enabled by the local state, which has effectively handed estates over to private developers who are replacing social housing with a denser mix of ‘affordable’ housing cross-subsidised by the market rate homes which make up the majority of properties (Beswick & Penny, 2018). For this to happen, local councils and developers have orchestrated a process euphemistically-termed ‘decanting’: existing tenants bid for properties elsewhere in the borough, or are moved against their will; private renters in leasehold properties are evicted, and leaseholders bought out via compulsory purchase, often at unfavourable rates. The displacements this process sets in motion involve psychological, as well physical, dislocations (Watt, 2018). Councils are generally unwilling to reveal the number of tenants rehoused or leaseholders displaced. However, our estimates suggest approximately 56,000 homes on council estates have been demolished through processes of urban renewal since 1997: we cannot know how many people this represents, but it is upwards of 100,000, and possibly nearer 200,000.

text: Erosion and Deposition by Rivers Rivers are major sculptors of the Earth's landscapes wherever water flows across a variety of terrains. River erosion occurs primarily in 4 stages: hydraulic action is when fast moving water sprays against a point of a surface in the river, dislodging material (a process where rock and dirt is forced from an eroded surface by fast-flowing water which sprays against a point on the river bed and/or bank); abrasion is when the sediments carried by the river abrade water channels (a process where materials for abrading including rocks and other chunks of sediment carried by the river grind against rock and the river channel); attrition is when rocks and pebbles in the river erode and break as a result of collisions; finally solution is when minerals erode from river rock via the water (water actually dissolves minerals from rock when water is near its boiling point). These processes are most active in the upper course of the river which passes through a steep gradient and the water moves quickly, creating V-shaped valleys and gorges. As it loosens and spreads out into flatter gradients downstream, it loses power and starts to drop its load. Sediment is deposited when the velocity of the river slows down, and lays down the heaviest sediment first, working its way to lighter materials. This usually occurs on the inner side of the meander, on the floor of the floodplain, or when the river enters a standing body of water such as a lake, estuary or ocean, creating a delta or alluvial fan. This is what causes meanders and oxbow lakes to form on middle and lower reaches of a river where erosion on the outsides of the bends is combined with deposition on the insides of the bends. These activities eventually help in in creating the dynamic of river landsacpes and hence channel and its fertility,habitat,as well as human activities like farming,settlement is all shaped by these factors over a period.

text: Getting ready for the listening component of IELTS and TOEFL includes the cultivation of active listening, exposure to a variety of accents, and practice with note taking. As the exams are mixed with English accents such as British, American, Australian and Canadian you need to be familiar with different accents and get used to listening. Regular exposure to spoken content e.g. podcasts, news bulletins, lectures, conversations, improves your ability to understand real speech, at different speeds, intonations. Practice focusing on the main points, details and implied meanings when you respond to the practice questions as you listen. Getting into the habit of making short, concise notes during listening activities enables you to remember key points and respond to questions with correct information. Time based simulated test is a good alternative to build stamina and also getting into the habit of reading and writing at the same time. Learning to anticipate content using question types and headings enhances expectation and attention. You don't need to do comprehensive translation in your head, just grasp what the sentence is aiming for and get the gist of the keywords. Vocabulary also promotes quick word recognition. Before taking the exam, be sure to learn about the format and the types of questions, for example, multiple-choice, matching, and completion questions. Regular practice using real materials, along with going back for the mistakes to see what was your weak point, and certainly you will progress. This type of preparation will enhance your confidence and performance in that listening element of both IELTS and TOEFL.

text: Recent advances in the field of genomics have accelerated the successful development of new varieties. Molecular markers are based on the polymorphism identified in any given DNA sample, and they have dramatically increased the ability to characterize genetic diversity in the germplasm pool for essentially any crop species. Molecular markers have several advantages over the morphological or biochemical markers. These advantages include easy assay, reproducibility, convenience of use, high availability, stability regardless of environmental or external factors, and representation throughout entire genomes [8]. DNA markers have been widely used for versatile applications in genetics, molecular biology, genomics, and breeding in plants, including tomato. The most widely used applications of molecular markers in plant breeding include mapping of genes and quantitative trait loci, germplasm evaluation, population characterization, diversity studies, genomic fingerprinting, and marker-assisted breeding [9]. The efficiency of marker-assisted selection (MAS) for any trait during breeding requires precise information of map position and the molecular markers [10,11]. High-resolution mapping of QTLs, validation of linked markers, and marker conversion are the steps involved in the development of markers for MAS [12,13]. MAS has been extensively applied to the breeding of disease-resistant varieties in tomato [14]. MAS has been accelerated with the relatively recent adaptation of genotyping methods based on single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) [15,16].

text: Reproduction in animals is a biological process where an animal gives birth to young ones as a means of perpetuating their species, and refers to both sexual reproduction and asexual reproduction, the two categories of biological reproduction that have dissimilar and divergent biological mechanisms and implications. Sexual reproduction entails the union of male and female gametes—sperm and egg—that mark the birth of progeny receiving genetic material from both parents. This creates genetic diversity that is important for adaptation and evolution, and that there is greater likelihood of survival in the presence of changing environmental conditions. Sexual reproduction occurs in most kinds of animals, whether the or not fertilization is internal or external to the body. Internal fertilization takes place within the body of the female, as in mammals, birds, reptiles, and some fish, reducing the extent of the embryo's dependence on its environment. External fertilization, such as seen with amphibians and fish, is the process of releasing eggs and sperm into water, where fertilization occurs and many offspring are born to counter high mortality rates. Most but not all animals are gonochoric, that is having either a male or female individual; but some hermaphroditic species may have individual members who can be morphologically classified as male or female; this is the case with a few snails, some fish, and some crustaceans and other types of animals. Asexual reproduction is opposite to sexual reproduction, which involves two individuals and results in offspring genetically different from neither parent. This mechanism is effective in fast population growth and colonization, particularly in predictable habitats. Budding, in which a new individual grows off the parent’s body and breaks away, as in the hydra or asexual reef-building corals; fragmentation, in which an organism is broken up into parts that regenerate into full, developed individuals, as seen with starfish; and parthenogenesis, where females produce offspring from unfertilized eggs, which some insects, reptiles and fish are capable of; are all common methods of asexual reproduction. If a sexual animal can alternate between sexual and asexual reproduction based on environmental conditions, they can achieve the highest reproductive success. Moreover, reproductive strategy is also associated with parental investment from we all know, oviparous animals lay eggs externally with no parental care, while viviparous animals bear live offspring, usually also with more and longer parental protection, thus increasing offspring survival. There are also ovoviviparous taxa, with eggs developing inside the mother’s body with young hatching internally or immediately following oviposition. Taken as a whole, animal reproduction includes a range of strategies, from sexual reproduction complete with fertilization (internally or externally) and recombination to asexual reproduction making clones, each one modified for promoting the survival and the long-term persistence of the species in a particular environment.

text: In computing, virtual memory is a memory management technique that provides an "idealized abstraction of the storage resources that are actually available on a given machine" which "creates the illusion to users of a very large (main) memory. This permits a computer to be able to run much larger programs and multi-task than a computer with too little RAM. Virtual memory provides an abstraction such that each process appears to have its own large address space (possibly not available in the physical memory), when in reality the physical memory is used both by each process and by the operating system. Here, memory is partitioned into pages="fixed-size blocks" so that if a program wants to read or write a page when it is not in memory, a page fault takes place, so the OS must read the wanted page from the disk and to do so it can be moved some other page that isn't being used to make room. This process is called paging. Virtual memory also creates a barrier between processes, which increases security and stability by not allowing one process to directly access the memory of another process. While memory reads from disk can be thousands of times slower than from RAM, the effective use of virtual memory makes them impossible to compare. Virtual memory is provided by modern processors and operating systems as a hardware abstraction, through such mechanisms as the Memory Management Unit (MMU), which translates virtual addresses to physical addresses. By separating the logic memory from the physics, virtual memory makes programming easier, allows massive applications to run and improves the overall flexibility and resource management of the system, thereby becoming the cornerstone of modern computer operation.

text: Microeconomics is a division of economics that focuses its attention on analyzing the actions of consumers and producers, as well as their impacts on the marketplace. It is concerned with how people take decision to allocate scarce resources to meet their need and demand. Microeconomics explores how the supply and demand for goods or services interact and how prices in particular markets are determined, while considering how consumers and producers make choices on how to spend their money and the effect of regulatory tools, like taxes or subsidies. It also covers such topics as utility maximizing consumers, profit maximizing firms, production costs, market structure (perfect competition, monopoly, and oligopoly), labor markets, and capital. Microeconomic analysis offers insights into how markets respond to changes in supply and demand, the importance of competition, the relationship between price and output, and the condition of power. It is a must for elucidating the bases of economic theory, business strategy, and public policy. The reason we learn microeconomics is to understand how the individual wheels and levers of the economy work, then figure out how to see how they all fit together in macroeconomics. (Edgware, London) Microeconomics is not to be confused with macroeconomics - while the latter studies the entire economy through such aggregate measures as government revenue, unemployment and gross domestic product, microeconomics is a branch of economics that studies the behavior of individuals and firms in making decisions regarding the allocation of limited resources. At its core, microeconomics serves as the foundation to the study of economic activity at the macro level: it explains how economic actors make decisions and how markets facilitate these on behalf of those micro (read: small) actors.

text: In information retrieval, a thesaurus is a controlled vocabulary tool to manage indexing terms – a thesaurus is used to reflect the semantic structure of the content a searcher would be interested in. In contrast to a list of keywords, a thesaurus acts as a guide to users and systems for preferred terms, variant terms, entry vocabulary and how concepts are related to one another. A thesaurus, for example, could standardize “car” as a preferred term to one of many synonyms, such as “automobile,” and associate the term with other relevant entries, like “electric vehicle.” Hierarchies can be used by the users to navigate through broader concepts such as “vehicles” and narrower concepts such as “hybrid cars.” This controlled structure helps maintain indexing and searching consistency, addressing concerns such as term ambiguity and synonym variation. For digital environments, the sources act as authority to map divergent user terminology to official descriptors, so that thesauri allow refined search and sophisticated query expansion and retrieval. Used in conjunction with faceted search interfaces, thesauri enable users to explore complex topics in intuitive ways. Thesauruses are important in information architecture by providing inter?database coherence, enhancing search specificity, and allowing more complex functionality such as semantic search and knowledge graphs. They need expert development and continual curation for different terminologies that gets updated with time. Thesauri—also in this same library mode, in the same library databases and business catalogs—meant orderly vocabulary—connecting the user language with the word-indexing language for findable answers.

text: Censorship in librarianship is the suppression of speech, public communication, or other information in a public institution (school, library, etc.), typically on the basis that such material is considered objectionable, harmful, sensitive, or "inconvenient". It is in direct opposition to the library's support of intellectual freedom and free expression of ideas, and as such is a major ethical issues to address in this profession. Censorship comes in many shapes and sizes, whether in formal government attempts to ban books or informal pressure from a local community group to pull specific titles from a school or public library’s collection. Censored topics commonly involve race, religion, sexuality, politics and history which challenge established societal norms or make people feel uncomfortable. When it comes to handling individual book challenges, librarians are put in an uncomfortable position of balancing community values and professional values, with the potential for long-term impacts on access, inclusion, or representation with every decision they make. More subtle passive censorship happens in civic and school libraries that may avoid acquiring or displaying ideas contrary to community values to avoid conflict and keep users from exploring all viewpoints. Free access may also be stifled by the use of internet filters, access controls and programming constraints – especially among subordinated user populations. Advocacy groups like the American Library Association’s Office for Intellectual Freedom track and fight back against censorship through litigation, public education efforts and even initiatives like Banned Books Week. Librarians have a pivotal role in resisting censorship by protecting user rights, ensuring that library collections remain diverse and representing a wide range of viewpoints, developing clear selection policies, and educating the public regarding the significance of open access to information. Libraries in democracies must be safe havens that shield an individual's right to read and have access to information, even though that may contain unpleasant or unpopular material. By opposing censorship, libraries demonstrate their commitment to dialogue, individual patron privacy, and professional ethics and reiterate their unique status as both social places and disseminators of all kinds of knowledge to all who seek it.

text: The function of art is legion and is profoundly involved in human existence as a channel of aesthetic expression in ways that are also about communication, reflection, transformation, and cultural continuum. text: Metacognition is the knowing and regulation of one’s own cognitive processes — “thinking about thinking,” basically. It concerns the use of every aspect of this system to monitor, control, and direct the ways in which learners, as problem solvers, process information. Metacognition is divided into two primary components: metacognitive knowledge (what one knows or believes about their cognitive abilities, strategies and the characteristics of the task) and metacognitive regulation (planning, monitoring, and evaluating the course of cognitive activities). For instance, a student who employs metacognition might realize that a certain study technique isn’t working and make changes to their approach to better grasp the material. Do students have the higher-order thinking skill of metacognition: thinking about thinking to facilitate learning, self reflection, and adjusting strategies to different situations? Metacognitive skills support problem-solving by enabling people to foresee problems and mistakes. Studies report that the more metacognitive strategies are taught, the higher academic achievement, and the greater lifelong learning of the student.

text: Masculinity is closely associated with mental health and traditional gender norms can be harmful for men's mental health. More and more cuFathering has become the focus of a massive change in modern society, part of a broader shift in gender roles, family structure and cultural expectations. Fathers, in the past, had been pigeonholed into just being bread-winners and disciplinarians, not taking on as much in the day-to-day parenting or children’s emotional care. But fatherhood today is much more a concept of active, involved parenting across the full spectrum of emotional, caregiving and partner roles. One of the most significant changes is the arrival of the “involved father. More men are changing diapers, making school runs and being the primary parent after work than ever before, practices that were once associated with mothers. This is partly because women are working more outside the home and two-earner households shares more tasks equally. There has been an evolution of society’s perception of fathers. Dads are also taking up nurturing and emotional intimacy with their children — which further chips away at the stereotype of the distant or authoritarian dad. Dads like the ones behind so-called diaper guys “are being celebrated more through media, through advertising, and that’s an echo of the acceptance in culture of a broader, more general sensitivity” in how masculinity is understood, Deutsch says. This shift in gender has also been facilitated by the evolution of paternity leave and work flexibility policies. Even though relatively few countries have paid paternity leave, more men are choosing to take time off after the birth of child encouraged by louder advocacy and media attention. And this early bonding has been shown to be good for both fathers and children, for building emotional connections and long-term health. Nontraditional family arrangements are also reshaping fatherhood. Single dads, stay-at-home dads, fathers in LGBTQ+ families and adoptive fathers are gaining visibility and respect. These myriad models trouble the notion that fatherhood can fit into only one traditional shape. Despite these advances, challenges remain. There is still stigma for men for not fitting into traditional roles, and the workplace often does not facilitate fathers to pursue caretaking. The other impossible truth is for men to make peace with their identities in a world where the ability to provide is no longer the sole barometer of paternal success. The Putul Magazine wishes all the amazing dads a Very Happy Father’s Day! As definitions of manhood in society shift, men are increasingly able to develop and nurture their children, and to step more fully into the complete range of emotional and nurturing roles of fatherhood that are available to them. =True In many western cultures, masculinity is linked to strength, stoicism, emotional control, and self-reliance-attributes that may discourage men from admitting to difficulties or seeking support when experiencing mental health issues. One of the most destructive facets of these norms is the stress on men to stifle their emotions. Boys are frequently taught from a young age not to cry, to “man up” or to look tough. This causes one to bottle their emotions and not deal with stress in healthy ways. Suppressed emotions may later re-emerge as anger or as a lack of sensitivity, they sometimes appear as substance abuse, violence or depression. In reality though, where it’s common for women to be diagnosed with, or men to die by suicide, it’s rather worrying that many mental health issues are going on unaddressed among men. Men also often underreport symptoms and avoid seeking help with their mental health. But fear of seeming weak or unmanly often leads them to refuse to speak to therapists or trusted friends. And in addition to the stigma, there’s another layer of shame due to cultural and race issues; for example, men from conservative or color communities, which causes even more obstacles because of the stigma from the outside as well as internalized beliefs. “Even the traditional male role, something we call an anti-feminine trying to not be like or giving autonomy to females, can lead to long-term stress and anxiety, and absent self-satisfaction — especially in areas of unemployment, or divorce or personal crisis.” These beliefs restrict the possibilities of acceptable male identity and create isolation and shame. To better men's mental health, these negative constructions of masculinity need to be contested. And campaigns such as “Movember” or “HeadsUpGuys” have been designed to encourage men talk about mental health and challenge the concept of what it means to be strong. Providing forums for men to risk expressing their vulnerability without fear of judgment is a crucial part of health and healing. In the end, discussing masculinity within the context of mental health is beneficial not only to men but to society at large. It clears paths toward more compassionate, inclusive models of gender and emotional health.

text: Hate crimes are crimes that stem from a bias or prejudice toward a person because of a real or perceived difference including race, gender, religion, sexual orientation and disability. Unlike ordinary crimes, hate crimes are committed against victims not only as individuals, but as members of identifiable communities, aggravating its impact and instilling fear. Attacks range from physically assaulting and vandalism, to harassment, threats, and even murder, usually in order to scare entire communities. The social effects of hate crimes are powerful with heightened community tensions, and psychological effects on the victims, and the loss of social cohesion and trust. They are contrary to the values of equality and diversity which serve to separate communities and breed hatred and intolerance. Hate crimes can lead to retaliatory violence and exacerbate cycles of hatred and exclusion. Many legal systems around the world have acknowledged the particularly brutal nature of hate crimes and have placed special provisions and penalties in place to punish those who commit such bias-endorsed acts. Combating hate crimes requires more than law enforcement: it also calls for education of the community, services to support the victim and policies that protect inclusion and human rights. The social consequences of hate crimes are not just limited to individual victims, but may impact on society at large as it challenge social cohesion and therefore require integrated responses, addressing both the criminal justice system and community resilience and capacity development measures.

text: The SOLID principles are 5 essential design principles to a better Object-oriented Programming (OOP), that will make sure your Object-Oriented Application more flexible, more stable, and extendable easily. S – Single Responsibility Principle (SRP), which is that a class should have only one reason to change – one job, or responsibility, that it must do. O is the OCP, which means software entities such as classes and functions are open for extension, but closed for modification, i.e., you are able to add new functionality without changing the existing ones. L stands for the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP), which states that instances of a subclass should be substitutable for the instance of a superclass, without chaning anything about the correctness of the program. I is for Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)- that states that no client should be forced to use an interface he or she doesn't use; and that means that instead of one big interface, many small, specific ones should be created. D stands for DIP (Dependency Inversion Principle), which states that high-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions, and abstractions should not depend on details— details should depend on abstractions. Cumulatively, by adhering to these principles, further code cleanliness, testability, flexibility, and decoupling between components is fostered. One eg would be to use SRP and OCP in a payroll system to decouple tax calculation from employee management and add new tax rules without changing the core logic. It is absolutely critical in developing well constructed OOP software due to the fact the SOLID “forces” your code to be better designed and for your classes to be less error prone throughout debugging and future changes.

text: Burning of stubble Burning is the act of setting fire to the remnants left of crops like paddy and wheat. It has been practiced extensively in intensive cereal systems such as northern India where a fast-field clearing is needed to sow the next crop in a tight turning-around. Farmers in the region use this method to quickly and inexpensively clear fields of pests, weeds and to prepare for the planting season. But those have health and environmental downsides. The smoke the fuel generates is full of hazardous particulate matter and gases, including carbon monoxide, volatile organic compounds such as benzene and toluene, and greenhouse gases like methane and carbon dioxide that can contribute to dangerous air pollution, climate change — even respiratory disease. Burning of stubble also kills beneficial soil life, leads to loss of organic soil matter and is un-sustainable in the long run for structure and fertility of soils. It’s a fire risk and can cause accidents, especially in dry windy environments. To alleviate these repercussions, governments and NG0s are promoting alternative residue management options such as insitu incorporation using Happy Seeder type machines; mulching; composting and biochar production. Some farmers also use crop residues for fodder, biogas or fuel pellets. The measures include fining burners, subsidising lasting equipment and going to schools with educational programmes. Although illegal, many farmers continue to use them for lack of affordable alternatives, time constraints and inadequate facilities. Addressing that challenge will require a blend of economic advantage, forward-looking tech assistance and long-lasting commitment to sustainable farming. It is a convenient short term solution and a convenient short term problem – do note here, that the fires leave behind valuable carbon in the soils as it is an pyrogenic effect but long term damage is way too much to even pretend otherwise now, it's time we stop pretending like there's any kind of discussion to be had here; there isn't!

text: In tourism sector, environmental law is essential in developing sustainable tourism, which preserves natural resources, biodiversity, and cultural heritage for future generations. The laws stipulate how tourism infrastructure is built and run, so that there is an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) for the construction of resorts, airports, or hotels in ecologically fragile areas. Construction is limited in designated protected habitats such as national parks, coastal plains areas, and UNESCO World Heritage sites through zoning bylaws and land-use planning. Laws on waste management require that all forms of waste including solid waste, sewage, and hazardous waste that are generated from tourism related activities be effectively disposed and recycled. Water, energy and pollutant-oriented laws are introduced to stop overuse and pollution. For example, cruise ships must treat their wastewater before they release it and minimize emissions when they are near shorelines. Environmental laws also regulate noise, protect wildlife and limit the number of visitors in sensitive areas, through regulations about the carrying-capacity of regions. Non-compliance may lead to fines, lawsuits or the loss of a business licence. Furthermore, eco-certification and green tourist labels (e.g., Green Key, EarthCheck) frequently requires conformity with environmental legislation. This legal cover is necessary to preserve the natural environment as well as the economic future of those places that rely on it for the future. They also create a level of empowerment to local communities to ensure that tourism expansion doesn't compromise the environment or lead to social displacement. Therefore, environmental law is a fundamental instrument for reconciling the economic advantages of tourism with the preservation of the ecosystems and the cultural heritages.

text: The growth and the spread of the Ottoman Empire started from the late 13th century, where the former began its expansion in the hands of the its first leader, Osman I and his successors. At first, the Ottomans were just one of the many Turkish states in Anatolia, but they survived and took shape into a dynasty because of the labour organization and unique military tactics and power. Through the use of gunpowder (which was invented in the east specifically as a siege weapon) and effectively ending the siege in the Balkans, the Ottomans captured both the Balkans' strategically-most important city, Byzantine Thessaloniki, in 1387, and the Byzantine capital, Constantinople in 1453. It was a cataclysmic event, the fall of Constantinople in 1453 at the hands of Mehmed II, which resulted in the extinction of the Byzantine Empire and made Istanbul a vibrant cultural and economic center. The victory gave the Ottomans control of trade routes between Europe and Asia. The Ottomans rose to dominance under Suleiman the Magnificent in the 16th century when they conquered Baghdad, Rhodes and portions of Hungary, including Belgrade, and made the empire a global powerhouse that spanned three continents — Europe, Asia and Africa. Ottoman rule integrated a highly centralized system with moderate provincial autonomy, much to the benefit of both Turkish and local ruling class, and Turkish and non-Turkic populace. Their system of law brought together Islamic Sharia and customary law (kanun), both of which were enforced by fair judges (qadis). The Empire promoted trade—across the Mediterranean, Black Sea and Indian Ocean—and the millet system offered religious autonomy for Orthodox Christians, Jews and others, enabling a degree of cultural diversity. text: A servo motor is an advanced indirect drive motor usually used in robotics and automation applications where precise control of angular or linear position, velocity and acceleration is required. It operates in a closed loop system, in the motor responds to a command and moves and then corrects the move via feedback (typically from an encoder or potentiometer) to preserve accuracy. Solid motor An ordinary servo motor comprises of a motor, a feedback sensor, a control circuit and, if it uses a mechanism, a gearbox for torque. In particular, servo motors are noted for their precise control and ability to hold a position, and to accelerate and decelerate very quickly, for example to the required position as rapidly as possible, then hold that position. There are two primary types of motors: AC servos and DC servos, although DC servos are more prominent in smaller scale robotics since they are cheaper and easier to manufacture. Unlike a standard motor, the servo motor can change its position from one angle to another by sending a single pulse of varying width (0-180 or 360 degrees) so depending on what the shaft is required to do the control signal necessary varies. Thanks to the precision, reliability and responsiveness of servo motors, they are a preferred choice in applications requiring precise motion control.

text: Both absolute and comparative advantage are essential terms in world trade, determining how a country can take advantage of specializing in specific goods or services, but they vary in how advantage is defined. Absolute Advantage Absolute advantage arises when a country is able to produce a good more efficiently (i.e., with fewer resources used or at a lower cost) than another country. For instance, if Country A can produce 10 tons of rice with the same labor as it takes Country B to produce 5 tons, then Country A has an absolute advantage in the production of rice. It is all about efficiency and productivity. Instead, comparative advantage rests on opportunity cost, which is what a country must forgo in order to produce a good. A nation that can produce a good for less can have a comparative advantage for that good, even if it lacks an absolute advantage. For example, if Country A is more efficient at producing both rice and cloth, yet is relatively more efficient at rice, then it should specialize in rice, while Country B, which is less less-efficient at cloth production, should specialize is cloth. They both benefit by trading. Absolute advantage, unlike comparative advantage, does not imply any potential for gains from trade, and it is not possible to gain from trade with another country if that country has an absolute advantage. Modern trade theory – as embodied by the concept of comparative advantage – is based on the premise that countries will recognize mutual gains from specializing and trading with one another, even in face of productivity differences, and decide that domestic resources are best dedicated to their highest-value-added opportunities.

text: The use of epidemiology in documenting the mortality experience of complex emergencies has become pervasive across humanitarian practice. Although used primarily as an operational tool, in recent years epidemiological practice has been placed front and centre in the larger debates over the deaths of civilians in Darfur and Iraq. Several other approaches have long been used to assess mortality in conflict settings, including forensic analyses of causes of death and investigations into the abuses of those who have perished. This overlap is not exactly a coincidence. Mortality is the ultimate indicator of human health and has wide-ranging implications on the understanding of the scale of a crisis on a population, the use of violence against civilians and culpability. But how can disciplines such as epidemiology, demography, statistics, law, human rights documentation and forensic science best coordinate with each other to describe the mortality experience of civilian populations? Each field has distinct objectives. There is a need to develop an understanding of these objectives to ultimately provide a coherent understanding of various numerical estimates and accounts. This will improve scientific communication and prevent confusion among the end users of these estimates.

text: Plant hormones, or phytohormones, are low-abundance chemical signals that direct diverse aspects of growth, development, and physiology in plants. They are made in one part of the plant and sent to another, where they can prompt activities like cell division, cell elongation, flowering, fruiting and responses to stimuli. Plant hormones are not secreted from glands, unlike in animals. There are five major classes of plant hormones: auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid, and ethylene. AUX are involved in cell elongation, root initiation, apical dominance, and tropic movements, including positive gravitropism. Gibberellins cause growth of stems and are involved in flowering and seed germination. They also promote seed and bud dormancy release and are commercially applied for fruit enlargement. Cytokinins stimulate cell division and shoot initiation, and retard senescence (aging) in leaves. The ratio of auxins and cytokinins shapes root or shoot growth in culture tissues. ABA ABA is basically a grow-inhibition hormone, which is a hormone related to inhibiting growth and promoting dormancy, closing the stomata when wateri is deficient, inducing plants' wateri pressure and resistance regulation, and so on. Finally, the gaseous hormone ethylene is involved in fruit ripening, leaf abscission, flower wilting, and is an essential signaling component of stress responses and mechanical stress adaptation. Other plant hormones are the brassinosteroids, jasmonates, and salicylic acid, which participate in many physiological process such as defense and environmental interactions in plants. These hormones frequently act synergistically or antagonistically to modulate plant development and responses to stimuli. Delineation of phytohormones has considerable applications in areas such as agriculture, horticulture and biotechnology including modulation of plant growth, increase in yield and post-harvest physiology.

text: Sudden Oak Death (SOD), a kind of plant disease, is caused by the pathogen of Phytophthora ramorum. It was firstly tested on Azalea and Viburnum dilatatum in Germany and Dutch in 1993, and presented to Lithocarpus densiflorus and Quercus in California coastal areas in 1996 [1-3] . It has a wide range of host plants, rapid spreading, and serious harmful consequences. The outbreak of SOD is influenced by various factors, such as geographical and climatic environments, host plants, pathogen’s physical characteristics and social factors [4]. Thus there are obvious spatial variations in its distribution due to the influence of different environmental factors [5-6] . China has very similar environmental and climatic conditions with the SOD outbreak areas, and additionally, it has large distributions of host plants (e.g. the Oak, Maple, Azalea and other vegetation). Some studies has shown that the pathogen may originate from Himalayas region, and the pathogen was also found in the ancient forest in Nepal and Taiwan [7-8]. Upon this background, there is quite high occurrence risk of SOD in China although there is no outbreak records in mainland China until now. Phytophthora ramorum is already included in the alien invasive species needing to be checked or investigated in accordance with the requirement of China’s State Forestry Administration on Warning notification on forestry pests that requires the relevant forestry departments in the mainland to carry out the special investigation on it.

text: Human trafficking is a type of modern-day slavery where people profit from the control and exploitation of others through force, fraud, or coercion to satisfy these needs for labor and services including commercial sex. It is among the rapidly expanding and lucrative international crimes and impacts several millions of individuals globally, men, women, and children. Victims are especially duped with promises of jobs, education or better environments, and end being held against their will, forced to lower themselves to circumstances that rob them of their freedom. Human trafficking usually preys upon the vulnerable, such as the poor, refugees or people living in war zones. It can happen across borders and within a country and is frequently enabled by criminal rings that benefit from the sale or rental of human beings. Traffickers control their victims through techniques such as debt bondage, threats, isolation and psychological manipulation. Human trafficking is not the same thing as human smuggling, in which people pay a coyote to bring them across the border, and the transaction ends upon arrival: one is consensual and ends, and one is coercive and continues. Eradicating human trafficking must be a multi-faceted approach; it should involve vaccination through laws, international cooperation, aggressive border policing, programme for identifying and protecting victims, and awareness building. The legislation in many countries is based on the UN Palermo Protocol, which focuses on prevention, protection and prosecution. Police also collaborate with NGOs and international bodies to rescue victims and break up trafficking networks. It is crucial to help victims to rehabilitate by providing medical services, legal aid, psychological care and social reintegration. Criminologists and human rights practitioners research trafficking trends, risk factors, and community based prevention programming. Because human trafficking is a clandestine and convoluted crime, it is hard to recognize and tends to be underreported; education, awareness, and multi-sector partnerships are all critical components of fighting trafficking.

text: Globalization is the term used to describe the process of countries becoming more interconnected through trade, technology, culture and communications. Bringing as well as economic growth and innovation, globalisation has far-reaching impacts on traditional social institutions such as family, education and religion. In Bangladesh, the process of globalization has brought numerous opportunities as well as challenges. The expansion of global media and internet access has introduced citizens to new ways of life, values and beliefs that frequently contradict traditional values. For example, a nuclear family structure is becoming the norm, with the migration of people to urban spaces for work and education. Satellite TV and social media spread global fashions, music and ideas about gender to Iraq and shape young people’s ideas about marriage, career and identity. In education, global trends have promoted the expansion of English-medium schools and the adoption of foreign curricula, which can isolate students from their own local culture and language. Millions of Bangladeshis have also emigrated to the Middle East and elsewhere for work, leading to the rise of transnational families and transformations of traditional family roles and economic arrangements. Religion too has not been left out by the wave of globalization, it can be promoted such that mutual understanding or a modern reading of religion is shared, but it can be a vector for cultural uniformity/ radicalization if left unchecked on the internet for example. Economically, globalization has contributed a fillip to sectors like garments and remittances but has also sent job security, damage to the environment and consumerism soaring. Non-governmental organizations and local organizations frequently find it difficult to maintain indigenous values amid the furious pace of development. And so as globalization has opened up Bangladesh to technology and capitalism, it has also pushed traditional institutions to the brink. In the meantime, a harmonious blend of modernity and culture is currently challenging policymakers, educationists and the communities.

text: Sensory adaptation is when sensory receptors become desensitized over time to a constant or stable stimulus. It enables organisms to decrease the importance of stimuli that are no longer biologically valid or do not demand a direct response at the time, and to reserve cognitive resources for recognizing new or changing stimuli. "Just as you notice a strong smell when you first enter a smelly room, but after a while don’t think about it, that kind of thing will happen with climate." This happens because ongoing stimulation leads to desensitization of the olfactory receptors. Sensory adaptation occurs in all modalities -vision (adjusting to low light in a room), touch (feeling the clothes you wear) and hearing (tuning out background noise). It is a passive and reflexive process that indicates the effectiveness of the sensory system to automatically prioritize new input. But not all senses adapt the same; for example, pain receptors, or ‘nociceptors,’ adapt less because constant awareness of pain is essential for survival. Behavioural adaptation is essential for perception and enables us to concentrate on the informative changes in the world, instead of becoming oversaturated by irrelevant background information.

text: There are numerous plant families out there, but a few shine as key groups because of the environmental and economic roles they play. text: Ohm’s law is a basic rule used to calculate various parameters of an electrical circuit according to the relationship between potential difference, resistance and current, or directly proportional to the current running through it if the physical condition (temperature, pressure or any other factor). This expression was introduced by Georg Simon Ohm in the 19th century, and it states that the current flowing through a conductor between two points is directly proportional to the voltage across the two points, and inversely proportional to the resistance of the conductor. It is usually written mathematically as V=IR. This linear relationship is actually a straightforward one; if voltage is increased, then current increases proportionally (assuming resistance is remaining constant). Resistance is a property that hinders the passage of electric current and is determined by a number of factors including the material, its length, cross-sectional area and temperature. Ohm’s law forms the basis of all circuit analysis, and we can calculate any one of the three values if the other two are known. This relationship is applicable for ohmic materials having uniform resistance as a function of applied voltage and current, but may not be valid in semiconductors, diodes, or other nonlinear devices. Ohm’s law is a very useful tool used in electrical engineering and physics to figure out circuits, electrical systems and current flow. This can assist SEO and many other areas of electronics, in driving low power devices and is a useful piece of knowledge to add to your portfolio of devices available. By connecting voltage, current, and resistance, Ohm’s law is still one of the simplest and most essential elements in understanding and using electricity.

text: IPE Views: The complex relationship between economics and politics IPE is a sub-discipline that deals in the relationship between economics and politics. It speaks to how economic policies, trade, investment, and financial flows between states are shaped by political forces, and in turn how political decisions and power relations within and beyond states are conditioned by economic circumstances. IPE analyzes the actors, institutions, and rules that constitute the global economy, including states, multinational firms, international organizations, and financial and currency markets. Key areas of discussion are international trade links, monetary policy, development plans, economic globalization, and the equitable distribution of wealth and power. Topics of IPE scholars include protectionist versus free trade policies; the developmental and redistributive effects of international monetary institutions such as the IMF and World Bank; the political aspect of globalisation that can be practiced by the advanced economies in the attempt to position themselves as a world hegemonic leading state; or the fiscal power of the developed world. The discipline acknowledges that economic policies are never purely technical but are thoroughly woven into political interests and power struggles. In this way, IPE offers valuable insights into the way in which economic interdependence drives international cooperation and conflict, impact of economic crises on the global stability and the way in which economic instruments can be used as a form of diplomacy or a tool of coercion. It is the economic-sociopolitical counterpart to think about the complications of the global system in an economically integrated but politically fragmented world.

text: Deficit budget A country’s budget is described as deficit budget if its expenditure is more than income and revenue during the fiscal year, excluding money from borrowings. This is because the government is spending more money than it’s making, and has to borrow to plug the gap. Budget deficits can be caused by various reasons such as economic slowdown which leads to lower income and corporate earnings and lower taxes and increased government expenditure for defense, subsidies and salaries. Unproductive tax systems and tax evasion, as well as structural problems such as low productivity or underperformance in exports, also play a role. In developing economies the shortfalls are more due to investments in infrastructure and welfare far outstrip existing sources of revenue. There are many other negative effects of an ongoing budget deficit. It also tends to push up public debt because more government borrowing is needed to plug the gap. This increases future debt-servicing costs, and can crowd out crucial spending in health, education or infrastructure. Persistent deficits can also put upward pressure on interest rates, deter private sector investment, and, in extreme cases, inflation, a loss of currency value, or both, if the deficit is monetized. And in the long run, constant deficits can drive down a country’s credit rating, raising the cost of external borrowing and undermining investor confidence. Nevertheless, temporary deficits are not harmful per se, so long as the spending is for investments that increase future revenues and economic growth. Yet governments must preserve a sound fiscal stance through the tax system, better control the spending and promote sustainable economic growth to avoid the negative long-term effects of perennial budget deficits.

text: Constructivism is an international relations theory that explains how social relations alter and transform international material social structures, based on identities, norms, and values. out of -- the internal arrangements within states, not the external mutual independent relations of states. Unlike realism and liberalism, in three broad principles which privilege objective structures and rational actors, constructivism believes that's * the * these most important structures in the state system are not a physical, they're social, and they're constructed, through, interaction, through language, and shared understandings. Most prominently developed by Alexander Wendt and other scholars in the 1990s, constructivism contends that “anarchy is what states make of it,” implying that the meaning and impact of the international system is a function of how states perceive and act upon it. The state does not just act in line with interests or security concerns, but its behavior is affected by histories, identities, cultures and norms that change at different times. For instance, the reason the U.S. is unworried about and does not see Canada as a threat, despite the fact that Canada has offensive military capabilities, is not the balance of power but rather shared norms and identity. Constructivist theories examine how international norms—like sovereignty or human rights or environmental responsibility—arise, diffuse, and affect state and nonstate behavior. They also explore how concepts such as nationalism or terrorism are socially constructed and endowed with coherence through the agency of discourse and policy. Constructivism joins the international and the domestic by understanding that internal ideologies, beliefs, and values account for foreign policy decisions. It also highlights the power of language, symbolism, and cultural narratives in the conduct of international affairs. While attacked for its lack of predictive value, constructivism casts a light on the dynamic character of world politics and the effects of ideas, identities, and social structures on international relations.

text: ADC and DAC are building blocks of mixed-signal electronics, such as the digital signal processor of a mobile phone, or of sound cards. An ADC (or A-to-D) is a device that redistributes a continuous physical value (typically voltage) and maps it as a number on the CPU can understand. This conversion consists of sampling the analog signal in time, and quantizing its amplitude level to solid values and then converting it to Binary. The resolution (peak to some number of bits) and actual sampling rate is used to specify an ADC's performance. For instance, a 10 bit analog to digital conversion has at 1024 levels. Applications range from sensor (use as a simple analog digital converter) and I/O (Interface one or more potentiometers and a button) extension to a full featured A-D Converter (use it together with the Audiolibrary or DTMF library to build a mobile 4-8 channel DTMF controlled measuringdevice with automatic identification or use it to control a stepper motor) or as a component in a high speed data acquisition system. On the other hand, a DAC is a component that performs exactly the opposite. It receives a digital input (usually from a computer or microprocessor) and generates an analog output. In these audio playback products, such as digital audio players and TVs, DACs are used to convert digital data stream output by the digital audio processing system to analog audio signals. There are many architectures in ADCs and DACs as SAR (Sequential Approximation Register), flash, delta-sigma in ADCs and ladder-type, weighted resistor types in DACs. This processes happens spontaneously because other isotopes are unstable, there is an imbalance in the nuclei protons/neutrons count and therefore the isotope will try to transform itself to one that has a balanced number of protons and neutrons. To reach a more stable state, the nucleus emits alpha particles (helium nuclei), beta particles (electrons or positrons), or photons (gamma rays). The decay of radioactive atoms is random, but statistically predictable for large groups of atoms. The decay scheme leads to the transmutation of one element into another and so forth, often until a stable isotope is achieved. This process is an important tool in various domains including the study of rocks, paleontology used to interpret all dating and chronology information of fossils, in medicine historical hiv dating for myeloma, to treat thyroid cancer, and even to kill harmful bacteria and microbes, and in power plants to generate electricity. The extent of decay is defined by half-life, which is nothing but the time that takes for a sample of radioactive atoms will decay to half. Radioactive decay is a first order kinetic process and it is not dependent on the amount of material present. Knowledge of radioactive decay has also been important in the study of nuclear physics and chemistry, enabling scientists to probe the structure of atoms, find new elements and create nuclear weapons. text: Mendelian inheritance The basic rules of genetic inheritance first described by Gregor Mendel in the 19th century based on his experiments with pea plants, and the basis for much of modern genetics. Mendel’s studies showed that characteristics are transferred as distinct units, now called genes, that are inherited from parents to their offspring in a predictable way. Mendelian genetics states that organisms have two forms of each gene (two alleles), one form inherited from each parent, and that those alleles can be dominant or recessive. Recessive alleles are only expressed if both alleles are recessive, and the observable trait or phenotype is determined by dominant alleles that mask the effect of recessive alleles in a heterozygous genotype. From his observations, Mendel established several important laws. The Law of Segregation The two alleles for a trait segregate during the formation of gametes, so each gamete carries only one allele for each trait. This is why children get one gene from each of their parents. The Law of Independent Assortment states that a gene or alleles of one trait do not affect another genes alleles during gamete formation (unless the genes are located very close on the chromosome or on the same chromosome and linked, then the alleles usually move together; known as linked genes). Mendelian inheritance is seen in traits that are determined by a single gene with no variation in the alleles of that gene, as seen in flower color of pea seeds. These regularities in patterns make it possible to use a Punnett square to predict the genotypes and phenotypes of offspring given an understanding of the allele combinations in the parent. But in real-life genetics is not so simple because you have incomplete dominance (1 allele is not completely dominant over another and heterozygotes show some degree of both genes), codominance (when 2 alleles are expressed in ~ equal amount), multiple alleles, polygenic inheritance (traits affected by multiple genes) and effects of the environment. Notwithstanding these complications, Mendelian inheritance still provides key vehicle by which the passage of traits from one generation to the next can be understood. It is important for research in sickle cell anemia, breeding programs, evolutionary biology. Mendel’s laws have become enriched from the discovery of DNA, chromosomes, and molecular genetics, but the original ideas concerning the separation of alleles and independent assortment continue to permeate genetic research and applications. Invisible individuals: The legacy of Mendelian inheritanceMendelian inheritance is the science of genes: the inheritance of discrete units that separate (segregate) and assort independently from generation to generation, which govern how inherited traits of an organism that can be considered the most fundamental discovery of classical genetics.

text: Atom's model by Bohr, Niels Bohr's 1913 model of the atom introduces electrons in quantized orbits to explain the stability and spectral lines of atoms (especially hydrogen). This latter subjection we have here overcome, as Bohr has shown us that electrons describe their revolutions around the nucleus in stationary orbits or energy levels, without radiating out any energy, against the laws of classical electromagnetics. These are the fixed energy states and electrons can move up and down between these levels through absorbing or emitting a photon having energy same as the difference between the energies of these states. This accounted for the observed line spectrum in the atomic emission and absorption. Bohr’s model predicts that an electron’s angular momentum is quantized, meaning that it has a value that depends on a fundamental constant. Bohr’s theory provided a successful model for the hydrogen atom spectrum and it introduced important ideas of quantum theory—though not yet sophisticated enough to account for more complicated atoms or the detailed form of the spectra. Nevertheless, it provided a framework for the development of quantum mechanics and atomic theory, as it first proposed that energy is quantized and that electrons possess wave-particle duality. The import of Bohr’s work crossed the classical/quantum divide, and its value is reflected not only in work stimulated by it but also in our developing understanding of atomic structure, chemical behavior, the nature of matter, in properties of atoms, ions, and small molecules and in biomolecules.

text: Maize, the commonly grown cereal, belongs to the genus oZea mays. Maize ( Zea mays L.)-commonly known as corn-is a grass family Poaceae plant and the third most widely grown staple food and feed crop worldwide. Maize, originating from Central America, has been grown for several millennia and has become a major crop all over the world because of its adaptation to diverse environments and high productivity. The plant is tall with broad leaves that bear ears with kernels that are the harvested grains. Maize kernels have different colors, sizes, and texture depending on the variety, and they are the most cultivated parts of the plant, many of which are used as a food product in human cuisine, as animal feed or as raw material for the production of starch, sweeteners, and biofuels. It is a C4 plant, which makes it very efficient at using energy, so it can grow in a hot and heavily lit environment. Maize can be grown in well-drained fertile soils with a good supply of moisture for optimum growth. It is cultivated in a wide range of agro-climatic zones, which makes it an important crop for food security in several countries. The botanical classification of the plant is used in scientific research and breeding, as well as for improvement programs, focused on increasing yield, resistance to pests and environmental adaptation. Introduction of genetics and genetic engineering in maize breeding has also resulted in the development of hybrids and transgenic varieties possessing enhanced characteristics. Knowledge about its botanical features is also useful for its crop management, its pest regulation and post-harvest industrial processing. On a larger perspective, Zea mays is central to the world agriculture with its nutritional, economic and industrial importance.

text: Reinforcement schedules are the rules that specify when and how often reinforcers are delivered, and they have a powerful effect on the speed, strength, and the consistency of learning. The two main forms are continuous and partial (intermittent) reinforcement; the former is when reinforcement is given after each occurrence of the target behavior, whereas in the latter reinforcement is given after some occurrences but not all. In partial reinforcement, this can be the fixed-ratio schedule (reinforce after a fixed number of responses [e.g., every 5 actions taken]), the variable-ratio schedule (reinforce after a varying/unpredictable number of responses [e.g., gambling]), the fixed-interval schedule (reinforce after a fixed or constant passage of time [e.g., weekly paycheck]), or the variable-interval schedule (reinforce after a varying amount of time passes [e.g., a text exchange at some random time in the week]). Variable ratios in particular are known for resulting in high, steady rates of responding and greater levels of resistance to extinction than those schedules based on fixed ratios due to fixed schedules of reinforcement leading more to post -reinforcement pause affecting patterns. Whether a continuous or intermittent schedule design is optimal depends on the goal, and intermittent schedules may also be necessary to sustaining behavior over time without continuous reinforcement.

text: Media businesses carry various revenue models to support their business, maintain content creation, and remain competitive in a dynamic market. Media for a long time consisted of news papers, radio stations and television stations, which were essentially supported by ads – ie businesses paid to offer their ad before or in between what the public wanted to consume. But as digital disruption rewrote consumer behavior and shattered attention across platforms, media companies have diversified their revenue sources. One important model is the subscription model, in which audiences are charged a subscription fee to access premium or exclusive content, such as that offered by newspapers, e.g., The New York Times, and web-based platforms, e.g., Netflix.” Meanwhile, the freemium model gives away basic content and charges for premium features or ad-free use. There are some pay-per-view transactional models, if you want to view something stream (or sports related) you can pay a certain amount to unlock the content. Another emerging model is sponsorship and branded content, in which companies work with brands on informative or entertaining projects that subtly promote a product or message. This could be the result of incentives to pursue alternative funding models like crowdfunding, and donation from individuals who are independents, non-profit or even public broadcasters by that get support from their audience through Patreon or direct contributions. It can also be another source of revenue that aims to remain editorially independent by being government-funded and in the case of public service media like the BBC or PBS granted to the media entity. Licensing and syndication also permit media companies to gain revenue and reach by selling their content to other platforms. Event hosting, merchandising, and the integration of e-commerce are also becoming additional revenue streams. Digital analytics and programmatic advertising have helped to improve monetization by selling ads more intelligently. But these models are not without their ethical and practical concerns, including how to balance user experience, the threat of paywall fatigue, maintaining editorial independence, adapting to technological shifts, and more. At the end of the day, sustainable media revenue models need to be: inventive, trusted by the audience, and flexible to maneuver the landscape of a rapidly changing media economy.

text: Soft Power—the ability to influence international relations through attractive cultural, political and foreign policy channels rather than with military might or coercion (Nye, 2004)—has been on display in the recent positive and peaceful shift in relations between the United States and Cuba. A simultaneous December 2014 announcement by U.S. President Barack Obama and Cuban President Raul Castro kicked off a series of initiatives that began with the release of prisoners in both countries who had been accused of spying (DeYoung, 2014; Federal Register, 2015). As of this writing, the soft power policies toward the island nation have included the re-opening of respective embassies, the loosening of travel and commerce restrictions, the commencement of direct commercial flights between the countries and a historic visit of the first sitting U.S. president in almost a century (Davis, 2016a). Cuba and the United States share a complicated history, going back to before the Spanish American War when the United States interceded to win Cuba’s independence from Spain (Perez, 1990). The Cuban Revolution of 1959 installed Fidel Castro’s communist rule, nationalized millions of dollars of U.S. business and manufacturing interests in Cuba and resulted in a cessation of trade (Suddath, 2009). The revolution launched an era of hostility between the two nations that lasted more than five decades. This period was highlighted by a series of contentious encounters between the two governments including the unsuccessful Bay of Pigs invasion by U.S. troops, the Cuban Missile crisis of 1962 and the return to Cuba from Miami of a 6-year-old refugee Elian Gonzalez, whose mother drowned in an attempt to escape to the United States (Barringer, 2000).

text: Intersectionality is a concept and analytic framework to understand how aspects of social identity, such as gender, race, class, sexuality, disability, age, and other similar conditions of difference, as they mutually constitute systems of discrimination and classification. The term intersectionality, coined in 1989 by the legal scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw, describes how people are oppressed or privileged not by one aspect of their identity but by the combined effects of multiple identities: race, age, sex, disability and more. A Black woman, for instance, may experience both racism and sexism differently than white women or Black men. Intersectionality: Intersectionality highlights the many different ways that people can be oppressed, and discourages us from thinking of social injustice in a one-size-fits-all fashion – because inequalities don’t affect all people in the same way and therefore cannot be ended using the same methods that work for one group as for another. This tool is key in feminist theory and activism, as it makes potential an, inclusive, Child Rights Advocacy that will empower and keep at the center the roots for the most affected, in multiple marginality.

text: The Indian Independence Movement was a composite movement, with a variety of reactions by the people of India toward the British empire's expansion. Indian farmers and craftsmen were economically ruined by heavy land tax, by de?industrialisation and exploitation of their resources, and by poverty and famine. Politically, there was no representative government, and the brigand-acts (ra? huk?m???) of the colonial regime and its lack of representation in Indian government angered educated Indians who had become aware of their place in an empire. Socially, the growth of a modern middle class of Indians trained in British values in the public schools led to political consciousness and to the development of a national identity. Revivalism Cultural revivals such as the Bengal Renaissance, as well as movements in other regions, revived pride in Indian cultures, languages, and religions and challenged colonial images of superiority. Landmark episodes such as the partition of Bengal in 1905, the Jallianwala Bagh tragedy of 1919 and repressive legislations added fuel to the nationalist upsurge. Rise of Indian nationalism[edit] The creation of the Indian National Congress in 1885 by A.O. Hume provided a platform to the demands for political reform and eventually for independence. Diverse leadership from men such as Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Jawaharlal Nehru, Subhas Chandra Bose and Mahatma Gandhi meant that there was a range of strategies from militant nationalists to advocates of non-violent civil disobedience. It was also the result of the global context, of the impacts of World Wars, of the weakening of Britain’s economic and military influence, and so on. The movement was a mass struggle that cut across religions, regions and classes, represented India’s extraordinary diversity and united all against the common aspiration for freedom.

text: Management of plant diseases can be achieved by integrating cultural, chemical, biological and genetic methods which work continuously to prevent the entry, decrease population and the severity of damage by pathogen. Cultural measures include crop rotation; sanitation (eliminating diseased plant material); appropriate spacing for air movement; correct irrigation practices to minimize overly moist soil; and healthy seed or planting material. These actions deprive pathogens of their favorite habitat and break up their niche. Chemical control Includes the use of fungicides, bactericides, nematicides, or insecticides to protect plants from infection or to kill pathogens and vectors. Nevertheless, chemicals should be carefully used to reduce risks for the environment, resistance selection and residues. Biocontrol relies on beneficial organisms (e.g. antagonist fungi, bacteria, or predatory insects), to suppress pathogens or their vectors by natural means. This ecologically-sensitive method is increasingly being considered as part of the IPM. Soybean is susceptible to a variety of diseases and genetic control of these relies on developing and using resistant or tolerant plant types that can resist or reduce the development of the disease. With the development of biotechnology, genetic engineering has made some plants resistant to disease. An integrated approach to disease management integrates these methods according to disease severity, crop identity, environment, and economics, in order to sustainably and effectively control plant diseases.
