text: The exchange rate corresponds to the price of one country’s currency measured in terms of another country’s currency, and it sets how much one currency can be exchanged for another. For instance, if 1 USD is equal to 110 BDT, then the exchange rate is 1:110. The exchange rate is vital to international trade, investment, tourism and financial transactions, by fixing the price of imported and exported goods, foreign investments and competitiveness in general. The methodology used to determine exchange rates vary according to the kind of exchange rate regime: floating, fixed or managed float. Unfavourable exchange rates remove products from the local marketIn a floating exchange rate regime, exchange rate is determined by the market according to the forces of supply and demand in the foreign exchange market. Interest rates, inflation, and economic growth are other mechanisms through which a government can impact the demand for, and value of its currency. Like a central bank rate hike in a country, foreign investment in a country can raise its demand for its currency, pushing its value up. Instead, a fixed exchange rate is established and kept up by the government or the Central Bank and the value of the local currency is tied to another currency, usually the US dollar or a basket of currencies. It's that rate at which the government has to buy or sell its currency, in the foreign exchange market, to keep it that rate. A managed float is where exchange rates are allowed to vary within a range, but then this band is breached, intervention is allowed. Exchange rates are important indicators of economic performance, one that can have an abrupt impact on inflation, exports, imports and foreign debt. Thus, settled and predictable exchange relations are critical to the smoothly running international economic life, and then to investor confidence.

text: The World Bank is an international financial institution that aims to reduce poverty by providing financial and technical assistance to developing countries for development programs (e.g. bridges, roads, schools, etc.) It is a component of the World Bank Group. Created in 1944 with the IMF, the World Bank lends money to developing countries and makes grants and loans for specific projects and programs to help countries build infrastructure, educate and promote health care for people, support agriculture, and strengthen governance. Its objective is to support long-term development of the country through financing projects that generating employment and human capital and will give an economy growth, hence prosper living standard. The World Bank is a five institution cooperative that serves as a bank for the government officials of its 184 member countries and two of its five agencies are: International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) and the International Development Association (IDA). The bank funds a range of projects, including constructing roads and schools, as well as shoring up institutions and fighting climate change. It also is integral to exchange of knowledge and policy advice, assisting countries formulate successful development strategies and reforms. The World Bank collaborates with other development partners, governments, and the private sector to increase investments and manage aid. The World Bank has been criticized for loans with excessive conditionality that is seen to deprive borrowing countries of sovereignty, and in certain cases the environmental and social impact of projects. But the bank is constantly changing, adding social guarantees and the goals of sustainable development, which are precedents for the world. At its base, the World Bank remains crucial for responding to global inequalities, building economic stability and helping countries along the journey of inclusive, sustainable development.

text: African history of the British Empire It is not just the history of the British Empire in Africa which fascinates, but also its long and complex history over a number of centuries. In the 17th and 18th centuries, the only British interests in the region were outposts for the Atlantic slave trade (see North-East Passage). It was not the case in the 19th century, however, as a “Scramble for Africa” resulted in a brutal sprint for land, in which European powers raced one another to capture African territory. Britain created colonies and protectorates in major regions like Egypt, South Africa, Kenya, Nigeria, and Zimbabwe. The British adhered to a policy of indirect rule in many areas, ruling through local leaders and exploiting natural resources and labor for the benefit of the empire. Economically, the colonies provided raw materials such as gold, diamonds, rubber and palm oil for Britain’s industrial expansion. The empire also established Western-style education, legal systems, and Christianity, with unintended consequences affecting indigenous cultures and societies. Wars such as the Anglo-Zulu War and the Boer Wars were in part, attempts by Africans and settlers to avoid British rule. The British Empire in Africa was wonderfully enriching for Britain, with devastating social upheaval, land dispossession, and racial segregation. Nationalist leaders demanding self-determination and equality fuelled anti-colonial movements through the 20th century. The British colonial legacy in Africa is both positive and negative, the British successfully modernized and developed much infrastructure of their empire, like governance they established, roads, rails, industries and so forth, but also left behind a legacy of long standing challenges like economic dependency, disunity due to ethno-ethnic tensions and political instability that many postcolonial nations continue to struggle addressing.

text: Human actions create major (and sometimes devastating) effects on animal populations across the surface of the earth, reducing the number of species either in the forms of extirpations, preventing the bearing of offspring, or driving creatures out of some of their habitats and into one which is much smaller. Loss of habitat, as a result of urbanization, agriculture, deforestation and other types of infrastructure expansion that break up ecosystems and provide less space and resources for animals to feed, breed and find shelter, is one major reason animal populations are shrinking. Chemicals, plastics, and industrial refuse cause air, water and soil pollution that directly harm health and reproduction of wildlife and can result in reduced population and death. Climate change, driven predominantly by the emission of greenhouse gases generated by humans, shuffles temperatures and precipitation, creating havoc with migration patterns, breeding schedules, food supplies — all the things animals are built to deal with by evolving, moving or simply disappearing. Overexploitation by hunting, fishing and wildlife trade threatens the survival of numerous species, especially those with slow reproductive rates or high economic value. Humans also deliberately or inadvertently bring invasive species into new areas where they can compete with or prey upon native wildlife, or spread diseases among populations, throwing natural ecosystems out of kilter and causing the decline of native species. These accumulating stresses often translate into decreased genetic diversity, which can make a population more vulnerable to diseases and other environmental changes. Conflict between people and wildlife occurs when animals move into the community, or when people encroach into wildlife habitat, leading to retaliatory slaughter or displacement. Conservation interventions, including reserves, corridors, sustainable use of natural resources, and the regulation of exotic species, are used to combat these impacts, yet human population growth and consumption/economic demand indicate that threats to species will continue to grow. Public education, research and international cooperation are invaluable in reconciling people needs with wildlife conservation. In the end, it is human behavior that decides the fate of animals and conservation measures are required to ensure that biodiversity and ecosystem service is there for future generations.

text: The primary concern addressed by this study is how to build sophisticated prosodic models for developing high-performance TTS systems for Chinese dialects (or subdialects) other than Mandarin. Prosody modeling for Chinese dialects can be categorized into three classes: the direct modeling method [2]–?[9] , voice conversion method [10]–?[12], and tone mapping/base-syllable-type sharing method [6], [13], [14]. In the direct modeling method, a dialect prosodic model is directly trained from a dialect speech corpus uttered by a single speaker by using prosody modeling methods including the Fujisaki model [2]–?[4], artificial neural networks [5]–?[7] , and hidden Markov models (HMMs) [8], [9]. However, due to underresourced conditions for many dialects, this method may encounter the difficulty of collecting an abundant dialect speech corpus to cover all essential linguistic contexts, prosodic events, and speaking rate (SR) varieties. text: Biosocial theory of crime uses biological and social factors together to create the hypothesis that a person can learn through environmental experiences as well as genetic predilections which will result in them following life course ways. In contrast to both sociological and biological models, biosocial theory states that while social factors (such as poverty, family conditions and level of education) influence anti-social behavior development with approximately the same weight as biological factors (neurological functioning, hormonal imbalances), exposure to these behavioral elements also reduces criminal thought. For instance, a dysfunction in the prefrontal cortex, which controls impulse control and moral reasoning, has been linked to violent acts and antisocial behaviour. So, too, low serotonin or high testosterone has been associated with impulsiveness and violence. Some genetic research — based on studies of twins and adopted children — has supported that idea, suggesting that behavior like aggression or risk taking could have a hereditary component. Yet such biological predispositions do not wholly determine behavior; they are molded and triggered by social influences like exposure to violence, neglect, drugs or peers. Biosocial theory states that people are predisposed to criminal or deviant behavior when they have specific vulnerabilities for each in concert with adverse experiences in the environment. It also adjusts for prenatal factors, like drug use or maternal malnutrition, that can influence brain development and behavior in adulthood. Critics caution that biosocial theories threaten to become either stigmatizing or biologically deterministic, both of which overlook the opportunity for social reform. But the theory has also given a lot to our understanding of criminal behavior in terms of inter-disciplinary debates and detailed studies of crime. It also directly informs treatment interventions such as behavioral therapies, drugs and early childhood interventions to address the biological and social roots of criminal behavior. At heart, biosocial theory allows for an inclusive approach to crime in which we take into account both nature and nurture as we try to understand and eradicate antisocial conduct.

text: Absurdist drama is a type of drama in which avant-garde and innovative plays are carried out by a person or group involving stereotypical characters in absurd situations, as in Samuel Beckett's Waiting for Godot. This type of theater arises from the ruins of World War II and a profound skepticism of traditional values communication and reason It took form under the existential philosophy of someone like Albert Camus and Jean- Paul Sartre. Those plays tend to have circular or fragmented plots, repetitious or nonsensical dialogue and characters mired in senseless dilemmas that symbolize the collapse of the logical order of things and the inadequacy of language to communicate meaning. This movement includes playwrights such as Samuel Beckett (Waiting for Godot), Eugène Ionesco and Harold Pinter. The conversations feature contradictions as well as pauses and silences that signal alienation, bewilderment, and the quest for meaning in a purposeless world. Absurdist theatre forces the audience to face uncomfortable realities in existence, breakdowns in communication, and the alienation of the individual. Unlike classical drama, it does not go for definite ending and character development, and instead it stimulates thought with its ambiguity, with dark humor. This type of theatre combines reductionist plotting and paleolithic sets, representation of symbolic actions or surrealistic images which constitute the bizarre world reflecting the absurdist condition of mankind. The significance of absurd theatre lies in its novelty, in that it seeks to break free from the traditional form of drama and to question the very foundations of meaning, order and human relationships which were so integral to traditional Western theatre; and it has become the most effective weapon of modern drama for philosophical reflection and social criticism.

text: Movement and Feeding They are all aquatic marine animals, and depending on the individual species, it can exhibit some interesting ways of moving (the spiny skin sea star walks in their tube feet), and some even more unique ways of eating (tricking snails to regurgitate their food and then eat it again).This is made possible by their unique water vascular system. This hydraulic system functions by way of a complex pumping network of fluid filled canals and tube feet that radiate from the body wall, and aid echinoderms move, breathe, grip, and even sense their surroundings. The slow and lumbering movement of most echinoderms can be attributed to the fact that circulation of seawater pushes and pulls against tube feet, providing the hydraulic power for their motion, which can be extremely effective as they gently adhere to and release from surfaces while traveling over them on a bed of hundreds to feet long tube feet. For instance, starfish with hundreds of tube feet on the ventral surface of the arms called adambulacral feet can clamber with an astounding adhesive capability despite creeping across uneven locations and in opposition to strong currents. Some echinoderms, brittle stars for example, move faster by bending those long, thin arms snake-like. The feeding in echinoderms is also varied and specialized to their ecological habitat. A number of species prey on bivalves such as clams, the stomach being able to envelop and digest the prey outside the stomach; the animal overcomes the bivalve by forcing its valves apart, and its relatively weak prey-muscles are subdued by a poison secreted by the predatory starfish from glands in its "pedicellariae". Most sea urchins eat algae, which they scrape off rocks using their specialized feeding apparatus called Aristotle’s lantern, consisting of a hard, calcareous mouthpart with an intricate series of teeth that can scrape and chew plant material. Sea cucumbers feed by grabbing detritus or sediment with their modified tube feet around the mouth and once they have a good amount, they move the package towards their mouth and take it inside of them, removing the usable microorganisms and other food from it. Some echinoderms are suspension-feeders, sifting small particles from the water on their sticky tube feet or using special appendages to capture and tame plankton and organic detritus.Thus, the WV system does not only mediate movement and feeding, but also serves for respiration and perception (Dathe and Richter, 1887), attesting for the multifunctionality of this morphological adaptation that is vital for echinoderm survival. With the specific hydraulic system and varied feeding habits, echinoderms are able to occupy various habitats and utilize diverse food sources, which are not only the predators, but also the grazers, scavengers and organic matter recyclers in the sea life.

text: The Magna Carta, signed under duress in 1215 by a recalcitrant English king, was a revolutionary constitutional document that set a course for centuries, limiting monarchical authority, establishing the principle of due process, and building the framework for a representative government in medieval England and beyond. Officially known as “Magna Carta Libertatum” (The Great Charter of Liberties), it was a document forced on King John that linked him to the law rather than elevating him above it. The charter contained many essential principles: no unlawful detention (through habeas corpus clauses), no unfair taxation (except through common consent), and no abuse of justice—judging honestly. While many of its provisions were of a feudal nature and unique to the barons, phrases such as “No free man shall be seized or imprisoned... except by the lawful judgment of his equals or by the law of the land” became universal touchstones of legal equity. In time, Magna Carta was reissued and amended, harmonising centuries-old English customs with changes in royal policy, and establishing what the king’s subjects could and could not expect from him. Its provisions served as a models for English common law and subsequent legal systems in the English speaking world. The charter’s aspirations also became the inspiration for documents as diverse as the English Bill of Rights, the United States Constitution and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and they embedded concepts like due process, judicial fairness and government accountability in democratic institutions. Narrow in its immediate effect and initial guarantee, the Great Charter over time came to symbolize and offer lasting political philosophy: the timeless idea that even kings are to govern under the rule of law — a building block of constitutional democracy and the defense of a free person.

text: Big Data is a term that describes datasets whose sizes are beyond the ability of commonly used software tools to capture, manage, and process in a reasonable time and accuracy, which are typically identified as having high volume, velocity, and variety (the three Vs) — large-scale, circulating, and various formats (such as text, image, video, and sensing data), for which there is a need to evolve techniques and technologies beyond those commonly used for the management of data. In information studies, Big Data analytics exploits machine learning, data mining, natural language processing, and parallel processing to reveal valuable patterns and insights, and it enables the applications of trend analysis, user behavior modeling, content recommendation, and collection development planning. Libraries are leveraging Big Data libraries, they analyze user search logs, circulation data, e-resources use, social media activities and environmental sensor data to enable personalization, workflow optimization, and strategic analysis. Yet Big Data projects present obstacles in data quality, privacy, ethics, and infrastructure costs. It will be a role for libraries to tackle these issues through clear policies, responsible stewardship of data, interoperability standards, training of staff, working with IT and data science colleagues. When implemented thoughtfully, Big Data allows institutions to enhance user engagement, promote access equity, minimize operational waste, and enhance evidence-based practice while upholding their ethical responsibilities for sensitive data.

text: There are three recognized kinds of transfer of property, sale, whereas, and exchange here transfer of property change over such, to give, would bind by contract discharging them. General In the general sense, a sale is the (play) exchange of a commodity for money or other valuable consideration. According to Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a sale is not an actual sale unless the price is paid or promised of payment and when it comes to the immovable property, if the value of such land is above ?100, then it is mandatory that the same would be registered in a sale deed. The word "gift" as defined in Section 122 of the Act is a voluntary transfer of property made out of doner's natural love and affection to make some return because as per the English laws, there can be no consideration for a gift also. Gift of property should be completed spontaneously of free volition without there being any pressure or deceit, and must be accepted by the donee while donor is still alive. It also has to be in writing and registered in the case of an immovable property. In comparison, an exchange is regulated by Section 118 of the Transfer of Property Act where there is an inter-transfer of ownership between two persons i.e. of one asset for another, neither being money. Whereas in sale there need not be any money, the consideration for exchange must be some other tangible property. For instance if one gives his land in exchange for a flat, it is an exchange not sale. In each of these three cases, it is necessary that the parties should be capable, and that the thing should'' be gluted by the law. Sales are money-making, gifts are expressions of generosity, and exchanges are quasi-barter-like reciprocities. All three forms of registration are compulsory where immovable property is involved to ensure legal and valid storage as well as evidence of ownership. While they’re the same as another in form, as you can see they have very different legal and practical implications when there is consideration (let alone, without consideration) and one has a gift intent.

text: The Dynamics of Power in International Relations Power in international relations is the capacity that one or another actor—primarily states, but also coalitions, institutions, and individuals whether they are political leaders, diplomats, generals, or terrorists—has to shape the behavior, attitudes, and material conditions of other states and nonstate actors in directions of its choosing. It is multidimensional, taking into account material power (military capability, economic resources, technological capacity) and relational power, or a state’s location in global networks, alliances, and institutions. Academics tend to differentiate between “hard power”, the stuff of coercion such as military intervention or economic sanctions, and soft power, forms of attraction, persuasion, cultural influence, diplomacy, normative appeal. The combination of the two—smart power—is the best approach to deal with such global, complex problems, some say. Power is not fixed; power is really power politics, power credibility, soul power and also legitimacy of power, power power as policy of all different sorts of analysis at varying levels of analysis—systemic (distribution of power), state (national strategy, national capability), as well individual leader behavior. Constructivists also explain that power itself is socially constructed in that perceptions of what power is are constructed by ideas, norms, and discourse. Power also sits at the heart of many of the key IR phenomena such as alliances, deterrence, peacekeeping, treaty design, and global governance. Bargaining dynamics from trade talks to diplomatic mediation are shaped by power asymmetry between states. The rise of new sources of power—cyber, normative, epistemic—also indicates the changing canvas of global politics. In the final analysis, power is still at the heart of IR theory and practice, given its role in determining what actors can do in terms of affecting outcomes, as well as their ability to protect privileges, ensure compliance with rules, and produce cooperation or competition in the inherently fragmented international system.

text: Political culture consisting of a patterned and shared way of thinking about how political and economic life ought to be carried out is defined as a cluster of attitudes, values, and beliefs in relation to the political system, authority, and the role of citizens. It is the essential social substructure of political life that influences political behavior, institutions, and politics. Expectations of government legitimacy, citizen participation, toleration for dissent, and conceptions of rights and responsibilities are shaped by political culture. For example, societies that have a political culture that appreciates individual freedom and pluralism generally encourage democratic systems, open discussion, and respect for civil liberties. On the other hand, culture that values order, authority and hierarchy are more likley to provide authoritarian rule or restrained political competition. Political culture is passed from one generation to the next by the process of socialization, and it is affected by history, education, and the media as well as by the more spectacular moral and ethical influences of great leaders and large chunks of the population. It shapes how citizens participate in politics, how much they trust in institutions and how likely they are to follow laws or engage in collective action. Reasons for these contrasting political cultures that go beyond differences in the polity include proximity to centers of power and the degree of access to the powerful. For instance, electoral turnout, party systems and mechanisms of conflict resolution are influenced by political culture. A healthy political culture underpins political stability and democratic consolidation, a fragmented or polarised culture begets instability and a lurch toward authoritarianism. Understanding political culture is important when the task is to create good governance structures which are in accordance with social and human values, and enable and foster political participation.

text: Mechanism-Based drug–drug interaction (DDI) prediction is important during drug development to predict interactions between a potential new drug and drugs currently on the market. Premarket modeling efforts aim to identify interactions between a new drug and drugs with which it might be coadministered early on, before much time and money is invested [2] [3]. Predictions made using drug mechanisms generally offer a qualitative, rather than quantitative, estimate of the magnitude of the interaction. Scientists can use these qualitative predictions to select the set of clinical trials necessary to establish a new drug's safety profile [4].

text: Corporate governance The system of rules, practices, and procedures by which a company is directed and controlled and through which it ensures accountability, fairness, and transparency in its relationship with all stakeholders. It provides a structure for arranging decision rights, and therefore power over the other parties, and for rewarding the different parties for maintaining their commitment to the firm. The building of trust and the reduction of risk, along with the sustainability of an enterprise and its long-term success, critically depends on good corporate governance. It helps keep companies honest, legal, and pursuing strategies that serve shareholder interests. Fundamental principles of corporate governance include independent board members; disclosure of information; accountability; stockholder rights; and risk management. The role of board of directors is pivotal when it comes to governance, as it directs management, establishes strategic direction, and protects shareholders' interests. Several mechanisms exist to enforce governance matter, among which audit, internal control and shareholder voting rights. Weak corporate governance can result in fraud, mismanagement, and loss of investor confidence, all of which can ultimately have devastating effects on a company’s reputation and revenue stream. Prominence of Environmental, social, and governance (ESG) (the broad concept that used for corporate responsibility), in recent years, which broadened the lens of corporate governance from an economic connotation to sustainability and social responsibilities. Regulations, such as the SOX in the US as well as corporate governance codes in numerous countries, offer directions and direct requirements with which one must be adhered and must be comply. For investors and shareholders, corporate governance is an important factor in assessing the quality and risk profile of the company. Corporate governance in summary, directs how a company should be run in an efficient and responsible manner for the benefit of all parties involved and at the same time, maximizing long term value creation.

text: Ecological succession is the orderly and gradual replacement of one community by another community in a certain area, where both the old and new communities remain end distinct from one another. It is an example of the changing nature of ecosystems (which is the process of succession) where, in a relatively predictable sequence, one community of plants, animals/agrobacteria and microorganisms are replaced with another until a stable climax community forms. Succession may start in barren areas, known as primary succession, such as on rocks, sand dunes, and in some areas after forest fires, when plants do not grow in the soil until it has had wood decay for some amount of time. In such extreme conditions, pioneer species such as lichens, algae, and mosses are the first to colonize an area, starting soil formation by breaking down the rocks and adding organic material. With increased depth and fertility of soil, grasses and shrubs become established first, then trees, resulting in increasingly complex communities. Secondary succession takes place in areas where an established ecosystem has been altered or destroyed in some way (such as by overgrazing, severe weather, etc.) but some life and soil is still present. Due to the presence of the soil as well as the seed bank secondary succession moves more quickly than primary succession. During succession, species replacement and ecosystem transformations in terms of the community composition and ecosystem function are influenced by biotic interactions, for example, competition, predation and facilitation. Abiotic components such as weather, soil type and disturbances are also influential. Natural succession enhances biodiversity, enhances ecosystem function, and stabilizes the cycling of nutrients and the flow of energy. The climax community achieved depends on local environment, with forests being common in the lowland areas. Knowing how ecological succession proceeds is important for ecological restoration, conservation planning, and predicting ecosystem responses to natural and anthropogenic disturbances. It demonstrates the resistance and resilience of communities and ecosystems; and the need to conserve natural disturbance regimes in order to maintain species diversity and ecosystem health.

text: A thesaurus in library science and information science is a form of controlled vocabulary that seeks to dictate semantic manifestations of metadata in the indexing of content objects. .Establishment of relationships between concepts by means of synonyms and other similar words and their usage (equivalence), and through hierarchical relationships such as broader (/narrower) and related terms (associative). Created as a solution to problems of variability in natural language, such as synonyms, homonyms, and polysemy, a thesaurus enables a user who enters a search for something like “car” to also retrieve items indexed under “automobile.” Aligning with international norms such as ISO 25964, thesauri define best practice in structure (term lists, hierarchies, relationships), language consistency, and maintenance. Thesauri enhance precision within library catalogues, digital repositories, and discipline-specific databases by forcing indexers to use the same term and by helping users to determine how to input search terms—providing suggestions and related concepts. They are powerful enough to implement features, such as query expansion, in which a user’s input is expanded with synonyms and/or more general terms to enhance recall. For particular domains (e.g., medicine or education), domain-specific thesauri—such as the Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) for medicine and ERIC Thesaurus for education—provide rich hierarchies, synonyms and vocabularies that support semantic search on the specialized literature. Maintenance of an thesaurus includes the tasks of the ongoing term maintanance, new concepts, depreceted terms, multilingual equivalences, adapting domain knowledge. Thesauri will play an ever?increasing part in ontologies and knowledge graphs, as linked data and the semantic web expand, together they will provide a shared terminology that will allow systems to work with one another. In short, a thesaurus organises information at the level of the word, makes retrieval better and faster, helps users to make sense of meanings everywhere, and helps diverse users to find things they can trust in complex search facilities.

text: There are a few strategic steps that will help you prepare for a job interview in English and make you feel more comfortable and better articulate your qualifications. Try to speak respectfully and well articulated English and avoid using filler words like “um” or “like”. Get used to the common interview varieties — face-to-face, telephone and video — and if applicable, test your technology in a trial run. On the day of the interview, wear a professional outfit and be punctual. At the end, be ready to ask insightful questions that demonstrate your interest and curiosity. Following the interview, e-mail a gracious thank-you note to show gratitude and reinforce your interest. text: Negative sentences indicate that something isn't so, doesn't happen, or denies the existence of an action or state. They are important in communication as they enable speakers and writers to deny statements, to reject offers, to contradict opinions, or to impose prohibitions. Negative sentences in English are often constructed with placing the word “not” immediately after an auxiliary or modal verb like is, are, was, were, do, does, did, can, will or have. For instance, the positive sentence “She is happy” goes from positive to negative as “She is not happy.” When the positive statement does not have an auxiliary: “He plays football”, then we introduce the auxiliary “do” in the negative: “He does not play football.” “Isn’t,” “don’t,” “can’t” and “won’t” are often employed for conversational ease, in casual writing. ic sentencesThere are ways to form negative sentences other than simply adding with some other negative elements like “never,” “nobody,” “nothing,” or “nowhere.” For instance, “Nobody came to the party,” and “I never eat meat.” Negative prefixes like un-, in-, dis-, or non- can also render words negative, like “unhappy,” “incomplete. The proper use of negatives is important when denying or absence must be conveyed without the potential for ambiguity. Misuse of negatives can cause confusion – double negatives often cancel each other out, subverting the writer’s intended meaning. All in all, negative sentences play a crucial role in language to express opposition, refusal or absence in communication in an accurate and efficient manner.

text: Terrorism is the use or threat of use of violence by groups or individuals to achieve political, ideological, religious, or social objectives by fear, intimidation, or coercion of a population, or by the manipulation of a population or government through fear propaganda. Unlike ordinary offences, terrorism has the strategic aim of creating ever more diffuse fear and instability, and many of its victims are civilians and symbols. Terrorism as a criminological matter Together with political science, sociology, psychology and international relations, terrorism is a complex phenomenon. Criminologists analyze profiles and motivations of terrorists, examining how individuals are radicalized, recruited and indoctrinated in group dynamics that turn normal people into extremists willing to use violence. It raises critical questions about how states respond, civil liberties and where the balance lies between security and human rights. Here, I present a review of how the criminological literature investigates how the social-economic, political, identity, and ideological contribution to terrorism. It also examines the efficacy and impact of counter-terrorism policies such as surveillance, intelligence work and armed interventions. Moreover, terrorism is a transnational phenomenon requiring international co-operation in law enforcement and intelligence sharing. Criminology's focus is primarily on prevention as a series of community-based strategies, combined with deradicalization efforts and with countering social, political and economic causes such as social exclusion and political oppression. Analysis despite its complexity Terrorism must be understood from a criminological perspective to develop informed policies that will protect societies and maintain democratic ideals.

text: Empiricism is a theory by which everything that is has a sensuous origin and that knowledge is impossible without the mediation of stimuli. It is the idea that the human brain is born as an empty white board, and what you know and who you are comes from your interactions with the world, and the people in it. Empiricism focuses on evidence that arises from the testing of ideas and the evidence that is provided by the senses that delivers the ultimate proof and or disproof of an idea or other mental content, which became the ideal method and approach in the early stages of the scientific method and of doing science in general. Empiricism, most famously formulated by John Locke, George Berkeley, and David Hume, describes the idea that knowledge is based on experience and, in particular, on experience of the senses, whereas rationalism ceases to understand experience independently of the senses. Empiricism maintains that ideas, beliefs, and statements of knowledge can only be ultimately groundable in the “sensory impressions” of an entity. This worldview has been responsible for the great progress of the natural sciences, medicine, and technology, with emphasis on observation, measurement, and confirmation. Empiricism is also confronted with problems, however, because it can't account for abstract ideas, such as those of mathematics or morality, that don’t appear to be directly based on sense experiences. Besides, the senses can be deceptive at times and reason, critical discernment, are requisite to perceive correctly. Notwithstanding these limitations, empiricism continues to play a central, though evolving, role in contemporary epistemology, which tends to promote a more concrete and pragmatic attitude toward knowledge, favoring experience and evidence over speculation.

text: The Law of Large Numbers (LLN) is a key theorem in probability-statistics which says, as the sample size increases, the sample mean approaches the population mean. That is, if we have enough number of observations, the mean of the sample estimates approaches E. There are two principle forms of LLN: the weak law, which says the sample mean converges in probability to the population mean; and the strong law, which says the sample mean converges almost surely (with probability 1) to the population mean. Both forms convey the idea that the more observations you have, the better your statistical estimates will be. This law is the foundation of a great deal of inferential statistics, the process researchers use to make inferences about population parameters from sample data. Look at the ratio of heads and tails if a fair coin is tossed many times; in the long run, we expect this ratio to approach 0.5, even if the ratio deviates for short period of time. The LLN also provides a rationale for using sample averages as estimates of population means and is fundamental in fields such as insurance, finance, and quality control, where long run averages are considered in decision making. Crucially, while the LLN ensures convergence in the limit, it does not ensure that for small samples, the sample mean will be close to the population mean, a common misunderstanding. Nor does it mean that extreme results will even out in the short run — a fallacy called the gambler’s fallacy. In application, the LLN provides researchers with a sense of confidence that with increased data collection comes increased accuracy and less uncertainty. But it is also an excellent demonstration of the Castleman Law which only applies when our observations are i.i.d. To put it differently, we all know that the sample statistics tend to get more and more stable and more representative as the sample size increases thanks to law of large numbers, so that we have some theoretical assurance on the statistical estimation.

text: Organic farming is a farming system that allows plants to grow and animals to be raised without the use of synthetic chemicals (pesticides, herbicides, fertilizers), supplemental genetic modification (GMOs) or growth hormones. Instead, it uses natural methods and organic substances to increase soil fertility, minimize pests, and keep nature in balance. This technique encourages diversity and soil health, as well as sustainable resource use. Organic agriculture also includes benefits to human health, safety, and cultural heritage, and is less harmful to the environment in terms of soil fertility, and water and energy use. Organic agriculture uses techniques such as crop rotation, green manure, compost, and biological pest control, as well as mechanical weeding and many other methods. The aim is to create food that’s environmentally friendly, healthy for consumers and profitable for farmers — while reducing pollution and saving water and other natural resources. Organic farmers typically try to enrich soil with nutrients through the use of natural fertilizers like animal manure or plant-based compost. They also promote soil structure and guard against erosion with cover crops and minimum tillage. Control of pests and diseases in organic farms is achieved through integrated pest management (IPM) techniques, the encouragement of beneficial insects, and the use of natural materials (such as neem or other horticultural oil and insecticidal soap) which are allowed under organic certification. Animal welfare Organic farmers allow access to outdoor spaces, and provide organic feed, is provided for animals. '*Certification standards in all parts of the world to vouch for organic practices( standards from certified institutions), group compliance to the strictest norms and regular audit and inspection * Officially recognised organic seals from certifying bodies. Although organic farming generally yields less per hectare than conventional agriculture, it has strong potential for long-term environmental friendiness due to the reduced chemical residues, enhancement in soil carbon sequestration, and increased biodiversity. Consumers frequently buy organic products for perceived healthfulness and environmental reasons. The demand for organic food is increasing internationally, necessitating an organic sector and marketing that are developed. In the end, organic farming is a more holistic method of farming that optimizes food production but also growing relationships between ecological stability and personal health.

text: Murder, and manslaughter, are both killings, but are different between the two in terms of intent, circumstances, and criminal culpability. Murder requires the intentional killing with “malice aforethought,” which is to say that the killer planned the act or intended to kill or do great bodily harm. It is the most serious form of homicide, punishable by the most extreme robes and penalties such as life imprisonment or capital punishment. Murder is compounded by degrees, depending on whether or not it was premeditated it is either first-degree and not premeditated but intentional -- or second-degree. Manslaughter, on the other hand, is when the killing was not premeditated or committed with the malice required for murder. Voluntary manslaughter occurs when a person kills in the heat of passion that is provoked by circumstances that would cause a reasonable person to lose self-control, like finding out about a spouse’s infidelity. This mitigates moral responsibility, in the form of acknowledging human weakness. Involuntary manslaughter refers to a killing that occurs due to the actor being reckless or criminally negligent however unintentional — for example, a deadly car wreck caused by bad driving. Manslaughter is considered to be a less serious crime than murder, since it is not premeditated or malicious. The legal distinction enables the justice system to tailor punishment to the perpetrator’s mental state and the circumstances of the killing. This distinction maintains some measure of justice: a person who kills without willing it should have less severe consequences than one who plans and murders someone.

text: Prep of a file for print is a specific process that marries those two worlds so when it’s printed (or your printer changes the design size), the printed image looks as good as the digital proof. First, you would choose your document size and establish your bleed areas (usually 0.125” beyond your trim edges) to make sure you have enough area to cut. Designers also have to work in the CMYK color mode (as opposed to RGB), since printers mix those four inks — cyan, magenta, yellow and black — to recreate colors. It are typical of those that must be in high quality (usually 300 DPI on prints and higher) to prevent pixelation. Typography should be outlined or embedded, allowing fonts to display properly even if the print shop lacks the original font files. Then, every single item, including key elements with important content--such as logos or text--needs to be confined within a safe margin around the outside of the page (typically 0.25 inches) to guard against unwanted cuts. Where transparency is involved in applying the effects, transparency should be flattened, especially for older print systems. File format is another important consideration: PDF/X-1a or PDF/X-4 are among the most popular file types for commercial printing due to their consistent preservation of fonts, images and color profiles. Make sure you export by adding crop marks and bleed marks. Pantone or custom spot colors must be properly named and applied for spot color jobs. For Mac users the only way to get a proper alert on a missing font is to preflight in InDesign or via Adobe Acrobat before saving the document. Fold and die lines should be placed on separate not-printing layers for projects with folds and die cuts. A proof copy or a physical sample (request one) is a good last-chance check of color, layout, and finish. Get your files right to prevent mistakes, costly reprints and receive professional quality print.

text: InterGOVs are organizations between sovereign states that are created by written agreements (treaties) and other such accords providing for joint action by two or more nations or interest groups. IGOs are also forums for diplomacy, negotiation and policy-making, for establishing trust and cooperation, for mobilizing cooperative initiatives across a wide range of issue areas –from security and economic development, to the environment, human rights, health, and trade. Some of the most recognized IGOs include the UN, the WTO, the IMF, the EU, and the AU. These groups also tend to have formal structures with leadership bodies, secretariats and legal entities that enable them to make agreements, conduct programs and shape state behavior. IGOs can enforce international norms through soft power instruments as peer pressure, sanctions, funding inducement and surveillance mechanism. For illustration, the UN supports peacekeeping missions, organizes humanitarian aid and helps grow global standards through its entities including UNESCO and WHO. The WTO sets the rules of global trade, and the IMF dispenses emergency loans and advice on how to set national policies, which in some cases have created turmoil. In addition to mainstreaming liberal norms, IGOs also foster multilateralism that can reduce strife among nation-states, improve cooperation, and create avenues for tackling global problems that no single nation can solve on its own. However, IGOs are often criticized for their efficacy, bureaucracy, dominance by more powerful nations, and lax enforcement records. Yet, despite these limitations, IGOs are essential institutions of the contemporary international order. They institutionalize diplomacy, increase state cooperation, and provide mechanisms for collective action in a world that has been increasingly defined by interdependence and the globalisation of risks.

text: Charlemagne or Charles the Great ( r. 768–814) was the King of the Franks, being later crowned by Pope Leo III as the first Emperor of the Carolingian Empire in 800 AD. He brought the majority of Western and Central Europe under a single rule, and after the re-energization of the imperial power as it fell on the continent. By military conquest he secured the Lombard Kingdom in northern Italy, drove the Saxons through the scarsa guerra, and established influence over the Marca Hispanica in what is now Catalonia. The importance of Charlemagne, politically and culturally, cannot be overstated. He restructured the empire into an administrative division of counties headed by counts, and established the missi dominici, royal envoys who as inspectors roamed the county under his authority to ensure justice and the application of the laws and his volumes of decrees—one unified, centralized political system. He personally provided education for some of the young men at his court, and welcomed foreign scholars, mostly from Ireland and Britain, to run his chapel and scriptorium, notably Alcuin of York. Charles also established a library of his own at the Palace of Aachen, and had created what would become the nucleus of the collection of the Library of Congress. His court in Aachen became an intellectual focus, producing the practice of standard script as handwriting, standard laws, and the adoption of Gregorian Chant. Charlemagne was a firm believer in the Church and undertook to spread Christianity throughout his dominions, although as he was conquering a new territory he employed missionary policy very cautiously. His imperial coronation at Rome symbolically proclaimed the resurrection of the Western Roman Empire, and led to the notion of the Emperor of the Romans as the symbol of a universal monarchy with its political and heretical connotations, and the rigid separation between Church and State became formalized: the Church and the Empire were no longer partners equal but separate in the workings of the world, but a tandem between the one and the other under the firm authority of Rome for many centuries. Subsequent dynasties, including the Ottonians and Capetians, used that name to refer to their legitimacy, and were known as the Carolingian dynasty. His establishment and promotion of Christianity[7] was a turning point in European history, though the relationship itself was initially that between the state and the institution.[8] The impact of his establishment of Christianity with or without the help of force is one of the great organising forces in European history.[7] Many of his cultural reforms were an attempt to make public life of his empire match the life of Christian identity.[7] He is a saint in the Eastern Orthodox, Catholic, and Anglican traditions.[9] Additionally, he is a canonized in the Armenian Apostolic Church. Taken as a whole, Charlemagne’s rule was a turning point in European history—a revival of imperial identity, intellectual exchange, and central governance that influenced medieval Europe, and helped pave the way for the early modern period.

text: Animals are a diverse group of organisms, which belong to the kingdom of Animalia, and they typically have certain features that distinguish them from other living entities, like plants, fungi, and bacteria. One of the fundamental characteristics of animals is that they are multicellular eukaryotes whose bodies are composed of specialized cells that have nuclei and membrane-bound organelles. Animals are also heterotrophic that is to say they are unable to make their own food like plants do; they rely on other life forms, be they plant, animal or both plants and animals to fuel them. Almost all animals are motile, meaning they can move about at least at some point in their lives, but some species of animals, such as corals and sponges, go through a sessile phase in their life. Most species reproduce sexually with distinct male and female gametes (sperm and egg), but asexual reproduction is not uncommon. In animals, there are stages of development: from a single fertilized egg to a multicellular embryo, and in many, a process for gastrulation and organ formation. Another defining characteristic is the development of specialized tissues (e.g., muscle, nerve) that allow animals to move in a coordinated manner and to respond rapidly to environmental changes (features that are lacking in the other kingdoms). The majority of animals have at least some kind of body symmetry — radial (like jellyfish) or bilateral (like humans) — which corresponds to how their body parts are arranged. Many animals have a digestive system in which food enters a cavity, the intestinal and extraintestinal lumen, and is broken down in a tube or a tube beginning with a mouth hole and ending with an anus hole. Besides, animals are equipped with sensory organs and nervous system allowing them to react rapidly to environmental changes, in a higher extent in - vertebrates. The animals of the world's ecosystems - from its oceans, forests, or deserts to its arctic tundra - display an amazing variety of adaptations to different environments. Animals vary widely in social structure, from solitary to highly social species with communication, cooperation, and even division of labor. Type of animals broken down into vertebrates (have a backbone) and invertebrates (don't have a backbone), and representing a wide variety of animals. Ultimately, multicellularity, heterotrophy, mobility, sexual reproduction, tissue specialisation and adaptability are the defining features of animals as a biological and ecological group, and amongst the most dynamic and fundamental members of life on our planet.

text: The theory of demographic transition was developed in the first half of the twentieth century by demographer demographers consider world-university-story (2). Transition theory is a model that gives an explanation of the transformation of countries from high birth and death rates to low birth and death rates. This theory is often broken down into four or five stages. In Stage 1, birth and death rates are both high, resulting in a low and stable population growth rate. This is a stage typical of pre-industrial societies where no health care, famine, and disease has kept the population from growing. The onset of the transition in Stage 2 is characterized as death rates falling because of advances in healthcare, we as a people are increasingly better about sanitation (not just in our own camp, the entire modern world), and the availability of food insuring that enough folk will pop out babies before Mother Nature — or someone else guaranteed a rise in death rates. Stage 3: Birth rates start to drop as countries become more urban, women gain better access to education and jobs, and family planning becomes available to more people. This slows the pace of population growth. At Phase 4 rates of birth and death are both low, thus the population is in balance. Some scholars suggest a fifth stage, in which birth rates drop below replacement, resulting in a natural decrease in population. This framework aids demographers in studying and comparing the population dynamics in different areas and historical periods. But, critics argue, it might not be applicable to all the developing nations, as cultural, political and economic influences can make demographic paths very different. However, the demographic transition theory is still a useful tool for studying population and planning.

text: Already in the 1940s, radio astronomers had been looking for smart solutions aimed at increasing the resolving power of their instruments. This goal was brilliantly achieved with the development of aperture synthesis (Ryle and Vonberg 1946; Ryle and Hewish 1960), acknowledged by the first Nobel prize for astronomical research, in 1974. Aperture synthesis is an interferometric technique aimed at synthesizing a very large effective aperture from an array of telescopes. This elegant method is applied in its utmost complexity in very-long-baseline interferometry (VLBI), in which the astronomical signal collected by physically unconnected telescopes can be combined. The angular resolution of an interferometer is proportional to the ratio ?/bmax, where ? is the wavelength of the radiation and bmax is the maximum baseline length, i.e., the maximum (projected) separation between two elements of the array. The major VLBI arrays currently in use, the Very Long Baseline ArrayFootnote1 (VLBA) and the European VLBI Network (EVN), are characterized by maximum baselines of the order of 10 000 km, and perform most of their observations at centimeter wavelengths. Their operation is crucial in the investigation of compact radio sources, and has advanced significantly our knowledge of the physical conditions of the plasma flow on milli-arcsecond scales, i.e., on projected spatial extents of the order of few parsecs. Radio interferometric observations capable of probing such scales are, therefore, decisive for obtaining a complete picture of the AGN phenomenon, particularly if used in synergy with high-frequency studies, in the optical, X-ray, and ?-ray bands (e.g., Marscher 2005).

text: Materials and tools Information resources include all manner of sources and assets that convey data, facts, opinions, and beliefs, and as media that includes text, images, audio and video, and can take many other forms, including, for example, computer programs such as software and electronic media, and as digital versions of traditional materials and tools, and each can be referred to as various types of resources such as materials and tools, sources, or assets: data, facts, information and narrative in text, image, audio, video, other multimedia, and other forms referred to as media or content.[9] Information resources can be divided into a variety of types, including: primary, secondary, and tertiary sources. Primary Sources Primary sources are first hand, direct evidence, or original materials on which other research is based, including original research articles, photographs, and paintings. Secondary sources are written accounts or conclusions not based on firsthand experience, and consist of works such as textbooks, reviews, biographies, reports, and scholarly reviews. Tertiary sources organize or summarize primary and secondary sources, for example, Reference works such as encyclopedias, almanacs, and bibliographies Indexes and abstracts Abstracting and indexing services. text: This article focuses on how Google generates revenue and the various significant ways in which this impacts upon the wider digital information ecology on the web. Search engines have been addressed from a wide range of academic perspectives including, but not limited to, computer science, law, politics, information retrieval, and new media studies.Footnote1 However, the role that Google’s advertising business model plays within contemporary capitalism is rarely addressed directly. This topic is crucially important because it impacts a wide-range of phenomena that might otherwise be considered non-economic, such as general online language use, and the incentives underpinning a range of content, such as fake news. In order to situate these issues within broader trends in contemporary capitalism, this article draws on Post-Fordist theory, which is outlined below, placing it within a digital context. This perspective highlights the extensive influence that Google’s revenue model has upon digital culture. Alphabet, Google’s holding company created in 2015, is one of the most valuable companies in the world.Footnote2 It has a market value of over $500 billion and in 2016 generated a revenue of $77 billion. Ask someone what Google does and they will likely reply that it is a search engine company. However, a more accurate description is that Google is an advertising company. 88.7% of Google’s revenue comes from advertising (Alphabet, 2017, p 22); although, as will be outlined below, Google’s modes of advertising deviate significantly from any existing forms of traditional advertising. The economic success of such a shift is producing dramatically widespread effects within many areas of society. This article addresses two in particular: the reification of online language and the rise of fake news. There are many other important impacts of Google’s advertising programmes, however, focusing on these two issues demonstrates the broad scope on which such a narrow economic model operates.

text: There are a number of challenges associated with the integration on to the transmission grid of recently emerging renewable-energy sources, such as PV and wind, owing to their intermittent and variable character. While conventional power plants can produce electricity when it is needed, renewables rely on the weather, which means the power supply is constantly fluctuating — an issue that can be challenging as grid operators try to ensure a reliable supply. Such vagaries call for sophisticated grid control methods and energy storage solutions to balance load in real-time. Another issue is the actual grid infrastructure, which in many locations is old and not designed to accommodate decentralized and bidirectional power flows from small distributed renewable sources. This will require substantial investments in modernizing transmission lines, smart grid technologies and information technology infrastructure to move power around effectively and avoid energy bottlenecks. In addition, renewable power sources are variable in nature, with frequency and voltage's natural fluctuation may damage equipment or induce blackouts without proper handling. Regulatory and market issues Regulatory regimes and pricing mechanisms often favor traditional sources of power generation, making it a struggle for renewable technologies to compete commercially. The high penetration of renewable energy sources requires forecasting tools that predict generation patterns for optimal dispatch. Then, of course, social agreement and the land used for renewable installations can sometimes present logistics and environmental problems. In conclusion, the integration of renewables for a more sustainable energy resource is important, but the technical and economic challenges as well as policy [6] of integrating them into the grid must be addressed in order to maintain a robust and stable grid.

Scenic An example of this is a good representation of stage scenery for amateur thrust stages. Lighting has to be very well considered as the audience is three-sided and you can’t have people standing in front of each other as well as not-blinded, but overhead and side lighting is effectively used. text: The social construction of crime A standpoint that is very important within criminology is that ‘crime’ is not something that simply exists, that is objective and fixed in its meaning. From this perspective, acts are not inherently criminal; society criminalizes certain acts depending on cultural, political, and economic factors. What is an offence in one society or at a particular time may not be in another, highlighting the variability and subjectivity in offence definitions. Law is made by the powerful, and usually furthers the interests and morality of the powerful rather than some general sense of harm or justice. For instance, drug use, vagrancy, or political protest could be selectively criminalized to dominate subaltern social groups, while harmful actions of powerful corporations or political actors may be ignored or punished less harshly. This view also underscores the influence of agents of social control—such as the police, mass media, and courts—in generating and applying crime designations. The media is an important factor in determining how the public perceives crime as it tends to sensationalise and frame crime coverage in ways that can magnify fear and affect the laws that are created. One of the central concepts in this theory, labelling theory, addresses how being labeled a “criminal” influence ppl tendency to be a “criminal” (becker1968) by internalizing the label, thus furthering their deviance in a self-fulfilling prophecy. The social constructionist view contests the idea that crime is a natural or self-evidently agreed upon category, and argues for a critical study of how power relations shape policing and social reactions to deviance.Generated on 2014-02-13 00:27:39 GMT / http://hdl.handle.net/2027/inu.30000045736511Common Law The laws of England and the derived systems, including the laws of the British Empire. Because these marginalized groups are over-criminalized, it is productive in understanding racial, class, and gender discrepancies in criminal justice to turn to them. Looking at crime as socially constituted provides a way of thinking that is less likely to entail “othering” and more attentive to fairness, for it puts into question whose interests are served by particular definitions of crime and advocates social justice.

text: The fundamental areas of philosophy traditionally are included in its branching: metaphysics, epistemology, ethics, logic, and aesthetics which relate to the basic aspects of human thought. Metaphysics poses questions regarding existence, such as the existence of God and the nature of reality. Epistemology addresses the nature of knowledge, and its sources, scope and limits, enquiring into what we can know, how we can know it, and how we can justify our beliefs about what we know. Ethics, also known as moral philosophy, explores what we think is right and good, virtue, justice as well as the good life, and it helps us determine what to do, both as individuals and as a society. For philosophy as well as science, logic concerns the structure of arguments and valid inference -- the same discipline is at home in works of philosophy and in treatises on the natural sciences. Aesthetics examines the nature of beauty, art, and taste, and the creation and appreciation of beauty. In addition to the aforementioned branches of philosophy, philosophy itself has an assortment of specialized fields of study, such as political philosophy, philosophy of mind, philosophy of language, and philosophy of science. These branches are interconnected much as metaphysical questions of the nature of Reality are connected with physics and as ethical considerations are connected with political theories. The variety of voices in philosophy serves to represent its commitment to comprehensively investigate diverse aspects of human experience, and the world more generally. Both branches apply different approaches but both are driven by the aim of clarity, coherence and critical scrutiny. They thus constitute a unified foundation of concepts with which to address basic problems of all fields, and of all experience.

text: The reactivity hypothesis postulates that exaggerated cardiovascular reactivity to acute psychological stress predisposes individuals to risk for cardiovascular disease (Manuck, Kasprowicz, & Muldoon, 1990; Obrist, 1981). Evidence consistent with this hypothesis has been derived from cross-sectional and prospective studies showing that higher levels of stressor-evoked cardiovascular reactivity are associated with future blood pressure status and hypertension (Carroll, Ginty, Painter, et al., 2012), atherosclerosis (Barnett, Spence, Manuck, & Jennings, 1997), and cardiovascular disease mortality (Carroll, Ginty, Der, et al., 2012). Indeed, a meta-analysis of 36 studies showed greater stressor-evoked cardiovascular reactivity to associate with adverse future cardiovascular health status (Chida & Steptoe, 2010). Considerable effort has been put into examining the bases of stable individual differences in stressor-evoked cardiovascular reactivity. Evidence from neuroimaging studies has extended prior animal evidence to implicate neural systems as partial mediators of individual differences in stressor-evoked cardiovascular reactivity (Gianaros & Sheu, 2009; Gianaros & Wager, 2015; Gianaros et al., ; Ginty, Kraynak, Fisher, & Gianaros, 2017; Wager, Ast, et al., 2009). For example, human neuroimaging studies demonstrate that the hippocampus and amygdala are limbic structures related to autonomic cardiovascular control during stress (e.g., Gianaros & Wager, 2015; McEwen & Gianaros, 2011), and a recent review has suggested that these brain structures may influence stressor-evoked cardiovascular reactivity via predictive neural processes that calibrate physiology with anticipated behavioral demands (Gianaros & Jennings, 2018). Although it is known that stressor-evoked cardiovascular reactivity is associated with concurrent activation in these corticolimbic systems (Gianaros & Sheu, 2009; McEwen & Gianaros, 2011; Myers, 2017; Wager, Waugh, et al., 2009), there is substantially less research examining if underlying morphological differences of the hippocampus and amygdala are associated with individual differences in cardiovascular stress reactivity.

text: Nuclear power plants and a wide range of other industrial processes rely on heat exchangers, which are devices that transfer thermal energy from a hotter fluid to a colder fluid without bringing the two into direct contact. In the nuclear industry, heat exchangers also transfer heat from the primary (reactor plant) system to the secondary (non-radioactive water/steam) system, in most cases in the rankine cycle, as part of a cooling heat rejection loop. One repeated application in a PWR is the steam generator that serves as a shell-and-tube heat exchanger. In it, thousands of small-diameter tubes running through a large vessel contain the high-temperature, high-pressure primary coolant, which is surrounded by cooler secondary water. Heat is transferred through the walls of the tubes into the secondary side which turns water into steam to run turbines. There is an inherent challenge to optimize the heat transfer efficiency, to minimize pressure drop and to be mechanically stable under harsh conditions. Selection of materials plays a critical role--stainless steel, Inconel and titanium are among corrosion, radiation, and thermal stress resistant candidates. Heat exchangers also exist in reactor auxiliary heat removal systems, emergency core cooling systems, and spent fuel pool cooling systems. Specific shapes may be used in other types of reactors, such as advanced reactors and fast breeder reactors, such as a plate-type heat exchanger, or a modular heat exchanger adapted to meet a particular thermal and flow criteria. Construction should also take into account maintaining accessibility, fouling resistance, and ability to inspect for tube damage or leaks. Safety is of prime importance: A breech in a heat exchanger can result in a secondary loop receiving radioactivity or a reduced nexus cooling capacity. Temperature differential abnormalities, flow rates and pressure change anomalies can be detected by today's monitoring systems to give early warning to potential failure. Good heat exchange is crucial for operation and safety in nuclear plants and heat exchangers continue to be one of the most designed and watched systems in the thermal cycle.

text: One of the early theories thinking about or considering how do we think about public opinion is also the theory of spiral of silence, come from Elisabeth Nolle-Neumann in the 1970s which really looked at kind of what are the dynamics that lead to the formation of public opinion and how certain things become dominant, and why sometimes certain kind of points of view are silenced. The theory posits that humans have a hardwired fear of social rejection that affects their willingness to state opinions publicly. And when they see their evidence as taking the minority or unpopular side of the issue, they refrain from sharing it (i.e., they self-censor) to avoid alienation or ostracism. That in turn generates a “spiral,” as dissenting views are successively shut down, thereby enabling the dominant view to become even more prevalent — and even less of a contained value war. Mass media have a significant role in this, both in amplifying a perceived majority view in coverage and in aiding social norms and a climate in which different views appear marginalised or ignored. This can lead to reduced intellectual diversity in the public discourse and sow political division, because people will think twice before saying what they think they see the social costs of being ostracized. The theory also recognizes the situations where the spiral can be shattered, such as when social backing exists for minority points of view, or when anonymity shields people from retaliation. But in the era of online sharing and social-media manipulation, the spiral of silence has adapted, with digital anonymity and counter-publics offering a venue for silenced voices to find some purchase — even as it helps cultivate echo chambers. The spiral of silence is one of the keys to understanding how peer pressure, media frames and public opinion mix and mingle to shape public attitudes and political participation.

text: Nelson Mandela (1918–2013) was a South African anti-apartheid revolutionary, political leader, and philanthropist who served as president of South Africa from 1994 to 1999. He was the country's first black head of state and the first elected in a fully representative democratic election. Mandela had been imprisoned 27 years for his role as a leader in the struggle to end apartheid, the official policy of legalized racial discrimination and segregation by the white minority government. On his release in 1990, Mandela led the formation of negotiations to achieve a peaceful transition from apartheid government by a white minority to majority rule and democracy. He won the backing of the vast majority of the country to become its first black president in 1994, after 27 years in prison as a heroic symbol of the struggle against white minority rule, and in doing so he drew on such a well of goodwill and reverence he embodied the ideal of leaning toward forgiveness, reconciliation and peace. Mandela’s presidency became a time of reckoning with apartheid’s legacy both through the easing of racial reconciliation via a Truth and Reconciliation Commission and the pursuit of social and economic development. Under him, the emphasis was on inclusivity and nation-building, not retribution and vigilantism, and he made the country’s path a beacon to the world for both reconciliation and human rights. Mandela’s influence stretched well beyond South Africa; he emerged as a hero to civil rights movements, anti-colonial crusades and democratic aspirations everywhere. The honors arrived, the Nobel Peace Prize — in 1993 — and he is a lasting giant in the fight for justice, a tough stand for resilience and dignity, and a healing force of talk and forgiveness. His legacy is reflected in every movement for equality, justice, and dignity in America and around the world.

text: Benthicalgae are important aquatic biota in riverine ecosystems. As primary producers,algae provide the main food resources for macro invertebrates and fish and play animportant role in energy cycling [1,2]. Due to their short life span, relatively complexcommunity composition and high sensitivity, benthic algae can integrate both short-term andlong-term environmental variation and a broad range of human stressors [3]. Thus, manymonitoring programs in the United States [4] and Europe [5-7] include diatoms asmainelements to assess river health. There are several diatom-based indices that have been developed in Europe using theZelinka and Marvan formula [8]. The indices take into account the variations of relativeabundance and tolerance of each taxon in the community, and have been widely acceptedas important indictors in river health assessment. The Descy Index [9] was the first diatomindex developed based on the pollution tolerance classification for diatoms. Thestandardized Biological Diatom Index (BDI) [10] was first developed and applied in Francefor the surveillance of water quality. The BDI index was revised (BDI-2006) [11] for bettersuitability to the European Water Framework Directive (WFD). Other widely used indicesinclude the Specific Pollution sensitivity Index (SPI) [12], Generic Diatom Index (GDI) [13],Trophic Diatom Index (TDI) [14], Commission for Economical Community Index (CEE) [15],Schiefele and Schreiner’s Index (SHE) [16] and Rott Saprobic Index (ROTT) [17].

text: 1) Subword: We have observed that Chinese sign language words are not unrelated to others, but they have a semantic relationship among each other. For instance, in Chinese, the word “kindergarten” means “the house of kids.” More specifically, the Chinese sign language word “kindergarten” is composed of front and back parts, where the front and back parts represent “kid” and “house,” respectively. Similarly, the Chinese word “station” means “the house of cars,” and the sign word “station” is composed of “car” and “house” parts. In fact, the two “house” parts in “kindergarten” and “station” are identical. In other words, the two “house” parts have the same hand shapes and trajectories. Accordingly, we can define three subwords: “kid,” “car,” and “house.” The “kindergarten” can be denoted by “kid–house” and the “station” can be denoted by “car-house.” Along this line of consideration, the smaller scale subword units are defined in the entire word domain. Consequently, we divide sign words into sequential subwords as output and model the subword sequence instead of words. In [2] and [22], the authors gave the inspiration and conducted the preliminary trial about subwords, while our work is more natural for SLR tasks as it has some main differences from [2] and [22]. For example, we do not define the specific word “phonemes” whose context properties are omitted during training [2], [22].
