text: The body as language: Physical theatre Physical theatre is a type of performance that by its nature utilizes the body as a means of communicating and telling a story, focusing on a more “physical” and less spoken mode of communication than traditional theatre. It's a mixture of dance, mime, circus, and theatre combined with dynamic, visually dazzling performances. Physical Theatre This “body-based” theatre rejects the idea that the actor’s body is a mere text to point towards meaning, and insists that, instead, it is the text itself. This type of dance frequently includes highly choreographed and stylized movements that convey meaning with body attitude, beat and space relationships. In physical theatre, when spoken language is used, certain physical exercises are done for global actors to retard the verbal action so their bodily being can be experienced as a unified center with potential for movement. It’s a call for actor/director/designer cooperation that would fuse lighting, sound and set around the zeal of physical action. This style is developed by companies such as DV8 Physical Theatre and practitioners such as Jacques Lecoq. Physical theatre frequently challenges notions of identity, power, and the human experience using non-traditional or innovative storytelling and performance techniques, to do so. It demands intense focus and team work among the actors, discipline, stretching, creativity. This methodology establishes a visceral, unmediated relationship between the performer and the audience making for an immersive and unforgettable theatrical experience.

text: Finding the point-to-point correspondence of related visual patterns is a fundamental problem in computer vision. Many applications such as stereo, motion estimation, object detection, and action detection benefit from accurate and fast matching algorithms. Visual matching is also a challenging problem because the imagery of an object may have large variations, e.g., geometrical transformations, deformations, and appearance changes in different viewing conditions. In this paper, we propose an efficient linear solution to the visual matching problem which yields reliable results even when there is large rotation, scaling, translation, deformation, and clutter. Different methods have been proposed to solve matching problems. The Hough transform [36], [1], [2] and RANSAC [35], [3], [34] are robust methods that have been widely used in object matching. The Hough transform requires a careful selection of its parameters (e.g., bin size) and breaks down in the presence of strong clutter. RANSAC is more resistant to clutter: It generates matching hypotheses for a small number of anchor points and then evaluates the hypotheses using all the model points. RANSAC becomes increasingly slow with weak features or strong clutter. To reduce the complexity, prepruning methods based on heuristics or General Hough Transform have been used [3] to remove unpromising local matches. However, when local feature matching becomes increasingly ambiguous, the prepruning process is less and less effective. Besides, the Hough transform and RANSAC find the overall geometrical transformation, but do not directly give point-to-point deformable object matching.

text: Job satisfaction is the degree in which someone feels satisfied or happy with their job and the work environment. It is an intricate, multi-faceted concept that is affected by different factors ranging from the nature of the job, pay, recognition, work-to-life balance, relationships with colleagues and supervisors, opportunities for development, and organizational culture. A happy employee with high job satisfaction is also more likely to be productive, engaged, motivated, and loyal — while dissatisfaction can manifest as frequently calling in sick, low morale, burnout, and high turnover. Theories like Herzberg’s Two-Factor Theory separate job satisfaction into hygiene factors (like pay, job security and working conditions) and motivators (like achievement, recognition, and personal growth). Hygiene factors when absent can create dissatisfaction although their presence themselves may not result in satisfaction unless the Presence of motivator factors. Likewise, Maslow's Hierarchy of needs suggest that meeting psychological and self actualization needs in work-life leads to satisfaction. Certainly contentment at work will also be based on what an individual expects from a job and what they get from the job. For example, a person that values autonomy would feel dissatisfied in an environment where everything is highly controlled. Questionnaires and feedback-tools are widely used in organizations seeking to measure and promote job satisfaction. Ways to raise satisfaction levels might include more employee engagement, more skill-building opportunities, rewarding people that perform, inviting people into making choices and creating a caring culture. text: Indemnity and guarantee are both species of contracts under the law of obligations that relate to third party liability, but some of their features and structures differ. Hence indemnity in India is a contract of indemnity as per Section 124 of the Contract Act, 1872 which is a contract by which the promisor promises to save the promise of a loss caused to him or by the conduct of the promisor or any other person. There are two parties: the indemnifier (the one who promises to compensate) and the indemnified (the one protected). The insurer, for instance, undertakes to indemnify the insured against losses from damage or loss. It is an original and underimpaired (or not subordinated) liability — once the loss has been suffered the indemnifier is liable, whether or not there has been a default by any other person. On the other hand, a contract of guarantee as explained under Section 126, represents three parties, namely, the creditor (to whom money is due), the principal debtor (the person whose liability is guaranted) and the surety (the person who gives the guarantee). The liability of the surety is collateral and is activated only when the principal does not perform or fulfill the duty for which the surety acts as guarantee. For instance, when A borrows from a bank and B signs as a guarantor, B will pay only when A defaults. A further distinction is that under indemnity the loss need not flow in consequence of the default or breach, whereas under guarantee the liability flows directly on the default by the debtor. Indemnity is for loss of a monetisable value in future uncertain events, while Guarantee has got to do with the promise to ensure the action of a third person. As a matter of legal risk, indemnifiers have less defenses available and may be subject to legal rights of the surety, such as rights of subrogation and indemnity against the principal debtor. So, although both cover against loss, indemnity is concerned with compensation and guarantee with performance security.

text: An oligopoly refers to a market dominated by a few large firms each of which is highly influenced by the actions of the others. Interdependence is the chief characteristic of an oligopoly, where each firm takes into the account the potential reactions of its competitors in determining pricing, production and investment decisions. Goods can be homogeneous (such as steel or cement) or differentiated (such as cars or cellphones). There tend to be high barriers to entry preventing new firms from entering the market because of limited firms, such as, economies of scale, government licenses or brand loyalty. It is difficult to predict prices in the case of oligopolies because collusive or strategic behaviour can come into play. Companies could join together in a cartel — the way OPEC manages oil output and prices — to coordinate pricing and output, although such collusion is illegal in many markets. Instead, they could pursue non-collusive conduct which involves attempting to ‘do better than,’ but at the same timemaintaining, the stability of present industry prices. Price stickiness is another common characteristic (firms tend to avoid being the first mover to cut prices for fear of opening a price war). Instead, they compete using non-price methods, such as advertising, creating new products or providing good customer service. Game theory is commonly applied within studies of strategy within oligopoly whereby firms react to rivals’ moves. Oligopolies reduce competition and tend to increase prices and lower consumer surplus, but their high profits encourage both innovation and investment. Airlines, telecoms and pharmaceuticals are typical examples. In conclusion, oligopolies are intermediate between monopolies and more competitive settings, they are simultaneously powerful and dependent making them politically important and difficult to regulate.

text: The transpolar potential is consistent with region-1 (J1) currents that are voltage driven but current limited, where the currents close through the ionosphere within minutes. Following the model of Siscoe (1982), the J1 currents also partially close through the magnetosphere with a time delay, forming the ring current and associated region-2 (J2) currents. In Paper1 (Rothwell and Jasperse, 2006), equivalent time-dependent circuit equations were derived and an empirical relationship established between the solar wind data measured at L1 and the penetration electric field. The ionospheric response to J1 and J2 was modeled after Nopper and Carovillano (1978) which includes the effects of a sun-lit ionosphere and a dipole magnetic field. The conductance at the terminators used in the Rothwell–Jasperse model had a much larger conductance gradient (and hence more realistic) than that used in the Nopper–Carovillano model. In contrast to the J1 current, the presence of J2 creates a westward electric field also just past 1800 h LT which shields the J1-produced eastward (positive) electric field. Therefore, the net post-sunset electric field is the difference between the J1 and J2 components. Since these two components operate on different time scales finding the net penetration electric field Eeq(t) at any one time is difficult.

text: A complex sentence is a sentence that includes one independent clause and at least one dependent (or subordinate) clause. An independent clause is a full sentence; it can stand alone and doesn't depend on any other element to work (although it may contain other elements). A dependent clause is not a full sentence. Subordinate clauses typically open with subordinating conjunctions that can include: because, although, if, when, while, since or even though. You can think of these clauses as extra details, explanations, or conditions on the main idea. For instance: “I was home; it rained.” Here, “I stayed home” is the independent clause and “because it’s raining” is the dependent clause. The sentence couldn’t be “because it was raining” alone, because then it would not be a sentence at all. Another sample: “Even though she was tired, she completed her homework.” The subordinate clause precedes the main clause. In the second example, note that when the dependent clause appears first, there is a comma between the clauses. Complexity sentences can be used to express detailed and subtle ideas in a way that is not possible with simple or compound sentences. They clarify cause and effect, sequence and time, conditions, and contrasts. For example: “If you work hard, you’ll succeed” (condition), “When I came, they were having dinner” (time) and “Though he is rich, he lives simply” (contrast). Academic and formal writing relies heavily on complex sentences because they are ideal for discussing a relationship between ideas. They enhance reading and writing abilities as well through a stronger grasp of grammar and structure. In short, in a complex sentence, a main point is combined with extra information in a ‘correct’ or grammatical way so that we can communicate more clearly, more fully and more accurately.

text: Stare decisis is of special importance in the field of criminal law for the benefit of maintaining stability and predictability of judicial decisions. Courts can simply be consistent with past decisions on cases involving the same or similar subject matter, producing a system of law where people, attorneys and the police know how the law is interpreted and enforced. This is particularly important in criminal law where the requirement for fair warning and widespread uniformity are axioms of justice. Precedent has the effect of treating like alike - there is less of a swerve toward arbitrary or prejudiced decisions - and it promotes the rule of law and confidence in the administration of the legal process. In addition, precedent allows criminal law to change with the times, answering the needs of society as it changes its cultural values, technology, and new types of cases though small modifications or turning over old decisions. There is a hierarchy between courts where higher courts have the ability to create binding precedent for lower courts, which follows in the form of a pyramid. The courts can reverse wrong precedents out of date to meet this new injustice or to adjust to the new development of the law. In criminal law, there are numerous aspects influenced by precedents – definition of offences, evidence thresholds, punishment, procedural rights, etc. It serves therefore as a conservative as well as an engine of legal evolution, reflecting the tension between tradition and change in the justice system.

text: The classical option pricing theory of Black and Scholes relies on the fact that the payoff of every contingent claim can be duplicated by a portfolio consisting of investments in the underlying stock and in a bond paying a riskless rate of interest; in other words, the risk of buying or writing an option can be completely hedged against. In such complete markets, there is a unique measure which is equivalent to the canonical measure (the "real world" measure) and which makes the discounted price process a martingale. The unique fair price of a contingent claim is then the expectation under this martingale measure of the discounted payoff at maturity, which is essentially the content of the famous Black-Scholes formula.

text: In the following, we describe observations by the Voyager 2 magnetometer (Behannon et al. 1977) at 4.4 AU of waves with linear polarization and spacecraft frame frequencies significantly greater than the proton cyclotron frequency when the mean interplanetary magnetic field (IMF) B0 is perpendicular to the solar wind flow velocity. There are several potential sources and interpretations for these waves, and each source implies specific wave characteristics that can be tested, but most sources and interpretations can be reliably excluded. At these frequencies, the two most likely plasma modes are whistler and Bernstein modes. Direct and unambiguous identification of the wave properties is difficult, but with the observed linear polarization and a strongly oblique IMF we argue that propagation at large angles to the IMF is likely. These facts, together with the observed spacecraft frame frequencies, strongly point to the Bernstein mode as the probable identity of the waves. Interplanetary magnetic waves arising from wave/particle interactions most normally fall into several classes. Low-frequency Alfvén or fast-mode waves frequently arise due to field-aligned and gyrating beams of energetic ions and are observed to be strongly polarized, parallel propagating in the same direction as the ion beam, and with magnetic fluctuations perpendicular to the mean IMF (Gary et al. 1984; Murphy et al. 1995; Lee & Ip 1987; Isenberg 2005; Joyce et al. 2010). Higher frequency waves can arise from field-aligned electron beams or gyrating ion distributions. For electron beams the dominant instability is the parallel-propagating and highly polarized whistler mode (Wong & Smith 1994). However, gyrating ion beams can produce whistler waves at small to modest angles of propagation relative to the mean IMF (Wong & Goldstein 1987, 1988).

text: Fusion energy is the process in which two light atomic nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus, releasing vast amounts of energy, which are similar to the reactions in our sun and other stars. It is fundamentally different from fission, where heavy atomic nuclei are broken into smaller pieces, and with it also energy is released. In fusion, hydrogen isotopes like deuterium and tritium join together under high temperatures and high pressures to overcome electrostatic repulsion. Fusion has several advantages over fission, such as its fuel is plentiful (deuterium can be obtained from water and tritium can be bred from lithium). Fusion results in very small amounts of long-lived radioactive waste in comparison to fission, and this contributes to its environmental advantages. And, of course, fusion reactions are immune to runaways chain reactions or meltdowns; they’re already inherently safe. Because it is difficult to create and sustain these extreme conditions for the time and volume necessary to produce net energy, controlled fusion has proved to be elusive in practice on Earth. Fission reactors, on the other hand, are a reality but they also pose issues related to radioactive waste, proliferation, and accidents. Fusion offers the potential of a near limitless supply of clean and safe energy if these challenges can be met. Around the world, there are continued research efforts into magnetic confinement, including stellarators and tokamaks, as well as other mainstream and alternative approaches to achieving usable fusion.

text: The steam generator in a PWR is an important component in the heat transfer chain between the primary loop of the reactor (which is radioactive) and the pretreated secondary loop (which is completely free of radioactivity). The steam generator is, in effect, a very large heat exchanger with thousands of U-bent tubes made of corrosion-resistant alloy. Reactor core coolant under pressure travels up through the interior of these tubes and transfers its heat to the secondary system water operating at lower pressure. This sub-cooled water under low pressure absorbs the heat and becomes a saturated steam. The steam is then sent into a turbine, which runs a generator to produce electricity. After passing through the turbine, the steam is condensed by cooling and returned to liquid form (water) in the condenser, ready to be pumped back to the steam generator. The steam generator has to achieve a delicate thermal-pressure balance: it should maintain high pressure (about 155 bar) primary loop water not boiling, and also secondary side boiling pressure (about 70 bar), in order to generate a sufficient steam flow. "The good performance in the operation of the steam generator is essential to keep good fulfillment of thermal efficiency, fuel performance, and safety of the reactor. The design is also critical for safety and accident protection as the containment isolates the radioactive coolant from the turbine-plants and saves it from being contaminated. Periodic inspection and maintenance is needed to make sure such problems as tube wear, corrosion, or tube foulants that could affect heat transfer and, in gross instances, allow radioactive material into the secondary side, are detected quickly. In short, the steam generator of a PWR powers the plant's electricity while protecting the reactor's heat exchange and containment barriers.

text: An operational amplifier (often op-amp or opamp) is a DC-coupled high-gain electronic voltage amplifier with a differential input and, usually, a single-ended output. It is a voltage amplifier with an extremely high voltage gain. It usually has 2 inputs designated inverting (-) and noninverting (+) and 1 output, and is used with dual voltages supplies such as ±15V. The most important characteristic of an op-amp is the open-loop gain that can be as large as 100,000, so that even the tiniest voltage difference between the inputs is manifested as a large output voltage. Which Means In all Cases op-amps are used as close loop with negative feedback so that gain is stable and output is predictable. With an inverting amplifier you put the input through a resistor into the inverting detector and project a result back to the same detector through another resistor. This feedback attenuates the gain, with the feedback gain being ?Rf?/Rin?. Op-amps have ultra high input impedance and low output impedance; perfect for buffering and signal manipulation. Applications Include: active filters, instrumentation, Cable AC Driv, function generator, power supplies etc. Nowadays op-amps may be purchased in small IC packages such as the uA741. Ideal op-amps are also assumed to have infinite input impedance, infinite output impedance and many assume zero noise as well. Summary Operational amplifiers are incredibly versatile in both analog and digital interfacing, offering you a superb combination of features: precision, availability, and convenience that have made them indispensable in countless electrical circuits and control systems.

text: Punishment in psychology is a consequence that is used to decrease the likelihood of a behavior recurring in the future. It is a fundamental principle in B.F. Skinner's theory of operant conditioning and is sometimes referred to as the ""pleasure and pain principle"" or the ""punch line principle."" It can de divided into two main types, positive punishment and negative punishment. Positive punishment is adding something unpleasant following a behavior, for example, reprimanding a child for behaving badly in order to prevent said behavior. Negative punishment, which removes a desirable stimulus, acts to decrease behavior, as when a teen’s phone is taken away when he or she breaks the rules. This strategy can teach your dog to fear you, and if you use treats or punishment, can create negative associations in the long term, e.g. if you use treats with punishment, your dog will start to fear treats or your dog may become anxious or aggressive if not trained correctly. Punishment is most effective when it is close in time to the behavior, is consistent, and corresponds in intensity to the behavior. It is an entirely different process to reinforcement whose goal is to cause an increase in behaviour, while punishment’s purpose is directly aimed at suppressing behaviour. Successful behavior modification frequently depends more on using reinforcement to make good behavior more frequent than on using punishment to deter from bad behavior – punishment may even accomplish the opposite by not showing a person what to do instead and damage relationships or self-esteem.Punishment and reinforcement operate in the opposite manner: Reinforcement increases a behavior that was done willingly, and punishment decreases a behavior that was done willingly.

text: According to Talcott Parsons’ structural functionalism theory society is a specific system which is made up of different components that contribute to the stability and maintenance of social order. In Parson's view, institutions such as the family, education, religion, and government serve important purposes for society to function properly. This knowledge is particularly pertinent for Bangladesh where modern and traditional institutions are operating alongside each other and determining the equilibrium of society. The family in Bangladesh, for example, is the playing field for righting and teaching values and cultures. The education system, which is inequitably distributed, serves to train youth for the labor market and to reproduce national identity. Religious, in particular Islamic, beliefs and practices provide a moral guide and promote social unity. During times of crisis–floods, pandemics, or political turmoil–religious institutions, families, and local government units converge to provide assistance, converging in the sense of Parsons’ functional integration. Even political parties — which can be such sources of instability — serve to organize public opinion and distribute power. Structural functionalism also explains why attempts to effect changes (legal reforms, gender equality, etc.), meet resistance—they disrupt existing functional relations. But if new institutions (including things like NGOs or online education platforms) emerge to fulfill functional gaps, they can be incorporated into the social order. Parsons’ theory is therefore valuable for understanding how Bangladesh sustains social solidarity against the backdrop of increasing urbanization, political adversaries and external influences. It has to be added that change is only sustainable if it is compatible with the purpose of society.

text: A mutation is a permanent heritable change in the sequence of a DNA gene; the term is generally restricted to relatively rare changes that have some significant physiological or pathological effect and that can be transmitted to the subsequent offspring. Such alterations can happen spontaneously, arising from mistakes made during DNA replication, or be triggered by external influences like radiation, chemicals or infections with viruses. Mutations may be point mutations (alterations to a single nucleotide), insertions, deletions, or chromosomal rearrangements. Mutations are critical in plants because they can create genetic variation, the fuel for evolution and for plant breeding programs. Mutations, of course, aren’t necessarily good; many are neutral or damaging, but some impart desirable characteristics such as disease resistance, higher yield or environmental adaptation. Mutations in germ cells are heritable, and thus can be transmitted to subsequent generations, leading to variability among species, mutations in somatic cells are not transmitted to the next generation, and concern only the individual plant. Mutations may be silent (no protein change), missense (coded for a different amino acid), nonsense (introducing a stop codon) or frameshift (since open reading frame will be altered) which affect gene expression differently. Induced mutations with mutagens are used in plant improvement to develop new cultivars with preferred traits. Molecular methods, including gene sequencing, are used to identify mutations of the gene in order to generate accurate genetic investigations. Although they are important for variation, unrestrained mutations can be harmful: they can result in genetic diseases or decrease fitness. Knowledge of mutation is also relevant for breeding and genetic conservation and for understanding evolutionary processes and, therefore, is a central concept of genetics and plant biology.

text: Escherichia coli strains are the major cause of urinary tract infections in humans. Such strains can be divided into virulent, UPEC strains causing symptomatic infections, and asymptomatic, commensal-like strains causing asymptomatic bacteriuria, ABU. The best-characterized ABU strain is strain 83972. Global gene expression profiling of strain 83972 has been carried out under seven different sets of environmental conditions ranging from laboratory minimal medium to human bladders. The data reveal highly specific gene expression responses to different conditions. A number of potential fitness factors for the human urinary tract could be identified. Also, presence/absence data of the gene expression was used as an adaptive genomics tool to model the gene pool of 83972 using primarily UPEC strain CFT073 as a scaffold. In our analysis, 96% of the transcripts filtered present in strain 83972 can be found in CFT073, and genes on six of the seven pathogenicity islands were expressed in 83972. Despite the very different patient symptom profiles, the two strains seem to be very similar. Genes expressed in CFT073 but not in 83972 were identified and can be considered as virulence factor candidates. Strain 83972 is a deconstructed pathogen rather than a commensal strain that has acquired fitness properties.

text: Slow and controlled release (SR, CR, respectively) are the most advanced pharmaceutical preparations, and provide a slow, controlled release of the active compound throughout a prolonged period minimizing administration frequency, and improving patient compliance. SR dosage forms are the products that release the drug at a rate that is slower than that of IR dosage forms, or that slow the drug release or absorption. This prolongation of the time course of plasma drug concentration variation can ameliorate adverse effects and enhance efficacy. But the time-release form in fact doesn’t maintain a constant release rate of the drug itself; it just keeps it circulating in the blood stream longer. Sustained-release delivery systems, on the other hand, allow a uniform or controlled release over a period of time of the drug delivery system and typically follow zero order kinetics wherein the rate of release is dramatically fixed independent of drug concentration. In this way it becomes feasible to control the plasma level more efficiently, improve efficacy and decrease toxicity. Both systems are constructed of different types of technology, such as matrix systems, reservoir systems, osmotic pumps, or biodegradable polymers for drug release modulation. Controlled-release often refers to special dosage forms or formulations in which the active substance is encapsulated in a system that controls the its release. These forms of application are of particular significance for substances with very short half-lives as well as those with a narrow therapeutic range and for those which have to be kept at a molecular blood dosage. Through greater dosing flexibility, they offer additional convenience and adherence for patients, reducing the risk of missed doses and having a positive impact on treatment outcomes overall. They also minimize the undesirable effects because they do not peak, and they can minimize drug wastage. For the design of SR and CR drug delivery forms a lot of background information on drug properties, release kinetics and patient characteristics is necessary. In summary, SR and CR dosage forms attempt to achieve an ideal drug therapy by extending the administration of drugs in predictable and effective manner.

text: A tariff is a tax by a government on imported goods, whether for protection, retaliation, or revenue. Overall, tariffs raise the cost of imports and drive down their competitiveness relative to locally manufactured goods thus incentivising consumers to opt for home-grown products. Tariffs come in a variety of forms. The most standard is the ad valorem tariff, which is determined as a fixed percent of the value of the imported good. For instance, a 10 percent ad valorem tariff for imported cars implies that the government takes 10 percent of a car’s value as a tax. A second category is the specific tariff which is a set amount of money applied for each unit of imported good, no matter the price—$5 per kilogram of sugar, for example. A mixed tariff is a combination of ad valorem and specific tariffs. And tariffs can be protective (to protect the home industries) or revenue-producing (to pay the costs of government). Tariffs may have positive and negative impacts. On the upside, tariffs can shelter nascent industries, save jobs and produce government bounty. But they frequently backfire and result in higher prices for consumers and fewer options, while other countries retaliate with counter-tariffs that can ignite trade wars. They may also waste resources by sheltering less competitive domestic industries and are welfare?reducing. Though tariffs can be employed for strategic national purposes, overdone or poorly executed tariffs can distort trade patterns and destroy international relationships. Most countries have lowered tariffs in accordance with trade agreements to facilitate freer and more efficient global trade.

text: Animal adaptation varies from structural, physiological, and behavior response that would allow animals to meet the demands of life in a specific environment. Structural adaptations are physical traits that enhance an animal's ability to survive in its environment, such as the thick fur of polar bears for insulating against frigid temperatures, the camouflaged coloration of chameleons to blend in with the environment to avoid predators, or the long neck of giraffes that allows them to reach the high leaves of savannas. Physiological adaptations are more internal processes, regulating and maintaining body functions such as body temperature, water balance and metabolic rate; desert animals such as the kangaroo rat, for example, use the minimum water they need by producing concentrated urine and are active mainly during the cooler night as opposed to the hot day. Some fish secrete antifreeze proteins into their blood to keep ice crystals from forming in freezing water. Behavioral adaptations refer to what animals do to survive, for example, migration in birds moving to warmer climates to avoid the cold, pack behavior in wolves that helps them hunt efficiently, or hibernation in bears with insufficient food resources. Animals could evolve reproductive strategies, too, such as having lots of offspring at once in response to variable environments or providing parental care to increase offspring survival chances. Over generations, these adaptations develop through the mechanism of natural selection, in which the survival and reproduction of individuals bearing the most adaptive traits is more likely than their peers. Adaptations may be general or very specific to particular environmental conditions, such as aquatic animals being sleek and having gills so that they can swim and obtain oxygen from the water, or as specific as having thumbs for precise manipulations (humans). Certain species have fascinating plasticity, wherein they can alter their behavior or physiology in a generation in response to changing environments, like adapting to different temperatures. It is the combination of these adaptations that allows animals to exploit a wide range of habitats, from the deep oceans to high mountain ranges, to thick forest to desert. Characterizing animal adaptations is also informative for conservation: Species often inhabit a sweet spot in their ecosystem, and the loss of habitat or changes in temperature threaten species that cannot adapt swiftly enough. To conclude, they make living in certain (physical and ecological) surroundings possible for some animals and allow the latter to survive and reproduce in the face of environmental challenges and oppotunities in their specific habitats, both thanks to a finely-tuned set of physical features, internal functions and behaviour patterns.

text: The six-factor formula is an expression in nuclear engineering used to calculate the effective multiplication factor (k-effective) for neutron multiplication in a nuclear reactor whether the reflected reactor is sub-critical, critical, or over-critical. It decomposes the complex neutron life cycle in six terms that characterize the neutron activity from production to absorption or leakage. These include Fast fission factor (?), the number of neutrons added to the system by one neutron's worth of fissions by these fast neutrons Resonance escape probability (p), the probability that a neutron will escape absorption by the fuel at resonance nuclear reactions while being slowed from the fast fission generation energy to the thermal fission range Thermal utilization factor (f), the fraction of the thermal neutron flux promptly absorbed in the fuel Reproduction factor (?), the number of neutrons produced by fission of actinide nuclei divided by the number of neutrons absorbed by those nuclei Fast non-leakage probability (Pf), the probability that fast neutrons will remain in the system Thermal non-leakage probability (Pt), the probability that thermal neutrons will remain in the system K-effective is determined by the calculation of a product of six factors the formula which describes this calculation is a measure of the reactors ability to maintain a chain reaction. If k-effective=1, the reactor is critical, i.e., the chain reaction is self-sustaining, 1 is supercritical. This equation is essential for design, operation and safety analysis of reactors and enables engineers to better design materials, geometry and operational conditions to support controlled fission. It provides a coherent, design foundations-based basis for analyzing core physics and is being applied in both theoretical and operational analyses of reactor core behavior.

text: Trajectory planning in robotics corresponds to finding a time-parametrized path that should follow the end effector or the joints of a robot to go from a given starting position to a goal with desired properties. It guarantees that the robot kinematically moves in a smooth, efficient and safe manner, considering physical limits, such as joint limits, velocity, acceleration, jerk (rate of change of acceleration), and obstacle avoidance. A trajectory is more than a geometric path; it includes how the robot moves along the path through time. In joint-space trajectory planning, the trajectory is provided as a function of time of each joint angle, which is suitable for tasks such as pick and place. Cartesian-space motions are defined by position and orientation in 3D space, allowing an easy to understand processes of moving of the end-effector in complex environment. Such techniques as polynomial interpolation (e.g., cubic or quintic splines), trapezoidal velocity profiles, and B-splines are employed to create smooth trajectories. Advanced widgets could use optimization-based or artificial intelligence (such as genetic algorithms or neural networks) for manipulation of dynamic obstacles or live changes. Motion planning is important for many robotic applications such as industrial automation, autonomous vehicles, and even humanoid robots to make sure their movements are accurate as well as within the capabilities of the system. Ill-designed trajectories can cause rupture motions, wear on actuators, barren collisions and also entire instability of a system, and consequently becoming crucial in all aspects of robotic control and performance optimization.

text: What is Investigative Journalism Investigative journalism is a type of journalism that requires in-depth, high-quality research from a journalist and can take weeks, months or years to fully uncover and understand the truth that is shrouded in secrecy. Not like breaking news, which merely reports current events and superficial information, investigative reporting digs beneath everything to uncover deeper forces at play, like corruption, fraud, abuse of power, and human rights abuses. Investigative journalism can be a long and tedious process, often requiring weeks, months, or sometimes years of work and the accumulation of mountains of evidence in the form of interviews, documents, surveillance, and data analysis. The role is not simply to chronicle what has taken place, but to describe why and how it has taken place (and who or what carried it out) -- the better to focus a reader or viewer's attention on authors of wrongdoing and the fallout of their actions. Investigative journalists are frequently confront a barrage of obstacles, from legal intimidation and political harassment to real physical danger. Therefore, they are bound to follow strict moral and legal rules to guarantee that what they have written is truthful, reasonable, and sourced. A few famous examples are the Watergate scandal revealed by Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein and, more recently, the Panama Papers, which revealed instances of tax evasion and money laundering by people across the world. Investigative journalism is immensely important in a democracy, for it helps to keep the powerful in check and citizens informed so they can demand change. It promotes transparency, upholds justice, and can elicit public outcry or government reform. But it is a model that takes time and resources and is endangered more than ever in today’s world of rapid-fire, click-driven media. Still, many journalists and outlets continue to do this extremely important work, sometimes with the help of grants or nonprofit entities devoted to public interest reporting. text: Ultrasonic sensor An ultrasonic sensor is a distance measuring sensor that works by sending out high-frequency (20 kHz or over) sound waves and measuring the exact time it takes for the sound to bounce back after hitting an object. It is primarily composed of a transmitter that generates ultrasonic pulses and a receiver that locates reflected (echo) waves. When emitted wave encounters an obstacle, it is reflected back to the sensor. The sensor then computes the distance to the object by using the time taken to send and receive the outbound pulse according to the equation: Distance = (Speed of Sound x Time Delay) / 2, because the signal travels to the object and back. The utilization of ultrasonic sensor in robot for object detection, level measurement and obstacle avoidance is very common. They also excel in applications prone to optical sensor failure from dust or dirt, low light or shine which can cause light reflection. But they can be affected by the temperature, the pressure of the air, or substances that absorb sound. Ultrasonic sensors are commonly used in mobile robots or drones for navigation or in robotic arms for object proximity during pick-and-place operations. Their dependability, ease of use, and cost-effectiveness have made them a staple with hobbyists and automation engineers alike for bay - robot kit. escort- robot kit. rugby- robot kit. soccer- robot kit._EDEFAULT distance measurement on a wide range of applications.

text: Groundwater is an important part of water resources in the world. Especially in arid and semi-arid regions, most water use comes from groundwater. Estimation of groundwater recharge is needed for sustainable groundwater resources management [1]. Many approaches have been used to estimate groundwater recharge, such as direct measurements, water balance methods, Darcyan methods, tracer methods, remote sensing methods [2]. Among of them, tracer methods for estimating groundwater recharge are widely used in arid and semi-arid areas. Particularly natural tracers such as meteoric chloride are popular because their ubiquitous availability and increased sensitivity at lower recharge rate [3]. Chloride mass balance (CMB) approach is to employ chloride concentration in the unsaturated and/or saturated zone for recharge estimation. This method is the most widely used technique for estimating groundwater recharge in semiarid and arid regions [4]. However, most of its applications in China were conducted in arid and semi-humid areas. In typical semi-arid climate, its use is still limited.

text: The difficulties and deficits observed in autism span a wide range as the disorder is characterized by various phenotypes. The spectrum of these phenotypes includes: difficulties in social interaction, verbal and nonverbal communication, and repetitive behaviors. Autism is recognized as an entity by itself, but autistic features are also present in several neurodevelopmental syndromes such as: Rett, Fragile-X, Angelman, Prader-Willi, Joubert, Tuberous sclerosis, and 22q13.3 deletion syndromes, among others [1]. One of those syndromes that includes autistic features is Smith-Magenis syndrome (SMS; Mendelian Inheritance in Man number (MIM), 182290). SMS is a microdeletion syndrome with an estimated incidence of 1:15,000 to 1:25,000 live births [2,3]. The phenotypes more commonly associated with SMS are a variable degree of intellectual disability, speech and motor delay, behavior abnormalities with sleep disturbances, self-injurious and/or aggressive attention-seeking behavior, and distinctive craniofacial and skeletal anomalies [3]. SMS is typically caused by a deletion of chromosome 17p11.2 that encompasses multiple genes, including the retinoic acid-induced 1 (RAI1) gene or heterozygous mutation in the RAI1 gene [4,5,6,7,8,9,10,11].

text: In the international relations sense, it refers to the core rights and freedoms to which all individuals are entitled no matter their nationality, ethnic origin, gender, religion or any other status, as established and safeguarded by international law. Such rights are civil and political freedoms like the right to life, freedom of speech, and the right to a fair trial, and economic, social and cultural rights such as the right to education, healthcare and a standard of living. Human rights have become transformed from primarily national issues to the core of global governance, framing national conduct and international diplomacy. The UDHR and ensuing covenants such as the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR) provide the legal foundation for human rights protection. States have duties to respect, protect, and fulfill human rights, but enforcing these duties is difficult because of the principle of sovereignty and political interests. Frequently, human rights abuses affect foreign policy and aid and intervention decisions; groups like the United Nations Human Rights Council watch for violations. Human rights diplomacy entails the balancing of recognition of state sovereignty with a determination to protect individuals from certain abuses (eg genocide, torture, discrimination). Responsibility to Protect (R2P) has evolved as a basis for international intervention where states neglect to protect their people. Human rights in IR are also connected with wider global concerns such as migration, terrorism and development, which revolve around the issue of their universality but also cultural relativism. Respect for human rights contribute to international peace and security by helping to reduce and respond to the root causes of conflict and instability, and therefore they are fundamental elements of the contemporary international relations.

text: There are numerous defenses in criminal law that may be available to the accused to challenge the state’s case or to minimize his or her culpability. They have been broadly classified as justifications (which plead the facts), excuses (which plead the absence of mens rea), and proce dural defenses (including all other defenses). Justification defenses maintain that although defendant's conduct would usually be considered criminal, the conduct was allowed under the circumstances; e.g., self-defense allows a person to use reasonable force to protect against imminent injury or death. It is a defence to do something contrary to the law in order "make the lesser evil prevail over the greater" which includes breaking into a cabin so as not to freeze to death. Defenses of excuse concentrate on the accused’s mental or physical status at the relevant time by claiming they were not capable, or did not intend, to be fully liable. The insanity defense contends that the perpetrator was so mentally ill or incompetent that they were unable to appreciate their behavior or know right from wrong. Claims that the accused committed the offence under duress are that are the accused was compelled to commit the offence by threats of death or serious injury and that the act was involuntary. Voluntary or involuntary intoxication Some vagueness also surrounds the issue of the role of a voluntary (or involuntary) state of intoxication on the level of culpability. Procedural defenses question the manner in which the prosecution obtained evidence, including failure to obtain a search warrant, violation of the right to counsel and prosecutorial misconduct, which could lead to dismissal or suppression of evidence. An alibi defense seeks to establish that the accused was elsewhere when the crime was committed, rendering participation in it impossible. Defenses are available, if at all, depending on place and time and standard of proof against which it was claimed and on the facts of the case. Defences are crucial institutions which contribute to justice by avoiding wrongful convictions and recognizing human frailty and just those special circumstances.

text: Metadata is “data about data”—structured or semi-structured data that describes, explains or contextualizes other data and that helps users and systems find, understand, manage and use information more effectively. Typical examples include descriptive metadata (information that provides information about other data; cataloging), structural metadata (information about the containers of data; how data is put together), and administrative metadata (information to help manage a resource; fall into this category, e.g., rights management). Metadata benefits discoverability – tags, or subject headings assist search engines (or OPACs) to identify relevant documents; interoperability, with building the ability to exchange information between systems using common standards like the Dublin Core or MARC; (and it supports (discovering preservation), by providing details about authenticity and versioning. By allowing users to apply filters based on date, author, topical tags, and format, a well-structured metadata system facilitates navigation and discovery. In library and information science, metadata makes it possible to find and organize resources; in the enterprise, metadata supports analytics, data governance, and integration between disparate systems. Low-quality or non-existent metadata causes “information islands”, decreasing accessibility, hampering compliance and increasing duplication or misinterpretation costs. As data volumes expand—particularly in big data and digital archives—metadata’s importance increases as a driver of automation, machine learning, and AI-powered discovery. A good metadata schemas should have the completeness while remaining usability, follow standards, and allow consistency. In brief, metadata is that which turns data into managed, interoperable, and reusable information assets — so it is key to successful information management.

text: Psychological and behavioral traits are under a considerable degree of genetic influence, with typical heritability statistics in the 0.40–0.60 range, but specific genetic variants associated with these traits have proved elusive. Since the first molecular genetic studies in the 1990s, there have been numerous reports of genetic association that have failed to consistently replicate. Early candidate gene studies selected variants for investigation on the basis of the known or presumed neurobiology of the trait of interest. However, it soon became clear that these studies were not delivering reliable associations—initial findings were typically followed by a collection of replications, partial replications, and nonreplications, so that over time the strength of evidence for any given association tended to decline. In stark contrast, genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have been extremely successful in identifying genetic variants associated with a range of complex phenotypes. In less than a decade, several loci associated with various complex phenotypes have been identified, through large consortium-based efforts (Tobacco & Genetics Consortium, 2010; Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium et?al., 2010).

text: The 19th-century British philosopher and political economist John Stuart Mill formed an understanding of liberty that remains incredibly rich as it evolved around the concept of individual freedom in tension with social responsibility. In his seminal essay On Liberty, Mill argued that people should be free to think, speak and act as they choose, so long as their actions don’t harm others — an idea since known as the harm principle. The freedom of soul, creativity and human progress, Mill was arguing, is what matters. He believed that the free expression of conflicting ideas, and also the prompt use of such method as will tend to correct the error of thought or opinion, or which shall repress the disturbing conclusion and lead, if possible to a better one, ought not, in the prevailing circumstances, of all times, to be unnecessary. Mill was also a supporter of protecting against tyranny of government and “the tyranny of the prevailing opinion and feeling, and to protect the minority against the tyranny of the majority.” He warned that society's pressures could convert one to a conformist, hence stifling one's self-expression and behavior. He was a champion of freedom of thought, conscience, and association, believing all of these to be crucial for personal and political development. But Mill also recognized that freedom must be limited when it comes to behavior that actually harms another, and that individuals must balance their rights against the wellbeing of the community. His ideas informed liberal democratic theory and civil rights movements, promoting tolerance, pluralism, and the protection of minorities. Both a libertarian and a socialist, if with a tidier whiff of paternalism and collectivism, Mill’s conception of liberty insists that to be free is not so much to be free to do what you want as to be free to develop your powers in a society that tolerates other views and ways of life. This nuanced understanding of freedom still signals fights over freedom of expression, personal freedoms, and social justice in modern nations.

text: Unemployment means a situation where people who would work at the prevailing wage rate are unable to find work. It’s a critical gauge of the economy as well and is reported as the unemployment rate — the percentage of the labor force that is unemployed. Explanation: Unemployment: There are different kinds of unemployment according to the causes and situation of the economy. Frictional unemployment is the temporary unemployment of workers who are searching for jobs or entering the workforce for the first time — it’s a natural aspect of job searching. Structural unemployment is a result of a disconnect between workers’ skills and job requirements, often a byproduct of technological changes, automation or changes in industry. Cyclical unemployment results from a downturn in the business cycle, where falling demand leads to lost jobs – most noticeable during recessions. Seasonal unemployment occurs in industries that only operate during certain times of the year, such as agriculture or tourism. Technological unemployment is one of the types of structural unemployment, which is a condition when labor is no longer needed or labor doesn't do the job, but new skills or specializations are about to be required. Crawling unemployment, which is widespread in developing countries, involves hiring many more workers than are actually required and is particularly prevalent in agriculture or family businesses. Low employment results in lower revenue, less retail spending, and economic waste. Fiscal policies, such as tax cuts and public works, and monetary policies, like changing the interest rate, are used by governments to offset unemployment, as are skill development programs. Knowing the forms of unemployment, they can consider to which they can provide short-term solutions for the shocks and which reveal longer-term structural problems.

text: The term library automation applies to the use of computers and other technologies to make traditional library tasks such as acquisition, cataloging, circulation, and the provision of reference more efficient. When manual or paper-based activities are automated, libraries benefit from increased efficiency, accuracy and user service. In a typical automation solution, acquisitions systems permit librarians to select and order materials online; cataloging modules enable staff to import, modify, or produce MARC metadata; and circulation modules automatically process check-ins / check-outs/fines/patron notices. Serials modules are used to track issues and to link to electronic journals and interlibrary loan systems interface with the libraries of other institutions for sharing resources. Automation on the backend can help libraries manage their inventory, run shelf-reading routines, access a reporting dashboard, and do budget analysis. Computerized user interfaces—such as OPACs and self-checkout stations—enable users to look for information and manage their accounts remotely or on site. Automation wears down mundane responsibilities such as double entry, overdue notices, and serials claims obligations, freeing up staff for such value-added services as reference work and instructional activities. More sophisticated automation systems could include RFID for self-checkout and security, robotic shelf reading, and analytics that make use of usage data to inform collection development and user experiences. Automation also facilitates the integration of electronic resources, as single sign-on access to e?journals, e?books and databases are provided. Automated solutions are an investment in infrastructure and training that are essential to how libraries work in the present day, both in terms of transparency and data-driven decisionmaking as well as the efficiency and service delivery that can be designed in even in a small public library or on large academic campus.

text: Theatre is instrumental in defining, articulating and reinforcing matters of cultural identity as a living context for individuals and as a community theatre can provide a forum for individuals to reflect upon shared history, values, beliefs, and traditions while embracing the challenges of change, diversity and inclusion. Through narrative, action, speech, song, dress and ceremony, theatre reflects the evolving cultural expression of a community, enabling the community to preserve, celebrate, and transmit its culture while enriching its sense of who it is as a community. It's a living repository of cultural memory, preserving myths, historical events and social customs that helps to form a community's identity, especially in those communities where oral traditions are paramount. At the same time, theatre is also a venue for challenging and reinterpreting cultural stories, particularly in places where migration, colonization, or globalization has fractured cultural identity—as cultural identities are often disputed, mixed, or changing. In dramatizing the clash between tradition and modernity, local and global, inclusion and exclusion, theatre provides a tool for individuals and communities to locate themselves in the swirling eddies of a globalizing world. It allows such historically subordinated or misrepresented voices as indigenous peoples, diasporic communities, or ethnic minorities, to regain control over their narratives and to claim their cultural visibility. Through community engagement and representation, the theater instils pride, strength and community, allowing people to both remain rooted in older forms of identity while embracing new ones in line with the current world. Plays that are specific to cultural contexts increase audience insight into the reality of their own and others' identities, and help to connect people to difference so that bridges may be built toward intercultural debate. In multilingual or multicultural societies, it can also play a role as a unifying force, celebrating difference as it investigates what connects people to each other. It also serves as an educational tool, particularly for the youngest ones, to learn about their roots and traditions in an amused and funny way. From all over the globe, theatre festivals, indigenous plays, and modern dramas all represent powerful forms of cultural identity, frequently assuming an important identity as important symbols of national, or regional pride. Theatre in the diaspora Theatre in diasporic contexts helps keep cultural connection and creates home for displaced/migrant communities. Finally, the relationship of theatre to cultural identity is both reflective and generative; theatre both reflects who we are and seeks to shape who we become, serving as a potent agent for individuals and societies to see themselves more clearly, confirm their values, and envision their futures.

text: Many situations in which language is used require not only the comprehension but also the validation of incoming linguistic information—that is, judging whether the comprehended information is true or false. Recent studies investigating the relationship between comprehension and validation support the assumption that validation occurs immediately and routinely during language comprehension (e.g., Isberner & Richter, 2013, 2014a; Richter, Schroeder, & Wöhrmann, 2009; Singer, 2006). All of these studies have used written materials as stimuli, thus limiting the extant empirical evidence for routine validation to the domain of reading. However, if validation is an inherent component of language comprehension (Cook & O’Brien, 2014; O’Brien & Cook, 2016; Richter et al., 2009; Singer, 2013), it should not be restricted to the processing of written language. Spoken language is often used in face-to-face communications that are characterized by a richer pragmatic context, which includes the physical environment in which the communication is situated. This context potentially forms the basis for validation. Moreover, for communication to be successful, listeners need to align their mental representation with that of the speaker.

text: In computer vision, we often need to learn characterizations of visual classes from examples. text: Ohm’s law The interrelationship between the voltage V, the current I, and the resistance R of an electrical circuit, expressed as V = IR and incorporated into the general theory of electrical networks, is ohm’s law; it is among the most basic of all concepts in electrical engineering. it there is a formula, I =V/R, with that I (current) is in Amperes, V is the potential difference in volts and R is the resistance in Ohms, explains that the current through a conductor between two points is directly proportional to the voltage across the two points and inversely proportional to the resistance between the points. For a given resistance and voltage, this law enables you to understand and calculate how much current will pass through an element in a circuit (e.g. a resistor). text: When it comes to memory, both quantity and quality matter (Koriat & Goldsmith, 1996; Koriat, Goldsmith, & Pansky, 2000). The quantitative aspect of memory refers to the likelihood that a given stimulus is encoded into and retrieved from the mental storehouse. The qualitative aspect of memory refers to the correspondence between the external stimuli and the internal memory representations, which can be operationalized as the inverse of the variability of memory performance. Although it is theoretically important to distinguish these two aspects of memory representations (Koriat & Goldsmith, 1996; Zhang & Luck, 2011), it is only until recently that these two aspects of memory have been simultaneously modeled in a single task to address theoretical questions (Bays & Husain, 2008; Brady, Konkle, Gill, Oliva, & Alvarez, 2013; Wilken & Ma, 2004; Zhang & Luck, 2008). The qualitative and quantitative aspects of memory representations can be mathematically modeled based on their independent contributions to overall memory recall performance in a delayed estimation task (Zhang & Luck, 2008, 2009, 2011). In this task, observers memorize some briefly presented memory items, such as colored squares, and then recall a given memory item after a delay of seconds (e.g., Zhang & Luck, 2008) or minutes (e.g., Brady et al., 2013), by reproducing the color of the memory item in a continuous manner.

text: The Non-Aligned Movement was founded in the context of the Cold War as a coalition of nations that aimed to forge their own way, without falling under the influence of either of the two superpowers that were leading the Cold War: the United States, and the Soviet Union. (IANS)Unified and setup formally at the Belgrade Conference in1961, the movement was born out of elder statesmen such as India's Jawaharlal Nehru,Yugoslavia's Josip Broz Tito and Egypt's Gamal Abdel Nasser, who came together with an aim to safeguard the sovereignty and self-dependence of newly liberated nations. Many were newly decolonized and wary of being sucked into the ideological and military competition that was shaping international affairs. The NAM advocated peaceful coexistence, respect for territorial integrity, non-interference in the internal affairs of another country, and arms limitation. It also sought to promote development and cooperation among developing countries, calling for a fairer global economic order opposed to neocolonial economic exploitation. Although the states which joined it differed greatly between Asia, Africa, Latin America and the Middle East, the Non-aligned movement was nevertheless a visible international force for the Global South during the Cold War era, pooling together over a hundred countries at its height. Although it faced difficulties in remaining united, given the competing national interests and the geopolitics, the movement wielded considerable influence on international relations, such as abiding to the principles of national sovereignty, and affirming the solidarity among smaller nations. Presently, the NAM remains an international forum for promoting peace, security, development and justice, though in view of recent global developments. such as globalization, climate change, and human rights, adjusting its relevance to the current world. If there is a legacy to it – and as with any master narrative there must be one – it is the rise of nations following their own foreign policy rather than simply falling into line with the superpowers, and is part of a wider narrative of humanity aspiring to equality and a self-determined place in the world.

text: Documentary theatre is performance that relies solely on real-life source material—interviews, court transcripts, historical records, and news reports—when compiling plays that consider factual events, social issues, and political matters. Documentary theatre rose to prominence in the 20th century, focusing on truth, original source materials, and privileged perspectives that may otherwise not be presented to the public. More committed than any work of fiction is to what really happened and to the real feeling of whatever it’s describing, it straddles journalism, history and art. Verbatim style The Documentary uses and being a style of theatre in Explicit reference to real peoplesUses of reallanguage and speech in scenes, rights to make more contemporary work. Between its intended purpose to inform, provoke audience thought and inspire social transformation, documentary theatre usually engages with topics such as war, injustice, human rights abuses and political scandal. Its style ranges from traditional reenactment to more experimental shows that incorporate multimedia, live narration and audience interaction. The very naturalistic nature of documentary theatre means that it also comes with a degree of ethical responsibility—ethical to the story’s subjects in the sense of respect and truth, if nothing else. It has also been used all over the world as a valuable weapon for campaigning and civic engagement – the live-ness of the performance making past or present history visceral and powerful. It’s true to its name: the power of the form to document memory, the experience of others, the process of feeling. Documentary theatre compels audiences to face uncomfortable truths and engage in discussions about social issues, and in so doing, it spans the distance/privileged line between experience and aesthetic.

text: The symbiosis that is established between the soil-borne arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) and roots of most land plants can provide many different agroecosystem services, such as an efficient use of soil nutrients, protection against biotic and abiotic stresses, and improved soil aggregation [1,2]. Recently, the importance of AMF for crop sustainable production has gained recognition and it has been shown that the association between wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) and AMF can positively affect plant phenotypic plasticity by increasing nutrient uptake [3] and the plant’s ability to cope with adverse conditions, such as high salinity [4,5], drought [6], or soil metal toxicity [7,8]. Thus, it is clear that the association of wheat with microorganisms affects its phenotype and it adds a source of variability that can have crucial effects on the functionality of the organism considered as a whole—the holobiont [9,10]. The holobiont is defined as the host organism and all of its associated symbiotic microorganisms, being the hologenome the summation of the genetic information of the host and its microbiota [11]. Accordingly, the putative contribution of other associated microorganisms, like bacteria, on the holobiont phenotype is not considered, when referring to wheat and its AMF symbiotic community. However, due to the known importance of AMF and impact in this system, we are arguably dealing with a most significant component of the holobiont. AMF can be horizontally transmitted through extraradical mycelial networks (ERM) and mycelial proliferation in the soil greatly extends the area over which plant roots may acquire soil phosphorus (P) and other major and micronutrients [12]. Individual plants can simultaneously associate with multiple species of AMF and vice-versa, but they can still exhibit considerable selectivity in their associations [13,14].

text: A logo is different visual mark-sheet-symbol-typhography-treatment representing a brand-organization-the most immediate and recognisable representation of an entity. A good logo is catchy, scalable, iconic, and functional to build brand identity, and if done right, it should be a complete visual representation of the brand in one glance. There are various kinds of logos that serve different branding functions. Wordmarks (logotypes) are logos that have text with a company’s name written in a distinct image — like Google, Coca-Cola, and Visa do. Lettermarks (monograms) take a brand name and reduce it to its initials (like IBM, HBO, and NASA). Pictorial marks (icons or symbols) are (pictorial) representation of a brand name in a way to be identified through images, like the illustrated apple of Apple or the bird in Twitter. Abstract marks employ geometric or symbolic images to produce a distinctive image — say, Nike’s swoosh — that doesn’t necessarily mean anything recognizable but will come to be associated with the brand over time. Combination Marks: These marks combine text with a symbol, making it versatile for marketing; Adidas and Burger King are common examples. Emblems contain some text in a badge or symbol—used commonly in older and more traditional industries like those in schools, old automotive and government seals (e.g., Harley-Davidson, Starbucks). Logos are much more than just embellishments; they are also an integral part of brand recognition, advertising, and trust. The kind of logo selected will rely on the brand, its strategy, its audience, and where and how it’s going to be used. Startups, on the other hand, may like combination marks for their flexibility and heritage brands may prefer emblems, to express tradition. A logo must be versatile enough to be used on every type of media from billboards to app icons, and should be able to work in black and white, as well as color. All in all, a logo should be an essential branding property representing the identity and ethos of a business through careful design and regular applications.

text: Media is a tool in the struggle for gender equality, when wielded to project the voices of the disempowered, to question discourses of domination, and to bring forth diverse, equal representations of people across the gender spectrum. In societies where traditional gender norms are well established, media have the potential to also challenge them by displaying alternative forms of femininity, masculinity and/or gender nonconformity. Media that empower features women, transgender, and non-binary individuals not as peripheral, metaphorical representations, but as distinct and developed characters who take an active role, have depth, and make their own choices. Media narrates, in documentaries, news, on digital platforms, telling gender injustices (wage gap, gender based violence, reproductive rights, or how much there is still work to do to have female politicians with a sharing ratio) that, making people aware, cries out for social action. Social media sites in particular have become a fundamental vehicle for grassroots gender activism, providing opportunities for instantaneous mobilization, the formation of solidarities, and the global sharing of personal experiences that contest structural gender inequality. As with independent cinema, feminist blogs, podcasts, and YouTube channels are attempting to change the conversation about gender, effecting a shift in editorial control from creators who are historically marginalized and whose perspectives have long been eclipsed by those of the mainstream. Additionally, inclusive advertising and public service campaigns can change societal attitudes, by normalizing, for example, different gender roles—men as caregivers, women in leadership. But, for media to really represent, it needs to move beyond surface diversity, and be about genuine representation: About giving a voice to the voiceless. That means providing behind-the-scenes support to the writers, directors, journalists and editors who bring with them authentic perspectives in the form of lived experience. Media literacy is also an important tool to enable audiences analyze (with a certain critical distance) messages on gendered content and stereotypes. Inclusive, reflective, and intentional media creates a cultural force for empowerment that can enable gender to be seen and experienced in new ways as we work to create a more just and fair world.

text: Economic development is the process by which a nation improves the economic, political, and social well-being of its people. It isn’t just about growing a country’s gross domestic product (GDP) but also opportunities for education, healthcare, jobs, and to fight poverty and inequality. Economic development generally refers to such structural changes as industrialization, improvement in agricultural methods, and establishment of urban centers, as well as other aspects of development, such as technological development and the physical aspects of infrastructure. It also calls for political institutions that are stable, good governance and inclusive policies that allow the proceeds of growth to be distributed among various social groups. The state has an important role to play in fostering economic development through investments in public services, regulations, tax and business incentives. World bodies, such as the United Nations, World Bank and International Monetary Fund (IMF) provide financial assistance, conduct studies and draw up plans. Economic growth can be measured in terms of indicators of GDP per capita, literacy and the education level, life expectancy, as well as the homoscedasticity and changeability of the Human Development Index (HDI). But critics say development has to be about more than economic statistics, and needs to embrace issues such as environmental sustainability, cultural preservation and human rights. 2.2.1.2 Now sustainable development as a focus, and it emphasis consideration of economic growth, environmental prote ction and social equity in balance. Problems like climate change, lack of resources, global inequality or corruption can jeopardize any developing process, particularly in low-middle income or politically unstable countries. Accordingly, successful economic development needs to take a long term, comprehensive perspective: economic, social, political and environmental. Ultimately, economic development is about building legal and economic institutions that enable everyone to live a productive, creative and meaningful life, and that ensure we treat future generations and all members of our species with dignity and respect.

text: Feudalism was the prevailing socioeconomic, legal, and political system in the medieval period in Europe, especially between the 9th and 15th centuries. Feudalism worked by tying everyone to everyone else in a chain of personal obligations and land holding. Monarchs awarded plots of land (fiefs) to nobles — dukes, counts, barons — in return for military service and allegiance. These aristocrats in their turn allocated land to vassals, to knights who owed them service and provided it on horseback. The serfs and peasants worked the land and in return paid taxes or provided labor in exchange for protection and a place to live at the bottom of the pyramid. Oaths of fealty, fixed duties and personal ties enforced rather than centralized law sustained feudal order. Castles, manor houses and fortified villages also increasingly acted as microcenters of power, defending the inhabitants against outside attacks. The feudal system molded the social fabric of medieval Europe: It encouraged self-sufficiency at the local level and community solidarity, while it was simultaneously reinforcing a rigid class system that revolved around birth and obligation. Feudalism enhanced the control of territorial fragmentation and localized security in a period of chaos, however feudalism led to restricted social mobility and consequently, centralized rule was inhibited. Manorialism — the economic side of feudalism — kept peasants shackled to their lord’s lands and underwrote aristocratic wealth through rents, labor and produce. The church mirrored these institutions, and for a time overlapped with them as spiritual and temporal authority. This system evolved and became increasingly complex: Monarchs built powerful bureaucracies and professional armies -- weakening the power of regional lords and contributing to the establishment of nation-states. Though it had already lost its effectiveness, as one of the older feudal states it left a mark in its organization and the political order and economy for centuries into the Middle Ages, in legal institutions, and in the rise of a monarchical form of government and the state in the Dutch territories.

text: There are different factors which hinder women in receiving appropriate, affordable and respectful care, from structural inequalities to cultural taboo. Common obstacles include the gender bias evident in medical research and treatment, causing symptoms to be dismissed or misdiagnosed, a lack of focused care for reproductive health issues that’s especially dire in some of the countries with restrictive abortion laws or weak maternal care and economic obstacles that keep women from accessing care because of cost, lack of insurance, or unpaid caregiving duties that make it difficult for them to get care for themselves. Marginalized women—white women of color, rural women, LGBTQ+ people and women with disabilities—experience repeated forms of discrimination and abandonment from the healthcare system. Male-biased healthcare systems may also neglect sex-specific problems such as menopause, pregnancy complications, or violence against women. Gender studies underscores the requirement for gender-sensitive inclusive and equitable health systems that prioritize patient dignity, informed consent, and culturally competent care for all.
