text: The Cold War was a significant period of global conflict between the United States and its allies on one side and the Soviet Union and its client states on the other that spanned roughly from 1947 to 1991. Its importance is associated with a process of structuring the international system after World World II as well as with a division of the world into two ideologically opposed camps – world of the capitalist democracy and that of the socialist communism – and with an impact exercised over world?wide politics, the economy and the military strategies. The Cold War involved no actual fighting; just a strategic arms race, as well as a diplomatic war (including an international campaign of propaganda and subversion) that despite the absence of direct hostilities there were many Jewish casualties. It helped develop military alliances such as NATO and the Warsaw Pact, and birthed decolonization movements that were both aided and fought against by the superpowers as they tried to exert control over new countries. The Cold War also fueled scientific and technological advancements, such as the spaceh race. It enshrined the doctrine of the deterrent, that shaped foreign policies across the globe. The bipolar structure of the Cold War inhibited some conflicts but also generated crises — like the Cuban Missile Crisis — that threatened nuclear war. The ideological war left a mark on culture, education, and international organizations and also on economic models and development concepts. The Cold War era closed with the fall of the Soviet Union and a unipolar moment, which gave the opportunity to the United States to reshape the world affairs, opening ways for globalization, democratization, and new types of security challenges. Its consequences still inform policies in relations, security and regional conflicts.

text: Sociology is the study of society, social institutions, and social relationships, in addition to the study of our behavior within these contexts. It is the study of how people interact with one another, how the collective behaviour of humanity is structured, the ways in which societies change, and the institutional bases for that social change. Sociology is a huge field that ranges over a large number of topics including family, religion, education, economy, politics, culture, social stratification, and social problems. The importance of sociology is greater in the context of Bangladesh as it contributes to understanding the intricate dynamics of interaction between the traditional and modernizing forces that influence society. Bangladeshi society is made up of various ethnic groups, and features considerable rural-urban differences, language, religion and colonial past, resulting in such issues as corruption, violence and discrimination that contribute to how people interact and establish systems. It can also help understand contemporary social issues, such as poverty, gender inequality, exodus to the cities and the challenges of development, that are essential for policy development. It offers valuable understanding of family, kinship, community, and social movements systems, which affect the social cohesion and conflict. Sociology - through the examination of social norms, values, and institutions - offers explanations of the enduring aspects of culture, as well as of newly emerging practices. It also contributes to addressing social challenges, including child labor, domestic violence and environmental degradation, by providing a methodology to identify underlying causes and societal consequences. On the whole, the challenges to sociology appear to be critical for gaining an integrated understanding of Bangladeshi society, for defining social policies and for ensuring social justice and sustainability in a rapidly changing social context.

text: It is imperative that the public and private sectors work together to reduce risk to disasters, in order to utilize resources and capabilities available in both government and the private sector to make countries in the region more resilient and better prepared to face disasters. Cooperation can serve to strengthen early warning systems, infrastructure resilience, emergency responses, and recovery. Bringing in the private sector, such as business, financiers and insurers, to invest in construction for building resilient infrastructure, insurance products and financing mechanisms for disaster risk to reduce economic loss. text: Narrative, Descriptive, and Argumentative Essay A narrative essay is written in paragraph form, using a main character to tell a story. A narrative essay either tells a story or describes an event from a personal point of view. It has a beginning, middle, and an end, and involves characters, setting, conflict, and resolution. The point is to get the reader into the groove emotionally when storytelling and make a mental picture. For instance, an essay on life events based on a childhood memory or a transformative event will be narrative. A descriptive essay, on the other hand, is more about creating a mental image of a person, place, object or location by way of detailed observation. It engages the five senses and contains strong adjectives, similes and metaphors. The aim is to make the reader live the scene from within. For example, to describe a sunset on the beach, one can resort to a descriptive essay. In comparison, the argumentative essay is more formal and analytical. It clearly states an opinion or thesis on an unresolved issue and concludes the thesis with evidence and support. The author needs to present counterarguments and make them appear to be weak. Issues such as climate change, education reform or online privacy often appear in argumentative writing. These essays each have a recognizable structure—beginning, middle, and end—but the voice, phraseology, and subject matter are distinct based on their objective. Understanding the distinctions can help writers select the appropriate model and strategy for addressing the topic and the audience.

text: Robotics A transformation matrix is a matrix describing a rigid transformation from one coordinate system to another. Generally, a transformation matrix is represented as a 4×4 homogenous matrix which holds both rotation and translation in a single format, which can be used to transform points or vectors from one co-ordinate system into another. It consists of a 3×3 rotation matrix in the upper-left corner, a 3×1 translation vector in the upper-right corner, and a bottom row of [0 0 0 1] to enable rotation-transformation with a 4th homogeneous coordinate. These are very important matrices in the forward kinematics formulation which is defined as estimating the position and orientation of a robot end effector with respect its base, given its joint angles/displacements. By cascading the separate transformation matrices, which are based on the D-H (Denavit-Hartenberg) parameters or another method for modeling the robot, one derives the overall transformation from the base frame to the tool frame. Transformation matrices also let one easily chain together a sequence of movements, because the composition of transformations is associative, which is highly desirable in simulation, animation, and real-time control. They are also employed in inverse kinematics, path planning, collision avoidance and visual servoing. In programming and simulation environments for robots such as MATLAB, ROS, V-REP, transformation matrices are a key ingredient when manipulating poses of objects, programming motion sequences and problems of setting up-positions between parts of a manipulator, or even between the robot body and the environment. Their incorporation of rotation and translation on an equal footing has made them one of the principal tools in robotics analysis and control.

text: Shape registration is a crucial problem in computer vision and medical image analysis [46]. Shape alignment, also known as global shape registration, aims to recover a global transformation, such as rigid, similarity, or affine transformation, that brings the pose of a source (also known as model or moving) shape as close as possible to that of a target (also known as template or fixed) shape. The alignment has extensive uses in recognition, indexing and retrieval, and tracking. Shape alignment algorithms are usually different from each other in three aspects: shape representation, energy function, and optimization method. Point-based representations are widely used since they can represent shapes of arbitrary dimension and topology. The Iterative Closest Point (ICP) [3], [54] algorithm is one of the most widely used point sets alignment methods. The ICP algorithm iteratively associates points between the source and target point sets by the nearest neighbor criterion and transforms the source point set to minimize distances between these associated points. It terminates until the change in the sum of those distances falls below a given threshold. There are a large number of variants introduced on the basic ICP concept [36].

text: There are several factors that contribute to vignetting. Some arise from the optical properties of camera lenses, the most prominent of which is off-axis illumination falloff or the cos4 law. Here, vignetting is a result of foreshortening of the lens when viewed at increasing angles from the optical axis [13]. Other sources of vignetting are geometric in nature—light arriving at oblique angles to the optical axis may be partially obstructed by the field stop or lens rim. To determine the vignetting effects in an image, the most straightforward approach involves capturing an image completely spanned by a uniform scene region, such that brightness variations can solely be attributed to vignetting [1], [11], [20], [28], [29]. In such a calibration image, ratios of intensity with respect to the pixel on the optical axis describe the vignetting function. Suitable imaging conditions for this approach, however, can be challenging to produce due to uneven illumination and camera tilt, and the vignetting measurements are valid only for images captured by the camera under the same camera settings. Moreover, a calibration image can be recorded only if the camera is at hand; consequently, this approach cannot be used to correct images captured by unknown cameras, such as images downloaded from the Web.

text: Types of hazards and disaster in Bangladesh Bangladesh is exposed to a variety of natural hazards in part due to its geographical location and the physical environment in which it is located, and in part due to its societal and economic conditions that do not allow the country to cope with the immediate and long-term impacts of natural hazards (Basher et al, 2011; ASRHRES-2011). The most common and severe natural hazards are floods: they extend wide areas during monsoon due to heavy rains and rivers overflow. Cyclones are also a significant danger, generating destructive winds, storm surges, and heavy rainfall that results in extensive flooding and damage, in particular in the coastal belt. The country also faces riverbank erosion that leaves hundreds or thousands homeless each year by washing away farmland and villages built on the banks of rivers. In the hilly northeast and southeast, landslides are risks, particularly during the rainy season. Bangladesh is also affected by drought in northern and western regions, which impacts yields and water availability. While rare, earthquakes pose a substantial threat given Bangladesh’s adjacency to active tectonic faults in the Himalayas. Furthermore, saltwater intrusion from rising sea levels and tidal inundation is putting coastal agriculture and fresh water supplies at risk. Since these challenges affect millions of people, livelihoods, assets and the economy, it is important that the country’s resilience is reinforced through effective disaster risk management, climate adaptation, and regional cooperation.

text: Climate resilience is the ability of people, communities, ecosystems and systems to survive, adapt, and grow, no matter what kinds of chronic stresses and acute shocks they experience. It is the capability to bounce back from shocks like climatic disasters to climate variability, and transform to minimize sensitivity, and maximize sustainability. Resilience to climate change is not only about bouncing back from damage to an exceedingly vulnerable state, but also about building forward, learning from climate disruptions, and improving adaptation to address future risks. This capability is related to social, economic, institutional, and environmental conditions, which are linked to accesses to resources, information, technology, governance and communication. Building resilience involves aligning risk management with development and climate adaptation objectives. It is about minimising exposure to hazards, enhancing adaptive capability and reducing vulnerability to the effects of climate. For instance, adaptive agriculture could include drought-resistant crops, better water usage and diversified activities to cope with increased variability in rainfall. Urban resilience includes infrastructure that can withstand floods or heatwaves, a fast acting emergency response force and thoughtful planning. Ecosystems in the presence of intact biodiversity and connectivity can buffer microclimates and deliver vital ecosystem services in times of climatic pressures. Enhancing climate resilience is critical to reduce social and economic losses, safeguard human populations and economic assets (including livelihoods, infrastructure and water and food supplies), and develop along sustainable trajectories under mounting climate variability and uncertainty. It involves the sharing of responsibilities between governments, communities, civil society, the private sector to develop policies, invest in adaptive technology, education, access and promote inclusive participation. Ultimately, climate resilience is an integrated strategy to help communities proactively live with impacts of climate change by minimizing risks and seizing opportunities for sustainable development.

text: Analog and digital signaling are basic forms of transmitting data from one system to another system through electronic systems or circuits. An analog signal has a continuous time and continuous amplitude, it could have any value within a range and it changes smoothly over time. It's used to model physical phenomena such as temperature, sound and light level. A microphone, for instance, translates sound waves into an analog voltage level that changes in a continuous manner as air pressure changes. On the other hand, the digital signal is a slew limited, discrete time13 signal based on binary values (zeros and ones), that changes not continuously but in step-wise fashion. Digital signals are obtained by sampling and quantization of analog signals. Whereas analog systems can be plagued by noise and distortion, digital signals can be reliably protected from noise, and they consolidated to save on storage, processing time and bandwidth by computers and other digital devices. Analog signals are used in older audio/video systems, analog sensors and other medical type equipment. In modern electronics the digital signal has taken over the formerly analog domain: computers, mobile phones, digital communication, data processing and storage. Analog systems are less complex, but are less accurate, whereas digital systems are more complex, but are able to implement error detection, compression and encryption. A record is playing analog music, a cd representing music in digital coding. One common use is to convert an analog signal (e.g., an analog audio signal) to a digital format for subsequent digital processing such as conversion to a type needed in a digital mixing or mastering console, or archiving in a sound studio. To sum up, analog signals are continuous and changing, reflect nature reality, but digital signals are discrete and constant, it is cater to the developing computer and communication technology.

text: Definitions Governmental publications Governmental publications Government publications are documents published by governments or government agencies either directly to the public or to other groups or entities in behalf of or at the order of those governments. They are authentic sources of information and in many cases are primary sources and increasingly important for legal, policy, historical research, and civic participation. These documents are published by organizations such as national archives, ministries, or statistical bureaus, often being made available through government websites, library depositories and legal databases, and they are archived in institutional and organizational repositories. Collections need metadata standards such as MARC and Federal Depository Library Program (FDLP) guidelines, as well as classification systems for government documents. Management issues involve rapid obsolescence of digital formats, keeping open access repositories, and ensuring legal authenticity. Government files might be private as well—needing redaction or access protection. For scholars, governmental publishing gives a taste of public controversies, social values, and decisions based on evidence. Government information libraries must support both subject expertise and servitization, and the re-use and navigation of complex legislative and administrational structures. In affording equal access to public records, libraries promote transparency, accountability, and educated citizenry participation in democracy.

text: Dust grains play a central role in the radiative transfer, chemistry, and thermodynamics of the ISM, and therefore also in the star formation process. For example, molecular hydrogen (H2), the fuel for star formation, forms on dust grains (Gould & Salpeter 1963; Hill & Hollenbach 1976). In addition, dust shields the molecular ISM from photo-dissociating UV radiation (Hollenbach & Tielens 1999), allowing the gas to cool, fragment, and star formation to proceed (Krumholz et al. 2009b). To understand the structure of the ISM and the lifecycle of dust, it is therefore essential to understand the variations of the dust abundance and composition as a function of environment and metallicity. Here, we carry out a study of the spatial variations of the ISM GDR in the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds (LMC and SMC). The Magellanic Clouds are ideal environments to constrain the variations of the GDR between ISM phases. They are relatively close, with the LMC at 50 kpc (Schaefer 2008) and the SMC at 62 kpc (Hilditch et al. 2005).

text: Vegetative reproduction is a form of asexual reproduction in plants, in which new plants are obtained from the vegetative parts of the parents, such as the root, stem, and leaves, the process of vegetative reproduction does not involve the formation of seeds or spores. This type of propagation offers a means of multiplying very quickly genetically identical offspring (clones) possessing all the favorite traits of the parent plant. Vegetative propagation may be either natural or artificial. Vegetative propagation in nature occurs in several manners: runners or stolons as in strawberry, runners as in Chlorophytum, rhizomes as in ginger, tubers as in potato, bulbs as in onion, corms as in gladiolus, or from adventitious buds on leaves as in Bryophyllum. These organs are the reserve food which form roots and new shoots in the new plant. Artificial vegetative propagation is a form of vegetative propagation that is found in the gardening and the agricultural work and that involves human intervation. This can be done by various methods, such as by cutting (quarter heel, half heel, root cutting), layering, grafting, etc. In an artificial method of asexual reproduction, the plant is created by the transformation of normal plant tissue (a single cell of the parent plant) in a test tube; this method is also known as micro propagation and involves the use of plant growth regulators (auxin and cytokinin) and a gelifying agent (agar). This process is particularly valuable for establishment of seedless genotypes or low seeded potential genotypes. The advantages of vegetative propagation are many:' it is more rapid than the growing from seeds, the quality of the crop can be better controlled, the properties of hybrids can be "made permanent' and plants which do not form seeds can be identically reproduced. But it’s not perfect either – there is low genetic variety and offspring are genetically similar hence more prone to pests and diseases. Nevertheless, vegetative propagation is extensively used in commercial agriculture, forestry and horticulture to produce superior performing and disease resilient plants as well.

text: Rural urban migration in Bangladesh is one of the largest demographic changes in recent times. This migratory process is about the movement of the people from village to city for various purposes like employment, education, medication or better standard of living. This move is good for economic growth and for the growth of cities, but it also has huge social and structural consequences. One consequence is the depopulation of rural areas, and particularly of young working-age men, causing labor returns in agriculture and traditional rural economies to rise. It impacts food productivity and weakens the social fabric of village life.” The urban population, however, is growing at an exponential pace, putting enormous strain on urban infrastructure, housing, mobility, sanitation and city services. This can lead to crowded slums, a rise in pollution and growth of a shadow community of informal labour where there is little regulation or job security. On a social level, migration from rural to urban areas results in the disintegration of joint families, who are removed from the immediate environment. It becomes a problem for the immigrants who go through an identity crisis or if they are socially or culturally alienated in the ruins. Yet, migration also has its positive repercussions with money flowing back into villages, increment in rural investments, new ideas and values entering into the realm of rural life. This migration, over time, has helped spur rural development in some cases, as families have used money earned in the cities to build houses, educate children and start small businesses. The task for the policy planners is to devise a trade-off between urban and rural de-velopment and to enable the latter to discourage unnecessary migration and, in doing so, support sustainable socio-economic growth. Rural-urban planning should be incorporated to manage the effects of this change more efficiently.

text: Information retrieval (IR) is the practice and research of searching for documents, and for information within documents, on the Web. Its area of concern is to find, retrieve and present information that most closely satisfies the user’s informational need, which not always is formulated in accurate terms. Information retrieval systems (e.g., search engines such as Google or library catalogs) are designed to assist users in finding relevant documents, web pages, records, etc, among large and often unstructured data collections. It differs from querying the types of databases found in modern SQL engines, in that it is textual and not a procedure-based query.Dictionary-based translation algorithm implementations like these must necessarily be configured for specific uses such as spam filtering, language translation, etc. Key issues in IR include how to index (indexing, associating words and phrases with documents), how to query (querying, interpreting or translating user input), how to match (matching, comparing queries to documents), and how to rank (ranking, ordering of search results by estimated relevance). The performance of an IR system is usually assessed using a variety of metrics including precision (how many returned documents are relevant), recall (how many relevant documents are returned) and F-score (the geometric mean of precision and recall). Artificial intelligence and machine learning have significantly reshaped information retrieval with advances from keyword to semantic search, from statistical to personal content recommendations and from providing structured lists of content to understanding the context of it. For instance, contemporary search engines utilize user behaviour, query history, and linguistic context to improve search results. Colleges and schools use IR libraries help their students to find books, journal articles, and other resources by subjects, authors, or classifications. In the enterprise, IR is used for knowledge management, customer support and data analysis. It also addresses the user behavior, the interface design and the query word formulation in order to study the user …ques. Efficient IR is important in this era of information overload, it serves as a navigation tool that helps users find accurate information quickly, and such efforts contribute positively to the decision-making process, and research productivity, while minimizing time wasted on unrelated contents. While digital collections grow, IR is an active area of both research and application in Information Science, affecting how people deal with information in almost every sector.

text: Theatre and the environment explores the way that theatre and performance have engaged with environmental issues to effect change, particularly at the level of conscience in favour of sustainable futures. Theatre achieves this by narrativizing, visualizing, and emotively immersing people in this way, making environmentally abstract and/or distant issues like global climate instability, tree-borne extinction, pollution, biodiversity decrease, and resource extraction more immediate, savvy, and exigent to the broadest cross-section of the public. This latter group of writers, often referred to as ecodramatists or “eco-theatre” writers, directly engage with environmental topics and are typically interested in marrying science with storytelling and metaphor to study the causes and effects of ecocide. These shows include characters trying to survive environmental catastrophe, indigenous voices on land and nature, and Orwellian visions of the future scarred by natural disasters, telling the viewers to pay attention to their own impact on the environment. Theatre becomes environmentally engaged also through its production practices, based on sustainable working methods like the recycling of set and costume elements, the saving of energy via the digital and other technical devices in use, or the choice of a site-specific performance in the bare nature in order to reduce the ecological footprint. In addition, immersive and participatory theatre forms allow audiences to feel and embody ecological issues, resulting in empathy and eonic resonance. Groups such as educational theater companies, community performative works, activist troupes often work side-by-side with scientists, environmentalists, and other neighborhood organizations to put on work based in scientific data that points to societal responsibility and possibilities for hope. It is often followed by discussions, workshops or calls to action that connect art to civic engagement. Furthermore, environmental theatre frequently resists the mainstream cultural mythologies of exploitation and anthropocentrism, proposing instead worldviews that promote interrelatedness, ecological equilibrium and reverence for non-human life. Theatre is uniquely positioned to offer ways for audiences to face uncomfortable truths, envision a more sustainable future, and contemplate what personal and societal transformations are necessary to respond to the environmental emergencies facing our planet. As it is, the event of live theatre also reminds audiences of its ephemerality, and its re-enacting of themes of impermanence and fragility is a reminder of the accidents of the natural world. In every genre and every culture, theatre remains one of the most vital tools of environmental communication; aesthetic and emotional force are harnessed for activism, creating a better understanding in the community of ecological problems. In so doing, it entertains, educates, and mobilizes; strengthening its position as a socially engaged transformative art as we navigate increasingly dire global environmental challenges.

text: Employee motivation is a factor, or factors, that cause(s) an employee to pursue work tasks or goals. Engaged employees are more likely to be productive, loyal and happy--all which supports an organization's success. Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory (otherwise known as the Motivation-Hygiene Theory) describes motivation in the workplace in terms of two separate kinds of factors: Hygiene factors and motivator factors. Hygiene factors are external to the work itself, and include salary, company policies, work conditions, job security, and relationships with peers and supervisors. And although the lack of them can become the source of dissatisfaction, they are not, conversely, the source of motivation or job satisfaction. Motivators: motivators are intrinsic to the job, such as achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, advancement, and personal growth. Such factors are associated with higher levels of job motivation and satisfaction. Herzberg’s motivational theory implies that to motivate employees, a business not only needs to tackle hygiene factors to prevent dissatisfaction but also boost motivators to motivate employees and enable them to perform. This theory has important implications for HR interventions aimed at promoting job enrichment, meaningful work and career development. It emphasizes the value of acknowledging employees’ psychological needs and the development of a work context that leads to satisfaction and motivation, the key drivers of the best possible organizational results.

text: Maxwell’s equations are four basic equations which determine the behavior of electric and magnetic fields and their relation to matter, as well as to one another. They were first laid out in the 19th century by James Clerk Maxwell, who consolidated into a single consistent theory but two very dispartate principles of electricity and magnetism in a theory he called electromagnetism. The equations are: Gauss’s law for electricity, which relates electric fields to electric charges; Gauss’s law for magnetism, which indicates that magnetic monopoles don’t exist and that magnetic field lines must be closed loops; Faraday’s law of induction, which explains how a changing magnetic field makes an electric field; and Ampère’s law with Maxwell’s correction, which says that electric currents and changing electric fields make magnetic fields. The most revolutionary thing Maxwell's equations did was to predict the existence of waves of electromagnetic radiation - light, radio, X- and gamma rays were all waves of a new type that travelled even in the absence of any material, and at a fixed speed, which Maxwell calculated was equal to the speed of light. This observation was crucial in showing that light is indeed an electromagnetic wave. Maxwell’s equations were the basis for a vast number of technological developments, from wireless communication, electrical circuits, radar and MRI machines to the design and construction of electric motors, generators and antennas, and the design and analysis of waveguides. They are also enablers for the set up of Special Relativity since Einstein built this theory focusing on the constance of the speed of light and that fact was built upon the works of Maxwell. In modern physics, Maxwell’s equations are considered among the most beautiful and most powerful that describe the behavior of the classical electromagnetic field in vacuum and matter. They are also an introduction to quantum electrodynamics (QED), which is a quantum mechanical theory of the electromagnetic interactions. That they are true explains a great deal, and the importance of Maxwell’s equations cannot be overstated: beyond property omnisweeps, they unite electric and magnetic fields into one of nature’s four fundamental forces coordinating a large portion of the physical world, powering modern civilization and only vaguely understood.

text: For almost a century, drug discovery was driven by the quest for magic bullets, which act by targeting one critical step in a disease process and elicit a cure with few other consequences. However, this concept is far from biological reality, and even the most successful rationally designed drugs (such as Gleevec®) show a quite promiscuous binding behavior, which has opened novel therapeutic possibilities [1]. Today, the emerging picture is that drugs rarely bind specifically to a single target, and this challenges the concept of a magic bullet. Indeed, recent analyses of drug and drug-target networks show a rich pattern of interactions among drugs and their targets, where drugs acting on a single target seem to be the exception. Likewise, many proteins are targeted by several drugs with quite distinct chemical structures [2]. Drug-repositioning strategies seek to exploit the notion of polypharmacology [3], together with the high connectivity among apparently unrelated cellular processes, to identify new therapeutic uses for already approved drugs. The main advantage of this approach is that, since it starts from approved compounds with well-characterized pharmacology and safety profiles, it should drastically reduce the risk of attrition in clinical phases. There are several successful examples of drug repositioning (for example, thalidomide to treat leprosy or finasteride for the prevention of baldness), although they were all found by serendipity and are not the result of well-thought strategies.

text: Abnormally low levels of oxygen in cells, known as hypoxia, characterize most solid tumors. Hypoxia is associated with malignant progression, invasion, angiogenesis, changes in metabolism and increased risk of metastasis. It also severely affects treatment outcome because hypoxic tumors are usually resistant to radiotherapy and chemotherapy [1–4]. Up to 60% of locally advanced solid tumors exhibit hypoxic (1% O2 or less, compared to 2 to 9% O2 in the adjacent tissue) and/or anoxic (that is, no measurable oxygen, < 0.01% O2) areas throughout the tumor mass. Studies in breast, uterine cervix and head and neck cancers suggest that the extent of hypoxia is independent of tumor stage, size, histology or grade [5]. Hypoxia is caused by several factors: inadequate vascularization (tumor angiogenesis is often characterized by aberrant vessels that have altered perfusion); an increase in diffusion distances that is associated with tumor expansion (oxygen has to travel further to oxygenate tumor cells because of uncontrolled tumor growth); and tumor or therapy-related anemia (caused by reduced oxygen transport capacity) [5]. Cancer cells can adapt to a hostile, low-oxygen environment and this contributes to their malignancy and aggressive phenotype. This adaptation is governed by many factors, including transcriptional and post-transcriptional changes in gene expression.

text: National income is the sum of monies received for all final goods and services produced by a country as an economic entity over an interval of time, typically one year, and is such domestically and the excess over imports from the rest of the world. It's an indication of a country's economic health and is an indicator of how well the entire economy is performing. National income aids in comprehension of the living standard, economic development and use of resources of a nation. There are various other concepts of national income, each presenting a different viewpoint. They are Gross Domestic Product (GDP), indicating the overall national product; Gross National Product (GNP), comprising of GDP plus net income earned from abroad; Net National Product (NNP), which is GNP minus depreciation; National Income (NI) at factor cost which means NI adjusted to indirect taxes and subsidies; Personal Income (PI), which is households’ income, including transfer payments; and Disposable Personal Income (DPI), PI less direct taxes, or the amount available to spend as well as to save. They are approached for analysis with different theoretical tools. For instance, GDP takes into account production within the nation while GNP considers international income, and hence GNP is more apt for countries with large overseas investments. The national income figures are crucial to the government's planning, policy-making, tax policies and international comparisons. They are also used to help businesses understand the trends. These taxonomies can help economists and policy makers to better assess the economic stability, distribution of income, and development needs of countries.

text: A dimensionless number that defines how effectively an AC (alternating current) electrical system converts electric power into useful power outputs. The power factor is the cosine of the phase angle (?) between the voltage and current and is expressed by the relationship PF = cos(?). The power factor can be expressed mathematically as the ratio between real power (W, watts) and apparent power (VA, volts-amps), as PF = Real Power / Apparent Power. Real power is the power that a device, such as a lamp, will use to produce work via such things as light, heat, or motion, whereas apparent power is the total power supplied to the circuit that consists of both the real power and reactive power (power that is stored and released from inductive or capacitive components). If PF=1 (or 100%), all power supplied to the circuit is utilized in producingwork. No energy is lost to waste and no energy is “stored” for later release (as magnetic or electrostatic fields). This is the condition of a circuit having no reactive (capacitive or inductive) elements, and is only attainable in purely resistive circuits. In inductive- and capacitive-based circuits, however, the current and voltage are no longer in phase and this leads to a power factor less than 1. Low power factor is inefficient because it results in the need for a larger current to achieve the same amount of useful power, which then causes larger losses due to increased current flows, and may require extra costly infrastructure, which must carry large surges of current. Power factor correction for large users may use switching devices such as large capacitor or synchronous condenser banks controlled to offset the inductive reactance of the load and thereby increase the power factor, making the system more efficient and allowing more load to run for the same fuel consumption. Utilities can levy surcharges to customers with low power factor because it burdens the power grid. Knowing and correcting a low power factor is essential in creating efficient electrical systems, as it lowers electricity bills and increases the life expectancy of electrical equipment as reduced heat results in less operating costs and line losses.

text: In the optical color–magnitude diagram (CMD), BSSs are bluer (hotter) and brighter than the main-sequence (MS) stars, thus mimicking a stellar population significantly younger than the "normal" cluster stars. As shown by Shara et al. (1997), BSSs are more massive than normal stars, suggesting that some mass-increasing mechanism drives their formation. Possible explanations involve mass transfer between binary companions, the merger of a binary system, and the collision between single and/or binary stars (McCrea 1964; Zinn & Searle 1976). Clear differentiation among these possibilities is difficult, since primordial binaries can sink to the cluster center, where stellar collisions may significantly alter their evolution. Similarly, gravitational interactions can generate new binary systems and possibly kick them out of the cluster core. With this caveat, we define primordial binary BSSs (PB-BSSs) as those formed by mass-transfer processes (possibly up to complete coalescence) in primordial binaries which evolved in isolation in the cluster. Collisional BSSs (COL-BSSs) are those generated by mechanisms where stellar collisions played a major role.

text: A form of tourism known as community-based tourism (CBT) is recognized as a sustainable and participatory means of tourism development that is committed to community participation, ownership, and benefit in the planning, management, and delivery of tourism experiences to empower communities, preserve cultural and natural heritage, and create the conditions for equitable economic development (Brown, 2015; Eaton, 2004; Mayaka and Rutashobya, 2014; Shiona, 2013). Contrasting with mass tourism models controlled by external investors or commoditized products, CBT is based on rich local heritage, local knowledge and local resources to provide visitors with genuine, experiences and very physical experiences like homestays, culture performance show, traditional crafts, trekking, storytelling, working in the fields This approach also keeps tourism earnings within the community and benefits local people—enhancing infrastructure, funding social services and alleviating poverty through consistent and inclusive jobs that bring income to women, youth and marginalized members of society. Environmental sustainability is a fundamental principle of CBT communities serving as custodians of their natural environment and adopt conservation measures, controlling external access, managing waste, and preserving biodiversity in order to protect ecosystems for future generations. Socially, CBT enhances community solidarity through the inclusion of participatory decision-making and recognition of cultural identity and traditional experience and skills that might otherwise be endangered by erosion. It fosters respectful intercultural exchange among hosts and guests, enhances local pride, helps preserve cultural heritage, and promotes community empowerment and sustainable development while balancing community desires with those of guests. CBT, in order to design and manage tourism enterprises that fail in line with visitor expectations and are consistent with local values, requires skills development, training and support with regard to hospitality management, marketing, language, and business development. Engaging with NGOs, governments, tour operators and academic institutions can mobilise technical help, funding and access to markets, but it is vital that local ownership is supported, and top-down approaches which limit community autonomy are avoided. Challenges to CBT involve the fair distribution of benefits in the community, sustainable growth control to prevent over-tourism, quality control, and navigating a competitive market. Such challenges can be overcome with transparent governance frameworks, guidelines, and participatory planning mechanisms that can help build trust between stakeholders. Finally, any attempt to better harness tourism’s potential for development would have to offer an alternative to extractive, unsustainable models of tourism in which the primary emphasis is placed on local economic benefits, cultural survival, nature protection, and social justice – all of which make tourism memorable for visitors but sustainable and beneficial to hosts, aligning the development of tourism more closely with other developmental priorities (development, poverty alleviation, resilience in the face of global change).

text: The World Tourism Organization (UNWTO)/Organización Mundial del Turismo (OMT) operates as a specialized agency of the United Nations, the UNWTO serves as a significant global actor, informing, facilitating, and bringing awareness to the work of the global tourism community and the public about the value of tourism to the economy and to society. As the world's leading international organization in the field of tourism, the UNWTO sits at the heart of global tourism policy and acts as a forum for tourism policy development and dialogue, recognizing the role and support of public policy to add value to the business tourism collected for governments, provide networking and partnership opportunities so that the business tourism industry can speak which facilititates knowledge sharing between tourism destinations to promote sustainable tourism development. Its mandate is to ensure that the social, economic and environment benefits of tourism are accessible to all – and that they are sustainable as well as including spiritual value. It is with this that UNWTO demonstrates leadership and promotes advocacy on major policy matters that include sustainable development, climate change, and poverty alleviation, gender equality, and tourism ethics including notably through its tools including the Global Code of Ethics for Tourism and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in which tourism is identified as a driver, a key priority for and cross-cutting contributor to achieving among other goals, decent work, reducing inequalities, and environmental sustainability. It is also a knowledge hub by collecting, analysing and sharing credible tourism statistics and market trends to guide evidence-based decision making of member states and industry stakeholders. By providing technical assistance, capacity building programmes, training workshops, and by partnering with local governments and the private sector, UNWTO helps destinations enhance policy and strategic planning for tourism, develop infrastructure, build and rise to the challenge of crises, from health emergencies to natural disasters and ensure the most vulnerable are included in the making and benefiting of the opportunities that tourism brings. UNWTO also fosters tourism in other ways, such as by pushing it as a form of cultural exchange and a promoter of peace, in promoting respectful treatment of the indigenous population's culture, protection of heritage sites, and mutual respect towards different cultures. It also supports measures to promote the safety and security of visitors, facilitate visa processing, and make travel accessible to everyone, including individuals with disabilities. The agency organizes major worldwide events such as the UNWTO General Assembly, regional conferences, and international symposia, where decision-makers, specialists, and industry players can address present and future issues and work on common solutions. By facilitating collaboration between the public and private sectors, UNWTO’s goal is to ensure that tourism can bring the maximum benefits possible, while minimizing as much as possible any negative impacts, including those related to overtourism, environmental damage and social upheaval. Ultimately, the role of the UNWTO is to take the lead and provide a platform for worldwide tourism to become more sustainable, more inclusive and more resilient, thereby, contributing to a more positive, meaningful and worthwhile growth of the economy, the community and the nature worldwide, making sure that travel remains a positive force for people and the planet at large.

text: Pteridophytes are vascular, seedless plants, spore bearing and form a link between non-vascular bryophytes and seed bearing plants such as gymnosperms and angiosperms. Ferns, horsetails and club mosses are some of the common examples. In contrast to bryophytes, which lack them, pteridophytes have xylem and phloem, conducting tissues for the efficient movement of water, minerals, and nutrients, and are able to grow much larger and to occupy a much greater diversity of habitats. They have true roots, stems, and more importantly, fronds or leaves, which unroll as they grow, circinate vernation, leaves with complex root-like organs that can perch above the soil like, in e.g., Dryopteris. The sporophyte is the conspicuous, independent plant and is the dominant phase in the life cycle of most Pteridophyta, whereas in most species the gametophyte is small short-lived, living in association with water where it is able to become fertilized. These are spore-producing plants that spores develop in structures called sporangia, which are typically found on the underside of leaves in sori (clusters). Despite this, pteridophytes still depend on water for effective sexual reproduction, since, like all bio-mytho-logical creatures, their sperm are flagellated and have to swim to the egg. Ecological importance In ecological terms the pteridophytes form a major part of the understorey system of forests including as well soil retention and nutrient clycling. Some species are good for land reclamation and ecological restoration, as they do well in disturbed areas. Economically, several ferns and some related plants are used most prominently for their ornamental value, most notably in horticulture. Some pteridophytes also have medicinal values in indigenous wound healing, fever and other diseases. Pteridophytes are important from an evolutionary point of view as they are one of the first plants to develop vascular tissues, which eventually allowed them to grow in an upright position and dominate the land. They are an important step in the evolution of plants because they bridge simple land plants and the more advanced plants with vascular seeds.

text: Advancements in the field of microscopy have pushed the boundaries of what was once thought possible. Fluorescent microscope systems such as very fast resonant scanning confocal (ribbon scanning), multiphoton, and fluorescence micro-optical sectioning tomography (fMOST) are all capable of generating very large multiterabyte whole mouse brain data sets. These technologies and techniques allow researchers to probe with greater specificity of observation and increased sensitivity in both resolution and frequency illuminating cellular level detail that was previously not possible -at a cost of increased data storage. These whole brain datasets pose a model problem for data archiving, access, and analysis: they are large; they are highly structured; they possess much information that may be useful beyond initial analyses (e.g. by other investigators, with distinct questions); multiple specimens must be analyzed for each experiment; they can be interrogated at many levels of complexity: elucidating properties of single synapses, single cells, brain regions, or the whole brain; diverse datasets can be rapidly generated with a range of different cell-types using readily available genetic resources (e.g. the library of Cre-driver mice used in neuroscience); and importantly, no single “average” value is going to capture the data represented within the collection. Finally, the archival library (composed of image collections showing connectivity between many distinct cell types and across many individuals) has significantly greater value than the individual images as a resource for understanding principles of neural connectivity across brain regions, circuit architectures, developmental stages and individual variations. Providing such a collection of datasets is non-trivial. It is not unusual for individual mouse datasets to exceed 10TB of storage and full-brain marmoset datasets to exceed 800TB. Due to limitations of data storage, individual labs frequently must decide the value of data immediately after collection, and allow discretionary deletion regardless of the reuse value of the dataset to the general scientific community. Furthermore, acquiring terabyte data sets from remote sources for reuse is generally infeasible for individual labs due to barriers such as the amount of local storage required, the amount of data that must be transferred, limitations of the bandwidth and the computational power required to harmonize the datasets to a uniform analysis standard.

text: William Shakespeare (1564-1616), known as England's national poet and the 'Bard of Avon', wrote 37 plays, 154 sonnets and two long narrative poems His plays have been translated into every major living language and are performed more often than those of any other playwright. Born in 1564 in the town of Stratford-upon-Avon, Shakespeare lived at least 52 years and wrote, by some estimates, a total of 39 plays, 154 sonnets, and a handful of other poems during his lifetime (which lasted 52 years and ended when his friends took him out to a tavern one night for some drinking, after which he died several days later from what most scholars think was probably a combination of a sudden fever and a case of bad sushi). His complete works, among them six tragedies, four comedies, four histories, and six romances, are considered the ultimate in dramatic repertoire and the epitome of human nature and emotion. In the mastery of the language he brought in new words, poetical tropes, and metrical forms that expanded English literature. Among those roles—Hamlet, Macbeth, Othello, Juliet— are figures who are so breathtakingly human and conflicted, and who encapsulate themes of love, ambition, jealousy, power, and mortality so universally that they continue to be fresh to audiences across cultures and through centuries. Shakespeare has also influenced a large number of writers and inspired a significant amount of literary output from his own time to the present. His works have been translated into every major living language and are performed more often than those of any other playwright. The universal and flexible nature of his themes make them capable of being performed in various cultural contexts and thus, ensure the continued popularity of his plays. And beyond his artistic accomplishments, Shakespeare’s work provides a window into his world — the social, political and philosophical currents of his time, around the turn of the 17th century, that was marked by Renaissance humanism and the pressures of Elizabethan England. The richness of his poetic beauty coupled with deep psychological insight transcends time. The significance of Shakespeare is not just as one of the multiple universal emotional translators but as the emotional architect, as he stands at some of the foundation of what is considered ‘us’, we being modern men and women of the Eurasian west (and the Pacific east, where we find Hogg and, for instance, Jane Reichhoff, whom Hogg adores), the English of Britain, the Australian of Sydney, Adelaide and Brisbane, of Hobart Town, the Americans of New York… all we who think a good deal about Shakespeare, and what his plays mean to us.

text: States are important, even pivotal, agents in the international system, playing essential roles in governing and controlling international politics. States as sovereign entities are responsible for domestic governance, upholding law and order, and providing services and foster social harmony all within their borders. And they have to handle foreign policy: diplomacy, treaty-making, conflict resolution, alliance building and international representation. States exert their economic sovereignty — steering trade, money and investment flows, and creating regimes such as tariffs, sanctions, and quantitative controls. Military Globally they possess military forces for defense, deterrence, or the projection of power, and even occasionally intervene, or conduct peacekeeping activities under international law. States ratify and enforce international law (under treaty obligations) — and either serve in international organizations or participate in shaping norms. They steward the earth and help shape the global commons on issues like climate change, public health, development and cybersecurity. Furthermore, the states are central funders and sites of global institutions, NGOs, and multilateral projects. Problems like pandemics or transnational terrorism caused states to work together through systems of collective security or regulatory regimes, albeit in competition with each other. The choices that states make is interpreted more or less through the lens of the various sub-disciplines of IR: the realists focus on power and security determinants; the liberals add concern for cooperative institutions; and the constructivists shift emphasis to identity and normative structures. States maintain a monopoly on central authority – and their behavior, policies, and legitimacy – determines the trajectory and stability of the international system - despite processes of globalization and external pressures.

text: Nikah is the Islamic marriage contract that helps in uniting a Muslim man and woman for marriage in religious and legal terms. It is a cherished contract, conditioned by the Islamic law, where consent of both the parties is the prerequisite and some legal formalities are followed. The primary elements of a nikah are one party's proposal (ijab) to the other, and the other party's acceptance (qabul) of the proposal in the presence of witnesses. The marriage is valid when at least two adult Muslim witnesses are present. Another vitally important condition to be fulfilled is the specification of the mahr or dower agreed to, that is what the husband promises to give to the wife. The contract, which may be oral or written, must expressly state mutual consent and the capability to marry. The bride's guardian (wali) typically also needs to grant permission, particularly if the bride is a minor or never before married, although different school of thoughts may have different opinions. In Bangladesh:Documentation: Under Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, it is mandatory to register a marriage, while marriage between a male and female residing permanently in Bangladesh should be registered under the same Laws.Requirements: Threshold requirement includes that the parties are not within the prohibitory degree of relationships, both are of sound state of mind, free from any sort of legal disability and are of age. The nikah includes a religious sermon and the signing of the nikah nama (the marriage certificate). Due to the Nikah, the rights of the spouses regarding inheritance, dower and legitimacy of the children are also safeguarded by law. Failure to observe legal formalities does not diminish the religious validity of the marriage, but creates dangerous ambiguity in civil and legal contexts. Nikkah is not only a contract but a sacred covenant with a focus on mutual respect, responsibility and social well-being.

Nonrenewable resources is also a cause of heavy pollution, greenhouse gas emission, and ecological disequilibrium. text: 1 Introduction Daylight and artificial light are two main types of illumination that are used in photography, filmmaking, and visual arts; both have distinctions, which affect the mood, appearance, and practicability of a set. Natural light is light that is found in nature and is not created by man, such as the light from the sun, the moon, fire, and even lightning. It is a wide, soft and dynamic light source valued for its variety and adaptability, throughout the day varying in intensity, color temperature and direction, that allows one to capture crowded of moods and atmospheres—from a warm golden hue at sunset or sunrise to the bright light of noon. People are used to seeing natural light because it is natural, and that makes exposure to it feel true and organic, giving an authentic and natural beauty to whatever we see, without needing a whole bunch of fancy equipment. It’s easy and effective when it works, but the downside is that lead times are often unpredictable because of the weather, light angles can change between one minute and the next, it can be tricky to control how in-your-face it is, and everything you shoot needs to be consistently lit and scheduled. On the contrary, artificial light is produced by artificial light sources such cameras flashes, incandescent lights, fluorescent lamps, LEDs, studio strobes or even specialized filmmaking lights. Other artists emphasize it has never been more clear that artificial lighting allows control over intensity of light, color temperature, direction and quality, allowing artists to stage a scene exactly as they imagine it irrespective of the hour or the weather. This control for continuity is essential when creating a professional production where you need the same lighting setup across different shots or locations. The artificial light may be altered with other tools like gels (for colored effects) or scrims (to diffuse light) to further control the light or its effects. Artificial light can feel only slightly less natural or more staged, but when employed judiciously, it is a necessary tool for indoor shots, shooting at night or when there is just not enough natural light to get the job done. Natural and artificial light often are combined by photographers and cinematographers who wish to enhance and blend their respective advantages, with a base of natural light supplemented by artificial light, or sometimes the other way around, bringing natural light through artificial windows in order to add time of day drama for instance. Learning about the distinctions between natural light and artificial light enable creators to make informed decisions on how they want to light their subjects and scenes, and all of this affects tone, clarity, and emotional conveyance within their visual storytelling.

text: A one-line diagram (sometimes called single-line diagram) is a simplified notation for representing a three-phase power system. Rather than depicting in detail all three phases of a power system on the SLD, the three are condensed into a single line, thereby providing a more easily understandable, analyzable and communicable map of the generation, transmission, distribution, and load entities on the SLD. It usually contain the primary devices such as generators, transformers, circuit breakers, buses, loads and protective devices and their ratings and relay-settings. The SLD is important for planning, operation, maintenance, and fault analysis because it shows the general overview of power flow paths, switching arrangements and the structure of the system without the detailed information, such as actual wire size and easyname/circuit number. SLDs are widely used by both engineers and operators to get a quick picture of the network status, which help in planning the expansions, protection coordination and fault analysis. The one-line diagram can be a critical reference for safety, engineering, troubleshooting and patience/comfort of operators working in Industrial and systems using Single Line Diagrams. Due to both the simplicity and transparency, an SLD can be a common tool employed to analyze and control EPS effectively.

text: Colonialism: The erosion of the social system of Bangladesh through the British colonial period. Traditional systems of governance, economy and social hierarchy were largely disrupted under the British but new institutions and systems of rule eventually played a role in modernising the country. One significant difference was the Permanent Settlement Act under which a new class of landlords, the zamindars, appeared and disrupted the centuries- old peasant communities. That system of economic injustice and feudal exploitation, had lingering impact on rural Bangladesh even today. The colonial education system sidelined indigenous languages and Islamic education in favour of English and Western knowledge and gave birth to a cultural and intellectual elite which was out of touch with its people. Furthermore, colonial governance exacerbated religious division, which fomented Hindu-Muslim antipathy and had implications for the partition of Bengal and eventually the formation of East Pakistan (which later became Bangladesh). Colonial urbanization was hampered, as it can be largely restricted to administrative or trade purposes, the result was also an uneven regional development. Colonialism had also brought a capitalist market, which threw traditional crafts and ways of life into turmoil. ?The local inhabitants had to either sell themselves for wages or starve. Social ascent was increasingly limited, and marked in contrast to the second class status of the civil servants and government employees. It helped to shape contemporary class structures and political alignments in Bangladesh. The colonial heritage also affected gender relations through restricted opportunities for female education and deeply rooted patriarchal values. Long after the British had left, many colonial institution and mechanisms, not least centralised bureaucracy, land laws and elitist education had continued to shape Bangladeshi society, as Khaled Ahmad observed the other say. Hence to understand colonialism is to understand the historical origins of the inequality, class distinction and culture of disunity of the Bangladesh social structure.

text: Types of Sentences Based on Purpose There are four main types of sentences in English based on purpose: Declarative: A declarative sentence makes a statement or argument about what is or is not the case. Each has its own role to play in communication. Declarative sentence tells something or states something. It is the most frequent type, and is terminated by a full stop. For instance, “She goes to school every day” is a declarative sentence. An interrogative sentence is a sentence that asks a question and ends with a question mark. It asks questions like “Do you like pizza?” or “Where is your bag?” An imperative tells someone to do something. Depending on the tone, it can be followed by a period or an exclamation point. For example: “Close the door.” or “Please be quiet.” Sometimes the subject “you” is implicit, even if it is not expressed in writing. The fourth is the exclamatory sentence that shows the emotion of surprise, anger, joy, or excitement. It always ends in an exclamation point! For example, “What a beautiful day!” or “I can’t believe this!” Understanding what kinds of sentences there are can help students write more interesting sentences. And each serves a purpose in everyday conversation, whether you’re being declarative, interrogative, imperative or emotive. Using one type over and over can be boring or make writing sound like machine speak. So, for example, a paragraph that consisted only of declarative sentences would be received as boring, while a combination of questions, exclamations builds rhythm and vitality. About different types of sentences is also has positive effect in punctuation, and grammar. On public speaking, school essays, and everyday small talk, the best type of sentence provides power to the message. To sum up, declarative, interrogative and imperative and exclamatory sentences are the foundation of communication, and they each fulfill a different and indispensable function in communication.

text: Reproductive strategies differ greatly between the species and are influenced by evolutionary pressures, environmental traits and an organism's life history in order to achieve maximum reproductive success and offspring survival. In general, these strategies can be ordered along one gradient, ranging from r-strategists to K-strategists. r-strategists, like insects, amphibians and many fish, produce very large numbers of offspring with little parental care, with survival of the young mainly left to numbers (as the vast majority of prey species do not mature after one year of birth, their offspring are born in areas of very high mortality, where producing a large number of offspring is crucial so that a fraction can survive). Such species usually possess a short life span, growth is rapid and early reproduction is early. At the other extreme, the K-strategists, who include many mammals, birds, and some reptiles, lay their eggs (or produce fewer offspring in other ways) which they invest more heavily in, and raise that smaller number of offspring with extensive maternal care, to attain a higher probability of advanced development and survival. These animals typically have longer gestation periods, longer periods of developing as juveniles, and parental behaviors feeding, sheltering, and teaching how to survive to offspring. Reproductive modes also are diverse—some are oviparous (laying eggs that develop outside the body of the mother), while others are viviparous (bearing live young that develop within the body of the mother). Yet another group is ovoviviparous, the eggs developing internally and the young being born live from the body of the mother. Sexual reproduction, using both male and female gametes, is widespread and introduces genetic variability, while asexual reproduction, observed in certain invertebrates and plants, enables populations to increase quickly without the need for a partner. Some species are also hermaphroditic, having both male and female reproductive organs, which may be advantageous for reproduction when their populations are small. Mating behaviors and reproduction is also quite variable, some species are seasonal in their breeding and base it on external stimuli such as a certain temperature or food availability, others are capable of year-long reproduction. Mate choice and competition are major selection pressures in much of the animal kingdom, influencing reproductive success and genetic fitness. Some organisms have external fertilization, rather than depositing gametes in to the water column, sperm and eggs are released in to the water and come together in the environment, where internal fertilization provides better protection for the embryo. Under extreme conditions, parthenogenesis allows females to reproduce without the participation of males. These multifarious reproductive strategies are symbols of life's accommodation to a variety of ecological niches and to the selective pressures exerted over it, indicative of a dynamic homeostasis, an artistic compromise beween the investment in energy, the prevailing environment, and the subsequent survival of the spawn that guides the continuity of life itself throughout the animal kingdom.

text: Electromagnetic (EM) field boundary conditions serve as the guidelines for the behavior of electric and magnetic fields at the interface of two dissimilar media. Such conditions require Maxwell’s Equations to be fulfilled in interfacial boundaries such as between air and a dielectric, or metal and vacuum. They tell us how the electric field, or the magnetic field, or components of the electric and magnetic field, change or are constant at a boundary. For instance, the tangential electric fields must be continuous at the boundary, i.e. there can not be abrupt changes in these field directions. Likewise, the normal component of the electric displacement field varies with the surface charge density at the boundary. Magnetic fields have similar boundary conditions for their tangential and normal components. Such conditions are key to the appropriate solution of problems of reflection, refraction, transmission, and absorption of EM waves with material interfaces. They aid in the design of antennas, waveguides, optical fibers and shielding materials by estimating how fields interact with surfaces. Surface currents, and surface charges induced by electromagnetic field are also governed by boundary conditions. In a pragmatic way, they also guarantee that solutions to electromagnetic problems are real and physical. Boundary conditions are vital to engineers and physicists in the fields of wave propagation, signal integrity, and electromagnetic compatibility.

text: A library catalog is a register, hopefully comprehensive, of all the resources found within the library's collection, such that users are able to find materials they are looking for any time, day, or night. It is the key access to the library s collection information, containing rich bibliographic records for all items in its collection including books, periodicals, maps, DVDs, electronic resources, and archival materials. Such records normally contain basic information such as the title, author, subject headings, date of publication, edition, call number, and location of the item in the library. Catalogues have gone from physical card catalogues, which are a set of cards that are physically filed at an index (or in some cases, by metadata), to digital search tools that help users findem media in a collection using terms, dates, and metadata. A record can provide multiple access points: author, title, subject, ISBN, or series, which would facilitate users to find what they need with their incomplete information. Cataloguing rules/conventions such as MARC (Machine-Readable Cataloguing) and RDA (Resource Description and Access) make it possible to create and share records that can be used across all types of libraries. Besides searching for particular titles, users can search through catalogs to find similiar works, check whether items are available, and place holds or renew items. An accurate and up-to-date library catalogue is essential for collection maintenance, selection, circulation control, and patron satisfaction. The catalog also serves as a record of the library collection, allowing the library to organize and access the resources by various formatting (and is also accessible to users who may be offsite). Many catalogs offer additional features such as reviews, user tags, recommender systems, and access to full text and e-books. In an era of digital libraries, library catalogs are typically accessed remotely through the Internet, and many museum libraries have made an effort to provide such access to their catalogs, although the need for interlibrary loans affordable only through regional or national consortia reduces the advantage of this trend. Library catalogs are more than a list; they are a living portal to knowledge that offers discoverability, access and exploration of a wide variety of topics and formats overall.

text: Control rods are an essential mechanical part of a nuclear reactor, which can penetrate into the core and be pulled out of the core to control the nuclear reaction, and absorb neutrons to decrease the neutron flux in the reactor core. They are constructed with materials having a high neutron-absorption cross-section, such as boron (in the form of boron carbide), cadmium, hafnium, silver-indium-cadmium alloys (see Nuclear poison). Material selection considerations include, neutron absorption efficiency, mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and compatibility of the material with the reactor environs. Control rods are inserted into the reactor core to increase reactivity, which increases power, and withdrawn from the reactor core to decrease reactivity and decrease power, including power down to the shutdown condition, known as reactor scram (or trip). Under normal operation, the rods may be partially inserted to adjust the fission rate rate, for stable and efficient production of energy. The reactor protection system closely supervises and regulates their operation to ensure safety margins. The rods need to withstand high temperatures, high neutron fluences and be resistant to corrosion without significant degradation or swelling that could limit extension and/or retraction. They are made as fail-safe components as well, which implies that they must automatically fall into the core by gravity or spring force if the power supply and the control system fail, to insure a prompt reactor shut down. Neutron economy should be also took into account in control rod design, in addition thermal-hydraulic effect because when they are inserted or withdrawn, coolant flow and heat is modified. Materials in control rod can deteriorate due to neutron irradiation and need to be inspected or repaired at certain intervals. There are various reactor designs each with diverse assembly and methods of control rod insertion, however they all share the basic concept of neutron absorption to control the fission process. In general, the control rods are indispensable for the safe operation and emergency response of the reactor, and take the key positions in the control systems of nuclear reactors.

text: Political participation is a popular and widely investigated subject in academic studies. This phenomenon, or rather array of phenomena, can be approached through various interlinked theoretical lenses. Some studies are concerned with the role and relevance of political participation in democratic systems (e.g., Barber, 1984), while others attempt to classify the different levels of political participation and types of participants (e.g., Arnstein, 1969) or identify the factors contributing to or limiting political activity (e.g., Verba et al., 1995). The present paper falls within the latter category, and more specifically within the domain of Internet and political participation research, as it explores how media and political landscapes mediate the contributions of Facebook to citizens’ political participation in Italy and the United Kingdom. Over the last decade an increasing number of academic studies have examined how digital technologies can contribute to political participation, with numerous publications focusing on social networking websites (SNSs), i.e., web-based services that ‘allow individuals to present themselves, articulate their social networks, and establish or maintain connections with others’ (Ellison et al., 2007, p. 1143). This course in scholarship can be arguably attributed to: the widespread and rapid penetration of SNSs across the globe; the role these platforms played in political protests and campaigns such as the Arab Spring and the 2008 Obama’s presidential campaign; the fact that, as stressed by Dahlgren (2009), the rise of the Internet coincided with citizens’ growing dissatisfaction with democratic political institutions and detachment from the political process—a phenomenon described as democratic deficit (Norris, 2011).
