text: Biological control on farms involves using living organisms (such as predators, parasites, pathogens, or competitors) to manage agricultural pests and diseases in an ecologically responsible manner. In contrast to chemical control, which can lead to environmental pollution, resistance and destruction of beneficial organisms, biological control utilise natural enemies of pests to lower their population to tolerable numbers. It is one of the most important tools of Integrated Pest Management (IPM), and conducive to the long-term sustainability of the agroecosystem. Types of biological control Three types of biological control are classi? cal, augmentative, and conservation. Classical biological control is used against long-established invasive or exotic pests. Augmentative control can involve rearing and releasing large numbers of beneficial organisms (e.g., lady beetles, Trichogramma wasps or entomopathogenic fungi) for outbreak control. These tactics also increase populations of retained natural enemies on a farm through management of habitat, reducing pesticide application, and planting noncropped flora. Insect pests, plant pathogens, and even weeds are the most common targets. For example, employing Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) bacteria to combat caterpillars, or introducing predacious mites to get rid of spider mite infestations. Biological control may also involve nematodes that parasitize soil-dwelling insects or fungi that colonize weeds. Although biological control is usually safe and environmentally friendly, it needs to be done with care, as the introduced enemy might damage non-target species. 2 We need the research and control to make sure it is effective and used ethically. Biological control not only minimizes the reliance on synthetic chemicals but also promotes biodiversity, soil health, and pollinator protection. It is a staple in organic production systems and is becoming more prevalent in conventional cropping systems as a sustainable approach. In other words, biological control is a sustainable way of a aiding what nature is already doing by providing additional resources to cultivate stronger, healthier farming systems.

text: Preventing crime is confronted with a variety of challenges related to the complex and multi-dimensional character of crime and the presence of social, economic and systemic issues. A major problem is the presiding social circumstances which cause crime – poverty, inequality, bad education, broken families, and unemployment – also need long-term and coordinated social policy action which goes well beyond policing. Another marginal factor is crime displacement, where crime is displaced elsewhere (in space, time, method, targets, or types of offence) as those for whom the measures are taken are no longer easy victims. The growing sophistication and variety of crimes, such as cybercrime, organized crime, and transnational crimes, require specialized expertise, sophisticated equipment, and international cooperation—factors that can place a burden on both resource allocation and coordination. Scarce resources and political concerns tend to emphasize reactive policing as opposed to preventive policing, such as investments in community programs and social services that would address underlying causes. And law enforcement doubt communities – particularly those of color ¬– hinder cooperation that the success of many prevention strategies rely on. It is also challenging to measure the success of prevention efforts and can depend on the local context. Addressing these high-impact problems is only possible with the help of cutting-edge and vibrant communities of researchers, including those who are considering new or challenging problems that are not at the forefront of mainstream research, developing and evaluating new methodologies, or challenging the status quo.

text: The Scientific Revolution (16th-18th centuries) radically changed humanity’s understanding of the natural world and European intellectual, cultural, and technological landscapes by articulating empirical science as method (and worldview). The revolution had its origins in the thinking of early pioneers such as Nicolaus Copernicus, who rocked the boat in 1543 by postulating that the universe is heliocentric — bucking a millennium and a half of geocentric orthodoxy. Kepler, whose accuracy of observation fostered mathematical precision in formulating his laws of planetary motion, which superseded the circular orbits with elliptical ones. Galileo Galilei made use of the telescope to study the heavens, and carried out a series of experiments on falling bodies, throwing into contention the Aristotelian account of motion and the heavens. Rene Descartes added a rationalist philosophy ("I think, therefore I am") to empiricism and shared themes with the work of humanists. Isaac Newton compounded these with his 1687 Principia where he stated that mathematical principles of the cosmic and the terrestrial mechanics were to be united in universal laws of motion and gravitational force. These conceptual revolutions changed not only physics and astronomy but methodology, leading to the now-familiar scientific method—systematic observation, hypothesis formation, hypothesis testing, and replication. This removed the privilege of knowledge from the religious and classical texts to the evidence-gathering examination. The radicalism funded technological advances — mechanical engineering, navigation, optics — that underpinned the Age of Exploration and later industrialization. It also altered social structure: education elites were can be looked upon with increased prestige by the successful advance of science state support for for research increased, and universities and scientific societies like the Royal Society or the Académie des Sciences appeared. To justify their Enlightenment beliefs in reason, progress and individual liberty, philosophers such as Francis Bacon and Voltaire turned to scientific rationalism. Scientific revolution also made its mark on modern medicine, which gave rise to anatomy, biology, and enlightened public health. Religiously and politically, the movement found itself at odds with ecclesiastical orthodoxy (think the Inquisition of Galileo) but, in the end, it ratified secular power in knowledge. In short, the Scientific Revolution gave the intellectual and methodological frame for modern science and the revolution of self?understanding in mankind on which a unique cultural progress and technology was constructed.

text: Several theories have been proposed to conceptualize the pathological processes inherent to schizophrenia, among others altered neurotransmission, autoimmune dysfunction and dysregulation of inflammation [1, 2]. The phospholipid hypothesis suggests that deficient uptake or excessive breakdown of membrane phospholipids or changes in membrane phospholipid composition may be associated with schizophrenia [3]. The hypothesis is supported by studies finding lipid abnormalities both in postmortem gray and white matter samples and from peripheral red blood cells of patients with schizophrenia [4]. Moreover, phospholipase A2 activity is increased particularly in the first-onset patients with schizophrenia and associates with structural brain changes, particularly in the prefrontal cortex and thalamus [5]. Nevertheless, the evidence for the phospholipid hypothesis is not conclusive [6]. Prior to the phospholipid hypothesis, a prostaglandin deficiency hypothesis was proposed [7]. Phospholipid abnormalities and prostaglandin deficiency may be related since prostaglandins are synthesized via hydrolysis of phosphatidylcholine (PC) by action of phospholipase A2, with another byproduct of this process being lysophosphatidylcholines (lysoPCs).

text: IPQC refers the process of monitoring and controlling the manufacturing of medications during the production processes to maintain the quality of the product. In contrast with final product testing, IPQC is a proactive approach whose task is to identify and resolve problems in the manufacturing process, rather than at the end. IPQC consists of the inspection of the quality of raw materials, granules, powders, compressed tablets, capsules, and liquids at significant processing points like mixing, granulation, compression, coating and packaging. Standard IPQC methods such as weight variation, hardness, thickness etc., disintegration time, moisture and microbial limit tests should be performed. Such testing assists in early detection of variances and permits remedial action to be taken in time to avoid the production of out-of-tolerance batches. IPQC is so important to standardisation, consistency and GMP (Good Manufacturing Practice). It’s also saving on waste and production costs as well as making sure patients are safe. This is because, in the local drugs and pharmaceuticals industry in Bangladesh, good practices of IPQC will ensure the reliability as well as integrity of the product in accordance with the regulatory compliance which lead to make local drugs and pharmaceuticals competitive at the global viewpoint. The IPQC workforce are all well versed in the use of SOPs, and accurate record keeping, vital of audits and inspections. Application of automatic monitoring and real time data analysis have enhanced the efficiency of IPQC. In general, IPQC represents an essential QA measure that protects drug product manufacturing, guaranteeing that safe, effective drugs reach patients.

text: The Media: First Responders in a Disaster The media is highly critical during disasters as it serves as a premier conduit for information distribution, public awareness, and accountability. Media broadcast (television, radio, newspapers, electronic media) the most current information about hazard events, as well as information on warnings, evacuations, and response activity, allowing the community to make informed decisions and take protective action. Coverage in the media informs the public regarding the scope and effects of disasters, and spurs support and fundraising for relief efforts. It is also an accountability mechanism, by which we report on the effectiveness, challenges and human rights aspects of the response.” Social media, in particular, enables instant messaging, crowd-sourced evidence and direct interaction with the affected populations. But media outlets have to weigh between a string of quick news updates and ensuring the right facts are out there, to prevent unnecessary misinformation and fear. On disaster coverage, ethical journalism means restraint, respect for victims’ dignity, verified sources and no sensationalism. Disaster preparedness can also be accomplished through the media by means of educational programming. Media and government collaboration with disaster preparedness organizations can help keep messages from getting muddled in translation. Barriers include restricted access to areas of impact, censorship and digital divide. Amidst this, the media continues to prove itself as an essential player in saving lives, recovery, and building resilient communities in disaster situations.

text: In spite of its potential in the biodiesel industry, commercial production of J. curcas L. is faced with numerous challenges including poor seed yield and non-synchronous flowering. Seed cultivation of J. curcas L. is often associated with heterozygosity, which affects the quality and quantity of the oil content. Propagation by cuttings also yields plants that are susceptible to drought and diseases [4]. Attempts to improve J. curcas L. through conventional breeding, radiation mutation, protoplast fusion and/or in vitro induction of polyploids has failed to produce improved varieties with the required characteristics [5,6]. However, the genetic modification and manipulation of J. curcas L., by incorporating genes that code for novel traits from closely related species to generate an intergeneric F1 hybrid, offer the opportunity for improvement. Crop development research worldwide is mainly focused on the improvement of the genetic makeup through techniques such as interspecific hybridization and genetic transformation via Agrobacterium tumefaciens and microprojectile bombardment [3,7]. Research into the genetic diversity of closely related crops helps in understanding their genetic makeup for improvement. The genetic makeup of Jatropha-related species such as R. communis L. has been extensively studied and reported [1,8]. R. communis L. possesses beneficial genetic traits for improving J. curcas. It is a wild plant that has been developed into an herbaceous crop with synchronous seeds, giving it a high seed yield that is easily harvested [9].

text: Spacecrafts are in a severe environment in space. Their surfaces are exposed to energetic and reactive particles, such as electrons, ions, protons and oxygen atoms, and ultraviolet light, including the particles exhausted from the plasma thrusters, during space missions. The environmental effect plays a crucial role in determining the spacecraft reliability and lifetime [1]. Although the number density of ions such as oxygen and nitrogen is smaller than that of the atomic oxygen in LEO, electrostatic interactions between the surface materials and the ambient plasma, such as the negative or positive sheath creation and the charging and arcing phenomena, frequently occur. The ions are accelerated in a negative-potential sheath on a solar array, and the current generated by the solar array is leaked by the impact of the ions; the solar array is still degraded by sputtering and arcing due to the collected ions [2], [3]. Accordingly, the environmental factors cause changes in the chemical structures of the spacecraft materials and their optical and/or electrical properties [4]–?[6].

text: The time response of a dynamic system is nothing but the way in which the output of system varies as a function of time under the action of some input signal like: step, impulse, ramp etc. It gives insight into how fast and accurate a system responds to changes or signals – transient and steady state behavior of the system. Time response is generally treated in two regions: the transient and the steady-state responses. The transient response is the first part of the response which represents what the system does right after the input changes, including how fast the response is applied, and if it overshoots the desired response, oscillates, or settles down, and how long it takes to settle. The steady state response is the response of the output for long time input after all the transients have died out and represents the output of the system due to the constant input. Time response analysis helps engineers assess the performance of a system through factors including rise time, peak time, overshoot, settling time, and steady state error, which aids in the design of control systems to achieve a desired speed, accuracy, and stability. Time response[edit] Depending of a mixing of their parameters, damping and feedback, not all systems have the same step response (critical, underdame, overdame) which makes this analysis quite important in robotics and automotive control as well as in industrial automation and electric circuits.

text: Social mobility is the ability of an individual or, occasionally, a group to move upwards or downwards in the social hierarchy or from one social class to another. Vertical (higher or lower) or horizontal (different occupation or job of same status). Factors such as education, vocation, income, gender, ethnicity, and political ties affect social mobility. With all this increase in possibility, one thing has become more visible in Bangladesh than ever before: upward mobility for the urban middle class, thanks to education, overseas employment and entrepreneurship. Families that were unskilled and used to depend on agriculture or manual labor have graduated to migration, remittances, or establishing a small business. The rapid expansion of English-medium education and private universities has opened up new opportunities particularly in urban settings. But it is the slide that is a problem as well, especially for the rural poor who are hit by climate change, landlessness, lack of work. Floods or river erosion are orthings that frequently eject families like Fuleswaree from their communities, dumping them in urban slums. Gender continues to be a major determining factor: while more women are working, for women, social mobility may be blocked by early marriage, domestic duties and workplace bias. Access to public jobs or resources is also conditioned by political affiliation, rendering mobility contingent upon connections rather than merit. In the countryside, caste-like distinctions and old power structures confined mobility for lower castes. NGOs and government programs that aimed to give microcredit, education, vocational training have provided ways out of poverty for a lot of people. Social mobility in Bangladesh is expanding, but uneven. The only way to ensure this is a more encompassing policy space than one where mobility is a privilege and not a capability.

text: Disasters are generally classified as natural, manmade (or anthropogenic), and complex, which are characterised by different origins and consequences. Natural disasters Natural disasters are those that are due to natural force and include geological events like earthquakes, tsunamis, vulcanicity and landslides; meteorological events like cyclones, storms and blizzards; hydrological events such as floods and avalanches and climatological events such as drought and wild fire. Such occurrences are often due to the process of the crust of the Earth, atmospheric and oceanic disturbances and are usually affected by seasonal phenomenon, climate variability and environmental degradation. Human-induced disasters come as a result of human negligence, incompetence, or malicious intentions. These can range from industrial and technological accidents (chemical spills, nuclear accidents, factory explosions), through disasters related to transport (train derailments, air crashes), fires, oil spills to conflicts like wars or terrorist attacks. Natural and technological disaster are the two primary causes of complex disasters, which may occur when a natural hazard, such as an earthquake, sets off a technological disaster, as evidenced by Japan's Fukushima nuclear disaster. Another example is the class of biological disasters, such as pandemics, epidemics and bioterrorism, e.g, the COVID-19 pandemic that has led to global health and socio-economical disruption. Disasters can also be divided by their cause into natural and human made, sudden-onset and slow-onset events such as earthquake and explosion, and drought and desertification, respectively. In addition, some experts add socio-natural disasters, the natural disasters that are exacerbated by human activity (such as deforestation that amplifies the risk of floods). An understanding of the types of disasters is useful for developing customized strategies for mitigation, preparedness, and response. For the purposes of mitigation to be effective and reduce impacts from either type of air pollution, specific knowledge, risk assessment, allocation of resources, and coordination among the parties involved are necessary.

text: Blocking is one of the most important things in theatre production, and it concerns coordination to design and control specific movements and location of actors on stage with respect to their performance in a certain scene, determining the way a story is visually presented and how the actors perform in relation to the full range of stage locations. It can be as simple as choices as to where characters enter and exit, where and how they stand or move in a scene, what gestures they make, and how to create stage pictures that communicate relationships, emotions, and the advancement of a story. The blocking does not indicate the movement of actors, but follows them during rehearsals, showing their positions on stage, and all changes in the stage not planned by the playwright, the author, are not letters written on the text, but created by the work in the rehearsal. Great blocking creates space, emphasizes important moments, and ultimately controls the rhythm and action of the play. It even takes into account practical factors like sightlines — ensuring every audience member can see what’s happening — safety, and interaction with scenery and props. In blocking, the director underscores power plays, closeness and space between characters, tension, or conflict, among other things, by staging characters not just moving closer together or farther apart but by moving or not moving them at all to act out mood, intention, and feeling that cannot be spoken. Again, blocking can determine the pace of a scene- as moments of quiet or physical action are blocked in such as way as to create space in which to hold the audience. It demands care to the capabilities and comfort of the actors, striking a balance between directorial vision and the demands of performing the show. Good blocking fits into the lighting and sound design, because they often depend on where actors are placed, they act as a cue for those departments and those departments can tell the cast, in any given situation, where they should go, what they should do etc. Choreography or stylized movement may be utilized in blocking to accentuate the play's style or message. In all, blocking turns the words and stage directions of a script into a living, spatially dynamic performance, and through it, storytelling, the physical expression of character and plot, is helped along. It's a skill, but also an art, indispensable for stage direction that makes look coherent, natural, visually interesting scenes that echo for a viewer and realize the text.

text: Urbanization is exerting a heavy influence on disaster risk accumulation by concentrating people and assets in such a dense manner that infrastructure, services and governance structures lag behind what is needed to effectively control risks. The rapid and haphazard urbanization could generate the spread of informal settlements into dangerous areas such as flooding areas, steep slopes, or soft soil, raising residents’ vulnerability to hazards (floods, landslides, earthquakes, and so on). Overcrowding, poor housing, sanitation and limited access to emergency services lead to increased disaster effects on urban populations, and particularly on vulnerable communities. Urbanization also imposes pressure on the natural ecosystems which serve as natural buffers such as wetlands and forests, decreasing their ability to offset disaster. The interconnected nature of urban systems, such as the transportation, energy and communication networks, implies that disasters lead to cascading failures with broad social and economic repercussions. On the other hand, well planned urbanisation provides opportunities to mitigate disaster risks through better land use planning, building technology, early warning and community preparedness. Institutions in urban areas are usually far more resourced and capable to reduce disaster risks, like compared to rural places. It’s urgent that integrated strategies include infrastructure development, social inclusion, environmental preservation, and governance reform to manage urban risk everywhere. Urbanization is a priority considering that more than half of the human population live in cities.In this context, the challenges of urbanization are paramount such that urban disaster resilience becomes a matter of priority for sustainable development and global disaster risk reduction.

text: Executive function is a collective term for the neural processes that enable effective performance and adaptation to novel, conflicting, or complex situations (Lezak, Howieson, Bigler, & Tranel, 2012). The cued go/no-go task is an experimental paradigm that requires activation of executive functions to achieve fast and accurate performance. In addition to the effectiveness of specific executive processes, however, it has been suggested that specific mechanisms that facilitate other processes are of key importance for optimal performance (Forstmann et al., 2008; Stuss et al., 2005). In the cued go/no-go task, several executive and facilitating processes can be investigated. Just like the activation of any other cognitive process, the effect of facilitation is reflected in altered neural activity. The present study investigates such alterations when instructing participants to optimize performance speed or accuracy in a cued go/no-go task while keeping other task aspects unchanged. That way, the executive processes needed to perform the task are the same in both conditions, while the relative facilitation of the different processes is affected.

text: The globalization is not a point, but a historical process both complicate and immutable, that separates nations, cultures, economies in conventions and technologies along the planet. There are several contributing causes, both historical and contemporary. One main historical driver was the Age of Exploration in the 15th and 16th centuries, when European powers created trade routes and colonized for­eign lands, forming the basis of global eco­nomic networks. The Industrial Revolution additionally boosted globalism in the 18th and 19 centuries by allowing on the one hand the mass production and on the other one enhancing transportation through the locomotive and steamboats and the move of commodities and people. In the 20th and 21st centuries, global transportation, communication (such as radio thoughts amateur people like cell phones and satellite television to navigate to the international barriers and international barriers of distance between trade and communication evaporated. Politically, too, there have been significant contributions: Post–World War II institutions such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the World Bank, and the World Trade Organization (WTO) advanced the ideas of free trade, economic liberalism, and interdependence. The collapse of communism and the advent of market economies in previously closed societies, led by China and Russia, opened new markets, fueling globalization. Courrporate expansion, particularly via multinationals, tied together production and consumption around the world. Furthermore, migration, diasporas and international tourism have developed links between far away countries and continued linguistic, religious and musical traditions brought to new places. Although economics are central to it, globalization is also an ideology, one with faith in capitalism, consumption, and a neoliberal policy script demanding open markets. However, globalization has been met with various controversies. Opponents claim that it has led to increased inequality, cultural homogenization, and environmental degradation. Yet its origins trace back to centuries of human expansion, technological development and policy decisions that have bound the world more tightly together.

text: As Japan has long portrayed itself as a “resource-poor” nation, it is interesting to examine the emergence and stabilization of the resource concept with its associated subtexts. In the current era when knowledge specialization is encouraged, “resource” is an appropriate concept to revisit because it facilitates a unified understanding of the various components of natural systems (water, land, forests, minerals, etc.) as an interconnected entity. Furthermore, the act of defining a resource from other potentially beneficial natural phenomena provides insight into the state of human relationships with the natural world. The resource concept thus opens up a common frame of reference for both natural and social scientists. Public interest in the state of natural resources was sustained until the two “oil shocks” of the 1970s; since then, it has gradually waned or else been neglected by the media and the government. As the gross domestic product (GDP) of Japan became the second largest in the world in the late 1960s, behind the United States, the supply of natural resources rapidly shifted towards importation rather than domestic production.

text: The distinction between validity and soundness is a fundamental paradigm in philosophy and logic used to separate an argument's form from its content. Validity is a feature of the logical form of an argument: if the premises are true, then the conclusion must also be true, but such truth-preservingness, cannot even be defined, in general, for some notions of content. In jargon then, validity can be understood to mean if the conclusion follows from the premises, whether the premises are true or not. For instance, the inference “if it rains then the ground is wet, it is raining; hence the ground is wet” is a valid one as the conclusion is an absolute consequence of the premises. Soundness, on the other hand, is a stricter property and implies that the argument is not only valid, but also that all the premises are true. And this can be so, in fact, only when one has sound arguments, because only in sound arguments is a true conclusion a result of both correct reasoning and true premises. Truth of the premises of a sound argument does not guarantee the truth of the conclusion, since validity does not guarantee truth-preserving properties of arguments whose premises are factually false. For example, “If pigs can fly, then the ground is wet; pigs can fly; so, the ground is wet” is a valid but unsound argument because the premise “pigs can fly” is false. Appreciating this distinction is a keystone in a methodologically sound treatment of arguments, since it distinguishes between formal logical correctness (validity) and empirical truth. Validity preserves consistency of reasoning, soundness preserves truth. This distinction is to be underlined, the philosophers say, to illuminate discussions concerning rational justification, and in order not to confuse the logical form with the factual content. This critical thinking is facilitated when one understands these ideas - he knows when an argument is structured well and when the conclusion is trustworthy.

text: Vulnerability analysis is a measure of the vulnerability of people, the community or an infrastructure that influences their capacity to anticipate, cope with, resist and recover from the impact of a hazard, including social, economic, physical and environmental conditions. It assists in recognizing who or what are most at risk and why, and informed targeted intervention for disaster risk reduction. The tools to assess need used are both qualitative and quantitative and include surveys, focus group discussions, socio-economic profiling and participatory vulnerability mapping. Leading determinants of vulnerability relate to poverty rates, age structure (children, elderly), health status, education, housing quality, availability of infrastructure and services, and rates of exposure to environmental decline. Institutional vulnerability, including governance performance and support to EMR, is also taken into account. Vulnerability is dynamic and may be context-dependent.” 21 It is also influenced by the locality in time, changing over time because of the urbanization, the migration or the climate change separatists can address. Hence, constant and participatory reassessment must be carried out, which includes communities in order to collect local knowledge and social dynamics. Geospatial vulnerability mapping through GIS aids in visualising the vulnerable areas compared to hazards and resources. Through understanding the underlying social determinants of vulnerability, including issues of inequality, marginalization or environmental degradation, assessments support strategies where social justice is integrated as part of the solution to any given hazard situation. Challenges are about data availability, multivariate dimensions of vulnerability, and quantification of social intangibles. Vulnerability assessment is, however, an essential component for the success of DRM informing policy decisions by helping to prioritize resources, devise inclusive policies, and to empower those most at risk of disaster losses in its exercise to lessen the cost of losses and build resilience.

text: In recent years, we have witnessed an exponential growth in the development and deployment of various types of cyber-physical systems (CPSs). They have brought impacts to almost all aspects of our daily life, for instance, in electrical power grids, oil and natural gas distribution, transportation systems, health-care devices, household appliances, and many more. Many of such systems are deployed in the critical infrastructure (CI), life support devices, or are essential to our daily lives. Therefore, they are expected to be free of vulnerabilities and immune to all types of attacks, which, unfortunately, is practically impossible for all real-world systems. One fundamental issue in CPS security is the heterogeneity of the building blocks. CPS are composed of various components in many ways. There are different hardware components such as sensors, actuators, and embedded systems. There are also different collections of software products, proprietary and commercial, for control and monitoring. As a result, every component, as well as their integration, can be a contributing factor to a CPS attack. Understanding the current CPS security vulnerabilities, attacks and protection mechanisms will provide us a better understanding of the security posture of CPS. Consequently, we should be able point out the limitations of CPS that make them subject to different attacks and devise approaches to defend against such attacks.

text: In real estate: The real estate or real property which is the subject of the lease the possessor of the real property (the landlord and lessor) the person who is given the right to possess the real property (the tenant or lessee) A lease is a contract in the form of a conveyance in which the right to possession and use of the real property is transferred. Regulated by the Transfer of Property Act 1882 in India, and other such legislation in other countries, in a lease, an interest in the property is transferred not ownership. Ingredients of a valid lease: (i) competent parties: landlord and tenant; (ii) legal subjects: the assets widely accepted for leasing (including real and personal properties of the real estate kind);(iii) duration-elements in lease must specify when it begins and when it ends-what is minor and what major (in both senses: short term/long term in tenure and/or in term of lease);(iv) the rent: the original amount of the rent stipulated as consideration; (v) transfer of possession and enjoyment: the lessor gives the lessee possession of the use of the property; (vi) Form of writing: a lease must be in writing and registered. Lease deeds are capable of being long term or short term, and the rights and liabilities of the parties are also defined by the lease deed. Termination may take place upon expiration, breach of term or by mutual agreement. The lease provides exclusive use rights and, where permitted, ultimate subletting rights are expressly provided. The tenant is responsible for the responsible use of the space, for returning the property when terminated. A license differs from a lease: a license may not create property interest and a license may be revoked at any time at the will of the proprietor of the property. Meaning thereby it creates legal rights & obligations and vested interest in immovable property of the lessee & so far as the lessor is concerned it guarantees legal security & a fixed liability.

text: Sustainable tourism is integral to travel, as it seeks to manage economic, environmental, and socio-cultural impacts, prevent long-term deteriorations of any target area and make life better for locals and visitors alike. Tourism can directly exert stress on natural resources, ecosystems and heritage but through sustainable tourism, the negative effects are intended to be kept to a minimum, while the benefits are increased. From an environmental perspective, sustainability encourages the use of such things as energy (e.g. using less electricity and other fuel types), waste (e.g. waste reduction, recycling, etc.), water (e.g. using less or protecting supplies), and the protection of ecosystems (e.g. rainforests, wetlands, etc.) in forest products production in order to lessen the industry's environmental impact. It is also an economic assistance by promoting community-based tourism, fair wages and re-investment in social infrastructures. text: Sustainability is a broad-based concept that entails meeting the needs of the current generation while preserving enough resources to enable future generations to meet their own needs. It combines three essential elements: economic growth, social inclusion and environmental protection, and acknowledges the need for sustainable, inclusive and ecologically responsible development. This became an internationally recognised ‘global norm’ following the 1987 Brundtland Report and has been enshrined in international policy agendas like the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Sustainability of economy implies that continuation of income and job opportunities are created without depleting natural resources. Social sustainability is interested in decreasing inequity, providing access to education and health care, securing human rights, and ‘giving a voice’ to people who feel powerless. Environmental sustainability combines practices such as conserving natural biodiversity, minimising carbon footprints, taking precautions against pollution, and ensuring the long-term management of resources. Unsustainable systems–such as rounds of deforestation, reliance on fossil fuels, and uneconomic consumption–sabotage ecosystems; it accelerates climate change and it hazards quality of life for future generations. Sustainable development requires the use of sustainable resources, clean technologies, circular economy solutions, and sustainable patterns of production and consumption. It also calls for international cooperation, inclusive policy-making and investment in green infrastructure and education. Sustainability is something in which businesses, governments and individuals all have a part to play. * And countries are increasingly taking steps that make economic and environmental sense, like investing in solar power, cracking down on waste, and creating jobs in green industries. Finally, sustainable development is not only an environmental question; it is a development path based on the pursuit of fairness of opportunity, resilience, and prosperity over the long term for all people and for the planet.

text: Late-time infrared emission typically indicates the presence of warm dust. The origin and heating mechanism of the dust, however, are not always well constrained. The dust may be newly formed or may have existed at the time of the supernova. If newly formed, the dust may condense from refractory elements in the expanding supernova ejecta or in the cool, dense shell of post-shocked circumstellar gas lying in between the forward and reverse shocks (like the post-shocked environment trailing stellar wind collisions in WR binary systems; Usov 1991). In both cases, several heating mechanisms are possible, including radioactivity, optical emission from the circumstellar interaction, and collisional heating by hot gas in the reverse shock. Alternatively, pre-existing dust may be collisionally heated by hot, shocked gas or radiatively heated by either the peak supernova luminosity or late-time optical emission from circumstellar interaction. In the latter case, an "IR echo" is evident due to light travel time effects. Multiple scenarios can contribute to the late-time infrared flux, as in the cases of SNe 2004et (Kotak et al. 2009; B. E. K. Sugerman et al., in preparation) and 2006jc (Mattila et al. 2008).

text: In recent decades methodological pluralism has become a mainstream commitment within British sociology, although incomplete in its realisation (Ayrton, 2017; Payne et al., 2004). text: Safety valves are a key part of nuclear power plants because of their role as a safety device which protects against overpressure in system such as a reactor coolant system, steam generators, and pressurizers. These valves should automatically open when system pressure exceeds the limit set, releasing steam or coolant to reduce the over-pressure condition to a safe operating level. When the pressure falls to a safe level, the valve closes to prevent escape of fluid or steam. Safety valves are essential for the protection of personnel and equipment from the devastating effects of over pressure leading to pipe and vessel ruptures and radioactivity release. Usually these valves are spring- or pilot-actuated devices and are carefully set to open at particular pressures. Pressurizer safety and relief vales are one of the most important valves in a nuclear reactor as they keep the pressure in the primary loop within so that it operates within safe parameters. Such valves are also important during plant transients or accidents, such as loss-of-coolant events or rapid trips, where pressure transients are more probable. Reliability and safety valves are required to be corrosion-, radiation- and thermal cycle-resistant; and there are periodic tests and inspections to maintain the reliability. Many are redundant — there are several valves in parallel — so that if one fails, others are available to do the safety task. They are elements of an overall safety and security programme and are linked with safety and emergency response analysis. The failure of a safety valve operated not as it should could have serious consequences which is why Safety Valves are regulated and the software has to be certified and the documentation have to be perfect. At the end of the spectrum, safety valves are a passive safety system mechanism to maintain reactor system integrity and containment under normal and accident scenarios, and are an essential last line of defense for pressure failure.

text: In power systems, the term faults is used to describe unusual operations in which undesired electrical connections are established, these actions may breaks the regular current flow. Based on the type of fault and the phases involved, faults are generally categorized as symmetrical and unsymmetrical faults. On the other hand a balanced fault or "three phase fault" is when all the 3-phase are short-circuited simultaneously to one another or earth with equal impedance. It is known as the worst type of fault due to it generating the maximum fault level, and it affects the system symmetrically i.e. balanced fault current in all the phases. It is rare, but important in system design as protective devices must be capable of withstanding such high fault currents. If the same fault occurs in one or two but not all the phases, on the other hand, it is sometimes spoken of as unsymmetrical and may be to neutral or ground. These are single line-to-ground faults, line-to-line faults and double line-to-ground faults. Asymmetric faults produce unbalanced currents and voltages which can unseat the system and result in damage to equipment if not adequately handled. Because power systems are naturally three-phase, the study of unsymmetrical faults becomes more difficult, involving the symmetrical component methods to decompose unbalanced systems into balanced components for calculation. Protective devices, such as relays, are set to quickly detect and disconnect both types of faults in order to maintain system stability, equipment integrity and safety. To design reliable protection systems and to ensure uninterrupted power supply during fault conditions, it is important to know the features of symmetrical and unsymmetrical faults.

text: At the centre of this essay is an argument about the kind of cultural and ideological work effected by the concept of dementia in contemporary popular culture in the global north. Without diminishing the challenges that living with dementia presents nor the importance of neuroscientific and medical research in this field, my focus here is on the ways in which the contemporary meanings of this complex syndrome (George et al., 2011) emerge at the intersection of science, politics, economics, bioethics and culture. This is to foreground the ways in which dementia operates as an ideologically freighted category, utilised and put to work to further particular political and ethical debates as much as it describes a set of pathological processes, a range of symptoms and a lived, embodied experience. (Burke, 2015, pp 9–10) In what follows, I explore the role played by current epistemologies of dementia in relation to ideas about life extension, regeneration and sustainability and the economic and ideological frameworks that underpin them. As Céline Lafontaine argues, in contemporary cultural discourse ageing has become a ‘crisis’ that “cannot be separated from the emergence of a bioeconomy based on the pharmaceutical industry, genetic engineering and the development of biomedical research as a whole”(Lafontaine, 2009, p 56). As a condition that tests the limits of current biomedical research, dementia plays a crucial role in the attribution of ageing as an intractable social and economic problem particularly for the economies of the global north. It is its role as an over-determined point of tangency upon which particular ideas about ageing, regeneration, human value, sustainability and futurity are played out that interests me here.

text: Ethically, moral questions are central in criminology research to protect the rights, dignity, and well-being of research participants and to preserve the integrity of the research process epistemologically. Since some are themselves vulnerable members of the society that are being targeted, ethical standards will guard against the exploitation, the coercion or the harm. Informed consent is a basic ethical obligation of researchers to explain to participants the aims, methods, risks, and benefits of a study and of participants to make a voluntary decision to participate or not to participate. Promises of confidentiality and non-identification by law enforcement are a way to alleviate the fears or identification (and demonization) as lawbreakers or as objects of criminal activity, the latter of which may be threatened by stigma, retaliation or legal revenge. They should not deceive unless it is absolutely necessary, and only when it is “eminently defensible by its value” should they do so, followed by debriefing participants. Proposals are reviewed for ethical standards by such groups as ethical review boards or institutional review boards. And it is also the duty of researchers to report findings truthfully – not to be bias and culture-sensitive pecksniffs! The obedience of ethical principles contributes to trust, participation and the legitimacy and social significance of criminological research. Its stakes include harm and legal consequences along with reputational damage to the discipline such that requirements for ethical behavior are inescapable for the existence of sound and significant criminological investigation.

text: (I) The dichotomy of cognizable and non-cognizable offences is well appreciated in the sphere of criminal jurisprudence and it has bearing on the working of the Police administration. A cognizable offence under Section 2(c) of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC) is one for which a police officer may, in accordance with the first schedule of CrPC, without the authority of a magistrate, initiate an investigation or arrest the perpetrator of the crime without an arrest warrant, detain the accused and also initiate an investigation, by taking them into custody. These crimes are generally serious in nature and involve serious crimes like murder, rape, dacoity, kidnapping, robbery etc, which are grave threat to the society and public order. A non-cognizable offence, as per Section 2(l), is one for which a police officer has no authority to arrest the accused or conduct the investigation without the order of a magistrate. These crimes are less grave, and they specifically include crimes like defamation, public nuisance, simple hurt, and cheating that may cause private harm but do not generally menace public safety in a substantial way. The First Schedule of the CrPC describes the offences as cognizable or non-cognizable, bailable or non-bailable. The difference is meant to allow the police to respond promptly in the more serious cases without first obtaining a judge's permission but still have the courts monitor and protect individual rights in the less serious cases. Nature of the offence also affects the mode of trial, investigative powers as well as the duties of the police. For instance, in a cognizable offence, the police are required to file an FIR immediately after receiving credible information, while the complainant in a non-cognisable case is required to go to a magistrate for his consent. As such, this classification serves to tailor a proper legal response between the exercise of state power and the individual’s freedom, and at the same time serves as means which promote the efficiency of and the justice in the criminal justice system.

text: Autoimmune disorders (AIDs), which as a group affect approximately 8.5% of individuals worldwide [1], are responsible for a substantial amount of disability and morbidity. Some AIDs are organ specific (for example, type 1 diabetes (T1D) targets the pancreas, autoimmune thyroid disease (AITD) attacks the thyroid gland), whereas others can affect multiple organs and/or be associated with systemic manifestations. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is the prototypic systemic AID that can affect multiple organs and can also be associated with significant systemic manifestations, morbidity and early mortality [2]. Most AIDs, including rheumatoid arthritis (RA), ankylosing spondylitis (AS), inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and multiple sclerosis (MS) have a predilection for specific organs (for example, the synovial joints in RA and the gastrointestinal tract in IBD) but are also associated with manifestations outside the primary target organ. Reasons for the diverse manifestations exhibited by different AIDs remain unclear, but recent progress in elucidating genetic susceptibility loci for this group of disorders promises to shed light on this important issue.

text: Despite of the astounding complexity of biological systems, the history of biology is marked by attempts to discern generalizable principles. Functional genomics and its ultimate integration with systems biology remain pivotal to enabling advances in experimental technology that provide detailed and comprehensive information about networks of biological interactions. The Functional Genomics and Systems Biology 2011 conference focused on recent, largely unpublished developments in sequencing-based approaches and computational methods, including their application to chromatin and proteome systems biology. Experts at the meeting also discussed advances in translating these findings to the clinic, with the ultimate goal of promoting personalized medicine. Here, we summarize some of the highlights presented at this exciting conference. A relatively simple genome and the availability of powerful methods for their genetic manipulation make yeast models the central paradigm in systems biology. Brenda Andrews (University of Toronto, Canada) presented the latest applications of synthetic genetic array (SGA) technology to proteome localization, allowing quantitative determination of subcellular localizations for the majority of yeast proteins. Published work from the laboratories of Andrews and Charles Boone (University of Toronto, Canada) exploited the SGA method to produce a genome-scale landscape of genetic interactions in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Integration of this technology with high-content microscopy screening of a green fluorescent protein fusion library allowed construction of abundance localization networks across the yeast proteome, including flux networks of dynamic protein localization changes.

text: Introduction Political theatre is a type of theatre that aspires to engage with, critique or even influence political ideas, structures and events, exploring the stage as a space from which to provoke thought, encourage action, disturb power and investigate ¿how life ought to be livedies. It purposefully confronts social injustice, power relations and ideological oppression, while drawing attention to the lives and suffering of the underclasses and the workings of systems of exploitation and oppression. In contrast to mere escapism, political theatre seeks to educate audiences about their role as political beings in society, and to promote critical reflection about pressing issues such as war, inequality, racism, colonialism, environmental destruction and human rights. Its methods can be anything from ‘realistic’ depictions of social conditions to the most stylized, symbolic and experimental efforts to break the boredom and passivity of the consumer and involve viewers both mentally and emotionally. Playwrights such as Bertolt Brecht famously invented devices like the "alienation effect" in order that the audience would not just identify with the characters but rather examine the social forces surrounding the drama. 1) Political Theatre It tends to be situationally-bound – a collaborative creation by performers, writers and directors in an attempt to address current issues and current characters. It has been a weapon of resistance and a tool of propaganda in the hands of revolutionaries and activists, governments and communities trying to shape public opinion or galvanize support for the causes they represent. Varieties of political theatre Street theatre, agitprop, documentary drama and participatory or immersive theatre are just a few of the creative forms in which political theatre may emerge, moving out of traditional theatres to extend its reach to new and diverse audiences. Its aims are not only to reflect political realities but to intervene in them, providing spaces for debate, solidarity, and the imagining of other worlds. Political theatre does its work by bringing to light what has been kept hidden, by interrogating dominant stories, and by speaking out of turn. It expresses the belief that art is not neutral but always an expression of power relations, and that performance can make those relations visible, critique them, undo them. But even when censored or silenced, political theatre has managed to 4 speak truth to power, employing metaphor, irony, and reversal to evade strictures and provoke resistance. At its core, political theatre involves the promise of putting the singular force of live performance in the service of confronting pressing social and political issues – targeted not towards having the audience see the world differently, but perhaps, to act to change it.

text: A Boiling Water Reactor (BWR) is used for the generation of electrical power and isot Whereas PWRs work at significantly higher pressures (usually 2200 psi = 150 atm), about the same pressure we have in our cars tires, BWRs operate at only a few times atmospheric pressure, ~70 atmospheres, which allows water to boil in the core of the reactor instead. Steam created by the system enters a turbine, which powers a generator to produce power. The former is easier to operate and less costly to build, but the latter has to remain free of radioactive substances, because the water used to drive it has been in direct contact with radioactive fuel. As far as the heat is concerned, every reactor design has safety features that are built into the reactor vessel to control the heat and pressure and also where the neutrons are absorbed by the control rods, which controls the fissioning back and forth. In such BWRs the neutrons and fuel rod, used to maintain a steady chain reaction, are slowed and cooled by water. They are easier to manufacture and because of swifter power changes and easier maintenance, but steam contami- nation has been an issue with much effort being applied towards control. text: Weathering and erosion are natural processes that wear down and carry rocks, minerals, and sediments on the Earth's crust. Weathering denotes the breakdown of rocks and minerals present in situ into smaller fragments by either physical, chemical or biological agencies. This is non-movement related and can be due to temperature, freeze/thaw cycles, root growth of plants or reaction with water and gases. Weathering can be classified as mechanical (or physical) and chemical. Mechanical weathering is the physical breakdown of rock into smaller and smaller pieces; there are no changes in the mineral composition of the broken rocks, not even a little bit. Chemical weathering results from chemical changes to the minerals that make up the rock (e.g., elements are removed by water, oxygen, or acids). What is erosion? Erosion, in contrast, is the process in which weathered material is moved (a) away from its source or (b) to another location by natural agents such as water, wind, ice and gravity. Rivers transport sediment downstream, glaciers pick away at and pulverize rock as they pass over it, wind picks up and moves dust-size particles of dust and sand, gravity triggers landslides or rockfalls. Over time, erosion leads to a change in the face of the earth; valleys are carved, deltas formed and sediments repositioned. Though weathering acts to weaken and prepare rocks for erosion, erosion is the addition of societal care that plays a more active role in working rock on its journey toward delicious soil and the rock cycle. Combined, weathering and erosion are an important part of shaping the surface of the Earth as well as providing necessary upkeep to our ecosystem.

text: The Western Roman Empire's collapse in 476 CE was the result of a centuries-long series of internal and external pressures. One major cause was political instability, particularly the rapid succession of emperors, civil wars, and military defeats, which may have frustrated attempts to address pressing economic and social problems. The empire suffered from the economic malaise with chronic inflation, heavy taxation, excessive forced labor, and the demise of trade that undermined agricultural and commercial prosperity of the cities. The empire was overextended, making it increasingly difficult for such vast borders to be defended against continuous pressure from groups like the Visigoths, Vandals, Huns, and Ostrogoths, whose migrations and invasions led to Rome being sacked. Increasingly it became less efficient, relying heavily on mercenaries whose loyalty was divided and were of inferior discipline. Social dissolution also contributed to the weakening empire: a falling population, increasing disparity between rich and poor, and the loss by urban Romans of civic pride undermined existing social institutions. Christianity’s rise also transformed the ideological order, with loyalty being redirected away from the state and toward the Church — sometimes leading to warfare between competing religious factions. Efforts by emperors, such as Diocletian and Constantine, to stabilize the empire through political and administrative reforms were not without problems—the reforms did stabilize the empire, but they also caused a collapse in the army, citizenship, bureaucracy, and the tax system, leading to a sense that the empire was falling apart. With the geopolitical transition the Eastern, or Byzantine, Empire became more powerful while the Western Roman Empire became more vulnerable. Although the Eastern Empire limped along for a millennium, Rome fell in 476 C.E., when the Germanic chieftain Odoacer deposed the last Western emperor, Romulus Augustulus. The fall wasn't fast or immediate—it was a slow, drawn-out capitulation as a failure or system failed spread between governance, economy, society, religion, military readiness and more, all weakened by non-stop attacks against one of the most powerful empires to ever exist.

text: The sum rule of probability is a basic rule for determining the probability of the occurrence of at least one of two or more events. The rule changes slightly whether the events are mutually exclusive or not. When the events are mutually exclusive, i.e., in case both of them cannot occur simultaneously (like throwing a die and getting 2 or 5), simple addition rule applies P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). This is just summing up the probabilities since each one does not intersect. For instance, in a fair six-sided die the probability of rolling a 2 or a 5 is P(2 or 5) = P(2) + P(5) = 1/6 + 1/6 = 1/3. However, this only holds when the events are mutually exclusive (i.e. if one happens the other one cannot happen), and if the events are not mutually exclusive (i.e. they can occur at the same time), then the rule should be modified to reflect the overlap so to not count it twice. Here, the general rule of addition is: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) – P(A and B). The item P(A and B) is the chance that both items occur, by subtracting it we avoid counting the cross over two times. For example, for a deck of cards, if A represents the event of drawing a heart and B is the event of drawing a king, then the probability of drawing a heart or king would be P(A) + P(B) – P(A and B). There is only one king of hearts, and it is in both events, which need to be removed. The sum and product rule are fundamental concepts not just in (theoretical) probability, but also in applied decision making under uncertainty. It’s useful for computing risk, planning moves and considering games where many outcomes are a possibility. It doesn't matter if you are working with the stock market, playing a game with friends, or trying to predict the weather: the addition rule is a way to combine different probabilities and still keep the logic straight.

text: A food chain is a series of species that are connected through their feeding, each member of which serves as a source of food or energy for the next. Often, this begins with a producer – in most cases, a green plant or other photosynthetic organism that makes food from sunlight. The producer is consumed by herbivore, which is subsequently consumed by carnivore, and on to tertiary and higher-level consumers, often culminating finally in apex predator. Decomposers, such as fungi and bacteria, decompose dead bodies, and circulate nutrients back to the environment. Food chains are basic models that emphasize energy transfer but are often overly simplistic ways of representing natural ecosystems, since many organisms are known to eat more than one kind of food and be eaten by more than one type of predator. A pyramid does not illustrate such complexity as well as a food web, which is linkages of different food chains showing numerous feeding relationships between members of a community. Food webs demonstrate the complexities of the flow of energy and the reliance of species on one another. They show how changes in one population can propagate through the ecosystem to impact others. Food chains and food webs are essential concepts in ecology as they show the flow of energy, balance of populations and the stability of the ecosystem. The relative length and complexity of food chains and webs differ among ecosystems, and these properties are linked with diversity and productivity. Studying them helps ecologists manage natural resources, save endangered species and predict how ecosystems will respond to change.

text: The basis on which coral reefs build up is the mass of skeleton formed from calcium carbonate by small animals called coral polyps. These are colonial polyps and they host endosymbiotic zooxanthellae, microscopic algae. The algae live in the tissues of the coral and photosynthesise – they create nutrients for themselves and enjoy a secure home. For the construction of coral reefs, several environmental conditions are required, such as clear and warm (23–29°C) shallow water, so that sunlight can reach down to the endosymbiotic algae that live on top of the corals; stable salinity levels in the water column: low nutrient and sediments concentrations. Larvae settle onto a surface, such as rock or dead coral, and begin to secrete calcium carbonate to form an exoskeleton, a process called calcification. Reef structures become more three-dimensional through time, as new generations of corals build from the skeletons upwards. Corals reefs come in three flavours, from the kind that lie right up against a coast (fringing reefs) to those which sit away from land, separated by lagoons (barrier reefs) or with a hole in the middle and typically some growing on or around a sunken volcanic island (atolls). Coral reefs are home to an oasis of biodiversity, including 1 2 A coral reef is a litmus test of ecol- ecosystem function and breakwater services (De’ath et al. They also serve to protect the coast by reducing wave activity and guarding against erosion. But coral reefs are highly sensitive to such shifts, particularly climate change. So when the water gets hotter, they "bleach", kicking out their algae, losing an energy source and eventually dying. Ocean acidification, caused by higher CO2 levels, also dissolves coral skeletons made from calcium carbonate so reefs become sterile. Pollution, over-fishing, harmful fishing technologies and coastal development are further threats. Conservation actions are aimed at decreasing local pressures, protecting reef habitat in the form of MPAs, restoring damaged reefs and ameliorating the effects of global climate change to maintain these priceless ecosystems for our children and grandchildren.

text: If one of the parties involved in a binding agreement does not meet his or her contractual obligations, you have a breach of contract and the wronged party can pursue legal recourse. The main form of relief is monetary relief, that is compensation or damages, which is money to make up for the loss sustained from the defendant's infraction. There are several kinds of such damages: compensatory damage (to compensate for the actual loss sustained), consequential damages (the loss resulting from the failure of the promisor to perform), punitive damages (should the breach of promise be willful), and nominal damages (where no actual damage was caused, but a legal right was invaded). Another type of remedy is called specific performance, where the court tells the party who breached the contract to fulfill their side of the bargain as it was outlined in the contract, which is common in cases of unique goods or services. Injunctions provide another form of relief, forbidding a party from doing something that would violate the agreement. Rescission enables the aggrieved party to annul the contract and to be returned to their original position. Restitution returns the benefit that the breaching party has received. If A paid B in advance for a service that B ended up not giving, for example, restitution required B to pay that money back. The selection of a remedy is determined by the character of the breach and the surrounding situation. The goal of the courts was to restore the non-breaching party to the same position that party would have occupied as if the contract had been properly performed. These remedies further the goal of contracts—to assure the performance of promises and to enable honesty in transactions, business and private.

text: Human rights hu·man rights Human rights are the rights and freedoms to which everyone is entitled by virtue of being human. Those rights include a broad array of protections and entitlements, from civil and political rights, like freedom of speech and a fair trial, to economic, social and cultural rights, like the rights to education, health care and a decent living standard. It took centuries for the concept of human rights to evolve, but they very likely were grounded in legal and philosophical traditions which themselves recognized the inherent dignity of human beings. Classical works like the Code of Hammurabi and religious commands provided the germ of ideas about what is just and morally required certainly, but the specific modern phrase ‘human rights’ was mainly coined in the Enlightenment, when the bringing together of a pre-modern idea of natural law were combined with a new focus on the freedom of individual people (re: Laura Maguire) by philosophers and lawyers. They included moments like the Magna Carta, the English Bill of Rights and the American and French Revolutions — which led people to ask questions about how to limit governmental authority and protect personal liberties. But the horrors of World War II, including the Holocaust, laid bare the catastrophic consequences of impunity for discrimination and oppression and spurred acceptance of the concept of an overarching system for protecting human rights around the world. Finally, in 1948, the United Nations adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), which packaged a wide-ranging set of rights and principles that it wanted to apply to all human beings regardless of race, gender, nationality or creed. Human rights have since expanded to include concerns about, for example, gender inequality, racial justice, the environment and the rights of marginalized groups elsewhere. Human rights remain unequal in enforcement, but they have been a bedrock of international law, diplomacy and activism, and have sparked campaigns and pioneering initiatives to confront oppression, discrimination and violence across the globe. The ongoing development of human rights is a reflection of the never-ending human aspiration for justice, equality and dignity for all of us.

text: Mulching, an agricultural practice involving applying a blanketing layer of filling (such as inorganic and organic materials) on the surface of the soil around crops, is widely recognized for its power to provide benefits in terms of soil fertility, moisture retention and yield monitoring. Organic mulches are the natural materials like straw, leaves, grass clippings, compost, wood chips, crop residues, and inorganic mulches are the artificial substances like plastic films, stones, gravel, or synthetic fabrics. The major advantage of mulch is water retention; it holds in moisture by blocking out the sun and wind, keeping soil environment stable and moist for roots while minimizing the need for irrigation. Mulching also contributes to soil temperature moderation, maintaining cooler temperatures during warm weather and warmer temperatures during cold snaps, promoting a healthy environment around plant roots. Weed suppression is a further important aspect: by shading germinating weed seeds in the soil with its smothering layer, the mulch prevents them from even germinate in the first place, so that it reduces the competition for nutrients and water and generally decreases the need for herbicides or manual weeding. Furthermore, organic mulches break down with time, thus returning organic matter and nutrients to the soil, with the added benefit of enhancing soil structure, aeration, and fertility, and enhancing the activities of soil microbes indispensable in nutrient transformations. Mulches also reduce wind and water erosion of soil by impeding the rain drops and run-oft from breaking up the topsoil. Mulch [Not only for agronomic purposes, mulching can help to increase the yield and quality of crops by enhancing the growth environment of the root system and releasing pests and diseases. It is a common practice in home gardening, orchards, vegetable gardens, and on large farms. Mulching is particularly useful as a water-saving strategy in water-deficient areas. Sustainable agriculture recommends mulching as an environment-friendly technique, which improves healthy of soil, saves resources, and avoids chemical input, and thus contributing to eco-friendly and hocistic farming practices.

text: Measure-valued diffusions are often motivated by first considering a class of prelimiting finite-population models. The dynamics in such discrete contexts are easily specified in terms of the behavior of the individuals in the population, and the composition of the population is naturally represented as a measure on the set, E, of possible types. Measure-valued diffusions then arise because the associated discrete measure-valued processes behave sensibly (after appropriate rescaling) in the large population limit. On the other hand, the discrete population models which keep track of the fates of individuals make no sense for infinite-population sizes. Thus, while it might be convenient in applications to think of the measure-valued diffusion as describing the evolution of a hypothetically infinite population, it is difficult to make this precise. Donnelly and Kurtz (1996, 1999) have recently given a discrete construction of a class of neutral measure-valued population processes. Loosely speaking, the idea is to "bring back the particles." text: They are huge, flowing bodies of ice formed from the accumulation and compaction of snow that is transformed over time, slipping under the pressure of its own weight, and reshaping the Earth's geology through which it flows. They commonly are divided into two categories, alpine (or valley) glaciers and continental glaciers. Alpine glaciers occur in mountainous regions and are confined to the valley by the morphology of the topography. They create sharp land forms such as U-shaped valleys, cirques, arêtes, and horns. Such glaciers tend to be much smaller and more localized, but can still be caused to exert significant erosive force. Continental glaciers (ice sheets) are enormous ice masses that cover landmasses and are not a part of the sea, such as Antarctica and Greenland. They are not limited, as alpine glaciers are, by topography and can spread in all directions. Ice-cap continental glaciers are a lesser variety, smaller than 50,000 km^2 in area. Other glacier types are piedmont glaciers, when valley glaciers spill out onto relatively flat plain and fan out; tidewater glaciers that end in the sea and calve pieces that become icebergs; and hanging glaciers, which cling to a steep mountain slope or cliff. Glacier types play a different role in erosion, sediment fluxes and sea level. In addition to affecting our quality of life, their distribution and behaviour are also particularly sensitive signals of changes in the climate, since small changes in temperature and in the position and frequency of precipitation can critically affect their expansion or retreat.

text: The fruit is the mature ovary of a flowering plant (or angiosperm), and the mature ovary with its attached seeds is the classically recognized and most widely accepted “fruit” (Givnish 2002). In angiosperms, after successful fertilization, the flower's ovary develops into a fruit and the ovules become seeds within the ovary. Fruits have a number of important functions: they protect the seeds as they develop, aid in seed dispersal, and sometimes supply food to animals and humans. There are three types of fruits, classified according to their origin and structure: simple fruits, aggregate fruits, and multiple fruits. Simple fruits arise from a single ovary of a single flower and can be either dry or fleshy. Examples are mango (a fleshy simple fruit) and pea (a dry simple fruit). Aggregate fruits are also composed of a single flower, but with several ovaries, and small fruitlets that eventually turn into a larger fruit (e.g., strawberry, raspberry). Many plant species have inflorescences from which a cluster of several fruits grow together in the form of a single structure, such as pineapple and jackfruit. With regards to texture, fruit can either be fleshy (such as tomato or orange) or dry (as in nut or bean ). It is common for succulent fruits to be sought out by animals in exchange for seed dispersal because of their attractive sweet taste and nourishment value. Mature dry fruits may split open (dehisce) along one or more seam to release the seeds, or they may stay intact (indehiscent). Some fruits, such as bananas, are capable of fruiting without fertilization, a phenomenon known as parthenocarpy, which produces seedless fruit. Fruits are important, ecologically (survival and distribution of species) and economically (food, vitamins, fibers, and income), not only for plant species, but also for the consumption of nutrients and health. They also have implications in plant taxnomy, and are often used by scientists to describe and classify different types of fruit based on their structure.

text: Supporting details are sentences or pieces of information within a paragraph that provide more detail about the topic sentence. text: Development of a numerical description of neutrino-radiation-hydrodynamic (RHD) phenomena presents numerous modeling challenges. These challenges result from complexity of the system—complexity stemming both from the sheer number of important physical components and from the diversity and variability of microphysical interactions among these components. In the core-collapse supernova problem, this complexity presents itself in a number of ways. There is complexity associated with interacting flows of matter and neutrino radiation. These flows exhibit coupling strengths that vary spatially, which change as a region evolves. There is typically strong coupling between matter and neutrino radiation in dense regions near the center, weak coupling in more diffuse outer regions of the core, and some kind of intermediate-strength coupling elsewhere. Where coupling is weaker, neutrino-radiation is not in local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) with matter. Adding to this is the presence of multiple species of neutrinos, which are coupled by pair-production processes and by exchange of energy and lepton number with matter. Hence, neutrino distributions span a large range of classical and quantum-mechanical behavior. There is also a complex nuclear chemistry present, which is mediated by both strong and weak interactions. Finally, the matter is described by a non-ideal-gas equation of state (EOS), which includes phase transitions and other complex behavior.
