text: The ozone layer is the portion of Earth's stratosphere that contains relatively high concentrations of ozone (O?) molecules, and it is located approximately 10 to 30 kilometers above Earth's surface. “What the Ozone Layer Does and About CFCs and the Ozone Layer,” The Ozone Layer Protection The ozone layer’s most important role is to filter out the sun’s harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation, most of the UV-B and UV-C radiation, that can cause human skin cancer, cataracts, and harm the human immune system, as well as damage plants and animals, including the ocean’s plankton, the bottom of the ocean’s ability to produce our food, and marine ecosystems. By screening out these destructive rays, the ozone layer serves as Earth’s natural sunscreen. Human activities, including the use of chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) in refrigeration, aerosol sprays, and industrial solvents, caused substantial depletion of the ozone, particularly above the Antarctic, the infamous "ozone hole." The 1987 Montreal Protocol, a global treaty, hastened the end of a number of ozone-destroying compounds and has been pivotal in the ozone layer's ongoing recovery. The recovery process continues and will last for many decades, but the role of the ozone layer is critical in the past and present equilibrium and protection of the biosphere from harmful solar radiation. Vigilance and compliance with international agreements are essential for full recovery and sustained stability.

text: Experimental theatre comprises a range of theatrical genres and practices, from the early avant garde to contemporary devised theatre and postdramatic theatre. From 20th century on, experimental theatre has most of the time been created to try and discover new forms, new processes or new modes of presentation rather than to devalue or to replace a traditional production. This tradition has gone against conventions — plot and setting linear narratives, attached from reality setting and characterisation — opting instead for fragmented, abstract or immersive performances that involve the audience in new ways. Experimental theatre often includes multimedia source such as video, projection, digital sound, and other elements which may overlap with the field of media arts. Influenced by avant-garde movements including Dada, Surrealism, and Theatre of the Absurd, it tends towards the philosophy of being nonsensical in nature, to regard the manifestations of absurdity in life, in general, as a logical response to a world made up of false logic. Directors and playwrights such as Antonin Artaud, Jerzy Grotowski and Peter Brook have been leading the way, focusing on physicality, ritual, and the deconstruction of language and form. Experimental theatre also deviates from the traditional theatre space and can be performed in atypical locations from a warehouse, to the streets, or online. Through their break with the convention of popular commercial theatre, the experimental performances call for a new awareness of what constitutes theatre and new spectatorial involvement.It is not about consuming but about interpreting, not about a passive reception but about an active spectatorship. This movement has had a major influence on today's theatre, allowing it to find new forms of expression, and serving as a means of democratizing stories and artistic voices. Although difficult or obscure, experimental theatre is necessary to break artistic barriers and widen the spectrum of human artistic expression.

text: In international law, human rights are considered to be those that are the most basic rights and freedoms to which all human beings are entitled, irrespective of what country they live in, what culture they belong to, and what religion they practice; or indeed, if they have any religion at all. These rights are included in numerous international treaties, conventions, declarations and covenants developed by international bodies in the years since the UDHR was written and signed into effect in 1948 by the United Nations. The human rights encompass, civil and political rights – which are all together known as the first-generation rights that are related to the right like life, liberty, freedom of expression; and economic, social and cultural rights, such as the right to education, health, and decent working conditions. Human rights are further secured in international law through international treaties, notably the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR), states are legally required to respect, protect and fulfil the former through binding positive action. International organizations including the UN, the ICC and regional organizations such as the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) oversee and implement policies to protect human rights. When the actions of a state violate these rights, individuals can turn to international legal instruments for recourse, but enforcement is difficult without the compliance of states. Non-governmental organizations and advocacy groups work on the front lines of promoting human rights by appealing to public sentiment, documenting violations and putting pressure on governments to adhere to international norms. International law makes human rights a priority, but the law’s power is only as strong as the commitment of states to enforce it, and the world’s will to must punish those who violate it.

text: Zero tolerance policingZero tolerance policing refers to a rigid form of policing built upon the enabling of enforcement officers to identify and punish relatively minor public order offenses in an effort to prevent more serious crime. Based on the "broken windows" theory, which holds that visible signs of disorder and minor offenses set the stage for more serious crime, zero tolerance policies are intended to maintain public order by addressing minor transgressions on the spot and without exception. This usually features heightened police presence, a high volume of arrests and citations for things such as loitering, vandalism, public drunkenness, plus high penalties for other individuals who dare violate the restrictions. Its proponents maintain that zero tolerance policing lowers crime, enhances public safety and sends out the signal that lawbreaking will not be tolerated. But over-policing, disproportionately against marginalized people, and strains between police and citizens are among the myriad criticisms of the site-based method. It can also result in minor behaviors being criminalized and mass incarceration. One criticism of the zero-tolerance style of policing is that it diverts resources from more serious crimes and also from looking into the cause of the problems. Implementation requires careful monitoring in order to prevent arbitrary and abusive conduct as well as to maintain community trust. The use of zero tolerance has been controversial, but effective, tool in policing to prevent disorder and ensure public safety.

text: Cultural tourism is a powerful tool for enhancing the visitor experience, honoring and recounting cultural heritage, promoting intercultural understanding, and supporting sustainable economic development in destinations by refocusing travel on the exploration and appreciation of a community’s traditions, history, art, architecture, language, rituals, festivals, spiritual beliefs, cuisine, and ways of life. It provides the travelers with authentic and deeper experiences rather than a superficial sight-seeing, concerning the soul-hood of a place: heritage and values through visiting historical monuments, museum & sites inscribed on the world heritage list of the UNESCO, local markets, indigenous communities and participation of events and cultural evening activities. In economic terms, cultural tourism creates an attractive source of income for local communities, bringing in several different types of tourists prepared to spend more in order to have the quality immersive experience, as well as create working positions in heritage conservation, guiding, handycrafts, performing arts, culinary heritage etc. This spending flows into the local economy through the multiplier effect, benefiting local small businesses, craftspeople, farmers and service providers, and driving inclusive growth in rural or marginalized areas where few other opportunities may exist for economic activity. Cultural tourism further prompts infrastructure provision, including roads, reception facilities, directional signboards and sanitation facilities, and is a benefit not only to the tourists but also to the local people. Heritage preservation Cultural tourism programme is, crucially, a means to conserve heritage sites and monuments, providing economic reasoning for government to invest in the maintenance of those old buildings and sites as well as traditional crafts, intangible culture including music, dance, stories and language, that would otherwise be wiped out by the wave of industrialisation or disregard for historical significance. It enables communities to determine the sharing of their culture: respectfully, locally, and on their own terms, not as symbols that can be vandalized or antibalized to capitalize on mass tourism. At the social level, cultural tourism is a catalyst of mutual understanding and peace between hosts and tourists, allowing them to exchange views, confront stereotypes and build empathy by building relationships beyond borders. It can also bolster community pride and unity, sparking a resurgence of traditions and fostering a sense of ownership of culture. But the potential advantages of cultural tourism are contingent on sustainable, participatory management that is sensitive to the cultural integrity of sites, minimizes the impact of tourists, resists over-commercialization and promotes equitable relationships in economic gains. This also encompasses community participation in planning and decision making, strengthening local capabilities in tourism for local operators, equitable benefit sharing processes and facilitating responsible marketing that brings respectful visitors. Local state and local governments, non-governmental organizations and the private sector all have a critical role to play in enhancing these efforts through policy development, funding, training and collaboration. In the end, the function of cultural tourism is to link the visitor and the host community by providing immersive, learning and transformative experiences while supporting the sustainable development, cultural preservation and economic prosperity of destinations around the world.

text: Glycolysis, which is the degradation of a six-carbon sugar to two molecules of pyruvate, is the principal route through which glucose is broken down to provide energy in the form of ATP and NADH. It exists in the cytoplasm of all cells and does not require oxygen to function (anaerobic). Glycolysis consists of ten enzymes catalyzed reactions and is divided into two stages: the energy investment phase and the energy generation phase. During the energy investment phase two ATP molecules are consumed for the phosphorylation of glucose to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. This is then split between two three-carbon molecules to yield G3P. In the energy rewarding phase, each G3P are catabolysed in a series of rections resulting in the production of four ATP(two per G3P)and two NADH forming two pyruvate molecules. The key enzymes are hexokinase, phosphofructokinase, and pyruvate kinase. Glycolysis provides quick energy and intermediates for the Krebs cycle and fermentation. It is especially important in organs that are dependent on glucose for energy, including the brain and red blood cells. As a summary, glycolysis is a main metabolic pathway for glucose metabolism that yields pyruvate, two ATPs and two NADHs as the most important energy and building block.

text: The willful and repeated execution of an action induces a series of psychomotor adaptations consistent with increased efficiency (Brener, 1986). At the neurophysiological level, the brain becomes better at discriminating processes that are functional to optimal execution from those that are not; with repetition, the former are enhanced and the latter suppressed (Hatfield, 2018; Hatfield & Hillman, 2001). The execution of an action is characterized by a distinctive spatiotemporal pattern in the EEG, involving oscillatory activity within the alpha frequency (i.e., around 10 Hz) band. Specifically, prior to and during movement, alpha decreases over motor areas of the cortex while concurrently increasing over nonmotor areas (Neuper & Pfurtscheller, 2001; Pfurtscheller, 1992). The function of alpha is to exert inhibitory control across the cerebral cortex, whereby higher alpha indicates stronger neuronal inhibition and less alpha indicates greater release from inhibition (Klimesch, 2012; Klimesch, Sauseng, & Hanslmayr, 2007). Based on this evidence, the gating-by-inhibition model (Jensen & Mazaheri, 2010) proposes that neuronal excitability is diverted away from regions showing higher alpha power (i.e., greater inhibition) and routed toward regions showing lower alpha power (i.e., less inhibition). Consequently, the alpha gating model describes a mechanism that explains how the brain accomplishes the activation of motor areas alongside the inhibition of nonmotor areas to achieve psychomotor efficiency.

text: Reader’s advisory is a niche library service in which librarians engage in one-on-one or group reference consultations, suggesting books or other reading material based on patrons’ interests, reading level, preferences, and moods — a mix of book smarts, human warmth, and situational pedicure. While reference helps answer factual questions, reader’s advisory is based on a subjective process—where personal reading tastes are revealed through discussions around genres, authors, pacing, themes, emotional tone, and previous reads; such as a patron who says “I loved The Night Circus—what should I read next?” suggestions like Erin Morgenstern’s The Starless Sea or Holly Black’s The Cruel Prince. “Librarians are on the front lines,” as Abrams put it, and they’re on top of new titles, new authors, diverse voices across genres — historical fiction, romance, mystery, graphic novels, memoirs, poetry — as well as backlist treasures and award-winners. Discussion strategies such as “read-alikes,” series discovery, theme browsing, and soft introductions to new genres with obvious analogies. Reader’s advisory can be cross-channel: in person, a friendly conversation at a service desk or cushy chair, through email or chat, on good-looking, thoughtfully curated shelves (doesn’t every library know the importance of a book display?), on seasonal reading lists, via bookish displays, social media posts, videos, community events and book clubs. It promotes literacy by building reading confidence, expanding horizons and encouraging a life long relationship with books. The walls of its digital gorge enclose as well young-adult, large-print, dual-language editions. Reader’s advisory is as much about connection, trust, reading joy, as it is about recommendation; librarians listen, remember, take note of emotional tone, and follow up with new reads over time. This service impacts user satisfaction, collection circulation, and library experience, contributing to the library’s welcoming and personal identity as a community space for exploring.

text: Artificial intelligence is becoming a crucial tool in solving crimes from predicting where a crime has the most likelihood of occurring to helping police officers gather as well as interpret information on-the-spot. Tools of artificial intelligence — including machine learning, facial recognition, natural language processing and predictive analytics — can help police agencies quickly interpret an ocean of data faster and more efficiently than humans ever could, finding patterns that they would never see in real time. AI can be used to examine surveillance footage and match the faces of suspects to those in facial databases, detect fraudulent banking transactions and, in city crime prediction systems that may lead to proactive policing. In cybercrime investigations, AI is used to search for malware, track darknet activity and trawl digital footprints. But AI in crime detection also presents significant ethical and legal challenges, despite all its promise. The dominant negatives are system bias, opaqueness, potential exploitation by customer organisations and human rights vacuums.” For example, facial recognition technology has proven more likely to falsely identify people of color and subject them to wrongful arrest. And, if it is trained on biased data, predictive policing could further propagate systemic injustices. AI can only be used to keep the public safe if it is open (and not mystical), accountable and part of a system that is governed by law. When used ethically, AI is the crime-fighting and justice-delivering technology of the future.

text: Climate justice is a concept that acknowledges the moral and political aspects of climate change, insisting that its effects and the burden of responsibility are not uniformly distributed across the earth or society. It contends that the people who have contributed the least to greenhouse gas pollution — typically low-income countries and marginal populations — suffer most from the impacts of climate change like extreme weather, rising seas and food shortages even though they have the least ability to protect themselves. Climate justice requires fair responses to these inequalities.Read a summary of how these are related and whyIf you are like me, you don't want to dig into life under the hood and actually solve root causes— like the breakdown of human community, or unsustainable patterns ofconsumerism. This involves among other things ensuring that climate and adaptation policies do not further social injustice but are informed and guided by principles of justice, human rights and sustainable development. It also emphasizes the role of participation and representation of vulnerable communities in shaping climate choices. Climate justice is based on equitable treatment for future generations under the framework of intergenerational equity, its question being who owes what to the future generations. The frame joins social and ecological justice and human rights arguments to call for climate policies that are fair, equitable, and provide opportunities for dispossessed peoples. Global collaboration, equitable financial mechanisms including climate funds, technology transfer as well as capacity building for vulnerable countries are also necessary to ensure climate justice. It means confronting institutionalized inequalities around race, class, gender and geography. Climate justice reframes climate change not only in scientific or environmental terms but as an ethical and political challenge and calls societies to embrace both vulnerable actors and resilient, sustainable futures.

text: Through the policy of price stability, the Central Bank contributes to the stability and sustainable growth of the economy. One of the its key role is to guide through the application of monetary policy tools the level of aggregate demand and money supply in the economy. This has led to central banks, through their monetary policy instruments, applying a contractionary monetary policy where the policy interest rate (repo rate) is increased to make borrowing more expensive. That dampens both consumer spending and business investment, cooling inflationary pressures. The act also performs an open market operation known as selling securities to drain excess reserves from banks. It could also raise cash reserve ratio (CRR) or statutory liquidity ratio (SLR) which is a proportion of deposits banks have to maintain with it, curtailing banks’ capacity to lend. By tightening credit these measures serve to brake excess demand, a frequent cause of inflation. The central bank also has a finger on the pulse of inflation expectations — it uses communication and policy signaling to shape public and market attitudes. It also produces information and forecasts that inform decisions by governments and the private sector. In emerging economies, where inflation can be erratic because of swings in food and fuel prices, the central bank might be expected to work with the government to promote fiscal discipline and to avoid excessive public spending. The central bank also serves, in effect, as a guardian of price stability, adjusting interest rates, managing liquidity, and fostering confidence in the monetary system to ensure that inflation is kept within a target band that is supportive of sustainable growth.

text: Windbreaks are planted or natural barrier that protects an area from strong winds, reduces soil erosion, and increases soil moisture in agriculture. Windbreaks are planted in various setback locations of an open field, crop field, rangeland, or building in or exposed to the wind-prone area to protect soil, crops, animals and buildings from wind damage such as wind erosion, wind desiccation, wind damage and windbreak related hazards. Windbreak trees are generally hardy, fast and dense growing, such as eucalyptus, poplar or casuarina. A well defined wind barrier can reduce wind speed away behind it up to 10 – 20 times its height, hence help reducing losses to wind and improve to microclimatic conditions. Windbreaks also aid in the conservation of soil moisture, by lessening evaporation, preventing dust, and protecting young plants and delicate crops. On farms, windbreaks reduce exposure, enhance health and productivity of livestock, particularly under extreme weather conditions. They can also add to biodiversity by providing refuges for birds and beneficial insects. Windbreaks add beauty to farmland and can also act as natural fences. In arid and semi-arid areas they are important in the prevention of desertification, stabilising sand dune and preventing wind erosion. Some windbreaks are multifunctional, providing additional products such as fruit, timber, or fuelwood. The design of a windbreak including species selection, orientation, spacing, and maintenance is important for long-term windbreak effectiveness. Windbreaks are a cost-effective, easily applied and widely adaptable technology in sustainable land management with multifaceted values for agricultural productivity, soil conservation and ecological stability of different farming systems.

text: Libel and slander are types of defamation—saying or writing untrue things about another person or entity in a way that damages that entity or person. There is one distinction to be made: the medium of communication itself; libel refers to a written defamatory statement, which can be published in newspaper, website, a magazine, or on a social media post to name a few, while slander refers to a spoken defamatory statement, made in private discussion, during a speech or on a public broadcast. Libel and slander - both of which are torts - are not crimes in most legal systems, but they are civil offenses and are thus potentially punishable under law. In order to be considered libel or slander, the statement must be false, must be presented as a fact, and must occur as a publication or communication to a third party, and must do harm to the person’s reputation. For instance, if a journalist falsely writes in a newspaper that a public figure was engaged in illegal activities without any evidence, that might be cause for a libel lawsuit. By contrast, if an individual falsely spreads rumors that a colleague is stealing from the company, that could be considered slander. Where public figures are concerned, the burden of proof for demonstrating defamation is usually higher. The individual can’t just show that a statement was false and damaging; she must show that it was false and published with actual malice — meaning the publisher knew it was false or recklessly disregarded the truth. This is a standard that was designed to safeguard free speech, to promote open debate on public officials and the issues. An accusation of libel or slander can seriously affect a journalists and media companies. Which is why professional journalists are taught to confirm our sources, back up our facts, and show restraint when floating bombshell charges. Media companies, for their part, bring in legal teams to vet potentially risky content. In short, libel and slander laws are supposed to shield people from the damages of false character attacks and libel!= slander while also weighing the public’s need to know and the free market of ideas. Knowing these terms is vital for responsible and legal journalism.

text: The outstanding judgment is the principle of res judicata is a concept enshrined in Section 11 CPC The term res judicata means, “a thing already decided”. It bars a re-trial of the same issue between the same parties in a new case after a court of competent jurisdiction has finally determined it. The ultimate purpose of this doctrine is to maintain the sanctity of judgments and to prevent the multiplicity of suits. The doctrine of res judicata is designed to promote judicial economy, to minimize inconsistent results, and to prevent the abuse of litigants and the legal System through multiple lawsuits. To be applicable, the said principle will require that there had been a prior suit between the same parties or their ancestors; the matter in issue directly and substantially was the same in both the suit; and finally the court decided the question raised in the same between the parties or their privies. For example, if A files a lawsuit against B for possession of a piece of land and the court rules in favor of B, A cannot file a second lawsuit against B on the same land claim, provided that the second such lawsuit is based on a slightly different issue than the first lawsuit. Res judicata bars relitigation not only of issues that werera.\vled, but also of those that might have been raised in that prior proceeding. It is also applicable to the execution of decrees and public interest litigations in limited circumstances. There are formal and material dimensions of the principle, which is crucial in keeping the law predictable. But it is not applicable where there is a fraud, or where the court below had no jurisdiction. In short, res judicata serves the interests of justice by avoiding the harassment of parties to litigation and by giving due respect to the finality of court decisions.

text: Coolant in a nuclear reactor assumes an important role that is paramount to the safety and efficiency of the reactor in producing electricity. Its principal purpose is to provide cooling for the heat production in the reactor derived from nuclear fission, although additional heat removal is often required to remove combustible materials following a loss-of-coolant accident. Without a proper coolant, the reactor core would heat up and eventually melt down, possibly causing fuel cladding failure, a leach of the pressure boundary or a catastrophic radiation release. It follows that the coolant to be used should satisfy some critical conditions, such as high thermal conductivity, chemical stability, resistance to radiation and compatibility with the materials of the reactor. The selection of a coolant depends on the reactor's type. Light water is used as a coolant and moderator in Pressurized Water Reactors (PWRs) and Boiling Water Reactors (BWRs). PWRs keep the water coolant under pressure to avoid boiling; the BWRs allow it to boil in the core. Heavy Water Reactors (e.g., CANDU) Deuterium oxide (D.sub.2 is used as coolant which acts as a moderator along with superior neutron economy. Some advanced reactors employ gaseous coolants such as helium or carbon dioxide or liquid coolants such as sodium, lead, or lead-bismuth eutectic, which have better heat transfer and enable higher temperature and hence higher thermal efficiencies. Apart from heat extraction, coolant also has a direct effect on the neutron economy in the core, because some coolants absorb more neutrons than others, thereby changing the reactor’s reactivity rent. Coolants are also a radiation barrier, especially in the case of liquid ones, acting as a shield. In an accident or loss of coolant situation, an emergency core cooling system (ECCS) injects coolant to the core to avoid over-heating. In summary The coolant is an essential factor in carrying away heat, retention of structure integrity and stable and safe running of the reactor.

text: Criminology is positioned to make significant contributions to the area of sustainable social development through addressing the root causes of crime, promoting justice, and creating inclusive and peaceful societies. By focusing on the social organization, economic conditions and psychological factors that generate criminality, criminologists can inform policies that eradicate inequality, poverty, marginalization, and violence—all obstacles to sustainable development. text: Dark matter is an enigmatic type of matter that does not emit, absorb or reflect light, making it difficult to detect directly by means of electromagnetic radiation. Although not directly seen, its presence can be inferred from its effects on visible matter, certain forms of energy such as radiation and the large scale structure of the universe. It is thought to make up 27 percent of the mass-energy content of the universe, far outweighing the ordinary stuff that makes up about 5 percent. Dark matter evidence includes excesses in galactic rotation curves, the gravitational lensing phenomenon, and the tilting and alignment of the cosmic microwave background radiation compared with the expectations with dark matter. Several candidates of particles for dark matter have been proposed, such as Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs), axions, and sterile neutrinos, but none have been observed directly. The identity of dark matter is among the most profound puzzles in current astrophysics and cosmology. Insight into dark matter is essential as it is a major contributor to the formation of galaxies, cosmic structure and the large-scale gravitational structure of the universe. “It’s hard to study such a particle, so scientists are searching in many different ways, hoping to produce dark matter in the lab or to detect it elsewhere, in the cosmos,” added Professor Kateri S. Donnelly, the LUX scientific collaboration spokesperson. Its discovery and study could have major implications for fundamental physics, and could illuminate new particles and interactions beyond the standard model. Dark matter, meanwhile, confounds our understanding of the universe’s material composition, implying that most of the matter in the cosmos is intrinsically different from normal matter, whose particles form stars, planets and life, and a rounding stalk of unexplored terrain for researchers to explore and understand.

text: Transition words Transition words are words or phrases that help establish connections between sentences, ideas, or paragraphs in a piece of writing. These are significant words because it improves on coherency – a logical and consistent relation of parts. Without transition words, writing becomes disorganized and difficult to follow. text: Four types of DC motor can be distinguished; these are separated as follows depending on how the connections between the armature and field windings are made: shunt, series, separately excited and compound. In a separately excited DC motor, the field is excited from an external independent voltage source. This design permits a great deal of control over the flux of the field and, as such, the speed of the motor, making it ideal for applications where it is desirable to have close control over the motor, such as in laboratory arrangement or control systems. Field winding of series dc motor is connected in series with the armature, as a result the field current will be directly related to the armature current. This, in turn, provides very high starting torque allowing series machines to be a popular choice for use in heavy duty applications such as traction, lifts and electrical cranes which require the motor to start under heavy load. They are, however, poorly regulated speed-wise and must never run unloaded, from which condition it may overspeed dangerously. The armature in the shunt DC motor is wired in parallel to the field winding. The latter effect is provided by the virtually constant field current, giving an almost constant speed irrespective of the load. Shunt motors are employed in lathes, blower fans, conveyors and blowers, for which speed control is important but torque is not as critical. Compound DC motors have of early as well as shunt motors, and both a series and a shunt field winding all letting the motor operate at a constant or consistent speed. Cumulative and differential types These motors are then further classified as cumulative and differential respectively. Cumulative compound motors have stronger starting torque and more uniform speed than series motors and are used in applications such as elevators and rolling mills. Compound motors which do not have this characteristic are known as differential compound motors, and are used where it is desirable to decrease torque while maintaining the current.rarely used.offer the reverse, increasing torque with load, but are designed to maintain a constant current. Different types of DC motor have certain advantages and disadvantages and choice is based on the requirements of speed control, torque, loading, and cost of application.

text: Routine activity theory Routine activity theory, first posited by Lawrence Cohen and Marcus Felson in 1979, is a control theory that eradicates the individual or social conditions; rather in this theory Cohen and Felson suggests that crime is a function of opportunities to commit crime. The theory states that for a crime to be committed, these three elements must be present at the same time (convergence in space and time). These elements are: a motivated offender, a suitable target, and the absence of a capable guardian. These three determinants are related to the activities and lifestyles of individuals and communities. For instance, when we leave our homes to go to work, go on vacation, hang out in crowded malls or otherwise we create crime opportunities through things like attractiveness of property and the reduction of informal surveillance. The theory highlights the fact that shifts in routine activities — be it the transition toward urban living, the increase in two-earner households, or spikes in online commerce — have the potential to have a strong effect on crime rates, by changing the presence of targets and guardianship. Implications Routine activity is a well-known criminological theory used in crime prevention programs, especially situational crime prevention, that attempts to design out offending opportunities by increasing surveillance, reducing property access and guardianship (e.g., the presence of police, neighbors, and the use of technological devices such as closed-circuit television cameras) in an effort to reduce criminal activity. It is also useful for explaining cybercrime, in which the offenders are actively seeking to exploit technological practices and insecure protection systems. A strength of the theory is that it’s very practical — it refocuses the lens from changing the behavior of offenders to changing environments so that crimes become more difficult to commit. Yet critics say it oversimplifies intricate criminal mind-sets and underemphasizes social, economic and psychological issues. Nevertheless, routine activity theory is a leading concept in environmental criminology and has inspired urban planning, community policing and public safety projects that have sought to reduce the opportunity structure to offend.

text: Current Transformers (CTs) and Potential Transformers (PTs) are instrument transformers used in power systems containing high voltage and high current for the measurement and protection of the power system. They are mainly used to reduce current and voltage values in both step on a large scale to manageable ones that can be tested with normal instruments and relays. It is low-turns primary (one to a few) and high-turns secondary (again, a few+). The CT produces a current that is proportionate to the primary current, and is often stepped down to a standard value such as 5A or 1A, which can be usefully fed to ammeters, energy meters or protective relays. On the contrary, a PT (also known as a voltage transformer) is used to reduce the high voltage input to a standard voltage (e.g., 110V or 63.5V): similar to a normal transformer, it has a high-accuracy ratio of turns in the windings to minimize its error in phase and magnitude. CTs and PTs are the indispensable parts of power substation, switchgear panel, and industrial electric facilities. Separation between the high-voltage circuit and measuring devices is also important for safe operation. The CT and PT secondary outputs are linked together to supply wattmeters, peak demand meters and protective devices, for example, overcurrent and differential relays. CT and PT error are represented by ratio error and phase angle error, and high-accuracy classes are needed for accurate metering. Finally, CTs and PTs participate in ensuring the safe and accurate monitoring, metering, and protection of apparatus carrying high-voltage and current in electrical power systems.

text: The term crime prevention, given its range of applications (from immediate opportunities that facilitate crime commitment through the collection of social factors), refers to those set of strategies that seek to reduce the occurrence of crime or its associated consequences. P roblems hoosing a crime prevention approach The most commonly used approaches fall into three large categories: situa- tional crime prevention, social crime prevention and community-based crime prevention methods. Routine activity theory emphasizes offending opportunities, arguing that criminal behavior occurs when motivated offenders converge with suitable targets in the absence of capable guardians, and situational crime prevention aims to reduce crime opportunities by changing the physical environment, including strengthening lighting, installing closed-circuit cameras, strengthening properties, and regulating access to potential targets. By making it harder or riskier for offenders to do something they shouldn’t, these can act as deterrents. It is the use of strategies that seek to address the underlying social problems that contribute to victimization, such as poverty, childhood maltreatment, and substance abuse, among others, with the goal of reducing crime. Community-based initiatives, especially community policing, favour a lock and key to solve problems in common and to gain trust and develop local solutions together among the law enforcers and the community. Alternative possibilities are legal system reform, programs to identify and assist at-risk individuals, campaigns to educate the public, and work to rehabilitate those who are released from prison. An effective approach to crime prevention needs to incorporate this variety of interventions and ensure it reflects the specific social and environmental factors of a local area. It is also critical to ensure that prevention is combined with robust enforcement and community engagement to create safer, more resilient societies. Indeed, a proactive, multi-faceted approach that situates immediate crime control in relation to long-term social development is the most hopeful strategy for preventing crime more broadly.

text: A concept of division of powers, or `separation of powers,' is inherent in democratic governments which divide the functions of government among three branches, the legislature, the executive and the judiciary. The functions and responsibilities of each branch are disjointed to avoid any part of them becoming too powerful in any part of the system. The legislature is supposed to make laws, the executive to implement them, and the judiciary to interpret and apply the laws. This separation provides a system of checks and balances, so that no branch has more power than the others; in other words, no branch can dominate. For example, the legislature may have the power to make the laws and control the public purse, but the executive will have the responsibility of administering those laws and may also have the power to propose them, the judiciary may rule laws or executive actions unconstitutional. This being interdependence, however independent, provides a shield against despotism, oppression and exercise of power. The doctrine was best enunciated by political philosophers like Montesquieu who believed that liberty is protected only when powers are divided and counterpoised. The separation of powers promotes transparency, accountability, and the supremacy of the rule of law, both in lawmaking by ensuring that officials do not act outside of the confines set by the Constitution. It ensures good governance by dividing and sharing powers, avoiding intertwining powers and thereby preventing enmity among branches. The principle looks different across countries: in presidential systems, like the U.S., the power of the branches is more clearly separated, while in parliamentary systems the executive and legislative powers intermingle, though not when it comes to the judiciary. For such a checks-and-balances system to function, strong institutions and an independent judiciary, free press, and vibrant civil society organizations to check government excesses are a must. Most importantly, however, the separation of powers is necessary to defend democracy and the freedoms of individual citizens, and to make government subservient to us and not the other way around.

text: Glycosides Glycosides are organic compounds (mostly carbohydrate) derived from plants, which consist of two parts - sugar part (glycone) and non-sugar part (aglycone or genin) linked by glycosidic bond. Hydrolysis of glycosides results in liberation of one or more sugars and a non-sugar part, which is often biologically active. The sugar part is involved in solubility and transport of the compound, and the aglycone confers pharmacological properties. According to the nature of the aglycone, glycosides are categorized into different types i.e., cardiac, anthraquinone, flavonoid, saponin and cyanogenic etc. Description Cardiac glycosides which include digoxin and digitoxin extracted from Digitalis purpurea (foxglove) are used to treat congestive heart failure and atrial fibrillation by enhancing the force of cardiac contraction. Anthraquinone glycosides are also used as natural laxatives, such as sennosides from the Senna leaf. Flavonoid glycosides (including rutin) have anti-oxidative, anti-inflammatory, and capillary-toughening properties. Saponin glycosides are contained in products of licorice and ginseng, and summarized to exert expectorant activity, immunostimulant effect and anti-cholesterol problem. Some glycosides, such as with amygdalin (a cyanogenic glycoside found in almonds, apple seeds, most stone fruits, &c.), contain small amounts of cyanide, which metabolizes into toxic hydrogen cyanide. The pharmacological effects, the absorbability and metabolism of glycosides are also influenced by the nature of the sugar moiety and the aglycon and also by the mode of processing in the body. Because of their diverse therapeutic effects, glycosides have a profound influence on traditional and modern medicine. Conclusion Glycosides belong to the group of non-selective-binding compounds.' These compounds are highly effective, naturally occurring substances that have become extremely useful medicaments for cardiology, gastroenterology and phytotherapy.

text: Multithreading is a programmatic means of allowing different parts of a single program to be run concurrently(i.e., concurrently from the point of view of the program; on a single-core system, two threads can only be executed one after the other, not literally simultaneously). Threads share not only the memory space, but are also executed independently, so that for example I/O, calculation or UI operations can run in parallel without waiting for each other and, therefore, improving performance and responsiveness. For instance, in Java, we can accomplish multithreading by extending the class Thread or by implementing the interface Runnable. Simple Java example Below is a simple example of how you can create a class that implements Runnable, run() method that describes what the thread will do and start a thread by calling start() on the Thread objects. Likewise in Python, you get "threading" module having Thread objects to which you can pass the target function, that can run in separate threads using start(). Multithreading becomes highly effective in web server or games or real-time systems where various processing have to be performed at a time. But multithreading brings problems of synchronization to prevent race conditions and deadlocks, and so forth. Thread interaction is safely managed by developers with the concept of locks, semaphores, and other synchronization techniques. Though threads allow true parallelism on multiple CPU cores, GIL (global interpreter lock) restricts multiple threads from executing Python bytecodes at once, hence they are more appropriate for I/O-bound operations. Java's multithreading, in comparison, supports actual parallelism on multi-cores. In short, multithreading improves the efficiency and performance of the applications while maximizing the user experiences as well by enabling simultaneous operation of multiple tasks of a particular application in a telephone.

text: Library planning is a systematic, participatory and focused process rooted in the exploration and evaluation of the future directions and services of a library, in light of the objectives of the unit it serves, as well as reader, user and patron needs, and general trends in the world at large. It starts with environmental scanning, looking at demographic trends, community need, technology advancement and budget projections, and includes stakeholder engagement with focus groups, surveys and advisory boards. This data... provides the basis for the formulation of a mission statement and strategic goals which may include digital transformation, user experience, growth of the collection, professional growth of staff, and physical plant improvements. A comprehensive needs assessment considers space use, accessibility, technology deficiencies, service track record, and evolving trends and issues. From this plan, libraries create operational and tactical plans that describe goals, schedules, owners, performance expectations, resources, and risk management. Planning shall also include facility reconfiguration such as outward facing layout, collaborative space, digital labs or expansion with architectural renderings and incremental implementation. Technology roadmaps shape investments in hardware and software--OPAC upgrades, RFID, e-resource platforms, analytics tools--and budget forecasting positions resources according to strategic need and grant opportunities. Professional development strategies assist training in new services, digital curation, or user-centered design. To track progress, libraries rely on dashboards, balanced scorecards, or evaluation frameworks that measure how many books they circulate, how people attend classes they offer, how many reference questions they answer, how many digital copies of books they offer for download, and how satisfied their users are. Effective planning is an iterative process Annual reviews allow for correction of course, realignment with organizational change, and training in response to changing user and technological circumstances. Ultimately, library planning is a pathway to mission-driven, data-informed, community-engaged, and sustainable growth as an institution—a way for the library to work ahead, continue to be responsive to change and ready for the future, while being both relevant and innovative.

text: Both robotics and mechatronics are multidisciplinary subsets of engineering/agriculture that utilize the combination of mechanics, electronics, and computing to design and build innovative devices, however they have different scopes and different applications. Robotics is a specialized field of mechatronics that involves the design, development, and use of robots—machines equipped with sensors, manipulators, and power supplies which enable them to perform distinct tasks automatically or semiautomatically. The work it encompasses includes mechanical design, the fusion of sensors, algorithms of control, and frequently, most important, artificial intelligence so machines can “see” the world around them and make decisions. Mechatronics however is a broader engineering field that also includes the combination of mechanics and electronics and computer control in the design of products and manufacturing processes, with devices such as washing machines, anti-lock braking systems (ABS) and acceptance testing machines being just a few testaments to this approach. All robots are inherently mechatronic systems, but not all mechatronic systems are robots. Mechatronics deals more with the cooperation of technologies which creates intelligent systems and products, stationary or mobile and robotics lays more emphasis on autonomy, completing tasks and the interaction with the environment. And finally, Robotics often involves more sophisticated computing requirements, for example AI and machine vision, than what we are typically used to in mechatronics. Hence, robotics is analogous to a more specialized, task specific field within mechatronics.

text: AN IMPORTANT component of life support systems in controlled environments (submarine, aircraft, spacecraft cabins) is air regeneration. Trace contaminant control is essential in maintaining a habitable and safe cabin atmosphere. Trace contaminants generated from equipment (degassing) and human (metabolic) processes may exceed spacecraft maximum allowable concentration (SMAC) limits for various exposure periods and need to be treated [NASA, 1996]. Conventional trace contaminant control technologies for life support systems include particulate filters, activated carbon/chemisorbent beds, and catalytic oxidizers. These technologies suffer from limitations that present significant challenges in advanced life support (ALS) applications such as the need for regeneration, high mass and space requirements for carbon adsorbers, catalyst poisoning, and high energy requirements for catalytic oxidizers. Thus, there is a need for innovative alternative technologies that have the potential of either replacing or supplementing current technologies in ALS applications. Nonthermal plasmas can be cost-effective in reducing volatile organic compounds (VOCs) from a variety of sources.

text: Climate adaptation strategies -Purposeful interventions or activities designed to change or maintain natural or human systems in response to actual or expected climate events. They are implemented to reduce harm or take advantage of new opportunities. These approaches include technical solutions such as building flood defenses or drought-resistant crops as well as institutional reforms like the revision of land-use planning or better disaster risk control management. Adaptation is anticipatory if it is accomplished before the impacts of climate on a system are manifested; conversely, adaptation is reactive if it is done after impacts have been experienced. It operates at many levels, from local action in communities to governance at the national and global levels. Important adaptation measures involve improving water management for changes in precipitation, sustainable agriculture for food security, protecting and restoring ecosystems as natural buffer, and ensuring that health systems are robust enough to cope with climate-sensitive diseases. Urban adaptation includes planning and maintaining resilient infrastructure, designing green space to mitigate heat island effects and ensuring secure housing and transportation systems. Social adjustment measures are development, education, social safety nets and enabling the less privileged. Technology plays a critical role, growing climate data, early warning systems and energy and agriculture innovations. Integrating adaptation into development planning leads to alignment and cost-effective resource utilization. These range from uncertainties surrounding climate projections, to the financing gap, governance limitations, and reconciling short-term needs and long-term sustainability. Effective adaptation demands engagement of broad constituencies, combining scientific and local and indigenous knowledge, and ongoing assessment and adjustment of strategies as conditions change. In general, climate adaptation plans are vital to reducing vulnerability, increasing resilience, and protecting livelihoods and ecosystems in the context of continuing climate change.

text: Editing is a foundational element of narrative storytelling that informs the rhythm, structure and pace of your story and first stage of world building: it’s what turns raw footage into an emotional, cohesive universe brought about by powerfully structured, on-brand visual messaging. Scenes and directing order the events of a scene, but the editor has the power to select shots and establish when those shots occur, which allows them to guide where a viewer is looking, focus on essential elements of a story and speed up or slow down how information — and therefore stories — are consumed. Editing can accelerate time via tools like montage, elongate moments with slow motion or repetition, or sustain suspense by controlling what the viewer sees and when. The rhythm of those cuts, jarring and fast or graceful and lingering, can produce feelings like excitement, tension, closeness or calm — whatever the emotional reaction that a director wants from you. Continuity editing within shots is what prevents the audience from noticing spatial or temporal discontinuities and enables them to become absorbed in the world of the story, but more stylized effects like jump cuts, match cuts, and cross-cutting can startle the viewer, add symbolic meaning or generate psychological tension. Editors also use reaction shots, inserts and cutaways to aid in communicating a character’s feeling, imply motivation or foreshadow events — effectively guiding character arcs and audience feeling in the process. When it’s in those talk scenes, that is by never cutting away from the pulse of a conversation and subtext flowing below it in editor>editor reactions, and when it’s action sequences, its about who is doing what and how we’re tracking their movement including both the why/how they got there as well as who/what caused them to do something else. Ironically, sound and music, which are often added during or after post-production in the form of scoring (as opposed to source/recorded music that identifies time or place – such as car radios) help tell a story through mood, tone and themes. With documentary and nonfiction, editing can guide structure by cutting in another interview or voiceover that may shift what argument/viewpoint is presented to the viewer. And even in those so-called “novelistic” or non-linear, impressionistic narratives, editing provides the sense of logic which makes the jumbled moments we’re mixing together from disparate time periods feel as if they belong together. Editors also collaborate closely with the director, camera crew and sound designers to tell the story through what we see and hear. The emotional heft of a single scene can also create vast differences according to how it’s edited, so an editor is another primary storyteller. After all, editing isn’t just a mechanical exercise – it’s an art that breathes life into a script and turns a pile-up of shots into one compelling narrative that moves its audience, viscerally as well as intellectually.

text: Reviews wield enormous power in the making of a theater production by determining how the public sees it, affecting the potential commercial success at the box office, influencing creative decisions, and adding to the larger cultural conversation a performance generates. Critics, through reviews unlocked in print, on Web sites, blogs and social media, offer audiences how-to-reads, pointing out what works and what doesn’t in areas like performance, direction, writing, set design and execution. Good reviews can help sell tickets, generate media interest and extend a show’s run; bad ones can dissuade potential audiences or force production teams into making changes. Theatre reviews can also assist those involved in producing a play as they are writing and developing it, and at the end of the production. For some shows, especially those that are smaller or less established, one major review can raise the show’s profile a lot and give it some legitimacy in the theater community. For large-scale commercial or institutional productions, reviews help to establish a reputation, raise funds and prepare the work to be eligible for awards or international touring. In addition, reviews also provide critical reflection – the wider social, political or historical framing of a production and encouraging readers to engage in deeper consideration of the issues the work addresses. So this kind of cultural criticism serves to not only legitimize theatre as a site of public discourse but also serves as a challenge to artists to be more reflective. But not all reviews have a positive impact: Overtly negative or biased criticism can demoralize creative teams or axe promising shows before they’ve had a chance to succeed. Furthermore, critics are increasingly lampooned during the digital age as they are no longer the sole authority on popular culture due to the internet, where the public themselves can comment on films and other popular culture. Today theater-makers must operate in this complex ecosystem where user comments and professional critique exist side by side, influencing one another and sometimes even the show’s destiny moment to moment. Reviews are also useful tools for learning in an educational and training context to be used as direct feedback to students and practitioners on how theatrical elements are perceived and interpreted. At their best—by providing that bridge between the stage and the audience—reviews promote dialogue, spur accountability, keeping the theater alive as a living, evolving communication. Whether rave or pans, reviews can leave permanent marks on a production’s legacy, affecting not only its initial reception but also its spot in theater history, academia and future revivals.

text: Freedom of the Press is a cornerstone principle of democracy which provides the media with the freedom to report news and express opinions without control, interference nor censorship by government and other powerful institutions. This freedom is grounded in the notion that an informed citizenry is critical to a functioning democracy, allowing its members to make informed choices, demand transparency from their government, and engage meaningfully in civic life. Press freedom enables journalists to investigate and report on issues that matter to the public—often matters involving corruption, human rights abuses or corporate malfeasance—without fear that their work will be met with censorship or punishment. It is enshrined in constitutions across the dozen, and international human rights instruments such as Article 19 on the Universal Declaration of Human Rights that guarantees the right to "seek, receive, and impart information and ideas through any media and regardless of frontiers." In practice, press freedom encompasses the right to information, source protection, criticism of authorities, and independent operation free from state or market control. Yet freedom of the press is not absolute and must be weighed in against other legal rights and interests including national security, defamation, as well as protection from hate speech. Yet freedom of the press is under attack in much of the world. Journalists are coming under severe threat -at risk of censorship, harassment, arrests, surveillance and even violence for doing their jobs. In some, the government utilises ill-defined laws or pressure tactics to control independent views, in others, corporate ownership or advertising pressure can suppress stories through more insidious forms of self-censorship. But in the digital era, freedom of the press also means the right to report and publish online free from undue restrictions.” Supporting a free press then comes down to things like ensuring that there are legal protections for journalists; that journalists are able to access public information; that the media isn’t being intimidated. At root, freedom of the press is not only a journalist’s right — it is everyone’s right to know; it is the right to question those in power; it is the right to demand accountability and to hold society to account.

text: Religious experiences cover a wide range of experiences, from seemingly mundane events to mystical experiences. These can be mystical, vision, and numinous or transformative experiences, and are typically characterized as moments of deep, integral insight, or a sense of unity, often with something beyond what is normally thought of as experience. Religious experiences have been interpreted as having metaphysical significance for instance see William James, evidence for religious beliefs, and have also been considered an important phenomenon in terms of the philosophy of religion, and in general, in the academic study of religion. They run the gamut from revelation to prayer and meditation to transcendence experienced in a spectrum of cultures and religious traditions. The character and interpretation of religious experience challenge us on the frontiers of epistemology (do such experiences yield knowledge?), phenomenology (what is their form?); and psychology (what actually causes them?). Critics claim that religious experiences can be understood naturalistically as events in the brain or mind, while defenders assert that they demonstrate access to a transcendent reality. Personal faith and the shaping of religious belief Religious experience frequently serves as the primary basis for individual faith, and the inspiration for individual doctrine as well, sometimes thought of as more immediate, more directly inspired, or more Spirit-empowered than doctrinal formulations. Philosophers still struggle with questions of how to evaluate, interpret, and include religious experience within wider philosophical and theological patterns.

The first stable compound produced in the Calvin cycle in the C3 plants is 3-phosphoglycerate (3-PGA), as they do not have a specialized compartment for initial carbon dioxide fixation. This happens within the mesophyll cells where the enzyme RuBisCO is fixing carbon dioxide directly from the atmosphere. But RuBisCO has a 2-fold affinity for CO? and O?, and under high temperatures, light and oxygen, it binds readily to O? instead of CO?, wasting energy in a process called photorespiration. Photorespiration makes photosynthesis less efficient and is a significant handicap for C3 plants such as wheat, rice and soybean. In the latter case, C4 plants have evolved a specialized strategy to reduce photorespiration and improve photosynthetic performance under high light and heat. In these plants the initial product of a carbon-fixing cycle is a four-carbon acid, the most common being oxaloacetate (C4), but also malate (C4). Carbon is fixed in mesophyll cells by an initial reaction with the enzyme PEP carboxylase, which does not compete with O? and is more efficient. The compound with four carbons is then transferred to bundle sheath cells where it releases CO? for the Calvin cycle. Such spatial separation minimizes interference by oxygen and also photorespiration. C4 photosynthesis is an evolutionary adaptation to hot, dry climates and is present in plants such as maize, sugarcane, sorghum and millet. These plants also exhibit higher water use efficiency, being able to keep photosynthesis active at partially closed stomata. Accordingly, the more widespread and adequate C3 photosynthesis is under cool, wet conditions, C4 photosynthesis provides a tremendous advantage under hot, dry conditions, and crops based on C4 photosynthesis are considered as key elements for future agricultural sustainability in the context of global climate change.

text: The Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW) of 1979 of was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly and is commonly described as an international bill of rights for women. As a legally binding international agreement, the Convention calls on signatory countries to end discrimination against women – whether it be in the legal, social or economic realm. CEDAW prescribes specific measures that all countries must undertake to guarantee women equal rights to education, employment, family life, and political participation, among others. It focuses on the need to remove the stereotypes of gender and to form real (as opposed to only formal-legal) de facto equality. CEDAW state parties are responsible for reporting to the CEDAW Committee, which oversees the implementation and makes recommendations. CEDAW has been ratified by more than 180 countries, but implementation has been inconsistent, and a number of powerful countries — including the United States — have signed but not ratified the treaty. CEDAW is often employed by feminist scholars and activists who use its provisions as a tool for advocacy and legal reform, and to link States parties' treaty obligations to their domestic laws.

text: The vast majority of the power used by the wireless sensor is dedicated to the radio transmitter for signal transmission. Therefore, the addition of local data-processing capabilities can prolong battery life significantly, due to the elimination of the requirement for constant high-throughput wireless data transmission. In addition, the combination of onboard signal-processing capabilities and a receiver can enable user-defined multimode operation, such as allowing the observer to switch between low-power event detection and variable rates of real-time biological-signal transmission. Therefore, a system that combines bidirectional communications with onboard computational abilities would be superior to a simple transmitter/receiver unit. Possible approaches for implementing a wireless biological sensor range from assembling commercial-off-the-shelf PC (COTS-PC) components [1] to custom-fabricating integrated circuits (ICs) [2]. COTS-PC components yield large power-intensive units with powerful communications and signal-processing capabilities, while custom ICs yield very specialized, compact, and power-efficient solutions. Unfortunately, investing in the development of custom ICs for digital signal acquisition, processing, and communication for nonstandardized applications (e.g., biological-signal recording), unlike cellular phones that operate on strict international standards (e.g., GSM, Bluetooth, etc.) may not be economically feasible.

text: Although clouds are among the dominant features of outdoor scenes, with few exceptions visual inference algorithms treat their effects on the scene as noise. However, the shadows they cast on the ground over time give novel cues for inferring 3D scene models. Clouds are one instantiation of the first law of geography, due to Waldo Tobler: “Everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things.” In a sense, we are applying this law to the problem of estimating a depth map from time-lapse imagery. The basic insight is that there is a relationship between the time series of intensity at two pixels and the distance between the imaged scene points. We describe two cues and present algorithms that use these cues to estimate a depth map. For the first cue, we compute the temporal correlation between pairs of pixels and observe that if the relationship between this correlation and 3D distance is known then there is a simple problem: Given an image and the 3D distance between every pair of scene points, find the 3D model of the scene that is consistent with the camera geometry and the distance constraints. However, the relationship between correlation and distance is unknown because it depends on the scene and the type of clouds in the scene. Thus, we derive and present a method that simultaneously solves for the relationship between distance and correlation and for a corresponding 3D scene model.

text: Although visual long-term memory (VLTM) has large enough capacity to store a virtually infinite amount of visual information (Brady, Konkle, Alvarez, & Oliva, 2008; Standing, 1973), not every information that we wish to remember is encoded. What limits our access to the unlimited memory storage? According to Atkinson and Shiffrin’s influential modal model of memory (Atkinson & Shiffrin, 1968, 1971; Rundus & Atkinson, 1970; Shiffrin & Atkinson, 1969), information is first encoded into short-term memory (STM) in which information is actively maintained. And this active maintenance is what grants access to long-term memory (LTM) storage. Despite its elegant simplicity, this model later received criticisms particularly on the proposed role of the STM maintenance in LTM encoding (Craik & Watkins, 1973; Naveh-Benjamin & Jonides, 1984). This criticism led to a discovery of the importance of the nature of encoding processes that information undergoes (Craik, 1983; Craik & Lockhart, 1972; Craik & Tulving, 1975; Craik & Watkins, 1973; Fisher & Craik, 1977; Moscovitch & Craik, 1976) and the characterization of the interaction between the encoding and retrieval processes became a central theme of LTM research. As a result, one aspect of LTM encoding proposed in the modal model—namely, its capacity limitation—received little attention to this date.

text: Correlation is a statistical analysis tool which measures a member and a strength of a linear relationship between two quantitative variables. It gives an idea in what way changes in one variable are related to changes in other. The correlation is a value ranged between -1 and +1 where +1 is a perfect positive linear relationship (-1 a perfect negative), which means as one variable grows, so does the other one. A correlation of 0 signifies no linear relationship between the variables. Correlation is not a cause but only measure the extent of the association between two variable. It has wide applications in many fields including economics, psychology, medicine, and social science to study relationships between two variables such as wages and education, blood pressure and age, and study time and exam scores. The Pearson correlation coefficient is the most widely used measure of correlation which measures the linear dependence between two variables assuming variables are loosely normally distributed. Other versions, like Spearman’s rank correlation, can be employed for non-parametric or non-linear relationships. Correlations are indicative of patterns, can generate hypotheses, and may inform further statistical modeling, but they should be interpreted in the context of data and research design.

text: Tempo estimation is a fundamental problem in music information retrieval (MIR), vital for applications such as music similarity and recommendation, semi-automatic audio editing, automatic accompaniment, polyphonic transcription, beat-synchronous audio effects, and computer assisted DJ systems. Typically, automatic analysis of rhythm consists of two main tasks: tempo estimation and beat tracking. The goal of tempo estimation is to automatically determine the rate of musical beats in time. Beats can be defined as the locations in time where a human would “tap” their foot while listening to a piece of music. Beat tracking is the task of determining the locations of these beats in time, and is considerably harder in music in which the tempo varies over time [1]. Both of these topics have received considerable attention and there is a large body of published literature exploring various approaches to solving them automatically.

text: A digital library is a library in which collections are stored in digital formats (as opposed to print, microform, or other media) and accessible through computers.The electronic content may be stored locally or accessed remotely via computer networks. Unlike physical libraries, the digital libraries of today are not just focused on the acquisition, organization, and long-term preservation of digital objects – they are also focused on the systems and software used by community members to discover, access and use these objects. These tend to have powerful searching engines and browse features that include radical browsing, full text search, as well as advanced functionality such as annotating, bookmarking, and linking to similar content. Digital libraries provide access to all users world wide 365 days per year whenever and wherever they are and allow distance educational, research and cultural activities thanks to removing geographic and time barriers. They advocate digital preservation through format choices which lessen technological obsolescence, and through the application of metadata standards (such as Dublin Core, METS) and protocols (OAI-PMH) to guarantee accessibility of content in the future. Services ranging from institutional repositories, digital humanities archives, discipline-specific collections, in which scholars can deposit and share research outputs that will then be open and visible for the long-term. User interaction is enhanced with interactive interfaces, recommendation systems, integration with learning management systems or bibliographical tools. But digital library collections also raise issues over digital rights management, licensing, copyright, privacy, access fairness, and maintenance of technology. They need to consider what open access should look like while working with legal, financial and ethical constraints. However, digital libraries constitute a natural progression of information institutions—merging the intellectual integrity of libraries with the potential and freedom of digital technology to better support the needs of today’s learning, research, and public interests.

text: Family is most frequently the origin of gender role expectations. From the moment babies are born, they are exposed to gender norms that are reinforced by family members, parenting styles, household role models and even the toys and clothes they are given. Without realizing it, parents may be sending boys messages about independence, assertiveness or strength, while encouraging girls to embody qualities like gentleness, empathy or beauty. These early messages help to define little boys’ and little girls’ understanding of what they should do because of their gender. The domestic division of labour also reinforces gender roles; whether children see that women repeatedly do housework and men work for money, or if this creates the impression in the child's mind that these roles are inevitable, it will help to employ these roles being natural or fixed. Siblings, relatives and culture also play a role in gender knowledge and expression. In some families, nonconformity to gender roles is discouraged or punished; in others, it is embraced and nurtured. As families change — through shifts in norms, or through same-sex or single parenting — they can become sites of resistance to traditional gender norms, promoting egalitarianism, open-mindedness and self-expression.

text: A passage’s tone refers to an author’s attitude or emotional feeling towards the piece’s subject matter or the audience expressed in a passage, conveyed through the author’s word choice, sentence structure, and writing style. It also factors into what readers think or feel about a body of writing. Formal and informal, serious and light-hearted, pleasant and sarcastic, pejorative and laudatory, optimistic and critical, you name it; the tone can be anything you want it to be, depending on what you have in mind for the article. Knowing the tone is important for readers to comprehend what emotional state the author held at the time the words were written. Readers can figure out the mood by considering the words used. For instance, positive words like “brilliant,” “uplifting,” or “joyful” indicate that the tone could be cheerful or enthusiastic, while words like “bleak,” “harsh,” or “tragic” indicate a negative or serious tone. Tone can also be seen through sentence structure — long, involved sentences are often formal or introspective, while short, sharp ones get things moving, generate excitement. Punctuation, like exclamation points, can indicate excitement, expletives or surprise, whereas question marks can indicate disbelief or curiosity. Also, the content of the passage — is it an editorial or a poem, or a news report or a personal account — can provide hints. For example, a speech to persuade may use a persuasive tone; the one on climate transformation can choose the tone of concern or urgency. Occasionally tone changes within a passage, particularly in lengthy texts, in which a writer may start humorously, but conclude solemnly. Readers need to be alive to these shifts to understand what the author is saying. The tone, if recognized as such, more clearly reveals the emotions, implications, and degree of seriousness behind a text which allows the reader to have a more insightful interpretation. For exams, the ability to identify tone is useful for inference, vocabulary, and author’s purpose questions.

text: As early as 2002, the International Ethics Committee of the Human Genome Organization (HUGO) stated that human genomic databases should be considered as global public goods [1]. In this statement, global public goods were defined as goods 'whose scope extends worldwide, are enjoyable by all with no groups excluded, and when consumed by one individual, are not depleted for others' [2]. Buttressed by the Bermuda Principles of 1996 [2] and mirrored in the Fort Lauderdale rules of 2003 [3], the common philosophy of sharing resources was reaffirmed in the 2008 International Summit on Proteomics Data Release and Sharing Policy in Amsterdam [4] and in the Toronto International Data Release Workshop of 2009 [5]. Finally, in January 2011, 17 major health funding agencies signed a joint statement on sharing research data to promote and improve public health [6]. However, the challenge is to take these fundamental values of sharing and access and to develop guiding principles and procedures that can be used as a basis for emerging practice. To begin, we consider data sharing as a form of data processing as defined by the EU Directive 95/46/EC on data protection [7].
