text: Data mining (also known as knowledge discovery in databases (KDD)) is the interdisciplinary process of identifying patterns in large datasets automatically or semi-automatically patterns, for example, in a database. It fuses statistical analysis, machine learning, database management and domain knowledge to identify hidden actionable insights. The actual course is sequential: business understanding, which defines goals and hypotheses; data collection and preparation, where various data sources may be cleaned, integrated, and formatted; modeling, in which methods such as clustering, classification, regression, association-rule mining, or anomaly detection are used; and evaluation and deployment, which assesses model performance and incorporates results into operational processes. You can use data mining to identify market segments or predict fraud and even to forecast when your equipment will fail or find hidden patterns in your data-mining output. Its forte is managing large volumes of data, of many types, and in a variety of formats, otherwise known as ‘big data,’ and transforming it into meaningful structures, such as decision-support models or predictive scores.” It demands a combination of skills (technical chops like programming and statistics, as well as domain knowledge and perhaps most importantly, the ability to critically assess the ethical consequences of algorithms, especially in relation to privacy and bias). However, data mining can be dangerous if not properly controlled as it can lead to abuse of information or misunderstanding. It’s a bridge between raw data and informed knowledge that mines untapped data patterns and turns them into strategic assets.

text: The volume or surface of a three-dimensional space inside which an end effector of a robot can effectively move is known as a robot's workspace. It provides the geometric limits of the physical range of movement for a robot, considering its structure, joint configurations and sizes. The workspace is dependent on parameters, for example, the number and types (rotational or linear) of drives, link lengths, and the number of degrees of freedom. A Cartesian robot, for example, will typically have box shaped workspace, whereas an articulated robot may be closer to spherical, or differ in shape. Work space can generally be classified into reachable work space, which is all the points on which the robot can reach and touch, and dexterous work space, at which the robot can arrive with arbitrary orientation of the end effector. It is particularly important in robotics, when designing or selecting a robot for a certain task, in that, if the workspace does not suit the robot, a potential task may not be capable of being fulfilled. Whereas a robot that has a limited workspace may be not be cost effective for the purpose of assembly at a large scale and paradoxically, a robot that has a large workspace may be too costly to use in a confined space. Simulation tools can be used by engineers to help visually layout the work area to achieve optimal coverage and to guard against collisions with peripheral objects.

text: Despite its vastness and seeming never-ending capacity to withstand the pressures placed on it by human society, it has been recognised for some time that the global ocean is not limitless. Worldwide, marine and coastal ecosystems are experiencing unprecedented levels of anthropogenic pressure (Halpern et al., 2008). The situation is global, with increasing evidence that humanity's effect on marine wildlife is substantial, impacting functioning and provision services in every ocean. This degradation of marine and coastal ecosystems has profound implications for societal use of the sea, and its ongoing management. A move to take better account of human dimensions within marine decision making is increasingly observed across different scales of governance, including international agendas (e.g. UN General Assembly, 2015); national policies (e.g. the UK Government’s 25 Year Environment Plan 2018); efforts across the globe to develop national and regional marine plans (Ehler, 2018) and a plethora of affiliated areas of legislation which speak to the human dimension of natural resource management (e.g. Welsh Government, 2016). Traditionally, discussions around marine and coastal management have positioned ‘people’ as the key driver of negative impacts for the global seas, with anthropogenic activities more broadly, cited as one of the most pressing challenges facing our seas (MA, 2005; Pascual et al., 2017). More recently, the conversation around marine and coastal management has started to shift, and there is a growing recognition of the role of individuals and communities as part of the solution (Jefferson et al., 2015). This draws on the concept of environmental citizenship and/ or stewardship, a concept that is not new, and yet is continually evolving (Bennett et al., 2018; Hawthorne and Alabaster, 1999), with recent forays into this field of research focusing on marine and coastal contexts (Steel et al., 2005 and Guest et al., 2015 focusing on ocean literacy; McKinley and Fletcher, 2010, 2012; Fletcher et al., 2012 examining the potential role and application for the concept of marine citizenship).

text: Neutron flux is a fundamental concept in nuclear engineering that describes the amount of neutrons that pass through a given volume in a sample in a certain amount of time. It is the number of neutrons that pass through one square centimeter of a target area in unit time, usually n/cm²/s. The neutron flux describes the number of neutrons and their energy distribution to support fission or absorption reactions. It has a direct impact on the rate of nuclear reactions in the core and thus power output, depletion, and material activation. Regions of high neutron flux suffer from faster fuel burn-up as well as higher doses on the structural materials. The design and operation of reactors rely on precise measurements and control of the neutron flux to ensure a stable safe fission reaction and to maximise fuel burnup 1. Neutron fluxes are measured using an array of instruments, such as neutron detectors, fission chambers, and activation foils. Core flux distributions are defined to obtain uniform power, while minimizing hot spots in the RPV that can lead to RPV damage. The neutron flux also is important for the neutron economy that is to say, how many neutrons are involved in sustaining and serving the chain that reactions versus those lost to absorption or leakage. Neutron flux for experiments with desired neutron intensity and suitable energies is important in research reactors. Predicting the behavior of the reactor in the various physical states and operation processes is possible due to a space and energetic distribution of the neutron flux, and this type of modeling is essential in reactor conditioning and operation regarding the reactor safety analysis and fuel cycle optics. As such, the neutron flux parameter is strictly necessary for the knowledge and handling of the nuclear reactions in order to maintain reactor security, efficiency, and long-life.

text: Image composition Focal length is important for image composition in that it can control perspective (i.e. how subjects appear relative to each other and the background), field of view, and depth of field. The focal length, measured in millimeters, is what defines how much of a scene the camera fits onto the sensor and how big or small things appear. A short focal length, i.e. 18mm or 24mm, will feature a wide-angle perspective, showing more of the scene and accentuating the spatial distance between the objects. This can emphasize perspective so that foreground objects seem larger and objects in the background are pushed farther back, a popular technique with landscape photographers, and can also create a little bit of drama. On the flip side, a long focal length in the range of 85mm or 200mm has a tight field of view and compresses perspective, pushing distant objects closer together and eliminating the depth between them. This compression effect is as desired for portrait photography, as it separates the subject from the background, for an attractive natural look with an out of focus background where the subject stands out prominently with a shallow depth of focus. Also, you can take a photo of a subject using a longer focal length from a more significant distance (which is a plus for wildlife or sports photography). Mid-range focal lengths, such as 50mm, are typically called “normal” lenses as they approximate the perspective of the human eye and are great all-purpose lenses. The focal length you select also has emotional and storytelling connotations - wide angles can make a scene feel large or impressive, for example, while telephoto lenses can imply intimacy or draw attention to details. And that altered focal length isn't merely the focal length, but whether adjusting that focal length means you in turn end up moving the camera closer or further away from the subject, which also produces changes in how the background relates to the subject. For example, Framing a subject with a wide-angle lens from a close proximity will may distort face features, while shooting with a telephoto lens from a far distance will keep the proportions of an object accurate. In sum, understanding and choosing the right focal length is crucial to getting the compositional effects you want in photography, as it is what ultimately determines how viewers will perceive and emotionally react to an image.

text: The exponential distribution is a continuous probability distribution that is often used to describe the time between events in a process in which events occur continuously and independently at a constant average rate. It is applicable to problems where waiting times are involved, such as the interval between arrivals at a service facility, the life span of electronic devices, or the time which elapses until a radioactive particle disintegrates. The exponential distribution has a single parameter ? (lambda) that is the rate at which events occur. The PDF is f(x) = ?e^(-?x) for x ? 0, and the CDF is F(x) = 1 - e^(-?x). The mean value, or expected value, is 1/?, and its variance is also 1/?². A defining characteristic of the exponential distribution is the memoryless property; the probability of an event occurring a certain length of time in the future is the same, regardless of how much time has already passed. That is, P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t). This characteristic of the exponential distribution makes it particularly useful for reliability analysis and queuing theory. For instance if an item of equipment has been operating for 10 hours, then it is just as likely to operate for a further 5 hours without failure as if it had just started running. This is in contrast with distributions such as the normal or Weibull, for example, for which the history of the variable impacts godwins its future probability. In applications, the exponential distribution is used to model the time between atomic events, i.e., events which occur with probability proportional to the size of a given small interval, namely with average frequency of events per unit of time. The exponential distribution is also used in Markov processes and survival analysis. Simple as it is, it faithfully reflects the nature of a wide range of natural and man-made phenomena where the random occurrence of events produces random time intervals, and thus it has found use in the fields of operations research, engineering, economics, and others.

text: Synaptic transmission is the way in which signals (or action potentials) are carried from one neuron (the pre-synaptic neuron) to the next neuron (post-synaptic neuron) or to target effector cells (e.g., muscle or gland cells). This process starts when an electrical impulse, also referred to as an action potential, is generated in the axon of a presynaptic neuron, and travels down the axon to the axon terminal. When the action potential arrives at the terminal, it causes the opening of voltage-gated calcium channels, and calcium ions flow into the neuron. This entry of calcium triggers synaptic vesicles (which are full of neurotransmitters) to move towards the cell membrane and release their contents into the synaptic cleft in a process known as exocytosis. Neurotransmitters then diffuse across the synaptic cleft and bind to specific receptors in the postsynaptic membrane of the next neuron or target cell. The binding can result in the opening or closing of the ion channels located at the postsynaptic cell, leading to excitation or inhibition depending on the type of neurotransmitter and the type of receptor (channel/protein and a few atomic details). When the signal is strong enough, this may cause a new action potential to be generated in the postsynaptic neuron. After release, the neurotransmitters are removed from the synapse by reuptake into the presynaptic neuron, enzymatic decomposition, or simple diffusion out of the synapse. This highly regulated process enables rapid, yet specific, modifiable communication between neurons - that permits diverse and dynamic functions including learning, memory, and behavior.

text: Inspired by previous work leveraging both similarities and dissimilarities between sentence pairs, we propose a new approach which uses only dependency relations as features for the task of paraphrase detection. This is an attempt to testify our idea, and we believe other sources of information beyond syntactics are useful as well, which are left to future work. A dependency relation is represented as a triplet, that is a dependency type followed by a head-modifier word pair: rel(head, modifier). After extracting dependency relations from each sentence, we align them to form a set of paired dependencies and a set of unpaired dependencies. The set of paired dependencies represents the similarities between the two sentences; similarly, the set of unpaired dependencies represents the dissimilarities. For dependency alignment, we follow the method adopted in [5], and use exact match for dependency type alignment, while resort to a English lexical database, namely WordNet [8], for computing word similarity between head pairs or modifier pairs. A word pair is aligned if their similarity is above a certain threshold. Two dependency relations are aligned if their dependency type is identical and their weighted sum of word similarities is above a certain threshold. We embed the dependency type and word pair with two disparate embedding schemes. Specifically, for the dependency type we simply use a randomly initialized embedding which is updated during training. For the word pair, we use off-the-shelf embeddings that are trained on a large corpus in an unsupervised fashion. Then these three embeddings are concatenated to get the embedding vector for dependency. We call it dependency embedding, which are then fed into a simple neural network that consists of only a few fully-connected layers for classification. This embedding technique is invented to facilitate learning with neural networks, which are more suitable for dense features like embedding vectors. An advantage of employing neural networks is sidestepping the need to weight dependencies manually as in [5], as our model learns a soft weighting scheme automatically

text: Research has characterized individuals with alcohol use disorders (AUD) as often participating in risky drinking despite knowledge of negative physical, social, and legal consequences (Ernst & Paulus, 2005; Fein & Chang, 2008; Fein, Klein, & Finn, 2004; Miranda, MacKillop, Meyerson, Justus, & Lovallo, 2009). This risk bias is often discussed in the framework of dysfunctional decision behavior (Bechara et al., 2001; Bjork, Hommer, Grant, & Danube, 2004; Euser, Van Meel, Snelleman, & Franken, 2011). Given that adaptive decision behavior is guided by balancing risks of potential negative and positive consequences (Brown et al., 2015) or weighing immediate rewards against long-term negative consequences (Mazas, Finn, & Steinmetz, 2000), this risky bias suggests dysfunctional evaluation of risk and/or outcome in AUD. Evidence from a variety of experimental tasks indicates faster and riskier choices associated with AUD, whether in abstinent AUD, adolescents at risk, offspring of AUD parents, or individuals with other substance use disorders (Erskine-Shaw, Monk, Qureshi, & Heim, 2017; Euser, Evans, Greaves-Lord, Huizink, & Franken, 2013; Euser, Greaves-Lord et al., 2013). Several moderators of dysfunctional decision behavior in AUD have been proposed, such as optimistically biased perception of one’s own risk (Klepper, Odenwald, & Rockstroh, 2016), indifference to the negative consequences of alcohol consumption (Kamarajan et al., 2010), and trait impulsivity (Dick et al., 2010; Kumar, Kumar, & Benegal, 2018), but the impact of these moderators and their interactions are not sufficiently understood.

text: The Fundamental Journalism EthicsThe primary is represented by which are moral standards or foundation that exist with an aim of conducting reporting in a responsible and credible manner, ensuring that journalists report the truth with integrity, fairness and accountability. One touchstone is truth — journalists must be fair, accurate and thorough. Equally important to accuracy and similar truthfulness – journalists must present all sides of a story, to provide fairness and neutrality while reporting without bias or favoritism. This means providing subjects the right of reply, and striking a neutral tone in the case of public interest. There is also the matter of independence, which is the ability of journalists to be impartial, whether politically, commercially or personally, and the freedom from any external pressure, whether it comes from advertisers, the state or interest groups. The humanity of journalism: These moral, ethical and aesthetic issues mean that the ethic of humanity places demands on journalists to be – for lack of a better word – gentle with their subjects and their audiences, to take care to avoid gratuitous harm, intrusion, exploitation, especially of vulnerable people or in traumatic situations. Accountability is crucial, too: journalists need to be prepared to accept and rectify errors, be transparent about decision-making and take on board public feedback in a constructive way. Further ethical considerations range from the safeguarding of privacy, the obligation to obtain consent in cases of reporting on private individuals or use of ‘delicate’ material, as well as the avoidance of plagiarism and showing due reference to all sources, etc. The rising importance of digital media has also underscored the importance of transparency in sourcing and incredibly rigorous fact-checking in the face of disinformation. In addition, journalists should adhere to professional codes of ethics such as those laid out by organizations like the Society of Professional Journalists or the Press Council, which clarify their obligations in this regard. Support for these principles defends the credibility of the press, promotes vigorous public debate, and makes our journalism a more critical check on the credibility of the powerful. In a politically-charged environment dominated by 'fake news', honest journalism keeps the truth accessible, dependable and uncompromised.

text: The solar dynamo generates magnetic flux inside the Sun, which is transported outward and emerges through the Sun's surface into the corona. Magnetic loops build up "closed" magnetic flux (connected to the Sun at both ends) in the corona. Some of these closed loops subsequently "open" into interplanetary space—that is, they are connected to the Sun at only one end with the other extending to great distances in the heliosphere or beyond. Owing to the very high electrical conductivity, open magnetic flux is frozen into the solar wind and carried out with it. The magnetized solar wind expands continuously outward from the Sun in all directions, filling and inflating our heliosphere and protecting the inner solar system from the vast majority of galactic cosmic rays. The balance between the opening and closing of magnetic flux from the Sun is thus critical and fundamental both to the solar wind and to the radiation environment of our solar system. Long lasting, radial "legs" are often observed along the flanks of a CME and persisting behind it. These legs are generally interpreted as evidence for at least some continued magnetic connection of CMEs back to the Sun and hence the opening of new magnetic flux with CME ejections. That picture is further supported by observation, in situ, of beamed suprathermal halo electrons streaming in both directions along the local interplanetary magnetic field (IMF) during the passage of an interplanetary CME (ICME) cloud (e.g., Gosling 1990, 1993, and references therein), which are commonly interpreted as signatures of direct connection of the ICME magnetic field to the solar corona in both directions, and hence of newly opening magnetic flux. However, less is known about the equally necessary process of disconnection that must be present to remove newly opened flux and prevent the IMF from growing without limit.

text: The accounting equation is the basic principle that is used throughout the entire accounting process, and shows the relationship between a business’s assets, liabilities and equity. It is also known as the accounting equation or balance sheet equation, and the equation is such that Assets = Liabilities + Equity, which means all business assets are either funded (liabilities) by borrowing or by the owner's investment and retained earnings (equity). Assets are items that the business owns and are used for the operation of the business, such as cash, inventory, equipment, receivable (payment owed to the business). Liabilities are obligations or money the company owes to outsiders (for example, loans, accounts payable and mortgages). Equity is that part of the owner’s interest left in the business after deducted total liabilities from total assets, includes the owner’s investment in the business and earnings not withdrawn. This equation should always be in equilibrium in a manner which accurately depicts the financial position of the company. One or more of these parameters are always affected by any trade, to ensure the balance remains. For instance, if a business takes a loan from a bank, both assets (cash) and liabilities (loan payable) rise by the same amount and that maintains the equality. If the company makes a profit, the equity grows from retained earnings. The equation is also the foundation of the double-entry bookkeeping system. It smoothes out the numbers, and provides other stakeholders with a clear signal about how the company pays for its assets, in terms of debt and equity. Understanding the accounting equation is vitally important to anyone who is learning accounting, as the basis of double entry accounting, it provides the structure for recording and reporting on all financial transactions, and also allows for simple analysis of a businesses health, by showing where the business stands in terms of assets and liabilities.

text: The Robot Operating System (ROS) is a volume-based open source robotics development environment implementing all the libraries and conventions required to write a complex robot application. Although ROS is by name a (non-traditional) operating system, it is not an operating system; it is instead a distributed communication middleware running above OSs such as Linux, which in turn, is used as a host for modular soft-development and for inter-component real-time communication purposes of robot systems. A key function of ROS is message passing between distributed processes (referred to as nodes in ROS) which specialize in tasks like sensing, actuation, localization, mapping and path planning. ROS abstracts some of the hassle of inter-process communication and lets us write more modular code where sensors, controllers and algorithms can work separately but still be able to talk to each other. ROS provides a variety of functionality such as hardware abstraction, device drivers, logging, visualization (e.g., RViz), and simulation (e.g., Gazebo) prepackaged. It has a rich set of programming languages, including but not limited to Python and C++, and a large community-contributed package ecosystem that allow for rapid development. ROS is used by the research and industry community because itâ€™s flexible, scalable and supports features of modern robots, including SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping), motion planning (through MoveIt), or computer vision (through OpenCV). Along with the release of ROS 2, advancements in real time capabilities, security and cross platform support have made ROS an even better fit for industrial and commercial robots. For all intents and purposes, ROS is the backbone of today’s robotics research and development work, serving as a universal platform that allows developers to create applications that are capable of working across multiple robot platforms from the start.

text: Personnel Management and Human Resource Management are two ways of managing people in an organization, and there are certain differences between the two in scope, definition, and approach. Personnel Management is frequently viewed as an old-school, administrative, reactive discipline focused on hiring, payroll, labor law compliance, and keeping employee records. It views employees primarily as production resources, and highlights rules, procedures, and the preservation of labor relations, striving toward employee welfare and industrial peace. By contrast, HRM is a more contemporary, strategic orientation to managing the needs of workers and sees them as sources of competitive advantage and as ‘partners’ in the pursuit of organisational objectives. HRM Combines people management with business strategies and systems, focusing upon policies such as recruitment, training and development, and management of performance, motivation, and engagement. It is centered around unleashing the full potential of employees, creating a good corporate culture and matching a workforce to the overarching needs of an endeavor. Additionally, while HRM includes all aspects of development and management, Personnel Management is largely centered on handling administrative and operAtional functions. A wide range of values are attached to work, fortes for HRM more participative style power of teamwork and involvement in decision making, in great contrast with Personnel Management, which practices departmentalization and compartmentalization. Due to technology development and globalization, organizations have been forced to utilize HRM in order to survive and to adapt in the face of changes, therefore HRM has evolved into an expansive, multifaceted function that is designed to support long-term organizational performance.

text: A seed drill is a device that sows the seeds for crops by metering out the seeds, positioning them in the soil, and covering them to a certain average depth. Manual broadcasting had led to irregular seed sowing, poor germination and low yield (Belavadi and Prakash, 1980). The seed drill transformed the way individual farmers worked, developed stronger strains of plants through selective breeding and helped make farming more efficient by reducing unnecessarily wasted seed. It is composed by some sections: the seed hopper, the tube and/or funnels to deliver the seeds in the field and the coulters/openers that make the furrows where the seeds are placed. Some of the newer seed drills even feature press wheels that help the seeds to be covered and lightly firmed up, while promoting better soil-seed contact. Seed drill has various advantages, including accurate sowing depth, proper spacing between rows, better germination rate, and which all together may enhance productivity and efficient utilization of resources. Modern seed drills can be modified to accommodate differing seed types and land conditions and are often used for sowing in conjunction with plant and fertilizer appliacators, potentially providing a fertilizing and sowing sevice in one pass. Seed drill machines can be manually-operated, ox-operated or horse-operated, and tractor-operated depending on the size of the farm and the available technology. The modern precision seed drills are GPS- and sensor-assisted, and calibrated to deliver seed in exact amounts, particularly important for high-value crops. Additionally, the employing of seed drills permits a better kill of weeds, due to the fact that the dense and uniform crop stand outcompetes the weeds more effectively. It also promotes conservation tillage as it reduces soil disturbance, helps conserve soil moisture, and improves organic matter. Seed drills are often marketed by governmental agencies and farmers' cooperatives who help farmers to pay for them or use them as extension tools to train farmers to use them in areas where they are less commonly used. In summary, seed drill is an indispensable implement in sustainable and mechanised agriculture that allows for better crop establishment, better use of land and the profitability of the farm, that can be achieved by the machine.

Whereas behaviour is observable and measurable, mental processes need to be studied indirectly through introspection, neuroimaging, and psychometric tests and experimental manipulation.

text: HRV is a relevant marker reflecting the ANS activities. ANS plays a vital role in modulating heart rates and cardiac output in response to physiological and psychological stress. It comprises of two self-regulatory systems, namely the sympathetic nervous system (SNS) and the parasympathetic nervous system (PNS). SNS and PNS activities are antagonistic. While an increase in SNS activities quickens heart rates, an increase in PNS activities slows down heart rates. The SNS is responsible for the fight-or-flight response in stressful situations, while the PNS is for resting and digesting in relaxed conditions. Due to the continuous antagonistic inputs from the SNS and PNS, the cardiac rhythm cyclically fluctuates slightly around the mean heart rate (Tarvainen et al., 2014). By measuring this fluctuation, the SNS and PNS activities, and their balance can be assessed since the rates and pressure intensity signals of the baroreceptors, situated in the aorta and the internal carotid arteries, will respond to the demand of the cardiac needs as a reaction to stressors experienced by the body. These responses are usually in the form of changing blood pressure levels, heart rates, and emotions, etc. As bio-signals, such responses can be measured by changes in heart beats which can be precisely represented by HRV using spectrum analysis, also referred to as frequency domain analysis.

text: Fertilization in plants is the joining of the male (sperm) and female (egg) gametes to produce a diploid zygote that will develop into an embryo. In the flower of a flowering plant, this process occurs after pollination and takes place in the ova contained within the ovary. Once a pollen grain has been deposited on a receptive stigma, it will germinate to initiate the growth of a pollen tube down through the style to the ovule. Two male nuclei enter the ovule via an opening in the integuments (micropyle). When the male gamete penetrates the embryo sac within the ovule, the egg cell and another male gamete combine the process of fertilization and give rise to a zygote. This zygote grows to form the seed embryo. The second male gamete is involved in a peculiar process known as double fertilization, which occurs only in angiosperms. Fertilization triggers a cascade of developmental events in the ovule that results in the formation of a seed, while the ovary develops into the fruit that protects and aids with seed dispersal. This serves not only for the initiation of the plant new life cycle, but also to maintain the transmission of genotype from the parents to offspring. Fertilization is crucial in preserving genetic diversity and adaptability in plant populations. In other non-flowering seed plants such as cycads and ginkgos, fertilization also occurs in the ovule, but the sperm are motile and are delivered to the egg(s) by pollen tubes. Irrespective of group, fertilization is the signature event in sexual plant reproduction and is the link that connects pollination to seed development and plant reproduction.

text: Track II diplomacy is informal and unofficial dialogue between non-state actors (such as academics, retired civil and military officials, public figures, social activists, etc) which can help resolve conflict (or, at least, mitigate its impact) by narrow the margins of misunderstanding in conflict areas, to reduce tensions and prevent the conflicts from escalating further. Whereas, in formal diplomacy, such talks often are impossible, for various reasons, in the process Track II they can take place without the press and without adding new political limitations. This adaptability allows for creativity when seeking solutions and may in turn minimize misperceptions and promote trust-building among groups otherwise riven by deeply held animosities or longstanding grievances. Track II diplomacy can also be regarded as a welfare activity when it contributes to prepare the ground for official peace talks, affects policy, or leads to policy change by presenting the officials with new ways of thinking or through the provision of additional technical expertise. These may include workshops, conferences, and back-channel discussions to encourage dialogue between party leaders or between those parties that may be marginalized outside official negotiations, as can be the case of minority rebel groups or smaller factions in the case of a negotiated settlement to an internal conflict in a State. Track II approaches have worked -- in many world conflict zones -- to break deadlocks, build confidence and ideas and bring to the table while pursuing peace. Significantly, although Track II diplomacy has no binding status, and is unofficial, the results of Track II efforts can exert considerable political effect and can become Track I diplomacy when supported by a country or international organization. This (official and unofficial tracks) approach has since become an increasingly important tool in contemporary conflict resolution and international relations, particularly in intractable, protracted conflicts where trust and communication are at a minimum.

text: Point estimation is a statistical method of providing an approximate value or a best guess of some quantity based on possibly incomplete or noisy measurements. For instance, to estimate the average height of all students in a school, we can take some students, each representing a good sample of the actual students, measure their heights and calculate the average sample, which is a point approximation of the population average. A point estimator is a specific kind of statistic used to estimate a parameter of a population from this single sample of data. Some simple point estimators are the sample mean (to estimate the population mean), the sample proportion (to estimate the population proportion), and the sample variance (to estimate the population variance). A point estimate is considered good when it has some desirable statistical properties like unbiasedness (its expectation is the true value of the parameter), consistency (it converges towards the true value as the sample size tends to infinity), and efficiency, that is it has minimum variance among all unbiased estimators. Although they are simpler to use and understand, point estimates have the drawback that they provide no information regarding precision or uncertainty about the estimate. In other words, two samples could give two different point estimates and it would not be accurate to ignore the variability and focus on only one point estimate. That is why point estimation are used to complement interval estimation (the most typical one being confidence intervals), which provides a plausible range of values for the parameter. Point estimates are ubiquitous in traditional statistics including business and economic forecasting, political polling, quality control, and medical studies. Whether one is attempting to estimate the average income in a population, the level of defects in a manufacturing process, or the value of a drug’s effect, point estimation is at the heart of converting raw data into a decision or action. To conclude, point estimation is an important aspect of the foundations of statistics to make educated guesses about populations using sample data, but only in conjunction with measures of uncertainty.

text: Slash-and-burn farming Slash-and-burn agriculture is a category of shifting cultivation called slash-and-burn based simply by the fact that this category has this name in the majority of the world's. This process temporarily fertilizes the soil because the ash residue will deplete the soil’s nutrients. Farmers then grow crops like maize, millet or root vegetables on this cleared area for several years before soil fertility decreases. When its productivity begins to wane, the land is left barren as the farmers move to the next patch of forest and the process is repeated. Shifting cultivation or slash-and-burn farming is a traditional farming method which involves the clearing of forest land for cultivation, where the land can be reverted to its natural state once the crops are harvested. Although it enables the indigenous peoples of some communities to do subsistence farming, it also has major environmental consequences when it is not practiced in a sustainable way. Persistent burning and clearing of forests leads to deforestation, habitat loss, loss of biodiversity, and increases in greenhouse gas emissions. It also causes soil erosion and degradation, robbing the land of productivity in the long run. But most slash-and-burn farming has fallow periods that give the forest system time to re-grow, and in between, it doesn’t have much impact on the environment. In the past few decades, population pressure and commercial logging have reduced the length of fallow cycles, accelerating land degradation and adding to climate change. Current interventions to reduce slash-and-burn include agroforestry, sustainable land management, and alternative farming strategies that seek to reconcile food security with protecting the environment. It is necessary that the socio-economic and cultural context is known and taken into account when developing interventions. The slash-and-burn tribes are a historic agricultural system that has had its advantages and disadvantages and needs to be managed sustainably to make it a low environmental impact practice.

text: The phrase "mens rea" meaning "guilty mind" is a basic principle that the state of mind (or intent) of a person committing a crime should be taken into consideration when he or she is accused of that crime. It means that to be convicted of most offences, what an accused person did (actus reus) should be coupled with mens rea (a guilty mind), or the state of mind of the accused person the time of offending. Mens rea can be in the form of intention, knowledge, recklessness or negligence, depending on the crime. Killing so demonstrative involves acting while a person has purpose to cause death, and reckless behavior may involve acting while knowing something constitutes a risk on the objective scale of riskiness. Mens rea, as a crime, separates bad acts from good accidents, so guilty minds get punished. Various crimes require different levels of mens rea; some are strict liability offenses, wherein the state of mind of the accused is irrelevant. Proving mens rea is necessary to just outcomes because to punish without a guilty mind would offend considerations of moral accountability. Q29.14 There are a number of tests and standards used in the common law to assess mens rea, including by reference to a subjective or objective test, and there are defences that could be said to negate mens rea by demonstrating lack of intention or incapacity of mind privately. The doctrine of mens rea is, in short, the morality of the criminal law which associates guilt or blame of the mind with legal accountability.

text: Gender is a major factor in determining the mode of criminal behavior and in explaining what kinds of crimes males or females commit, how often they commit them, and in what social environment they commit them. By the numbers, guys do the majority of the crimes--and a higher percentage of very serious crimes like robbery, assault, and murder--while girls more often end up being perps in cases of lesser crimes--usually property offenses or status offenses such as shoplifting or running away. This difference is attributed to a combination of biological, psychological and social reasons. Hormonally, masculinization (i.e. testosterone) has been related to increased aggression and risk-taking. On a psychological level socialization process, its foundation is based on traditional sex roles, where there is an encouragement and reinforcement for boys to be dominant, competitive, and assertive, and girls to be nurturing, compliant, and passive, which in turn affects behaviors and life decision-making. Sociological explanations, such as those of the gender role hypothesis and feminist criminology, stress how patriarchy restricts opportunities for offending and socialises individuals into roles that are more virtuous. For instance, female offending is frequently associated with victimization, abuse, and economic deprivation, suggesting that women follow a distinct route to crime compared with men. The justice system itself could have different standards for genders; women may be sentenced less harshly since they're seen as vulnerable, or because women are often the primary caregiver, and men may get harsher sentences. In addition, victims’ gender shapes victimization patterns and victim responses to crime. Recognizing these differences is important for developing gender-responsive crime prevention programs, rehabilitation, and policies that are inclusive to the specific needs and experiences of all gender identities throughout the criminal justice system.

text: Cache memory is a tiny, ultra-fast memory unit that is located between the processor and the main memory, that caches copies of the data from the most frequently used main memory locations to prevent the average time to access memory from the processor slowing down. Since main memory (RAM) is far slower than the processor registers (registers) or cache, a portion of the program stored in RAM accesses through the cache to achieve high efficiency of the computing. When the CPU wants data, it looks in the cache first (cache hit). (fast) – if required data found – (hit): access quick (slow) – if required data not found – (miss) fetched from slow main memory – (since required) – loaded in fast cache. Cache works in layers: L1 (smallest and fastest, within the CPU core), L2 (larger and slower), sometimes L3 (shared between cores). Using LRU (Least Recently Used), among other algorithms, the cache is wiser about what data to evict when it runs out of space to make room for new data. Cache Cache exists to speed up execution of loops and repetitive tasks by keeping data on hand as close to the CPU as possible. Depending on the architecture, it can hold an instruction, a data, or both. Cache coherence protocols guarantee data coherence in multi-core CPUs. In general, cache memory can help to increase the performance of the CPU by keeping on hand such specific types of data to avoid making repeated slow fetches from slower main memory.

text: Conflict theory According to Karl Marx’s conflict theory, which has been the framework for the analysis of class conflict, there are two primary social classes in the conflict model: the bourgeoisie (owners of production) and the proletariat (laborers). MARX: Capitalist societies are inherently unequal and the ruling class simply uses labor as a means to make money, the result is class struggle and revolution. It is of particular significance in the case of Bangladesh, being a country plagued with high levels of socio-economic disparities. Much of the wealth is in the hands of industrialists, landlords, and political insiders, while most people work at low-wage, labor-intensive jobs including for jobs in garment industries, farms and informal labor markets. The ready-made garment (RMG) sector is only one conspicuous instance: factory owners are making a killing, while workers — mostly female — endure long working hours, difficult conditions, and minimum wage levels. The divide between urban and rural, differences in land ownership, a small land owning class and limited upward mobility can be seen as class divisions. Moreover, corruption and nepotism when it comes to access to education, health care and work keep the working class in poverty. Intermittent labor protests and union strife are consistent with Marx's prophecy of conflict over exploitation. While Bangladesh did not spawn a Marxist-type revolution, class inequalities have spawned social movements that seek to increase the minimum wage, secure better labor rights, and obtain a more even allocation of resources. Marx’s theory then becomes a useful framework for examining the socio-economic structure of Bangladesh, which are influenced by class struggle within not only the political movement but also social policies of the country.

text: Nationalism and populism increasingly impede international cooperation and multilateralism by favoring national over global interests and undermining the ethos of collective action. Nationalist and populist movements tend to favor policies of sovereignty, protectionism, and “zero-sum” thinking, where what is good for one country is bad for another. This approach can manifest as withdrawal from international agreements, abandonment of multilateral institutions (such as United Nations or European Union), or reduced collaboration on important global challenges like climate change, trade or security. Populist rulers may also employ nationalist claims to mobilize internal support and to describe international cooperation as contrary to national interest, thereby reinforcing domestic and international divisions. The nationalist/populist wave has led to some countries leaving trade deals, such as the TPP and the EU (Brexit). Such movements can also further anti-immigrant feelings and undermine global efforts to deal with the world’s growing waves of migrants and refugees. Moreover, the upsurge of nationalism incumbently questions the validity and efficiency of institutions like the international ones, and puts even more hurdles on the way to reaching a consensus on global issues. The breast-beating focus on the challenge between great powers overlooks the breakdown in the capacity for genuinely multilateral negotiation, as countries across the board look increasingly toward their own territory or other self-proclaimed (and not always territorially related) interests. Nationalism and populism may offer extensive short-term political rewards for certain leaders, but the longer term costs are, time and time again, a more fragile global system of order, diminished international solidarity, and a greater challenge to tackle issues that require collective efforts, such as pandemics or climate change.

text: A nursery is a place where plants are propagated and grown to a desired age through an internship process for planting on location. Nurseries offer controlled environment for moisture, soil, light and temperature, for healthy and active growth during the most vulnerable phases of a plant. They are important for successful crop establishment especially for fruit trees, vegetables, flowers and forestry plants. In case of nursery, a number of methods including seed sowing, grafting, cutting, layering and tissue culture is used for producing high quality planting material. Nurseries certainly support higher germination rates, more uniform germination, and the resistance against pests and diseases and, consequently, good crop yields. They also enable farmers to cultivate plants outside of their natural growing season so that production can remain constant. Commercial nurseries are businesses which operate on a large scale to grow and sell seedlings to the public. In nurseries, the right care is watering, more than weekly, fertilizing, insect and virus control, as well as hardening off the plants for adapting outdoors. The supply of high quality nursery stock is required in forestation, reforestation and agroforestry programs, to support environment protection and sustainable agriculture. It helps in the minimization of crop loss by transplanting only healthy, vigorous plants from the nursery. Furthermore, contemporary nurseries use facilities such as greenhouses, mist chambers and shading nets to enhance growth conditions. The failure of many crops to cause by an insecure nursery management makes nurseries are one of the indispensable in the agricultural production system.

text: High-key and low-key lighting are two different lighting techniques used in photography and cinematography which can affect the overall tone, mood and visual impact of a scene. High-key lighting involves bright lights with virtually no shadows and low contrast and gives a clean, soft look with an upbeat feel. This setup generally employs two or more lights or heavy fill from strong lights to cancel out deep shadows and reduce the lighting ratio, which is perfect for scenes that require a sense of joyousness, wholesomeness, or an open feeling. It frequently appears in comedy, musical theatre, advertisements, and daytime television where it is less contrasty and more legible overall. High-key backgrounds are usually white or light colored, allowing you to maintain the beautiful light in general. In comparison, low-key lighting creates a more stark difference between light and shadow which leads to more prominent shadows with higher contrast and a more sinister, edgy or mysterious feeling. It's illuminated contrast lighting that requires a bright Key light and not much if any fill light, and accentuates and emphasizes the shadows across your subject and BG to add depth, tension, and visual interest. Low key lighting is used in thrillers, film noir, horror, and dramatic scenes to create suspense, conflict, or emotional intensity at the center of the narrative structure. text: Readability and legibility – two fundamental principles in typography, and from there, in design, but used frequently to indicate how easily a message can be understood by the audience. Although the terms are often used interchangeably, they describe different dimensions of text processing. Legibility refers to the degree of ease with which one character or letter can be identified from another. It comes down to how distinct the letterforms are — how easily one can recognize an “I” from an “l” or an “O” from a “0.” A few factors for legibility, which are all aspects that relate to the typeface design: the shape of the letters, inter-letter spacing, thickness / lightness of the letters, and if certain characters stand out. A very legible font that prevents misunderstanding (confusion) in signage, user interfaces, or wherever there is some crucial need for quick recognition. Readability, meanwhile, is about the ease of reading and understanding blocks of text. This involves elements such as font size, line length, line spacing (leading) paragraph structure and overall design. Even a readable type face is unreadable in a long, tight paragraph or a bad color contrast. For instance, while white-colored text on light gray background is technically readable, it does not have enough contrast to really be readable. Readability is vital for body text, articles, how-tos, and anything that needs to be read to be comprehended. These three aspects of readability and legibility are not only influenced by the medium (print or screen) and target audience, but environmental factors (e.g. glare on screen, dimly lit room etc) need to be taken into account. The design principles of accessibility also demand high readability for impaired users (such as those with poor vision or reading disorders). A combination of the two is what good typography is all about: no struggling required to unravel the text; the reader can concentrate on what the text is actually communicating. In other words: legibility makes characters visible, readability makes text flow, and both are prerequisites for effective visual communication.

text: Two major types of root systems exist, fibrous roots and taproots, but they can also parallel a combination of both types or be modified to suit the plant's environment. The Tap Root System The tap root system has the radicle as the primary root and is found in dicotyledonous plants. It is made up of one main meaty root (the taproot) that stretches into the soil and branches out into smaller lateral or secondary roots. Examples are carrots, mustard and mango. Taproots are often used in storage (as in beetroot or carrot), and where penetration lower into the soil is required, as with sweet clover. However, species like grasses, wheat and rice have a fibrous frying-pan type of root system in which leaves are borne on the stem. Here, the taproot is evanescent, and many roots of similar diameter arise at the base of the stem, creating a dense mat. Fibre roots are capable of de-ersting the soil and uptake nutrients from the upper soil layers. The third kind of roots, adventitious roots, develop from a part of the plant other than the radicle — a stem, a node, or even just a leaf. In some cases these roots may also be referred to as brace roots, and they often function later to prop up the plant in the soil. Functions of roots For support Roots may help support the plant, and may emerge from the base of the stem, above the ground. Root systems are also influenced by the actual) role plants have in their environment and how this environmental feedback acts on the plant root system (e.g. pneumatophores in mangroves grow upwards to facilitate gaseous exchange in waterlogged soils, and buttress roots in tropical trees to give added support for shallow soil). It also helps vines to cling to things. These varied types of root systems do not simply anchor and absorb but are also important for water uptake, mineral nutrition, carbohydrate storage, reproduction and general plant stability. Knowledge on type of root system is crucial in agriculture, horticulture and in soil conservation, since it affects how a plant interacts with the environment, competes and survives under different conditions.

text: World War II Bretton Woods system, the famous international monetary order created in 1944 at the end of the war, which became the architecture for post-war global economic system. It set up institutions to foster monetary stability, economic growth and postwar reconstruction such as the International Monetary Fund(IMF) and the World Bank. In the system currencies were pegged to the US dollar, which in turn could be exchanged at a fixed rate for gold, and trade and investment barriers were muted by fixing the exchange rates to further decrease the risk of rate fluctuation. The object of Bretton Woods was to avoid a recurrence of the economic dislocations of the 1930s and the war that followed, by promoting international cooperation among nations. the system facilitated the economic war recovery and supported the expansion unprecedented global that took place during the decades subsequent to the war. Despite the collapse of the fixed exchange rate system in the early 1970s and the subsequent floating of currencies, the Bretton Woods institutions continue to be key players in global economic governance. Their portfolios have expanded to include from poverty reduction, to crisis management, to development finance. Bretton Woods marks the departure towards multilateralism and institutionalize economic cooperation; it continues to define how states grapple with the challenges of global finance and development.

text: Definition A nation is a cultural, religious, and/or ideological community of individuals that share a common identity and elements of common culture, history or language, often possessing or seeking its own independent government or state and inhabiting a particular territory. The term Common Notion, is intended to express the idea that the National Movement exists within and beyond the limits of the state, as in the case of Kurd, Basque or Palestinian, the common denominator of the identity of that movement does not tie in with any particular state. By contrast, a state is a political and legal entity with a territorial boundary, an administration with a central authority that makes laws and is capable of excluding people or goods, of collecting taxes, and of representing its population in international diplomacy. States are sovereign and are considered the dominant entities in the international system according to international law. Though the nation-state suggests a harmonious correspondence between national identification and state organization, indeed many states are multiethnic or multinational, while many nations are stateless or (below the surface) cross border. Here the difference becomes politically salient: nationalism often fuels the call for self-determination—a state for a culture—whereas state-backed programmes seek to homogenise national identity across a diverse population. Statehood entails international recognition, protection under international law, and the holder of international obligations, whereas nationhood can affect internal identity, legitimacy, and political mobilization. There are internal problems such as internal conflict or oppression of the minority or secessionist movement, and the foreign policy can also be shaped, where a diaspora nation advocates for its kin across international borders. Accordingly, whereas “state” indicates an institutional and legal framework, “nation” conveys a sense of collective identity and shared consciousness – two entwined yet conceptually separable foundations of political life.

And with the war widely covered by the media, graphic images of combat unfolded around the world in living rooms, shaping public opinion and political discussion. Ultimately, the United States pulled out in 1973, and in 1975 North Vietnam took Saigon, uniting the country under communist leadership. The Vietnam War had significant effects: It changed U.S. military strategy, foreign policy, helped trigger the civil rights and countercultural movements, and left Vietnam in a shamble, economically and socially. Internationally, it revealed the constraints on superpower meddling, and illuminated the difficulty of nationalist struggles in the shadow of Cold War politics. text: The ancient Greek tragedians were playwrights who wrote plays that were part of a series of plays representing a single theme; their works are traditionally marked by beginning with a prologue and ending with a messenger's speech, and the chorus (limited to 12 singers and dancers) was used rather than the modern actor. Among these three tragedians there was a good deal of rivalry and tension in the development of the genre, and while there are certain conventions of style that are shared between Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides, each brought his own challenges to, and spin on certain of these conventions, as well. Aeschylus, sometimes called the “father of tragedy,” brought the second actor to the stage, making dialogue and complicated interactions possible beyond the chant of the chorus. His plays—including The Oresteia trilogy—are pageantlike and also significant for the questions they pose about myths and about moral, religious, and civic life. Sophocles advanced the dramatic form by adding a third actor and was also known for his deeper character development. His best known plays are Oedipus Rex and Antigone, in which he explores such themes as fate, the position of the individual versus the state and the role of humans as pawns of the gods. Euripides' realistic treatment of characters stands in stark contrast to his contemporary, Sophocles, whose 'heroic' characters are often stereotypes. His plays, including Medea and The Bacchae, confront audiences with morally complex female protagonists and are not afraid to criticise the gods. These tragedians were all selected to compete in the annual contests for Dyonisian festival in Athens. Their plays are typical of the advance stage, with a formal structure, poetic language and chorus commenting on the action and reflecting respectively. The Greek tragedians have been known to present pivotal concepts like catharsis, hamartia (tragic flow.), and dramatic irony. Their spirit lives on in literature, theatre, and philosophy around the world, as their exploration of universal themes and of what is best in man is just as relevant to us today.

text: The so-called corona loss is that the air around the conductors is ionized due to the strong electric field, leading to the loss of power in high-voltage transmission lines. When the voltage drop in the vicinity of a conductor becomes to high, the air molecules are ionized, and a visible discharge called the corona effect is produced. This ionization is accompanied by a weak blue flash of light, a hissing sound due to creation of ozone and audible ticks due to generation of gaseous ions. Corona loss leads to continuous discharge of electrical energy to the atmosphere which decreases efficiency of power transmission. It also induces radio interference and noise, which may be an issue in urban areas. Corona loss is influenced by the surface shape and condition of the conductor, its size and shape, the spacing of the conductor, operating voltage, atmosphere condition such as humidity, air pressure, and altitude. Corona loss is minimized for conductors of bigger diameters and with perfectly smooth surfaces while it is maximised for conductors with rough or damaged surfaces. The electric field intensity reduces and share of corona loss in total loss decreases in both cases. Though generally corona loss is a small fraction of total loss of transmission, at very high voltage such as extra-high voltage (EHV) and ultra-high voltage (UHV) lines is more and more distinct. Consequently, the understanding and avoiding of corona loss is important in high-voltage power transmission system design and operation in order to achieve efficient, reliable and environmentally-friendly system operation.

text: Fear conditioning paradigms rank among the most fundamental and widespread experimental procedures to elucidate the neurophysiology of aversive learning across different species (Maren, 2001). Discriminant delay fear conditioning involves presenting initially neutral, conditioned stimuli (CS), in various modalities, one of which (CS+) coterminates with an aversive unconditioned stimulus (US), such as a mild electric stimulation, while the other (CS-) is always presented alone. Fear conditioning is often probed by measuring autonomic responses. Several studies have demonstrated differential pupil size responses to CS+/CS- in cats (Oleson, Ashe, & Weinberger, 1975; Oleson, Westenberg, & Weinberger, 1972) and humans (Greenberg, Carlson, Cha, Hajcak, & Mujica-Parodi, 2013; Hermans et al., 2016; Kluge et al., 2011; Pollak et al., 2010; Reinhard & Lachnit, 2002; Reinhard, Lachnit, & König, 2006; Visser et al., 2016; Visser, Kunze, Westhoff, Scholte, & Kindt, 2015; Visser, Scholte, Beemsterboer, & Kindt, 2013). This resonates with a rich literature showing that pupil size is influenced by a wide range of neuropsychological processes in humans (Granholm & Steinhauer, 2004) such as perception of various arousing stimuli (Bayer, Sommer, & Schacht, 2011; Bradley, Miccoli, Escrig, & Lang, 2008; Hermans, Henckens, Roelofs, & Fernández, 2013; Korn & Bach, 2016; Prehn et al., 2013; Preller et al., 2014; Võ et al., 2008). However, there is a lack of universally accepted quantitative methods for analyzing pupil responses, and the approaches used at present are rather inhomogeneous and unspecified. They typically rely on methods such as peak scoring or calculating the area under the curve (AUC) within ad hoc defined time windows.

text: The most common presentation of invasive meningococcal disease is meningitis, while fulminant meningococcal septicaemia has a higher mortality rate [23]. Critical cases may develop disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) and acute adrenal haemorrhage. In cases with severe meningococcaemia, intravascular thrombosis and haemorrhagic necrosis can cause dramatic widespread purpura fulminans with potential infarction and gangrene of limbs [21,23]. Meningococci can also cause pneumonia, which occurs in 5–15% of patients with invasive meningococcal disease [24]. Other syndromes associated with meningococcal disease include acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), conjunctivitis, otitis media, epiglottitis, urethritis, arthritis, pericarditis, conus medullaris syndrome and cranial nerve dysfunction, especially of the 6th, 7th and 8th cranial nerves. Severe pericarditis, which is likely to result from an immunological reaction thought to be endotoxin-related, can complicate massive tamponade [21,24,25]. Early administration of antibiotics is the key factor leading to full recovery. Empirically, a third-generation cephalosporin (e.g., cefotaxime, ceftriaxone) should be given once the diagnosis is suspected. Penicillin G is still the drug of choice if the antibiotic susceptibility of the causative meningococcus is known. Alternatively, chloramphenicol can also be effective [26]. Despite the availability of effective antibiotics, the mortality rate remains at 10–15% of all cases [27]. Without treatment, the mortality rate associated with meningococcal disease can be as high as 70–90%. Up to 25% of survivors of meningococcal disease have lifelong sequelae, such as hearing loss, neurological disability (e.g., mental retardation, seizures and cognitive dysfunction), hydrocephalus, renal failure, skin scarring or loss of a limb [24]. However, survivors who do not display gross neurological damage can often show more subtle neurodevelopmental sequelae, e.g., the impairment of cognitive ability and behavioural limitations are factors that can influence academic performance in mathematics, reading and writing [28,29].

In Bangladesh, socialization starts from home where family that serves as the first agent transfers cultural norms and values, religious beliefs, language and gender roles to children. Families are often spread out or at the very least nearby and close relations enhance social norms and collective identity. Schools are also important actors of socialisation through which children are taught formal knowledge, discipline or social responsibility, and the opportunity to interact with other pupils from different backgrounds, which can increase their social knowledge. Religious institutions and practices, including the religious school mosque or madrasa, temple and religious festivals, are a potent force for moral and ethical socialization that inculcates not just faith-based values and beliefs but also group membership. Aside from family, peer groups (in adolescence primarily) are the most important crucible of social learning, as attitudes towards modernity, fashion, education, and career aspirations are formed in these institutions of unmediated social control. Mass media, with television, newspapers and now the digital media increasingly influencing, values and social norms which is reflected in their selection of food. The socialization process in Bangladesh is determined by the juxtaposition of traditional rural values and the press of urbanization, resulting in stability and change. The process of Socialization also includes role playing and learning the social roles of age, sex,and status, thus reinforcing the social order. In fact, socializing agents collaborate enabling individuals to join society, preserve cultural values, and adjust to new circumstances.

text: Proteins are large biological molecules, or macromolecules, consisting of one or more long chains of amino acid residue monomers. These monomer units are used for constructing sequences of blocks (polymers). Fifty percent of human body weight is water, and 20% of it is protein. They participate in the regulation of almost all cellular activities, such as enzymatic catalysis, transporter activity, communication, cell motility and immune responses. Proteins are made from long chains of just 20 different kinds of building blocks called amino acids, which are linked together by chemical bonds called peptide bonds, and they have different activities according to their precise shape. Although proteins have different functions and their lengths can vary quite a bit, their structure consists of four levels: primary, secondary, tertiary, and quaternary. The primary template is the linear ordering of the amino acids on a polypeptide chain. The secondary structure is defined by local folding patterns, stabilized by hydrogen bonds. Tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional shape of a single polypeptide, precisely determined by the interactions between the side chains of the amino acid residues, including hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, and disulfide bridges. Quaternary structure is the arrangement of two or more polypeptide chains to form a functional protein. Classification of proteins may be fibrous (collagen), globular (enzymes, antibodies), and membrane proteins. They are produced in ribosomes and fold and receive post-translational modifications to form functional molecules. Changes in protein shape can cause loss of function, as in Alzheimer’s or sickle cell anemia. Proteins found in diet supply necessary amino acids that are not synthesized in human body. Summary: Proteins are essential biological molecules that play an extraordinarily diverse and crucial array of roles in living systems, and which have a very specific structure.

text: Degrees of freedom In robotics, DOF is a measure of how many independent movements and parameters define the movement of a robot or its components. One DOF corresponds to one specific axis of movement: linear displacement (x, y, and z positions, e.g. forward/backward, up/down, left/right) or rotational movement (pitch, yaw, and roll). For instance, a basic robot arm that merely goes down and up has one degree of freedom, while a multifaceted robot such as the human arm which consists of joints at the shoulder, elbow and wrist is capable of having six or more degrees of freedom and drive in any direction through rotation too. Number of DOFs in robots indicates their flexibility and ability to move— the more DOFs, the more complex and accurate the movements, a necessary condition in the case of assembly, painting or surgery type of tasks. In almost all applications we have seen, a robot has 6 degrees of freedom: 3 translational (The robot can move on X, Y and Z), 3 rotational (The robot can rotate along X, Y and Z). Knowledge of DOF is important in the design, control and programming of robots since it strongly affects the robot’s ability to accurately position and move its end effector in a constrained workspace. It is also heavily used in forward and inverse kinematics.

text: The only difference between natural and man-made disasters is in their cause; however both can create crisis, destruction and trauma. A natural disaster is a major adverse event resulting from natural processes of the Earth; examples are floods, hurricanes, tornadoes, volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, tsunamis, and other geologic processes. They are such things as earthquakes, tsunamis, volcanic eruptions, cyclones, floods, droughts and also fires caused by lightning or spontaneous combustion. They can be very hard to forecast, they tend to strike without a moment’s notice and they can can be made worse by other factors such as deforestation or climate change. Natural disasters can have catastrophic consequences, though their happening is generally not determined by man while its vulnerability of man is important. Artificial disasters are the result of the acts of humans or negligent human action, and system failures. These range from industrial accidents, such as chemical spills, nuclear meltdowns and transport disasters, to terrorist attacks, building collapses and armed conflict. It can be attributed to human errors, inadequate maintenance, absence of safety codes or intentional damage. The important difference is responsibility: Man-made disasters are avoidable with proper regulation, technology, training and governance; natural ones can only be mitigated in their effects, not avoided altogether. But in today’s world the line between the two is increasingly obligatory: natural disasters like floods can be exacerbated by poor urban planning and uncontrolled development. Likewise, anthropogenic climate change is also exacerbating how often and how powerfully natural disasters occur. This distinction is crucial for both disaster preparedness and risk-reduction policies, because, while man-made disasters require a systemic overhaul and accountability, natural disasters need predictions, early warning systems, and strengthening resilience. Rehabilitation and long-term recovery efforts that include both types of programs are needed to reconstruct communities and reduce risks in the future.

text: Blazars include BL Lacertae (BL Lac) objects and flat-spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs). BL Lacs show featureless optical continuum, and are believed to be the beamed counterparts of the FR I radio galaxies (Browne 1983; Antonucci 1993; Urry & Padovani 1995). Xie et al. (1993) claimed that the parent population is FR I and FR II (G). FR II (G) is a radio galaxy whose optical type is that of a galaxy. Owen et al. (1996) also proposed that FR II radio galaxies should be regarded as a part of the parent population of BL Lac objects. From observations of blazars, it is known that they vary on diverse timescales. Variability timescale of blazars can be broadly divided into three classes, namely, intraday variability (IDV) or microvariability, short-term outbursts and long-term trends (Fan 2005). Significant variations in the flux of a few tenths of magnitude over the course of a day or less is often known as IDV (Wagner & Witzel 1995). Short-term outbursts and long-term trends can have timescales ranging from a few weeks to several months and several months to years, respectively. In about the last two decades, the variability of blazars in radio to optical bands on diverse timescales has been reported in a large number of papers (e.g., Miller et al. 1989; Courvoisier et al. 1995; Heidt & Wagner 1996; Takalo et al. 1996; Sillanpää et al. 1996a, 1996b; Bai et al. 1998, 1999; Fan et al. 1998a, 1998b, 2002, 2007a, 2007b; Xie et al. 2002b; Gupta et al. 2004, 2008a, 2008b, 2008c; Cellone et al. 2007; Ciprini et al. 2007, and references therein).

text: We know that social media including Twitter, Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, YouTube and TikTok has become more and more important to how to libraries and information organizations are getting content out to users, community engagement, and addressing equitable access. These communication channels allow libraries to communicate services, events, and materials in real time across many platforms to many different kinds of patrons, give patrons the quickest way of receiving information they may care about, share the fruits of librarians’ selective labor, whether book recommendations or faculty publications or highlight materials in an archive, and to have a directed and interactive conversation with patrons, whether this means doing a live stream or engaging with patrons via polls and hashtags. Social media campaigns can call attention to summer reading programs, digital literacy initiatives and other campaign targets, as well as encourage community participation through responses (likes, shares, comments), comments and direct messaging. Using analytics, libraries can monitor reach, engagement, and the demographics of the people served, and use that information to build on the most effective content and strategies. Digital social outreach is also facilitated for underserved or remote communities through digital social media, allowing equal opportunity regardless of location. But it takes disciplined policies on tone, privacy, moderation and accessibility — including visuals with captions and linguistic inclusiveness. Libraries can also offer misinformation tracking and digital media literacy instruction on social platforms, translating the authority of the institution into the trust of the public. Integrated within broader communications strategies, however, social media becomes a dynamic space of librarianship—a shared knowledge, a community, and an institutional currency.

text: As the scholarly literature has duly pointed out (Rooduijn, 2014; Taggart, 2004), populism is not always and everywhere synonymous with far-right, extremist, sovereignty-demanding movements. In Europe one sees left-wing parties such as Syriza and Podemos sharing themes and rhetorics (like anti-elitism) with the parties on the other side of the political/populist spectrum, even if starting from a different ideological perspective. It is also evident that several traditional parties and their leaders, be they in government or not, at different political latitudes, have adopted rhetorics and tones that undoubtedly resemble those of movements and leaders that define themselves as populist. These are clear examples of what Mudde (2004) calls the ‘populist Zeitgeist’, i.e., that populist discourse has become mainstream in today’s politics. If all politicians are affected by some sort of populist zeitgeist, it is legitimate to ask if there is at least a difference in the intensity of recourse to populist tones, assertions and allusions. One cannot expect leaders like, say, Angela Merkel or Mariano Rajoy, suddenly to convert to a bullying populist language. It is, however, conceivable that they endorse some bellicose demands on behalf of critical sectors of their public opinions that are typically addressed by populist leaders. It is the tone and the presence of some key features of populist discourse that mark the difference.
