text: Memory is complex and is a process that occurs from the interplay of three principal memory processes, that is encoding, storage, and retrieval, in the to explain how the brain encodes, stores, and retrieves information. For one, encoding is what happens when we encode information out of sensory information, getting into to a form that our brains can store and then use. This involves converting these stimuli (be they sights, sounds, experiences) into mental representations, with attention, perception, and association to render them: meaningful. During the storage time frame, the code can be held in certain place or preserved across a certain duration according to the meaning of the code. Bodenhausen assumed storage involves different types of memory systems: sensory memory, short-term or working memory, and long-term memory components. Retrieval, at least the way many of us think of it, is the effortful part when you are reaching into storage, pulling out the information and bringing it to the top of the mind, as when you remember the name of someone’s phone number or recite a list of facts on a test. Success of retrieval depends on the depth of encoding and storing of the information and is influenced by cues, context and emotion. The memory abilities that are dependent on these three phases is crucial to memory success and relevant to learning, problem solving, and decision-making. Disruptions in any of these processes can cause memory products to be forgotten or to be remembered in error.

text: Many of the readers are certainly familiar with linked lists, as they are one of the fundamental data structures at the core of computer science curricula. The main idea behind linked lists is that different units of information can be “linked” one after each other and then accessed sequentially. The unit ofinformation in a linked list is called node. A node contains the data that has to be stored and a pointer to the following node. A pointer is an abstraction of the physical location of a node in a computer’s memory. To retrieve the information contained in a node, it is necessary to “follow the pointer.” A list starts with a pointer to the first node, called a header. The end of a list is indicated by the null pointer. A common graphical representation of linked lists uses boxes and arrows. A box represents a node; it is divided in two parts, one representing the information fields, the other representing the pointer to the next node. An arrow, starting from the pointer part of a box and ending to another box, represents a link between two nodes. For example, Figs. 3 and 4 show representations of linked lists within the interface of iList. To effectively master linked lists, students need to understand the static properties of the structure and the dynamic operations necessary to store, organize, and retrieve information from it. More complex operations are built on top of basic ones such as traversal of a list, insertion of a new node, and deletion of an existing node.

text: The effects of climate change on the storage of medicines include raised temperatures, variable moisture and extreme weather, which may impact upon the stability, efficacy and safety of medicines. Some medicinal products specifically vaccines, biologicals and antibiotics; may require high level of storage temperature and humidity control to ensure their stability throughout the shelf life. Warm ambient temperatures and high humidity — both of which are more likely as a result of climate change — accelerate the chemical degradation of medicines and cause physical changes like a loss of potency, variations in how quickly a tablet is dissolved and physical damage like clumping or discoloration. Such decay could result in suboptimum drug delivery to patients through the failure of treatment, the occurrence of side effects or the emergence of antimicrobial resistance. “We have very few days left with the stockpile we hold, and we have not been able to meet the local needs, let alone fulfill the international needs,” said Mahmood Ali, a Bangladeshi scientist who runs the group that manufactured the vaccine. “This is particularly dangerous now as there is a global outcry.” Like most poor nations, Bangladesh is highly susceptible to shortages caused by inadequate storage infrastructure, unreliable power supplies and a struggle to maintain cold chains to keep the vaccine cold, particularly in hard-to-reach rural locations. In addition, disasters of a nature like floods and cyclones due to climate can disrupt supply chain, destroy storage and lead to stock outs. These impacts will need to be offset by those manufacturing pharmaceutical products and caring for patients, investing in climate-resilient storage such as solar-powered fridges, robust packaging, and more extensive temperature-monitoring protocols. Enhancing the regulation control on the product storage and staffs being educated to store properly in unstable climate also seemed to be essential. Clearly, it would be necessary to incorporate the impacts of climate change on the storage of health care goods into efforts to safeguard public health and ensure continuing access to quality medicines when the world is warming.

text: A similar concept is arms control, which is the attempt to limit the development, production, stockpiling, proliferation, and deployment of weapons, usually (but not always) with the goal of preventing or limiting armed conflict. Unlike disarmament, which seeks to be rid of weapons completely, arms control is about the management and regulation of weapons systems to improve stability, lower the risk of war and prevent escalation in time of war. Arms control can pertain to chemical, biological and nuclear weapons as well as to a variety of systems and equipment such as small arms, and international arms control efforts may involve such areas as production, stockpiling, proliferation, and (more specifically) for chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear weapons. Arms control can even regulate the growth of racially superior weapons. Arms control is typically exercised through the use of diplomacy which seeks to impose such limitations upon consenting participants through international treaties and agreements, although it may also comprise efforts by a nation or group of nations to enforce limitations upon a non-consenting country. familiar terms such as above-mentioned}`, transparency, verification, and confidence-building also are arms control terms. One of the most prominent arms eliminations agreements is the Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (START) between the United States and Russia, under which each signatory agree to reduce their stock of long-range nuclear weapons. Others have included the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty, the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC) and the Biological Weapons Convention (BWC). Such agreements typically include verification processes and supervisory bodies, like the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW), that oversee adherence and probe infractions. Arms control contributes to security by helping to mitigate distrust and misperceptions, particularly when tensions arise in international affairs. Helps to save resources by preventing arms races and developing them for the progress of the society. But arms control has some steep hurdles, among them mistrust, changing power dynamics, the refusal by some countries to stick to old agreements, and shiny new devices (such as hypersonic missiles or systems of autonomous weapons) that make those old agreements less effective. The past erosion of some key treaties — with the U.S. and Russia exiting the INF Treaty, for example — has led to fears of a new arms race. In spite of these difficulties, however, arms control still provides for an essential tool in global security architecture, which helps to enhance predictability, prevent conflicts and foster a more stable international order.

text: Smartphones, tablets and body-worn cameras equipped with audio interfaces and wireless communication modules can be used as scalable and flexible ad-hoc microphone networks [1]. An important task when a group of people record the same event with their devices is to enhance the input signals and to localize sound sources [6], [7]. In order to employ traditional microphone array techniques with ad-hoc networks, specific challenges such as device localization [2], [3] and clock synchronization [4], [5] have to be addressed. Blind source separation (BSS) is suitable for processing signals captured by an ad-hoc microphone network and can extract the speech of an individual from a mixture of speakers talking concurrently, without prior knowledge of the location of the microphones [8]. BSS employs independent component analysis (ICA) to estimate a demixing network to recover the sources from the mixture exploiting the statistical independence of the source signals [9]. For the mixing network to be invertible, ICA typically requires the number of microphones, M, to be equal to the number of sources, N.

text: Victimization surveys are particular types of research instruments in the field of criminology that are designed to directly survey individuals about their experiences as a victim of a crime (even if it went unreported to the police). They are designed to measure the hidden figure of crime—how much crime goes unreported or undetected—so that the true levels of crime and the nature of crime in society can be gauged. Generally administered via interviews or questionnaires, victimization surveys(question victims about their exposure to different types of crime within a specified period (from burglary, assault, and theft, to domestic violence). And they collect details on the nature of the crime: reporting behavior and effects on victims. Such surveys are useful to learn about the social and demographic correlates of becoming a victim and about the nature of law enforcement response. As victimization surveys are not based on official records, they can uncover discrepancies between reported and actual levels of crime, and also identify at-risk groups. We acknowledge challenges such as recall bias, willingness to report sensitive experiences, and limited sampling, yet such surveys are crucial for informing public policy, resource allocation and the needs of victims, offering a victim-centered viewpoint of crime.

text: Both the repo rate (repurchase rate) and reverse repo rate are powerful tools the RBI uses to control inflation, which in turn brings economic growth. The repo rate is the rate at which RBI lends to commercial banks short-term funds in exchange for government securities. It is a yardstick for lending rates across the economy. RBI Repo rate hike impact on Banks When the RBI increases the Repo rates, banks are able to borrow less money in repo and have to shell out more to borrow and when the bank borrow at higher rate, they on their part lend at even higher rate; thus, reducing the credit off take from the market. On the other hand, a cut in the repo rate will reduc the cost of borrowing for individuals and companies as it becomes cheaper for banks to borrow, leading to an increase in money flowing into the markets, thereby, helping boost investment and consumption. The reverse repo rate is the rate at which the RBI borrows money from banks and is a tool used by the central bank to drain excess liquidity from the banking system. The hike in reverse repo rate makes it attractive for the banks to park their surplus funds with the RBI, a move that will help restrict money supply in the economy and check inflation. Cut in the reverse repo rate makes it less attractive for the banks to park idle funds with the RBI and consequently more funds are available for on-lending. Taken together the repo and reverse repo rates make the monetary policy corridor, which the RBI uses to strike a balance between sky-rocketing inflation and slowing economic growth. These rates can be used even by the RBI to regulate the availability of credit and interest rate, and are thus, very powerful tools in the hands of the monetary authorities.

text: In Java, and equals() are used to compare but with different purposes. The operator performs reference or identity comparison for objects, which checks whether two variables point to the same memory location or object. For primitive types, such as int or char, compares the literal values that they contain directly. But when you compare the two objects, it does not compare the content or internal state, it just checks whether both references (ea and b1) point to the same object in memory. Whereas the equals() method (of the Object class) can be overridden by objects to compare the contents, or the logical equality, of one object with another (not the reference). For instance if two distinct String objects both hold the same set of characters, calling equals() on the two of them will return true, but if the two are different instances, then if(!s1 == s2) might return false. equals() is overridden in many Java classes to make meaningful comparison between their fields, like Integer, String, user defined classes and so on. One should also remember to override equals() appropriately in their class along with their hashCode() overridden to have predictability in collections such as HashSet or HashMap. Using for object equality is a bug waiting to happen:riegler. In conclusion: use == when comparing if two references are the same and equals() when comparing the actual content or state (value).

text: Modus tollens is yet another essential and valid type of deductive reasoning, and is referred to by the nickname “denying the consequent”. It is analogous to modus ponens as it is a fundamental inference rule in classical logic that works from negating the conclusion rather than affirming the premise. The modus tollens as structure is as follows: if P ? Q;¬Q?¬P If “If P then Q” is true, and Q is not, then P cannot be the case. For instance consider the proposition “Its raining implies the ground is wet”. If we notice that “The ground is not wet,” then by modus tolens we can infer “It is not raining.” It is the reason in an eminently testable sense in so far as it can be used to disconfirm or falsify hypotheses and assertions. A belief that something should happen when it does not supports believing that it does not happen. Modus tollens is the partner of modus ponens, permitting reasoning in two directions: from antecedent implications to consequent events and from failed consequences to nongenerated antecedents. Its soundness is what makes it critical in fields like the philosophy, law, mathematics, and science to determine falsifiability. For example, in the scientific method, a hypothesis which predicts an observation can possibly be invalidated if the observation is not observed, which is the form of modus tollens. Modus tollens also helps grasping the concept of negation and conditionals. Simple as this looks in its expression, modus tollens is possessed of deep consequences for epistemology as well as for reasoning, lending support to the critical thinking enterprise of eliminating the false and clarifying the true.

text: Plant biotechnology is a field that entails applying technology on life (plants). It is a vast field that entails producing new products in a larger faster way, deviating from the conventional way of doing the same. It consists of using plant cells, tissues or organs and transferring genes to engineer better crops that bear advantageous traits, such as higher yields, resistance against pests and diseases, drought tolerance and better nutritional value. Plant biotechnology embraces conventional techniques including hybridization, in addition to such new innovations as genetic engineering and molecular breeding. It is crucial to meet some of the world's major challenges such as food security, climate change and sustainable agriculture. Because gene-editing allows for precise changes to the DNA, biotechnology becomes capable of adding genes from unrelated species, a process not available to traditional breeding. Furthermore, plant biotechnology is enabling the production of pharmaceuticals, biofuels, and biodegradable materials, thereby fostering industrial innovation. The field encompasses in vitro culture methods to grow pathogen-free plants, marker-assisted selection for speed breeding and genome editing techniques such as CRISPR. Its use reflects ethical, environmental, and safety concerns, aimed at achieving positive effects while reducing risks. On the whole, plant biotechnology has transformed crop improvement, reduced dependence on chemicals and offers prospects of providing food for the expanding world population in an environmentally responsible manner.

text: Restoring livelihoods is an important element of post-disaster recovery because it goes to the heart of the economic and social health of individuals or communities affected by such disasters. Families can lose their homes, their crops, their livestock, their businesses, and the infrastructure and capital necessary to provide for themselves and their families. Without early and effective restoration of their livelihoods, affected communities are at risk of sinking further into poverty, food insecurity and social isolation and becoming dependent on humanitarian assistance in the long term. Restoring livelihoods includes many efforts such as cash, seeds, tools, training and market access for people to once again engage in planting, trade and other productive activities. This would be complemented by the assistance to workers in the informal sector, small- and medium sized enterprises and mini-cooperatives that are the lifeblood of many local economies. Restoration of means of livelihood helps in the psychosocial recovery and is one way of regaining normalcy, dignity and self reliance. It also diminishes displacement and migration pressure, keeping families and communities together. In addition, combining livelihood recovery with DRR contributes to the resilience of economic activities to future shocks, contributing to sustainability. Gender-sensitive response is important because women and other vulnerable groups may face greater obstacles to economic recovery. Disrupted supply chains, impaired infrastructures, and shifts in environmental conditions warrant cross-sector cooperation and innovative interventions. In the end, the restoration of livelihood is more than just economic improvement, it is also stitching back a social fabric and enabling a community to rise above adversity.

When an earthquake raises or lowers the seafloor, that movement displaces the water mass above it, which forms waves that radiate out from the source at 800 kilometers an hour in all directions. At sea, tsunami waves can hardly be more than ripples in the open ocean, but close to shore, waves can accelerate and stack up, gathering speed and size and becoming a solid wall of water and debris. Tsunamis can travel across the entire width of an ocean basin and inundate coastlines with relatively little warning and can therefore inflict severe flooding and destroy infrastructure as well as claim lives. Advance warning – much like ocean buoys and earthquake monitoring – is crucial to alert coastal communities. Preparedness Evacuation is among the best ways to decrease the impact of tsunamis.

text: A chemical emergency is the release of a hazardous chemical which could harm people's health; disrupt the environment; create publicity; or require the need for action in a public emergency. These incidents mainly take place within manufacturing, warehousing or transport processes of dangerous substances, but also happen with misuse of chemicals in agricultural, military or terrorist activities. Catastrophes may include gas leaks, explosions, spills or water and soil contamination, usually leading to acute and chronic health disorders. In the short term, burning, suffocation, becoming poisoned, and death can occur, while long-term exposure can cause cancer, mutations, and reproductive defects. India’s 1984 Bhopal Gas Tragedy is one of the most lethal chemical disasters ever, with a methyl isocyanate gas leak from the Union Carbide plant being responsible for thousands of deaths and hundreds of thousands of injuries. The Seveso disaster in Italy (1976) when a dioxin-cloud was discharged in the environment and large numbers of animals died, people were evacuated and health problems also persisted long term. In the US, the 1979 Three Mile Island accident, a nuclear incident, also exposed the hazards of chemical radiation. More recently, in 2020, a similar huge explosion, sparked by improperly stored ammonium nitrate, devastated Beirut, Lebanon, killing more than 200 people and laying waste to parts of the city. Chemical accidents are frequently caused by inadequate maintenance, poor safety training, feeble regulation, or ignorance of international safety standards. To avoid chemical disasters necessitate strict industrial safety norms, storage & labeling of chemicals, training up of emergency responders, training on public awareness. It is also essential for real time monitoring systems, periodic safety audits and enforcement of environmental laws. Chemical disasters require rapid evacuation, decontamination, medical management and containment of the chemical spill to reduce the impact of the disaster. When industrialization becomes more globalized and environmental problems occur, the significance of chemical safety and international cooperation and sustainable development trend to prevent large-scale events are brought into sharp focus.

text: The term international media is used to refer collectively to all those media that are distributed across borders and attract audiences with a global dimension, and that may communicate universally (other definitions exist), such as international broadcasting, international news and international music. It counts multination news groups, entertainment business, digital sites and social media platforms that transmit popular content across international audiences. Global media players include those like CNN, BBC World News, Al Jazeera, Reuters, Netflix, YouTube, and Meta platforms, such as Facebook and Instagram. These media continuously image information, entertainment and commercialism across the world, constructing viewers' opinion and cultural identity in different societies. World press is an important pillar in the awareness about world events, facilitation of international dialogue, and providing access to broad spectrum of cultural content. It also facilitates transnational business, diplomacy, education, activism and emergency communication in times of pandemics or natural disasters. Yet the global media is not problem-free. It is often seen as embodying the interests, values, and identities of dominant media producing countries — mainly the United States, Western Europe, and Japan — and therefore to some extent is serving their interests by ceding the ground of local - or at least national - culture, identity, and news absorption. A supposed desired effect of media globalization would be the information and the culture would flow freely across borders, in a way that would promote a shared civil society that is based on "democratization, human rights and social justice". Concerns have been raised regarding the diminishing diversity of media ownership, press bias, and the influence of corporate power. Language, technology disparities and censorship also prevent global media from being truly inclusive. Beyond that, in the digital age, global media is heavily impacted by algorithms, data analytics and artificial intelligence, with a lot of what users see affected, posing privacy, misinformation and echo chamber issues. Challenges aside, the world's media are a tremendous force for global connection, cooperation and understanding across cultures. It has continued to develop with the spread of communication technology, acting as a driving force in shaping the 21st century globalizing society.

text: Make in India, a major national initiative of the Government of India launched in September 2014 to transform India into a global manufacturing hub. The main goals of the program are to increase manufacturing sector’s contribution to GDP from currently around 14% to 25%, create millions of jobs and contribute to both domestic and foreign investments. The scheme is designed to facilitate business by assigning greater powers and freedom, rationalising regulations, building infrastructure and promoting innovation and skill development. It targets 25 such sectors including automobiles, electronics, defence, textiles, pharmaceuticals and renewable energy. Make in India permits 100 FDI in most of its sectors, which has attracted investor confidence and inflow. The program also promotes creation of smart cities, industrial corridors and logistics hubs in order to drive industrial growth. Although it has appealed to substantial investment, and has boosted India's rank in ease of doing business benchmarks, it grapples with land acquisition problems, infrastructure deficiencies, the complexities of labour laws and the urgency of skills development. Yet Make in India is a cornerstone of India’s economic doctrine of self-reliance (Atmanirbhar Bharat) and sustainable industrialization, seeking to minimize import dependence, enhance India’s exports, and make India and Indian manufacturing centre-stage in global manufacturing value chains.

text: Immersive theatre It is an exciting and innovative medium of live entertainment which transgresses conventional seats-based practice and allows its audiences to be active participants in the creation and telling of the story. Immersive theatre erases the line dividing performers from the audience and usually occurs performer audience unconventional, transformed spaces such as warehouses or historic buildings, where onlookers are encouraged to walk around rooms, examine odd corners, open cupboards and sometimes interact directly with character, or impact the story they encounter and how it unravels. And this participative dimension provides a variety of multi-sensory stimulation around the viewer; it’s sight and sound and touch (it might even be smell or taste), so that the story is not only seen in “here and now” terms, but in a much more immediate, personal and, indeed, emotional way. Immersive theatre leans into experiential storytelling, building meticulous, real-seeming universes for the audience to inhabit and explore to learn plot points, character drive, and thematic throughlines on their own or through guided experiences. This format is often nonlinear in narrative, with several scenes happening at once and branching storylines, requiring multiple viewings or group discussion to fully grasp the multilayered story. Space and lighting design, sound, setting, and props become meticulously integrated for authenticity and engagement, resulting in the space as part of the performance. Immersive theatre actors must strategically maneuver around audience, script lead, and improvise to ensure the performance's integrity and structure remain intact. By decentring the stage and by making the audience more than just spectators, spectators become active participants, or could even be said to co-create meaning in this form of theatre. With Immersive theatre, it goads for one to feel more emotionally involved in the experience or to provide a stronger sense of presence in the experience and therefore becomes a more memorable and individualistic one. It has risen to prominence in the last few decades as artists and creators look to experiment with the way stories are told and how the real-time possibilities of an audience might be used to address contemporaneity and social interaction. Immersive theatre is a big logistical ask that demands tight collaboration across the technical and creative teams, but it changes storytelling by giving the spectator permission to participate- and it's a breath of fresh air to see things from new perspectives as well as nervous system shaking collective experience. All in all, immersive theatre welcomes its audiences to travel deep into a narrative world, obliterating the division between the artifice of art and the reality of life, and allowing them to step into and become part of the incredible, transformative world of the theatre.

text: Cognitive Internet of Things (IoT) technology features advanced machine intelligence toward improved data sensing and analysis [1], [2], which is particularly appealing to applications involving sensor networks. text: ALARA is an acronym for “As Low As Reasonably Achievable,” and it represents a cornerstone of radiation protection safety. It is set up to limit radiation exposure for both workers and the public, even if doses are within regulatory limits. The fundamental concept is that there is no level of ionizing radiation exposure that is absolutely safe, and for this reason all exposure should be minimized as much as reasonably possible below allowable limits, taking into account technological, social and economic considerations. ALARA is not only a regulatory mandate but a proactive philosophy in radiological safety. It is achieved using a combination of engineering controls, administrative controls, and personal protective equipment. Engineering control measures may consist of shielding, containment, and automated handling systems to limit exposure to radioactive materials. Administrative controls involve the use of work policies such as time restricted in radiation areas, maximizing the distance from the source, the use of dosimetry to monitor, and the use of proper staff training. For instance, in medical applications such as radiology departments or nuclear medicine, while users adhere to the ALARA principle by optimizing imaging protocols to use the minimal dose needed to produce diagnostic quality images. Exposure is controlled by planning, handling remotely, scheduling of maintenance and area monitoring in nuclear power plants. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) and the International Commission on Radiological Protection (ICRP) are regulatory organizations that require “as low as reasonably achievable” (ALARA) be practiced and impose exposure limitations based on current scientific knowledge of radiation effects. The standard dose limits There are standard dose limits for occupational exposure of 50 millisieverts (mSv) per year in some countries and lower for the public. ALARA encourages an ongoing attempt to drive exposures to doses well below the limits set by law and it promotes the safety culture that is intended to ensure radiation exposures are as low as reasonably achievable, and a fundamental principle of radiation protection around the world.

text: Recently, there has been much interest in instabilities in plasmas containing dust particles. Nonlinear processes such as stimulated scattering of electromagnetic waves, decay of ion acoustic waves into dust acoustic waves, dust-induced modulational instabilities of ion waves, etc., have also been studied [1] [2]–?[8], [13]. Shukla et al. [4] found that the decay of an ion acoustic wave into another ion acoustic wave and a dust acoustic wave is possible if the decay wave propagates in a direction opposite to that of the pump wave. This is expected since in the long-wavelength regime, there is a huge difference in the speeds of the ion and dust waves, and the frequency and wave-vector matching conditions cannot be satisfied if both the pump and decay waves propagate forward. On the other hand, at short wavelengths, the phase speed of the ion acoustic waves is significantly reduced [9], and one would expect that decay processes with all waves propagating forward may become possible. In a dusty plasma, short-wavelength ion acoustic waves can propagate without suffering much damping in a fairly large window of the parameter space [3]. Furthermore, the charge of the dust grains can vary on a time scale which is much shorter than that of its motion, so that both the ion and the dust acoustic wave dispersion relations can be strongly modified by the charge variation.

text: Politics is technology, ish: It influences how we communicate, how we participate, govern and secure ourselves. Technical innovations also steer the agenda, as they introduce new spaces, e.g. cybersecurity, data governance or Ethics of AI. Digital divide in politics Inequitable availability of technologies has the potential to lead to social and political imbalances. text: Previous studies have revealed an evident temporal correlation and magnitude scaling relationship between magnetic reconnection rate in the low corona and mass acceleration measured in coronal mass ejections (CMEs) or filament eruptions in a number of solar eruptive events (e.g. Zhang et al., 2001, Qiu et al., 2004, Jing et al., 2005). Such a phenomenological relationship may be explained by interaction between eruption and reconnection shortly after the onset of the disruption. On one hand, the upward motion of the magnetized plasmas stretches the magnetic field lines below the flux rope, which serves to boost magnetic reconnection. On the other hand, magnetic reconnection changes the topology of the fields surrounding the flux rope and helps reduce the magnetic tension force that binds the flux rope to the solar surface, hence enhancing acceleration of the expulsion. However, the role of magnetic reconnection is not fully understood in different kinds of magnetic configurations in varying magnetic environments as described by several flare-CME models, such as the flux-rope model (e.g. Forbes and Priest, 1995) that envisages a bi-polar configuration and the break-out model (e.g. Antiochos et al., 1999) invoking a quadruple configuration. These models also show differences regarding whether the flux rope is pre-existent before eruption or formed in situ by magnetic reconnection during the disruption, and whether magnetic reconnection takes place below or above the magnetic flux structure to be hurled out. It remains unclear whether these varying surface and coronal conditions will result in significantly different flare–CME relationship (e.g. Low and Zhang, 2002). The issue will be examined observationally by detailed case studies.

text: Intersectionality (a term created by Kimberlé Crenshaw) is a tool for examining the ways that different aspects of identity (gender, sex, race, class, sexuality, ability, nationality, etc.) can combine to create simultaneously overlapping and interlocking systems of power and oppression. Intersectionality is central to activism by making sure that movements are inclusive, fair, and respectful of the variety found in the experiences of marginalized groups. Traditional feminist or civil rights movements too often focused experiences within a dominant group within those categories — white women or cisgender men — leaving out the needs of black, queer, disabled or poor people. In its place, intersectional activism acknowledges that pursuing justice in a one-size-fits-all manner causes many whose lives intersect at multiple identities to be unjustly left behind. For example, a campaign for gender equality that does not tackle racism might inadvertently ignore the unique obstacles to employment or health care that women of color face. Equally, advocacy efforts for LGBTQ+ rights that center solely on white cisgender gay men may neglect violence and economic marginalization against trans people of color. Intersectionality requires activism to be attuned to the ways in which different modes of oppression intersect and reinforce one another — and in the process, to produce more sophisticated policy advocacy, coalition-building and resource allocation. It also contributes to solidarity across movements — linking struggles against racism, sexism, ableism, homophobia, and colonialism — and when it has teeth, it holds organizations accountable to those most affected. Intersectional activism calls leaders to elevate voices from the margins, to create campaigns of inclusion and to ask how privilege operates within movements themselves. It also moves beyond the language of representation to that of structural change where structures that cause and are influenced by exclusion are critical targets of change. That’s why intersectionality doesn’t just make activists more effective, but also ensures that justice is neither incomplete nor selective. It is a transformational lens that moves movements closer to the lived realities of experience, and hence moves social change closer to true justice and true comprehensiveness, and consequently to true endurance.

text: Risk analysis for disasters is a systematic process to identify, analyze and evaluate structures at risk, their vulnerabilities and capacity, and estimates of the expected frequency and potential impact of disasters on a given area. It facilitates decision makers to understand where and how risks evolve, prioritize actions, allocate resources and formulate disaster risk reduction strategies that work. It starts with hazard identification—whether a natural or human-made threat —such as a quake or a flood, or a chemical spill—that could do harm. Second is vulnerability assessment – the extent to which people, infrastructure, ecosystems and economic systems are exposed to such hazards and how prepared or resilient they are to them, taking into consideration factors like their socio-economic conditions, their physical exposure, and their level of preparedness. Capacity assessment looks at resources, skills, institutions, and technologies that could help that can prevent or manage impacts. Risk assessment, by incorporation of such factors, estimates the likelihood and impact of future losses and provides a basis for the establishment of risk maps and early warning systems. It influences land use planning, infrastructure engineering, emergency preparedness and public policy aimed at minimizing risk exposure and enhancing resilience. Sound risk practice in a holistic manner calls for multi-disciplinary approaches, including geophysical data, socio-economic research and involvement participatory methods with local communities. Challenges include limited data, uncertainties in hazard prediction, and dynamic vulnerability through urbanization and climate change. Nonetheless, ongoing risk assessments updating and validation are essential for adaptive management. In nutshell, the risk assessment is one of the key tools of disaster management in promoting the planning based on proactive evidence that protects life, livelihood and development gains.

text: In the circuit theory of electrical networks, sources are classified as either independent or dependent (or controlled) sources -- the former in the traditional sense and the latter is an instrument based concept which represents sources for which current or voltage can be specified. Independent sources are theoretical components that maintains a given voltage or current irrespective of the rest of the circuit. They exhibit a predictable behavior - for example, a 5V independent voltage source delivers 5 volts regardless of the rest of the circuit it is connected to, and a 2A independent current source flows a steady 2 amps, always. These sources represent batteries, ideal power supplies, and signal generators in practical use. Dependent sources (i.e., controlled sources) are such elements for which the source function (voltage or current) depends on a second voltage or current elsewhere in the circuit. They are characterised by voltage- or current-control and are said to be of 4 types, VCVS (voltage controlled voltage source), CCVS (current controlled voltage source), VCCS (voltage controlled current source) and CCCS (current controlled current source). For instance, a VCVS could output twice the voltage of that measured across some other element in the circuit. Tunica sources are applied to devices like transistors, amplifiers, and operational amplifiers which are controlled by input signals. Their addition is essential in nodal and mesh analysis to perform an actual model of electronic devices that respond dynamically to circuit changes. Although the external sources impose the initial energy states on the system, a dependent source represents feedback; it supplies the mechanisms of interactions within the circuit, such that the gain and the signals can propagate in a complex fashion. Understanding the principle of both is an important topic in circuit analysis especially for linear systems and so-called small signal model for electronics and control system.

text: Rehabilitation is challenging for vulnerable people from financial, institutional, social, and environmental, among other, perspectives. To tackle these challenges, it is necessary to find a common language among various sectors, to involve civil society, to create transparency, to build capacities and to finance adequately. text: One of the primary products of beekeeping (or apiculture) is honey, which is natural sweet substance made by bees using the nectar of plants. Honey is produced by bees, after nectar or honeydew has been regurgitated, dehydrated using the heat of the humane body, stored in wax honeycombs inside the hive, and extracted by stash keeper. It has become valued worldwide for its distinctive taste, nutritional value and medicinal preparations that consist of sugars, mainly fructose and glucose, enzymes, vitamins, antioxidants and trace elements. But honey is not the only tasty product we get from bee farming. The others are beeswax (for candles, cosmetics, and medicine), royal jelly (a nutritious secretion for health supplement and beauty care), propolis (a resin with antibacterial and antifungal effects), and bee pollen (a superfood containing proteins and various nutrients). Beekeeping Beekeeping, which is crucial from an ecological perspective, because bees play a very significant role in pollination that greatly increases the yield and quality of crops such as fruit, vegetables, nuts, and oilseeds. May be of more economic significance than even honey. Beekeeping is a passive hobby as well as an active industry for many, and means of income for thousands and millions of people across the globe. It's good for sustainable rural development, it's good for biodiversity conservation, it's good for food security. The modern beekeeper is challenged by the phenomenon of colony collapse disorder (CCD), pesticides, loss of habitat, climate change, and diseases, such as Varroa mites or Nosema. Eco-friendly beekeeping practices are practiced, including safeguarding native forage, being mindful of the sources of harmful chemicals and maintaining hive health. Hungarian and international (including Europe, North America, Australia and New-Zealand) governments and NGOs contribute to the development of apiculture by training, grants, and developing the market. text: Normalisation is a design procedure in which data is structured so that it can be stored within the least amount of listeners and least amount of inheritance or dependency by categorizing the data and distributing it into tables that are linked by relationships. Something like this can increase data integrity and efficiency, as the same piece of data is stored only once. The process includes even so-called normal forms, the First Normal Form (1NF), which says that every cell of a table must contain simple values and that the value must be atomic and no record can have multiple values in a cell -- replacing repeating groups. 2NF(Second Normal Form) It is based on 1NF and It is rebuilt the tables in any manner, when there are partial dependencies, that is, all the non-key attributes are fully functional dependent on the entire primary key. That prevents sharing data but eliminates duplicates generated by attributes that only depend on part of a composite key. Third Normal Form (3NF): – All non prime attributes are fully functionally dependent on the primary key – No transitive dependency with non prime attributes – No functional dependency among prime attributes or among non prime attributes. This also reduces redundant data and ensures the consistency of data. Applying normalization from 1NF to 3NF makes database more scalable and easy for maintainance, overhead benefit is reduced of data to be corrected, increased query performance. But if you over-normalize it, you could get very complex joins, so designers tend to balance their level of normalization based on practical performance considerations.

text: In reality, soil erosion is the process by which the top layer of soil (referred to as topsoil) is removed or displaced due to natural forces, such as water and wind, or as a result of human activities, such as deforestation, overgrazing, and poor farming practices. The fertile soil contains organic matter, nutrients and microorganisms that are necessary for plants to grow, and the loss of such resources can dramatically reduce agricultural productivity. Erosion by water happens when raindrops hit the soil and wash the soil particles away with the surface runoff creating rills and larger gullies if it is not stopped. Wind erosion is most common in desolate, dry, or over farmed areas, where there is not enough vegetation to hold the soil and in places the wind is able to carry the broken soil off over long distances and cause plumes of dust. Soil erosion is detrimental not just to soil fertility, but also to aquatic ecosystems and water quality because of its effects on rivers, lakes, and reservoirs—sediment, for example, which comes from soil erosion, is a major pollutant of waterways and a complicating factor in such problems as flooding. The activities of humans are speeding the process of soil erosion through the destruction of protective vegetation cover, causing the soil to become exposed to direct impact of forces that induce erosion. The impacts of soil erosion are less agricultural productivity, land infertility, and destruction of infrastructure. Contour plowing, terracing, planting cover crops, mulching, and leaving forested areas intact are used to help prevent soil erosion. Such practices decrease the velocity of surface runoff, increase water infiltration, and anchor soil. Sustainable land management methods are essential for protecting soil health, sustaining ecosystem equilibrium, and achieving food security. A lack of proper erosion control can cause the disappearance of topsoil, which is rich in nutrients and essential for plant growth, and soil degradation in general, with? long-term consequences for the environment and man’s sustenance all over the world.

text: Factor analysis is a statistical method used to describe variability among observed, correlated variables in terms of a potentially lower number of unobserved variables called factors. Unlike PCA, which seeks to explain the total variance, factor analysis tries to explain the common variance among the variables in order to identify latent constructs underlying observed measures. In psychology, education, marketing, and social science, it has been widely employed to uncover underlying traits (e.g., intelligence, personality, consumer preferences) that are unobserved and cannot be directly measured. The manifest variables are treated as linear composites of one or more latent factors plus specific factors. The method estimates factor loadings, that is, the degree of relationship between each observed variable and the latent factors. Two primary types are exploratory factor analysis (EFA), applied when the factor structure is unknown, and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), which is used to test specific hypotheses about factor structures. Assumptions in factor analysis include multivariate normality and adequate sample size for reliable and meaningful solutions. Thus, rotation procedures such as varimax or oblimin are frequently used in order to attain a factor pattern which is simpler and easier to interpret and to maximise high loadings while minimising low loadings (Tabachnick, & Fidell, 2001). Factor analysis helps to streamline the research process and provide a method of reducing dimensionality, developing questionnaires and testing theories and is useful because it can explain the complex relationships between variables.

text: Unfortunately, almost all studies only investigated COP behavior within quiet stance tasks with the instruction “to stay as still as possible,” and are limited to only a few minutes, due to fatigue. However, prolonged standing tasks require repeated changes in body posture. Duarte and Zatsiorsky [15] investigated unconstrained standing, permitting the subject to change position as required over a prolonged standing task up to 30 min. During unconstrained standing, very low frequencies in the COP displacement were observed, indicative for long-range correlation or a long memory process. While Duarte and Zatsiorsky investigated unconstrained standing sway, only a few researchers have investigated the COP behavior during sitting tasks, or sitting postural sway. Harborne and Stergiou [16] have investigated the postural control development in children. They found that the emerging postural control behaves in a nonlinear way. Boker et al. [14] employed three techniques to investigate seated postural sway of sitting infants in a moving room experiment, namely, surrogation, mutual information, and falsest nearest neighbors (FNNs). They concluded that a linear stochastic model is insufficient for describing infant sitting behavior. The COP time series exhibited strong evidence of nonlinearity. This seems to be evidence that seated sway behaves in a nonlinear fashion. However, the change in seated sway over time has rarely been investigated.

text: Inverse dynamics are the joint force and torque calculations needed to generate a certain motion (e.g., joint positions, velocities, and accelerations) of a robot. Clearly the reverse of forward dynamics, which calculates the resulting movement from applied forces. Inverse dynamics employs the kinematic and dynamic models of the robot—usually obtained through the Newton-Euler or Lagrangian approach—to calculate the motor inputs that are required to follow a desired trajectory. This is particularly important for robot control where high precision, speed or force regulation is desired, such as manipulators grinding or polishing industrial parts, humanoid walking or surgical robotics. In other words, Inverse Dynamics calculates how much torque the motor of each joint must exert at each instant in order to move exactly along a given desired trajectory, taking into account the effects of its inertia, gravity, the Coriolis and centripetal forces. These are basic operations in a control model based control method such as a computed-torque control, a feed-forward control or an adaptive control, where a robot is moved stably and precisely even when its payload and/or an external force applied thereto are changed. Inverse dynamics have also been implemented in biomechanical research to analyze human motion, estimating joint forces from motion capture data. Computational costs are high in the case of more complex robots with many degrees of freedom, but efficient recursive algorithm such as Newton-Euler Recursive Algorithm come to reduce the computational tasks drastically. Inverse dynamics on the other hand is a technique used in simulations to achieve realistic animation of robots or assess the actuator specification in the design process. Inverse dynamics makes an essential contribution towards implementation of intelligent, safe, and efficient robotic behavior in the real world by connecting desired motion to the necessary physical inputs.

text: A z-test is any statistical test for which the distribution of the test statistic under the null hypothesis can be approximated by a normal distribution. It is based on the premise that the test statistic sampling distribution is normal under the null hypothesis. The z-test gives you a z-score, which tells you how many standard errors your sample mean is from the purported population mean. The z-score is then compared to critical values from the standard normal distribution to determine whether or not to reject the null hypothesis. Z-tests assume large samples (usually n > 30), for which the Central Limit Theorem guarantees that the sampling distribution is normal even if the source distribution of the data is not. It is appropriate to compare means, proportions, or differences in means. The z-test is direct and computationally simple, and widely used for quality control, in clinical trials, and in social science research. But, if you do not know population Variance; and your sample size is small, you should use t-test. In general, z-test is a basic inferential technique for hypothesis testing and constructing confidence intervals on known or large-sample variances.

text: Through their service as stewards of information, educators, preservers of culture, facilitators of technology access, and champions of intellectual freedom and individual rights, librarians determine not how the future is shaped, but how scholars and learners can research, learn, and build upon that future. … means: "unity," because "their business is linking people to knowledge ethically, inclusively, and meaningfully, such that every person and every community have the resources and opportunities they need to learn and develop and to make informed decisions." Librarians in public libraries offer access to books, e-resources, internet and programming that support education, job seekers, civic engagement and lifelong learning. They teach the information literacy skills needed to conduct research in academia, librarians provide research consultations, digitize and preserve digital content, and offer support in scholarly publishing. School librarians promote early literacy, critical thinking, and digital citizenship with students and related to curricular objectives and educational results. See, e.g., “The Evolution of the Profession of Special Librarian” from Special Libraries Association Special Librarians work for companies, hospitals, law firms, broadcasting companies, and newspapers, among other institutions, and have a specialized focus or area of expertise. In addition to their role in information provision, librarians promote social inclusion in a number of ways, by providing safe, welcoming spaces for people from marginalised groups and providing outreach services such as mobile libraries, multilingual resources and services for those with disabilities. They advance intellectual freedom as they resist censorship and ensure access to the broadest range of information; they protect the privacy of users from intrusion into their personal or reading habits, whether the intrusion is by the state, other users, or third parties; and their services are provided, and access is allowed, without charge. In the digital age, librarians are also technology guides — helping visitors navigate e-books, databases and online learning platforms, and sometimes even emerging technologies like artificial intelligence or virtual reality. They archive and preserve cultural memory via archives, through oral histories and also through digital repositories. Librarians serve as trusted public servants that often work with educators, policymakers, and community-based organizations to address social issues such as misinformation, digital divides, literacy gaps to name a few. Their efforts are the foundation of an informed, just and literate society. In other words, librarians are more than the guardians of books; they are active agents of information, access, and social engagement in a rapidly changing world of complex information.

text: Capacitance is the extent of the ability of the system to store electric charge per unit difference in potential between two conductors or plates. It measures the charge (Q) a capacitor can store given the voltage (V) applied to its terminals, and is mathematically defined as C=VQ?, where C is the capacitance, in farads (F). Capacitors are manufactured devices for which capacitance is intentionally introduced and comprise two conductive plates separated by a dielectric. Application of voltage causes positive charges and negative charges to accumulate on the opposing plates to produce a potential between them, while energy is stored in the resulting electric field. Capacitance is proportional to the area of the plate, the distance between plates and the nature of the dielectric between them. Increasing the plate area and the dielectric constant increases capacitance; increasing the separation between the plates decreases capacitance. Capacitance is a key concept in electronics and electrical engineering, contributing to changing the characteristics of circuits by allowing voltage and current to be controlled dynamically. Capacitors are part of simple power supplies; they are used to store energy in electric fields, in the electromagnetic fields used to apply locomotion to the World's Fastest Car, and in the circuits that produce industrial-strength magnetic fields. In AC circuits, the presence of capacitors has a large impact on the phase and impedance (as a function of frequency) of electrical signals, and they are used in many different applications, including filters, oscillators and tunable tuning circuits. The capacitor’s stored energy is inversely proportional to the voltage, allowing for efficient transitory storage and release of energy. Beyond these simple capacitors, internal capacitance is often a non-ideal dependence (and in fact may be a complex function) for many systems such as transmission lines, sensors, and even electronic devices like multi-layered chip capacitors and can often only be roughly quantified or predicted by simulation. Capacitance plays fundamental role in the design and analysis of electrical devises and systems, and has become a backbone of modern technology.

text: There are many forms of tourism, each of which define tourist through their motivations and the types of experiences they prefer to seek in destinations around the world. The most popular of them, is leisure tourism, which people undertake for holidays or vacations and also travel to beaches or seaside resorts. Cultural tourism is oriented to visit the heritage, art, lifestyle, traditions and the milestones of a nation; and is related to the history and the culture of a society. Adventure tourism targets adrenaline junkies who partake in physically demanding pursuits, be it hiking, climbing, diving, or zip-lining, among others and typically in the remotest of locales. Eco-tourism is defined as “responsible travel to natural areas that conserves the environment, sustains the well-being of the local people, and involves interpretation and education” and encourages the traveler “to minimize impact on the environment while taking an active and awareness stance on his or her surroundings”. Medical tourism is the practice of a patient going to a different country for either urgent or elective medical procedures, depending on their condition, and the type of procedure offered in their native country. Wellness tourism is focused on enhancing one's physical, mental, or spiritual well-being and is involved with activities like yoga retreats, spa treatments, or holistic health programs. Business tourism, also referred to as MICE (Meetings, Incentives, Conferences and Exhibitions), is travel for business combined with recreational interests. Religious and spiritual tourism – these are pilgrims and seekers visiting holy places, temples and festivals worldwide, for example Mecca, the Vatican or the Ganges river. Sports tourism involves participating in, as well as witnessing sporting events ranging from the Olympics to local marathons or school/church baseball leagues. Among the many types include educational tourism, where the purpose is to engage with other cultures or to learn in an educational environment, and in some cases the visitor is worthy of such a rule. Rural-based and agritourism transport visitors to the countryside to experience farm life, traditional activities and local food experiences away from the commercial city. Gastronomic tourism draws food lovers looking to discover regional dishes, cooking techniques and food markets. Dark tourism refers to visiting certain destinations related to tragedy, conflict, disaster, or death, where we inevitably do some reflecting and remembering. Eco-culture tourism promotes good behavior, inclusiveness and empowers local residents, it is about ensuring that tourism works for people at both ends of the tourist and guest equation. One could also add niche forms like virtual tourism and space tourism, facilitated by technology and globalization. Each form of travel presents different prospects for hands-on discovery, education, connection, and together they add up to a narrative about how people engage with the world and how places evolve to accommodate myriad traveler needs and interests while considering environmental, cultural, and economic consequences.

text: I DENTIFICATION of potential therapeutic drug molecules for a disease of interest, which is known as “drug-discovery”, is a critical step in new drug development. Traditional drug discovery practice in the pharmaceutical industry usually follows the “one drug - one target” approach, which seeks to identify drugs that act on individual molecules that are involved in the pathological process [1]. However, this approach ignores the systemic nature of human diseases and may account for a significant increase in the attrition rate of new candidate drugs due to low efficacy and serious side effects [2], [3]. Specifically, the pathological process of a disease usually involves extremely complex interplays between many functionally related biological molecules within certain disease-related pathways [4]. Targeting a single component in a disease-related pathway may not provide sufficient interference to the whole pathological process, which may result in unsatisfactory therapeutic efficacy. Moreover, it does not allow researchers to investigate the effects of drug molecules at a systems level, limiting its utility in evaluating drug safety and toxicity in early drug development stages [5]. Pathway-based drug discovery recently emerged as an appealing approach to overcome the limitations of the one drug - one target approach [6], [7], [8]. Instead of focusing on the interference of drug molecules on individual targets, pathway-based analysis seeks to understand the effect of a drug molecule on a whole biological pathway. The knowledge about the effects of drug molecules upon the diseaserelated pathways would allow researchers to identify more effective candidate drugs. However, currently not much is known about the complex relationships between drug molecules and biological pathways, and an important first step is to infer associations between them before delving into their complex relationships

text: Containment during the Cold War refers to the foreign policy strategy pursued by the United States in the USA and its allies to prevent the spread of communism following the end of World War II. A term devised by diplomat George F. Kennan in 1947, containment was built on the idea that communism was fundamentally expansionist and had to be blocked primarily through a blend of diplomacy, economics, and military force that would not set off a war between superpowers. It was an attempt to contain Soviet power by backing anti-Soviet allies politically and militarily, as with the Truman Doctrine (pledging aid to Greece and Turkey to oppose Communist insurgencies) and the Marshall Plan (economic aid to rebuild Western Europe and bolster capitalist societies). Truman’s containment strategy induced many proxy wars, like the Korean War and the Vietnam War, in which the U.S. intervened to try to prevent the spread of communist movements. The ideology had an effect on U.S. domestic policy as well, including anti-communist efforts such as McCarthyism. Although containment did succeed in preventing Soviet expansion in most of Western Europe and elsewhere, it also helped foster decades of bio-political and military tension, arms competition, and ideological polarization in the Cold War decades after the Soviet Union's dissolution in 1991.

text: Non-parametric techniques are characterized by less restrictive assumptions about the nature of the data than parametric methods. Parametric tests make specific probability distributional assumptions (i.e., normal or Gaussian) and require interval or ratio level data with homogeneity of variances. They extrapolate using means and variances. On the other hand, non-parametric tests do not require a specific distribution of the data, and can be applied to ordinal data, nominal or continuous data with non-parametric characteristics (not screening for a specific shape of distribution). Non-parametric tests often use ranks, medians or frequencies, rather than raw scores, making them less sensitive to extreme values or skewed data. A general heuristic is that non-parametric tests have less statistical power when parametric assumptions are satisfied, but are more robust to violation of these conditions, especially if sample sizes are small or the data distribution is not normal. Examples are the t-test, ANOVA, and the Pearson correlation which are parametric, and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Mann-Whitney U test, Kruskal-Wallis test, and Spearman’s correlation which are non-parametric equivalents. Non-parametric tests are generally more flexible but are less informative; they deal with medians or orderings, rather than means or variances. Parametric or non-parametric method is selected accordingly to the data set and the research objectives, and we use the non-parametric test as a supplementary alternative to the parametric test when such needs are not satisfied.

text: The endocrine system is responsible for regulating and coordinating many of the body's processes that occur over a long period of time through the release of naturally occurring chemicals called hormones that travel through the bloodstream to specific cells and organs. It works more slowly than the nervous system because it does not use rapid electrical signals, but the effects are broader and last longer than those of the nervous system, and it helps to regulate processes such as growth, metabolism, reproduction, development, mood, and homeostasis. It is composed of a number of specialized glands including the pituitary, thyroid, adrenal, pancreas and gonads, which secrete hormones into the bloodstream to regulate various body functions. For instance the “master gland,” the pituitary gland, operates other endocrine glands and essential processes — growth, water balance, to name a few — through hormones such as growth hormone and antidiuretic hormone. The thyroid gland, which regulates metabolism by releasing hormones that affect how cells convert nutrients into energy, and the adrenal glands, which produce cortisol and adrenaline to help the body respond to stress, are just a couple examples. Insulin and glucagon are secreted by the pancreas to control blood sugar levels and achieve energy availability and energy balance. Hormones produced and secreted by the ovaries and testes control sexual development, reproductive cycles, and behaviour. The nervous system and the endocrine system work hand-in-hand, via the hypothalamus, which connects the two systems and strives to keep the body in homeostasis: in balance, no matter how things are changing on the outside, neurons always control the hormone levels. Hormone levels are regulated by negative feedback and, using a variety of mechanisms, maintained within an appropriate range to prevent excesses or deficits, to achieve homeostasis. This delicate balance ensures that the physiological status quo is maintained even when constantly challenged by changes in the external and internal world. Furthermore, it has effects on mood, immune functioning, and even higher order cognitive functions, so it’s no surprise the endocrine system is essential to health and quality of life. A malfunctioning endocrine system can result in many life-threatening diseases; for example, diabetes, thyroid disorders, growth disorders, and infertility. In conclusion, the endocrine system is crucial for the homeostatic coordination of the organism as a whole by secreting hormones that control growth, metabolism, reproductive function, stress, adaptation to a changing environment in harmony with the other systems and structural organization required for the animal’s internal milieu, maintaining its physiological state and functional integrity and serving its survival and functional needs in evolution among all the species.

text: Oxygen is transported in living animals by respiratory and circulatory systems which take it from the environment to the cells of the body where it is needed for metabolism to take place producing energy. It all starts with respiration, when oxygen is acquired from the air or water the animal lives in, through respiratory organs like lungs, gills, tracheae or skin, depending on the animal’s environment and how it has evolved. After the oxygen diffuses into the blood or other body fluid, it binds to respiratory pigments, proteins which help increase the solubility and thus carrier of oxygen. The most common respiratory pigment in vertebrates is hemoglobin, which is contained in red blood cells and allows for oxygen to be picked up in the lungs or gills and for carbon dioxide to be released in the lungs or gills. Other pigments, such as the copper-containing hemocyanin and the iron-containing hemerythrin, are also found in some invertebrates and provide the same vital oxygen transport function. The circulatory system (either open or closed) leads to the distribution of oxygenated blood or hemolymph to the entire body. (Campbell, 469) Closed circulatory systems, as in vertebrates and some invertebrates, keep the oxygen-rich blood contained in vessels, which allows for more efficient delivery and regulation of flow, whereas open systems circulate hemolymph more loosely through body cavities. In some small or simple animals such as flatworms or insects, oxygen may instead diffuse through the body surface directly to the cells, bypassing the tracheal system or blood. In addition, pH, temperature, and CO 2 concentration affect the affinity of respiratory pigments for oxygen, which permits animals to modulate the release of oxygen as a function of metabolic demand (Bohr effect). Some animals have evolved insulating mats of lung, or gill mass and other adaptative devices, such as higher concentration of hemoglobin in the bloodstream, to help the oxygen diffuse.” These changes can increase the flow of oxygen into their systems, like a hyperbaric atmospheric chamber that surrounds their internal organs. In general, the transport of oxygen is a multiple-effect process with gills for uptake, pigments for binding and release, and circulation for distribution, all functioning in integration to provide the animal with the ATP required for its vitality. This efficient oxygen delivery is necessary for cellular respiration, which underpins aspects of animal life including movement, growth, and reproduction, and highlights the range of strategies animals have evolved in different habitats.

text: Equality is the notion that all people are to be treated justly, and possess equal moral value, and should have equal access to culture, the political system, and other social institutions. Conceptually, equality implies that no one is better or worse, that higher or lower does not convert into unearned advantages or disadvantages based on wealth, position or power. There are different ways to conceive of equality, such as political equality (right to vote), legal equality (equal before the law), social equality (access to education and healthcare), and economic equality (accessible resources). Various theories argue about the degree and form of equality -- some promote full equality of outcomes, others aspire for equality of opportunity. Equality is a central value of most concepts of human rights and democracy, generating values of inclusion, fairness and recognition of difference. But the road to equality is complicated and societies need to address a legacy of injustice, entrenched discrimination and structurally embedded inequality. Philosophers also face the challenge of reconciling equality with other values, like liberty and meritocracy. The contemporary social justice movements are drawing attention to the fact that the fight for an equality has not yet been won and have brought it again to the center of practical and theoretical ethical and political reflection.

text: Preparedness and mitigation are two elements of disaster management to minimize the affects by natural and anthrogenic-hazards. “Mitigation” comprises measures that either prevent the occurrence on new risks or reduce the scales of existing risk (disaster prevention) and long-term activities meant to minimise a community’s exposure to natural hazards. That can mean both structural measures — building higher and stronger flood levees, for example, or constructing earthquake-resistant buildings, storm shelters and firebreaks — and non-structural ones — things like enforcing land-use regulations and improving zoning laws, preserving wetlands that absorb floodwater, protecting natural buffers like mangroves and forests. It also involves risk assessments and hazard mapping, thereby of affected communities and susceptable populations in the need for targeted interventions. The aim of mitigation is to prevent disasters happening, or if they do occur, the death and property damage is reduced and economic disruption constrained. On the other hand, the preparedness is about being prepared for when a disaster comes so that we as individuals and we as communities, we as institutions are ready to do something when a disaster happens. This includes developing plans and training for emergencies, conducting drills, preparing response forces of the police and public, establishing communication systems, training logistics support personnel and stocking resources that would be required in case of an emergency, including early warning systems. Readiness might also be using people to carry out Public Education for Awareness, which is when you raise awareness among a group so that the risks are known and possibilities for changes are considered. It is creating readiness systems; essentially how to deal with disasters in a constructive fashion — which will reduce the chaos and allow better coordinated efforts in time of emergency. Whereas mitigation lowers the likelihood and magnitude of the hazards, preparedness in-creases capacity to respond. The two are interdependent and can only grow on the basis of sustained investments, policy support, community engagement and government, nongovernmental organization and private sector cooperation. Mitigation and preparedness represent approaches to damage control for disasters that are founded on prevention, ones that not only save life during events but also accelerate recovery and build long-term resilience in hazard-prone areas.

text: An isotope is a variety of a chemical element which has the same number of protons and electrons, but is heavier or lighter than normal because it contains different numbers of neutrons than are present in the most common form of the atom. Since an element has the same number of protons and this number defines the identity of an element, isobars of a given charge are chemically the same but have different physical and nuclear properties because of different neutron count. For example, carbon has isotopes such as carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14, where the numbers indicate the total number of protons and neutrons. Stable isotopes of carbon include carbon-12 and carbon-13, while carbon-14 is radioactive and is used in radiocarbon dating of decay of organic materials. The difference of neutron number and proton number is called the neutron excess; if this is large, a lot of ? ? decay can occur and the nuclei are not stable. Isotopes may form naturally, or they may be man-made, by means of bombs or in laboratories or nuclear reactors. They find applications in a large number of domains, with medical – in the form of imaging or cancer treatment (radioisotopes development) –, industry – as tracers or in quality control –, or environmental studies – to trace pollution or investigate climate change – being only a few examples. There is an analog in nuclear engineering, which becomes significant: fissile isotopes such as uranium-235 and plutonium-239 are fissionable and can serve as a source of neutrons, as can fissionable material which can be used in a chain reaction; fertile isotopes such as uranium-238 are not fissionable, but they can be converted after the fact to a fissile isotope when they have been subjected to a neutron flux. Isotopes are also central to nuclear reactors, cancer therapy and scientific research. I’m also studying isotopes that I am repelled by in fields like geochemistry and astrophysics, in which ratios of these isotopes provide hints about the origins of planets and the operations of the universe. The small but vital differences in isotopes are the reason they are so integral to scientific research, technological applications, and our everyday lives — as the minute differences in atomic composition can wreak havoc.

text: Fuel fabrication is the industrial process of turning enriched uranium into nuclear fuel that can be used in nuclear power. UO2 powders are first pressed and sintered to small cylindrical fuel pellets. These pellets have to be treated under strict specifications of density, purity and mechanical resistance, to garantee a reliable and efficient reactor operation. The pellets are then inserted, once manufactured, into long, thin tubes made of materials resistant to corrosion, such as zirconium alloy (the fuel rods). These rods are thereafter covered and bundled or otherwise treated in whatever fuel assembly or bundle pattern called for by the reactor. The parts have to be manufactured with close dimensional tolerance and free of contamination in order to perform reliably at high temperature and radiation in the reactor. Some quality-control tests are performed—crack detection, density/metallurgical measurements and chemical composition measurements, for example. The fuel fabrication plant is physically protected from intrusion due to the radioactive nature of the materials and because the fissile content may well be proliferation sensitive. The fuel assemblies, each of which is built to exacting specifications, are brought to nuclear power plants to be inserted into a reactor core; there, they hold the fissile material that feeds the chain reaction. Fuel fabrication represents a critical aspect of reactor safety, performance and fuel cycle economics.
