text: Introduction Official herbal monographs are standard documents containing scientific data on medicinal plant and herbal substance. These monographs are used by pharmacists, health professionals and researchers in order to confirm the identity, quality and purity, efficacy and safety of what can only be described as herbal drugs. Generally, the information covers scientific name, source of the plant, morphological, anatomical features, active principles, methods for identification, storage conditions, therapeutic uses, dosage, contraindications and adverse effects. Official monographs are published globally such as the monographs developed by the World Health Organization (WHO), European Pharmacopoeia (Ph. Eur.),United States Pharmacopeia (USP), British Pharmacopoeia (BP),and Indian Pharmacopoeia (IP). The WHO has published monographs on more than 100 drugs of natural origin covering PHARMACOPOEIAL AND TRADITIONAL MEDICINAL PLANTS scientific data and traditional use. The USP Herbal Medicines Compendium establishes quality specifications for botanicals in dietary supplements. In Europe, the EMA produces community herbal monographs through its Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC) which contributes to the supervising of traditional herbal medicinal products in EU member states. In Germany, Commission E Monographs are very famous for the assessment of the effectiveness and safety of herbal drugs. Such monographs also contribute to safety and quality of herbs and are essential to safeguarding consumers and their confidence in herbal medicines. They are also used as legal criteria for manufacturing and authorities in the licensing and marketing of herbal products. Conclusion Official herbal monographs are important instruments in guaranteeing the safe and effective use of herbal medications, by achieving uniformity, standard, and evidence base of prescription and dispensing practice in traditional and modern pharmacy.

text: Globally, refugees and IDPs number over 32.9 million [6], and "reproductive health needs do not disappear upon displacement" [4]. Relief efforts have traditionally focused on acute-phase survival, including HIV prevention and basic emergency obstetric care [7]. However, reproductive health spans relief and development and is essential for long-term survival [7, 8]. This is particularly true of contraceptive services, whose functioning requires sufficient staff training, counselling skills and supplies, and client trust that service quality is good and supplies will continue. In many camp settings, fertility rates and gender-based violence increase, and maternal and neonatal mortality can be high [7, 9]. For example, a World Health Organisation (WHO) study estimated 25–50% of maternal mortality among refugees as due to unsafe abortion, indicating considerable unmet need for contraception [10]. Implementing agencies now recognise the need to provide contraceptive services. However, despite moves to improve provision, barriers to access and acceptability remain [11–14].

text: Sustainable tourism transport is confronted with various interconnected problems: environmental, infrastructural, financial and social. From an environmental point of view, tourism transport – especially air travel and cruise shipping – is one of the largest CO? emitters, which cause both climate change and local air and noise pollution. This adds urgency to the question of decarbonization strategies and the adoption of clean energy. Logistically, airports, roads, rail systems and cruise berths are overwhelmed, resulting in delays, danger and a poor experience for visitors. They require significant investment and planning, which is itself a slow process. Economically, the finance of transport infrastructure is commonly based on public–private partnership, route subsidies or tourism levies–challenging to design and politically sensitive. From a social perspective, increased transportation access can disrupt localities, increase property values and change neighborhood dynamics, with some residents pushing back. In addition, access is not always equitable, with far-off or rural destinations left behind, and the benefits of tourism may be confined to its less exposed destinations. Complex regulation — from international air routes to maritime laws, cross-border rail and urban transit — needs to cohere across jurisdictions. Not to mention safety, security, and health protocols (pandemic controls, for example) also add layers. Some solutions (e.g., EV fleets, smart traffic systems) require technology adoption, but financial and knowhow barriers hinder this as well. Finally, people’s comfort, speed and price expectations place pressure on operators to find innovative and sustainable solutions. Tackling these challenges requires joined-up stakeholder engagement across tourism, transport, urban planning, technology and environment.

text: Newton’s 1st Law of Motion, also called the Law of Inertia, states that an object at rest will stay at rest and a body in motion will remain in motion with the same speed and in the same direction unless acted upon by an unbalanced force. This law brings out and illustrates the natural reluctance of a body to change its state of motion. For instance, if a ball is on the ground, it will generally remain there unless someone kicks it. And in the same way, there’s nothing about a ball rolling on a frictionless surface that says it has to stop moving, other than something like friction of a wall, stopping it. The law brings about the notion of inertia; that is the resistance of an object to changes in its motion. The more mass an object has the more inertia it possesses and the more force it takes to change its motion. Newton’s First Law: Newton’s first law is a cornerstone in classical mechanics. It also questions whether motion needs a force to bear on it to keep it going, concluding that a force is only needed to change its state. It was a revolutionary concept because prior to Newton, everyone thought that an object needed a continuous force to keep it moving. Azoury In our experience of real life, objects (due to friction and air resistance) tend to eventually slow down, unless something keeps pushing them, but under ideal circumstances (like one finds in space), an object will continue to move in a straight line forever once it is given a push. Forces and the fundamental law of motion: Newton's First LawThe first law of Newton describes simply how forces alter the motion of objects and is valid for both daily activities and for celestial mechanics. It instructs us that in the absence of net external force, an object’s velocity will remain unchanged — and hence no acceleration will take place, and it will either remain at rest or travel in a straight line at constant speed.

text: Subnetting allows a network to be divided into smaller, more efficient subnets, (ie: broadcast domains) and therefore increases available IP address space while controlling the flow of network traffic within a network. It means that you’re borrowing some bits from the host part of an IP address in order to make a network more or less granular.The borrowing bits themselves are specified by something called the subnet mask. For example, the IPv4 address 192.168.1.0 with a subnet mask of /24, which means that 24 bits are used for the network portion of the address (the first three numbers) and 8 bits are used for the host address allowing for 256 possible addresses (but only 254 can actually be used for hosts). You could subnet using 2 bits of the host portion, giving you a 255.255.255.192 (/26) mask, which would mean four subnets at 64 addresses (62 usable). The subnets are 192.168.1.0/26, 192.168.1.64/26, 192.168.1.128/26, and 192.168.1.192/26. A small network is created by each subnet, making it easier to manage traffic and preventing clogging of the network by broadcast traffic. Subnetting also fosters the more efficient assignment of IP addresses, adjusting the subnet size to fit the size of the organization, as well as better security, as it isolates groups of devices. Routers mask those packet destination addresses and look up the resulting bits to determine which subnet a packet is destined for. In summary, subnetting increases the flexibility, scalability, manageability, design, and performance capabilities of an IP net­work by virtually breaking larger IP networks into smaller, easily de­signable pieces.

The admission and conduct of travelers is controlled by immigration and visa policies. Finally, dispute resolution mechanisms—courts, arbitration, mediation—deals with conflicts between tourists, operators or host governments, often by way of pre?set ADR clauses or national consumer bodies. text: Original, first-hand records or artifacts are primary sources, and these are the most common type of source that one would use when studying history: letters, diaries, official records, photographs, artifacts, speeches, newspapers, or testimony. They are firsthand accounts of historical happenings from the very people living them; ideal for context, language, and perspective. By contrast, secondary sources are works of analysis or interpretations of events created later by historians and scholars—like books, articles, documentaries, or essays that rely on primary sources to tell a story or make an argument or develop ideas. The difference is a matter of distance: primary sources are material from the past, while secondary sources are the reflections upon that material. Both are valuable: primary sources as the empirical base and secondary sources as the scholarly frameworks in which the raw materials can be placed, examined, and interpreted. Knowing the distinction is useful to historians as they assess the reliability of sources; primary sources may have the authors' biases despite their explaining to some extent the authors' way of seeing the world and secondary sources could include a theoretical or interpretive bias. The importance of critical engagement — cross-referencing sources, testing the credibility of one’s sources — cannot be overstated. Understanding the difference also foregrounds the kind of analytical skills involved in the construction of history, preparing students to engage substantively with original evidence that they are also being trained to keep in conversation with other scholarly sources.

text: A transformer is a passive electrical device that transfers electrical energy between two or more circuits through electromagnetic induction. Transformer is most commonly used to increase (‘step up’) or decrease (‘step down’) AC voltage levels while keeping the corresponding current levels the same. It is based on the principle of mutual induction, through which a change in current in the primary winding creates a this induced voltage in the secondary winding. The most elementary form of a transformer consists of two windings, a primary and a secondary, wound on a common laminated softly magnetic core in order to achieve better magnetic coupling as well as to minimize losses of the energy that is being transferred. When an alternating voltage is applied to the primary winding, it produces an alternating magnetic field in the core that is linked to the secondary winding. This time-varying magnetic flux through the secondary is, according to Faraday’s Law, what causes an EMF to appear across the secondary coil. The ratio of turns on the primary and secondary windings sets the line voltage conversion ratio, Vs?/Vp?=Ns?/Np??, where V is voltage and N is number of turns. If the secondary coil has more turns than the primary, it’s a step-up transformer when a current is passed through the primary wire — if fewer, a step-down transformer. Transformers are the key components in a power system which enables the efficient transmission of electricity over long distances by stepping up voltage, thereby reducing current and, accordingly, transmission losses. At the output end, voltage is reduced to a safe level for household or industrial use. Transformers will only operate with AC as a result of the required changing magnetic field. Voltage regulators, isolation and impedance matching are other uses. Having no moving parts, transformers are extremely reliable and efficient, and have assumed a vital role in the electromagnetic infrastructure of the modern technological society.

text: The behavior of a team and the way in which it performs is often a product of team dynamics. These dynamics influence the way in which the group's members can work together, how they communicate, how they resolve conflicts between themselves, and how they hope to inspire change. A high-performing team has good dynamics. They trust each other. They approach that mutual trust with clear communication and with each person in a well-defined role and with mutual respect and understanding. That leads to better functioning, higher productivity, creativity, and job satisfaction. Conversely, detrimental team dynamics – like bad communication, embedded disagreements or cliques, bossy personas, or lack of responsibility – can lead to the failure to meet objectives, low morale, and time wasting. There are many things that influence team dynamics such as the style of leadership the team has, the size of the team, the diversity of the team, the organizational culture and the personalities of the people in the team, but these are just a few. For instance, a leader who is controlling and who does not permit open forums for communication and participation can stifle dynamics, while an authoritarian or laissez-faire leader can interfere with collaboration. The stage of team formation also has dynamics implications, tagged by Bruce Tuckman on the model: forming, storming, norming, performing, and adjourning. During storming members may argue for their own personal concept, however when properly guided and given time teams usually move to the performing phase. Good teamwork and group dynamics are crucial when it comes to problem-solving and creativity on complex or interdisciplinary projects.” Resources such as regular feedback, team-building exercises, conflict management tactics, and role clarification can go a long way to bettering morale. In today’s increasingly diverse — and virtual — workforce, managing team dynamics can be more challenging, but no less essential. Organizations that prioritize creating great teams achieve higher employee engagement levels, lower turnover, and stronger teams overall. And finally, leaders and managers will need to recognize and navigate the dynamics of their teams in order to build high performing, cohesive teams to drive long-term success.

text: The Popular and the Elite The principal difference between popular and elite theatre is in its audience,its artistic articulations means, its accessibility and its culturallocation in relation to society. Pop theater is made with a broad general audience appeal, and can contain things in common like entertainment, humor, feelings, stories which would logically resonate with man. This would usually include genres such as musical theatre, melodrama, farce, and comedy, as well as more serious drama Character representation is often a result of typecasting, so the areas a re non-specialist, however, some non-specialist performers are highly regarded. Theater that eats itself has everything you’ve ever seen or hear in it because the thing is created from all the stuff that we’ve all already seen or heard. This kind of theater is generally whatever the trend is, pop culture or pastiche-y, and whatever seems like a crowd-pleasing thing that can make money. On the other hand, elite theatre -also known as highbrow or avant-garde theatre- addresses a smaller, more culturally educated, and often more academically audience. It tends to favor artistic experimentation, intellectual complexity and innovations of form and content. High calibre theatre productions might experiment with abstract ideas, non-linear narratives, even minimalist staging, testing the boundaries of what theatre could and should be, the boundaries that traditionally audiences had to push more against as viewers. It’s not unusual to find these shows being staged in established institutions, festivals or quirkier experiment boxes - and in some cases they’re harder to get to because of ticket prices, language or obscure references. Popular theatre attempts to entertain and establish an emotional rapport with a wide range of people, whilst elite forms strive to engage viewers through new ideas and challenge the boundaries of what it is possible to put on the stage or think about. The difference also mirrors larger social systems; elite theatre is perceived as possessing high culture, and awarded cultural capital, institutional recognition, and artistic legitimacy, while popular theatre is seen as low culture, has mass appeal, and (with the exception of commercial theatre) is derived from a working-class tradition. But this dichotomy is far from clear-cut: many performances and audience responses mix the two, and there are indications that the hierarchy is being overthrown by audience choice. Elite and popular Elite theatre in some cases has a direct influence on popular productions, with styles/criteria, such as themes, often being borrowed, popular theatre can also deal with very serious social commentary in an accessible way, thus muddying the clear border between 'entertainment' and 'comment'. Additionally, the contemporary moment is marked by cultural and technological changes – in the form of digital media, community-orientated performance, and globalized theatre practices – that have helped to dismantle the binaries of elite and popular theatre. In short, the distinction between popular and elite theatre is not merely of content, or form: of who they are for, of who and what they assume where, when and how. Appreciating the former two while the latter ones are actually understandable enrich our conception of theatre as a complex changing art genre, catching all social elements of the human community.

text: Radiation detection systems are the key devices for the detection, measurement, and monitoring of the levels of radiation to keep people in safe work and living environment in radiation environment such as health care, industrial, research, and nuclear power plants. Such instruments are capable of detecting multiple types of ionizing radiation, such as alpha particles, beta particles, gamma rays, X-rays and neutrons. One of the most widely used instruments is the Geiger-Mueller (GM) counter that responds to ionizing radiation by producing electrical pulses when radiation ionizes gas in the detector tube. GM counters are small and inexpensive and are effective in monitoring beta and gamma radiation, but the response is marginal at high radiation fields or for accurate dose measurements. Scintillation detectors rely on substances such as sodium iodide crystals that emit light when exposed to radiation. This light is then turned into an electrical signal by a photomultiplier tube, that enables the sensitive and accurate measurement of radiation. They are commonly applied in nuclear medicine and environmental monitoring. Ionization chambers quantify the charge produced by ionizing radiation in an enclosed gas-filled chamber, and provide an accurate measure of very high dose-rates of radiation, which is why they can be used for calibration and monitoring of the reactor. Proportional counters act similarly, but provide energy discrimination. He-3 detectors and boron trifluoride (BF?) counters are commonly used for detection of neutrons. Personal dosimetry involves the use of passive dosimeters (i.e. film badges or TLDs) and electronic personal dosimeters (EPDs) which are worn by radiation workers to provide a record of cumulative radiation doses over time. Area monitors and portal monitors are located at the entry and the exit of facilities to identify contamination or unauthorized radioactive material passage into or out of the facilities. Instruments need to be calibrated on a regular basis and operators trained how to.

text: There should be no division between domestic and international politics when it comes to human rights,” said Mr Abdessamad. “Human rights are the rights we all enjoy simply because we are born as human beings, regardless of our nationality, ethnic origin, gender, religion or anything else.” These rights - which can differ legally, politically, and geographically – are found in international instruments such as the United Nations (UN) adopted Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) (1948), and subsequent covenants in different areas spanning from the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. Within international politics human rights are both normative prescriptions and legal duties that guide the behaviour of states internally and externally. There has been an increasing focus on human rights in international diplomacy, humanitarian interventions and development policies. International organizations including the UN Human Rights Council, the International Criminal Court, and regional courts oversee compliance and work to hold perpetrators—including states and individuals—responsible for genocides, war crimes or crimes against humanity. Human rights language directly challenges conventional understandings of state sovereignty by making clear that governments have obligations not only to their own peoples but also to the world at large. This has given rise to discussions regarding humanitarian intervention, the R2P doctrine, and the supposed tension that arises from reconciling national interests and universal moral obligation. While the adoption of human rights is still an uneven and contentious project around the world, and elicits political and cultural rejectionism in many quarters, it clearly is one of the normative pillars of international law and diplomacy, based on the widespread universal commitment to dignity, justice, equality, and freedom. Their safeguarding also supports peace, security and sustainable development, as it addresses the root causes of conflict and advances inclusive governance.

text: Intellectual freedom is the right of every individual to both seek and receive information from all points of view without restriction.It _provides for free access to all expressions of ideas and is protected by democratic societies as a primary value.?This free access to information and ideas istempered by constitutional analysis of the nature of the medium involved as well as the manner in which the content is provided_.? Intellectual freedom encompasses two dimensions—the freedom to have or seek information and the freedom to express ideas without restriction based on the content of the speech.?Personal rights to intellectual freedom encompass the freedom of access to information and freedom of expression.??It is a core ethical tenet of library and information science, and a specific ethical obligation of professionals in the field. It promotes the ability of people to read all about an issue, expose themselves to all opinions, and then form a balanced opinion without the hand of censorship, the bludgeon of coercion, or the shadow of reprisal hanging over their heads. Libraries support intellectual freedom and resist efforts to censor or remove materials, and does not tolerate any interference with the rights of individuals to use the library’s resources including any attempt to monitor or collect information about a user’s inquiries or resources used, or to analyze or suppress what a user reads or views. It is a principle codified in interpretive statements such as the American Library Association’s Library Bill of Rights and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (Article 19), both of which proclaim freedom of expression and the public’s right to know. Intellectual freedom also includes the right to read, and the right to have access to reading and viewing matter regardless of age or the origin of the material, as well as the right to read or not to read or view the materials provided. It may be difficult for a librarian to combine community values or insider pressures with professional obligations to defend intellectual freedom. Any of these factors—book challenges, filtering software, surveillance technologies—can and will erode this right, unless we consider them carefully and openly. Library intellectual freedom also encompasses more than materials through programs, exhibits, and digital content, libraries must design inclusive environments where curiosity, creativity, and critical thinking thrive. Amid the era of misinformation and polarized discourse, intellectual freedom also includes helping users to become media literate, to critically evaluate sources, to navigate difficult information scapes. Libraries that stand for intellectual freedom stand not only as storehouses of knowledge but champions for free inquiry, free expression, and the freedom to read and learn—democratic principles that foster everyone’s freedom to think, speak, and know for themselves.

text: Prisons are centrally important to the criminal justice system as the institutions that hold, discipline, and rehabilitate the individuals who have been convicted of crimes. Their basic function is to protect the public through a) secure, humane custody of offenders; b) prevention of future offending by means of incapacitation; and c) dispensation of just retribution for punishment imposed by the courts. Historically, the prison system punishes, but today's correctional philosophy is moving more towards rehabilitation and reintegration. Prisons offer education, vocational training, and mental health and substance abuse treatment, as well as counseling tailored to the causes of criminality. These services are designed to lower the possibility of repeat offense by providing the offender with the necessary skills and tools to live lawfully upon release. Correctional institutions also are responsible for controlling and regulating order and safety within the institution walls and incorporate handling of conflicts and humane treatment. In addition to imprisonment, correctional agencies administer community supervision through programs like probation and parole, combining surveillance with assistance to help offenders successfully reintegrate into society. But correctional institutions are under enormous strain: Overcrowding, lack of resources, violence -- and public confrontation with conditions -- are among the problems. Now the pendulum swings as scholars and policymakers wrangle with how we might best balance punishment against rehabilitation, increasingly convinced that corrections that lead to positive changes in people and to lowered social costs. Finally, corrections is a critical component of the administration of justice, the protection of the public, and the correction and rehabilitation of offenders in a manner that ultimately enhances community safety.

text: The media – including all forms of media; print, audio, video, broadcast and internet [ii] – plays a significant influence in shaping public opinion, public behaviors and public culture (including gender roles) in any society. In Bangladesh, the mass media, which include television, print media, radio, and film and more recently social media, are crucial actors in the perpetuation and contestation of conventional gendered norms. On the one hand, stereotypical images of women as passive, emotional, housebound and secondary to men are still very common in mainstream media. In countless TV dramas and films, women are shown to have more of a domestic function, while men are depicted as decision-makers and breadwinners. Advertisements often uphold these gendered expectations, with women selling beauty products or kitchenware, and men being used to selling technology or financial products. These representations make it difficult for us to think outside the box on gender, and prevent us from being able to fully comprehend what a man or a woman is or is not. But media has also become a medium for empowerment and change. Millions listen as many awareness campaigns in this part of the world on domestic violence, child marriage, girls’ education, sexual harassment have been done on the radio and TV. Social media, in particular Facebook and YouTube, have provided an outlet for women and gender rights activists to denounce, expose and mobilize public opinion. Photo Women journalists, filmmakers and influencers are emerging more as they lever pages followers to challenge sexism, spotlight women’s accomplishments and reflect progressive values. And while there are certainly significant opportunities there despite, or perhaps because of, it is the media in Bangladesh that itself often mirrors sexism, with the paucity of women in positions of influence or press freedom to report on sensitive gender issues.. And here, still, too much biased reporting and insensitivity in covering gender-based violence. Hence, the media has a moral responsibility to more actively promote gender equity by way of gender-sensitive content, decision-making that is inclusive of women and leverage its influence to help shape society attitudes to lead to more equitable and balanced futures.

text: English has a pervasive presence in the Bangladeshi educational system and is widely considered a pathway to educational and professional success. English is taught as a compulsory subject in all schools (bengali and english medium both) from the time when a child starts school, from primary school till higher secondary. English is more important in higher education. The requirement of English for academic texts, lectures, assign¬ments and examinations is indeed an essential commodity for most institutions of higher learning in Bangladesh (Atiur, 2001) and there is no exception to public or private universities where English has been identified as a medium of instruction, particularly in areas of engineering, medicine, business and social sciences. Papers, dissertations, and international partnerships are typically in English. English is also an important language for studying abroad and students need to go through various testing such as IELTS and TOEFL to be accepted. Most government schemes, including the Secondary Education Quality and Access Enhancement Project (SEQAEP) are aimed at making English language education better through teacher training and updated course material. Challenges such as constrained access to good quality English teachers in rural areas persists despite these initiatives. But being fluent in English is a mark of social status, a ticket to a better job and a conduit to global information. And those with good English frequently land the best jobs in the public and private sectors. English debate, spelling bees, and English clubs in schools also support learning in the classroom. In summary, English has become tightly entrenched within the curriculum-based-policy in Bangladesh, and it is not only a subject itself, but also the channel to global knowledge, job-market, and success.

text: A volcanic eruption happens when magma, a mixture of molten rock and gas from the Earth’s interior, gets pushed up from pressure and heat and makes its way to the surface, which also contains dissolved gases. At great depths within the Earth, it heats up so much, that the rock melts, forming a low-density liquid called magma that is lighter than the surrounding, much more dense, solid rock. As this magma rises, it creates cracks in the earth’s crust, and may pool in a magma chamber just underneath a volcano. As the magma continues to pile up, the pressure within the chamber grows. They are also pressurized by gasses such as water vapour, carbon dioxide, and sulfur dioxide that are dissolved in the magma. When this pressure is greater than the strength of the overlying rocks this pressure causes the crust to crack and the magma is expelled through the vent resulting in an eruption. Influenced by the viscosity and gas contents of magma, eruptions can be explosive or effusive. Associated with these is an explosive eruption that could produce considerable ash and rock fragments that could be hurled into the atmosphere – should the magma be rich in silica (such as andesite or rhyolite) then it has a greater propensity of being explosive - leaving behind pyroclastic flows and ash clouds, that can travel for long distances. Effusive eruptions instead include relatively low viscosity (very runny) basalt magma that fountains or flows calmly like lava rather than explodes. The impact of a volcanic eruption may be immediate, or it may be cumulative, with outcomes adding up over the long-term. At the local level, they can obliterate landscapes, bury communities and take lives. On a worldwide scale, massive eruptions can release ash and sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere, which can affect climate by blocking sunlight, temporarily cooling the Earth. Volcanoes are most often found where tectonic plate boundaries are drawn together or pushed apart: in the mid-ocean ridges and above subduction zones of converging tectonic plates. Hotspots, similar to those in Hawaii, are another style of volcanic setting where magma rises from deep within the mantle away from plate margins. Tracking volcanic activity with tools such as seismometers, gas sensors and satellite images enables scientists to forecast eruptions and give early warnings. For risk management, particularly of those communities dwelling close to active volcanoes, an understanding of volcanic processes is crucial.

text: Information policy is the regulating policy for information, and more generally the regulation and management of information.[2] Information policy includes those aspects of information-related policy that contain, disseminate, or otherwise affect information. It encompasses a wide range of issues, including freedom of information, intellectual property, privacy, telecommunications, public access to government information, and free expression. It provides a set of legal, ethical, and technical standpoints when collecting, storing, moving and sharing information. Policies at the organizational level cover compliance with laws such as GDPR, HIPAA, and copyright as well as establish data ownership, access permission, record keeping, and breach response. It also governs terms of use, metadata protocols, quality targets and interoperability specifications, and digital preservation policies. Information policies help us to appropriately manage information so that it remains confidential, maintains its integrity, and is available when needed, yet is accessible to us and reused to help us operate and achieve our operational, accounting, and strategic goals. On a societal level, national information policy regulates public access to government information, supports open-government efforts, provides for equitable digital infrastructure, and regulates media standards. Properly crafted policies ensure a balance between transparency and privacy, between innovation and risk mitigation, between archival needs and storage limitations. They are periodically updated to account for new technologies, evolving threats, and changing regulations. Without strong data policies in place, companies face regulatory fines, security vulnerabilities, data silos, and inconsistent practices that affect decision-making and reputation. Accordingly, policy must be co?created—working with legal and IT professionals, information professionals, as well as stakeholders—to develop clear, enforceable, and flexible policies, which align the information flow with ethical,legal, and strategic considerations.

text: Direct detection via high-resolution imaging holds great promise for extending comparative exoplanetology across the full range of planetary ages and orbital radii. Direct detection programs are vital for studying the outer regions of extrasolar systems (where analogs to our own gas giant planets should reside) since those planets are inaccessible to transit searches and can only be discovered with decades-long surveys by radial velocity programs. Direct detection also offers a window into the detailed atmospheric and evolutionary properties of exoplanets since they are amenable to photometric and spectroscopic study. Finally, young exoplanets should be much hotter and more luminous than their older counterparts (Marley et al. 2007; Fortney et al. 2008), so they are easier to detect and should offer a window into the very early stages of planet formation and evolution. Young planets and outer planets will provide critical new tests of the formation and evolution of planetary systems, as the two competing models of planet formation ("core accretion," Pollack et al. 1996, and "disk instability," Boss 2001) make very different claims about when and where planets should form. Disk instability should preferentially form planets in outer solar systems, and typically will do so within ?1 Myr after a star has formed. In contrast, core accretion is much more efficient in forming planets with small orbital radii, and the assembly process should require ?3–5 Myr to form gas giants analogous to our own Jupiter and Saturn. Furthermore, almost all gas giant planets are expected to migrate both inward and outward in their orbits due to gravitational interactions with the protoplanetary disk and with smaller rocky bodies (Ida & Lin 2004; Tsiganis et al. 2005).

text: In nuclear reactors, the fuel materials are the types of matter that can be underwent a nuclear chain reaction, These materials can generate large amounts of heat, so it can be used to produce the electricity. The most usual fuel for commercial nuclear reactors is uranium as pure uranium dioxide (UO2) which is coated in a thin layer of metal, generally zirconium, that allow the tightly packed together pellets to form rod of approximately 1 cm in diameter and several metres in length. These rods are grouped into fuel assemblies which are loaded into the reactor core. Natural uranium is composed primarily of uranium-238, and very much lesser percentages of the isotopes uranium-235 (the fissile isotope used in nuclear reactors and nuclear weapons) and uranium-234. Enriched uranium, which contains a higher-than-natural concentration of isotopes of uranium-235 is favored for power reactor fuel to maintain a power level and adequate fuel lifetime with fewer absorbent impurities. In some reactor designs, such as nuclear fast reactors, plutonium-239 (^239Pu) can be used as well, e.g., one proposed in the Generation IV program called a Molten Salt Reactor. The fissionable material needs to have a high melting point, good thermal conductivity, dimensional stability under irradiation, and be chemically stable. Uranium dioxide is attractive because of its high temperature stability and chemical resistance although its thermal conducticity is low in comparison to metals. Thus advanced fuels may employ additives or other compositions to enhance performance. Metallic fuels, like uranium-zirconium alloys, have better heat transfer characteristics and more dense form in some research, and prototypical reactors. Fuel based on thorium is also being developed, for example for molten salt and high-temperature reactors, because thorium fuel is both abundant and has favorable atomic properties. The fuel is contained in cladding (often of zirconium alloy) to prevent the release of radioactive fission products into the coolant. Fuel over time has the effects of radiation damage,fission gas build-up, and structural changes ultimately leading to "spent fuel" which must either be cooled and stored or reprocessed. Every aspect of the design, fabrication, and use of a nuclear fuel is controlled by rigorous quality assurance/quality control criteria and by a system of regulations to assure that the safety of the reactor and the efficiency of the fuel cycle are achieved.

text: To adapt to daily and seasonal environmental cycles, living organisms need to vary their metabolism, physiology and behaviour within strict temporal programmes that tune them to the alternating demands and opportunities of night and day, summer and winter. Consequently, evolution has furnished them with intrinsic biological clocks, which confer the critically important adaptive ability to anticipate, and thereby prepare for, these environmental cycles [1]. This preparative anticipation is evidenced by the bewildering array of overt circadian (and seasonal) rhythms, hard-wired into nature. For example, the photosynthetic apparatus of cyanobacteria and higher plants is up-regulated in advance of dawn to maximise light-harvesting efficiency, whilst circadian activation of the human adrenal gland drives increasing secretion of corticosteroids, also in advance of dawn, ensuring optimal physical and mental performance immediately after waking [2,3]. The intrinsic nature of these rhythms and the clocks driving them is revealed experimentally by testing the effects of temporal isolation of individuals within an unchanging environment. Under such constant conditions, circadian rhythms persist, thereby demonstrating their control by an endogenous timer [4]. As with all biological systems, however, the period of the “free-running” rhythms varies slightly between individuals, and is only approximately, not exactly, one day (hence circa-dian). Under natural field conditions, however, synchronisation of the circadian mechanism to the environment sets the period to exactly 24 h, and also sets the phase of the clock, matching internal time to the appropriate solar time.

text: 2.1.2 Factorial design in ANOVA Factorial design in ANOVA is the investigation conducted for the independent categorical variables, called as factors, in two or more numbers with multiple levels in order to investigate the effects of individual factor(s) as well as the interaction effects of combined factors on the dependent variables. Unlike one-way ANOVA, which tests the effect of a single factor, factorial ANOVA lets the researcher test the main effects of each factor and the interaction effects that are when the influence of one factor depends on the level of another. For instance, a 2x3 factorial design could have two gender(between groups were male and female) and three treatment type (within of three levels of treatment type) and recovery. Factorial designs allow researchers to study more than one factor at the same time in an experiment, and consequently enhance the efficiency of the experimental process that leads to a greater appreciation of challenging situations. The decomposition categorizes total variation according to that explained by each main effect, two-way and three- way interaction(s) and residual error. Interaction effects are particularly relevant, as they indicate whether the effects of the factors are independent or combined with one other on the phenomenon to be analyzed. It could help in theory and practical implementations by revealing complex interactions between variable pairs. Factorial designs can be between-subjects (a different set of subjects for each level of the factor) or within-subjects (repeated measures), or mixed. The latter design complicates the analysis but offers more interpretive richness and control. Normality, independence, and homogeneity of variances are assumed, and interaction plots are frequently used to illustrate effects. To sum up, factorial ANOVA designs allow for the simultaneous consideration of several factors, the separate and joint effects of these factors, and thus the making of finer distinctions about the processes that affect a dependent variable.

text: Sampling is the act, process, or technique of selecting a suitable sample, or a representative part of a population for the purpose of determining parameters or characteristics of the whole population. As researching an entire population is rarely feasible, almost all social research is conducted on a sample rather than the entire population, and researchers must sample only a portion of the population to generate results capable of being generalized from the sample to the population. The selected group is referred to as a sample, and the entire group from which the sample is drawn is the population. Sampling plays a key role in the field of statistics and research by providing analysts an opportunity estimate population parameters, testing hypothesis, and making prediction without analyzing all members of the population from which sample has been created. In order for sampling to be successful and produce accurate results, the sample must be representative of the population, or those characteristics that describe the population, must be proportional to the sample. There are two major types of sampling: Probability Sampling A sample chosen from a larger population by using a chance process or a random number generator in which each member of the population has a known probability of being chosen and non-probability sampling in which no probability is attached to members of the population as a basis for selecting them. Some of the probability sampling techniques are, simple random sampling, stratified sampling, cluster sampling and systematic sampling, and each of these has their own methodologies and applications. Non-probability techniques are convenience, quota and purposive. Sampling is closely related to ideas like sampling distribution, standard error, and confidence intervals which are used to quantify the uncertainty and variability of estimates coming from it. The sample size is an essential factor in such case as well; the larger the sample, the more accurate the estimates, though such collection may require more resources. Inferior sampling may result in bias, which decreases the validity of inference. Sampling is applicable to a variety of fields such as opinion polling, medical research, business market and quality control. At the end of the day, sampling allows investigators and decision makers to study diverse populations to quickly draw inferences that may be applicable to broader groups.

text: Circulation and Readership are the two most commonly used indicators for assessing the penetration and effectiveness of print media such as newspapers and magazines. Circulation is a measure of copies being distributed within an audience (or to the public). It’s a number that tells you how much of the physical product is in the hands of readers. Advertisers, for whom circulation data can determine the potential visibility of their ads, are likely watching the matter closely. On the other, readership is a wider concept that accounts for all those who have actually read (or interacted with) a publication. Because newspapers and magazines can be read by more than one person in a given household or office or at a kiosk, they are considered to have a higher readership. “Readership” also includes pass-along readers and presents a truer picture of a publication’s influence. Both metrics are important to publishers and advertisers alike. Accurate circulation and readership figures enable media houses to establish advertising rates, demographics of readers and content strategies. These numbers are frequently audited by independent companies to guarantee transparency and honesty. In more recent years, such metrics have been enhanced to account for digital copies and online readerships. That contrast is vitally important for print brands looking to make the leap to digital. Also, where circulation provides the journalists with an actual number, readership is qualitative and tells things like “engagement” of readers, loyalty and favourite content. The circulation of a publication is essentially the number of copies sent out, while readership is the number of people who actually read them. When combined they build a snapshot of a publication’s reach, relevance and efficiency in the ever-competitive media environment.

text: Indifference curves are much more recent and modern than this approach in explaining consumer preference and rational consumer choice among different combinations of goods; it comes from microeconomic theory. An indifference curve is a graph showing combination of two goods that give the consumer equal satisfaction and utility. The underlying concept is that on a line, a person is indifferent betweenany two points on the same line because the same utility is obtained from both. These curves look downward sloping and bowed towards the origin to reflect the law of diminishing marginal rate of substitution: as a consumer consumes more and more of one good in place of another, they need an ever-increasing amount of the other good in order to keep the same level of satisfaction. Indifference curves further from the origin depict higher utility. Consumers are assumed to be rational and prefer more consumption to less, with their preferences being complete and transitive. Indifference curve technique departs from an older cardinal utility theory in that it is supported on ordinal utility, where consumers’ preferences are ranked rather than measured in amounts. This tool gives a richer understanding to consumers’ choice of trade-offs as opposed to one-dimensional utility numbers. Indifference curves are overlaid on budget constraints (which represent the consumer’s income and the prices he or she faces) to show how consumers reach equilibrium. This balance is reached when the budget line is tangent to an indifference curve, in other words the combination of goods that the consumer can afford and prefers the most. To sum up, indifference curve analysis is a useful device to represent consumer choice, preference ranking, and the impact of changes in both money income and prices on consumption decisions.

text: Terrace farming Terrace farming is a type of farming that consists of different "steps" or terraces that were developed in various places around the world. They are constructed by carving into the slope and then constructing retaining walls that create flat areas to slow water runoff and reduce erosion. A form of agriculture that allows for efficient use of land, some of this form of farming even incorporates the steeper sides of hills that would be otherwise useless. The terraces provide control to the water, help to retain moisture, prevent soil erosion and maintain soil fertility, and enhance agricultural productivity. Terracing has ancient roots, and was practiced by various cultures around the world early in history including here in the Himalayas across South Asia, the Andes in South America and the steep slopes of the Mediterranean basin. Rice, wheat, barley, maize and vegetables are some of the crops grown in terraces according to the local climate and soil, it is evident from the use of their unique combination of brick/ or stone walls. Although labour and capital are required to build and maintain terraces, the manifold benefits accrue in terms of food security, land management and environmentally sustainable practices. Terrace farm manages flowing water and stops landslides and flooding by stabilizing slopes. It also supports biodiversity, by supporting healthy soil and water. this traditional farming system remains one of the most important climate smart adaptations for food production in harsh environments traditional agro ecological systems are those that are sustainable and resilient to the stresses of agriculture. In summary, terrace cultivation is a significant manner of cultivating on hillsides and conserving soil and water.

text: India’s Five-Year Plans, which were launched in 1951 with the creation of the Planning Commission, were overarching economic development plans intended to direct progress across multiple sectors in a centralized manner. The early plans focused on the rapid development of heavy industry — in steel, coal and machinery — in a bid to get the economy up on its feet. They emphasized public sector growth, infrastructure investment, and import substitution to become self-reliant. Agricultural development and land reform, along with poverty reduction, assumed greater importance in subsequent plans, particularly through the Green Revolution that aimed to increase agricultural output. Gradually, Education, Health, Rural Development, etc. defined the essentials of the plans. The plans also stressed regional balance to mitigate differences among states in regards to development. From the 8th Plan (1992) India began to integrate its economy with world markets and reoriented its economy towards a more market-driven approach and began to further liberalize its regulations since then. Some have criticised the plans, which fixed quantitative production, investment, employment, and social targets for each enterprise, as rigid and inefficient. The Planning Commission developed the Plan and represented it through while NITI Aayog after 2015 discontinued the Five-Year Plan regime. The Five-Year Plans, as we inherit them, are a legacy in form of providing and shaping institutional mechanisms of planned integrated development in India, and that also as an instrument of India’s socio-economic transformation during the span of a little over seven decades.

text: Clouds occur when warm, moist air rises, expands and cools, with the water vapor it contains turning into tiny water droplets or ice crystals when it encounters microscopic particles such as dust or salt in the atmosphere. This starts when the sun heats the surface of the Earth which, in turn, heats the air above it, making it less dense and causing it to rise, known as convection. As the air rises, it meets increasingly lower pressure and thus expands and cools. When the air cools down to its dew point – the temperature at which it gets completely saturated – there is condensation and clouds start to develop. The character and height of these clouds are a function of atmospheric conditions, including humidity, temperature, and wind. Rain happens when these small droplets or ice crystals in clouds adhere to one another and coalesce into larger droplets, which becomes heavy enough that gravity can overcome the air’s ability to suspend it and pulls it toward the Earth. It falls as rain, snow, sleet, or hail, depending on the temperature of the air within the atmosphere layers between the cloud base and the ground. Snow will literally snow on ground when it is below the freezing point over the whole atmospheric column and if that snow falls into ground-level air that is warmer and the snow melts. Upward drafts in thunderclouds can lift water droplets high enough for them to freeze andm coalesce into hailstones. The entire cloud development and precipitation sequence is vital for the water cycle, which moves water from the atmosphere to the ground and its ecosystems and thus maintains sources of freshwater.

text: The dower, known as mahr, is the gift or payment offered by the husband to the wife upon marriage as part of Islamic law. The marriage contract in Islam has a special place for bride price or consideration, called a louqayah, and it is favorably recommended. The mahr may be immediate (prompt) or deferred at the option of the woman; however, it can be paid upon the death or divorce of the husband. Mahr amounts and conditions are left up to the couple involved and may include non-material (e.g. spiritual) requirements even though the mahr is typically money or an object describing by the parties which is meant to be used by the bride (an example may be: farming equipment, money for furthering education, household items). Mahr is described as a right of the wife in the Quran, though some scholars argue that it’s more aptly called a “gift.” Mahr has a few reasons – it can act as a form of financial protection to the wife if the marriage were to break down, it demonstrates the husband’s commitment and ability to maintain the relationship, and it also can serve as a form of acknowledging the parties’ commitments. In judicial perspective, mahr is the wife's property and cannot be acquired from or seized by any other individual such as, the groom, his parents or the in-laws. In Bangladesh, the Mahr in the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance is derived from the concept of mahr under Muslim Personal laws. Where the husband does not pay the mahr, the wife is entitled to approach the court for remedy, be it the payment in, before or after divorce. The centrality of the mahr to Muslims sends a message of equilibrium and the virtue of wife rights and duties and balance as well as justice and respect to the personality of the wife.

text: Self-report studies may also provide more or less visibility to criminality, as the respondents report on their own criminal acts or victimization; however, such studies are often subject to various constrains that may affect reliability and validity of the data. Honesty and social desirability effects are key phenomena posed by respondents unwilling to report the true extent of their criminal activities - partially for reasons of stigmatization and deterrence and partly for reasons who appearing in a revealing positive or neutral light. Memory recovery questions can lead to the creation of distortions, particularly if the event occurred long ago or was traumatic. There may be sampling bias if some parts of the populations, e.g. active offenders, or specific sub-populations are less likely to participate and the results may be biased. The severity of some crimes is so questionably intense and sensitive that there would be likelihood of misunderstanding and false admission thus leading to under reporting in which case the quality of data may become suspect. Ethical issues concern among other things the development of questionnaires, how questions are formulated, and insurances about anonymity to stimulate honest and truthful replies. This notwithstanding self-report data still have utility in criminological research as they can be used to identify broader patters of unreported crime and the findings can be triangulated with other sources of data, bearing in mind the limitations of the approach.

text: There are two fundamental modes of animal reproduction based on both how the embryo develops and how offspring are delivered: viviparity (birth) and oviparity (egg). Oviparous applies to animals that lay eggs, and also to those which produce eggs that hatch outside the body and receive no further nourishment from the mother (cf. digesting egg yolk as in placental mammals). This is the case with most birds, numerous reptiles and amphibians, fish in general (as opposed to sharks), many invertebrates. Egg laying animals have, in effect, taken the bet, most heavily on investment in wards like hard or leathery shells, hidden nests and defended burrows and many many offspring which help to keep some margin of odds tilted their way. 5) Parental care varies dramatically; some species lay and leave eggs, while others — including most types of birds and certain kinds of reptiles — incubate and protect them. In stark contrast, the uterus versus maternal/uterus being a part of the definition, development in viviparity and a live birth as opposed to from an egg. The embryo is directly nourished by the mother, typically through a placenta in most mammals. This strategy has improved protective and less predictable developmental environments that are associated with higher mean offspring survival, but lower total offspring. Viviparity has evolved independently over time in many diverse animal groups, including most mammals, some reptiles (such as certain snakes and lizards) and a few species of fish and amphibians. There’s also an intermediate form — ovoviviparity — in which the young grow inside the mother’s body, but not by feeding directly from it, as if it were a placenta; using instead supplied nutrients such as yolk; and the baby animals are born live when they’re fully developed, a mode we see sometimes in sharks, snakes and some insects. The evolution of live bearing is often associated with habitats where it is unproductive for the animals to lay eggs due to temperature fluctuations, predation, or other ecologically negative conditions. The former allows larger number of off-springs, possibly at an even lower energy per egg cost, while the latter increases protection and development costs for neonates on expenses of lesser fecundity and more maternal investment. Both strategies compromise between reproductive efficiency and survival in time (and facing evolutionary selection and the ecological environment). These two extremes of oviparity and viviparity taken together are a clear illustration of the astonishing diversity in reproductive and developmental adaptations found apparently everywhere across the animal kingdom, and how nature comes up with different ways that species can maximize their reproductive fitness simply by mixing and matching these various levels of parental investment in offspring.

text: Measured concentrations of ozone in the upper stratosphere (altitude 35–45 km) show a statistically significant increase at mid-latitudes and the tropics since around 2000. This increase is consistent with the predicted recovery of stratospheric ozone resulting from decreasing concentrations of ozone-depleting substances (ODSs) in the atmosphere. Apparent increases in the total ozone column (i.e., ozone concentrations integrated over all altitudes) have been observed at most latitudes since 1996. However, these increases are not yet statistically significant because of natural variability and compounding factors, such as the buildup of greenhouse gases. The only exception is Antarctica, where a significant positive trend in total ozone has been observed.2 Decreases in UV-B radiation at the Earth’s surface in response to the recovery of stratospheric ozone have not been detected yet because such changes are still masked by varying attenuation of UV radiation by ozone, clouds, aerosols, and other factors. Carbonaceous aerosols resulting from combustion include black carbon (BC), which is primarily released at elevated temperatures from burning of fossil fuels, biofuels, and biomass, and brown carbon (BrC), which is produced by the burning of organic matter at lower temperatures such as by forest fires. The wavelength dependence of the absorption of UV and visible radiation by BC is relatively small. However, measurements from the ground and space at Santa Cruz, Bolivia, confirmed that the absorption by BrC has a strong wavelength dependence in the UV with the largest absorption observed at UV-B wavelengths.19 These Aerosol effects are much larger in the UV than in the visible region. By considering the different fractions of BC and BrC, the study concluded that absorption by BrC at this site caused an additional 20–25% reduction at the shortest UV-B wavelengths reaching the surface (i.e., 305 nm) compared to the BC-only absorption. If confirmed, unaccounted reduction in surface UV-B irradiance by BrC could be important for health risk assessments.

text: Three types of radiation are released, emitted as a radioactive element decays: alpha, beta and gamma radiation, which differ in their qualities, composition and how deeply they can penetrate. Alpha radiation consists of alpha particles, which are helium nuclei containing two protons and two neutrons. Aplha particles, if inhaled or ingested can't even penetrate paper, or human skin and tend to cause a lot of damage (to life though). Beta decay is high-energy electrons (negative particles) or positrons (positive particles) ejected from the nucleus while one neutron decays (or an extra-nuclear particle decays) into a proton. Betas are smaller and faster than alphas, with some penetrating power„ -that is, they go through paper but are easily stopped by aluminum foil. The electromagnetic radiation of highest energy is gamma radiation, which is emitted by the decay of a nucleus. Gamma rays have neither mass nor charge, and thus don’t have a problem penetrating through most matter; thick lead or concrete are needed to stop gamma rays. Gamma rays penetrate the human body and are instrumental for medical imaging and cancer treatment but can be harmful in large doses as well. For a number of reasons such as radiation protection, nuclear medicine, industry and environment safety, it is worthy of to have knowledge about their character. They differ in their ionizing power, biological effects, shielding requirements, and therefore which nuclear materials are used in which applications.

text: Market structure is characterized by the options and processes that are available to the buyers and sellers in a market. Four categories of market types or structures are perfect competition, monopoly, monopolistic competition and oligopoly. Three of these structures are distinguished by the number of firms, the product, the ease with which new firms can enter or old firms can leave the market, the control of price, and the type and level of competition exercised in the market. Under the perfect competition, many small firms sell an identical product such that no one company has any control over the price of the product. Instead, a monopoly is a market where there is only one seller and no close substitutes, making the firm a price maker. Under monopolistic competition a large number of firms sell a product with slight differentiation; some market power exists as firms were ok to produce and sell, with competition being aggressive thanks to identical goods and freedom of entry. Oligopoly: Whereby the market is dominated by a few large firms which may produce either homogeneous or differentiated products. In an oligopoly, firms are interdependent as one firm’s actions (in terms of pricing) will affect another firm. They can be competitors, but also partners, which is why the structure is intricate and strategic. These are supplemented by markets where duopoly (one of the special cases of oligopoly) or monopsony (market where one buyer faces many sellers) prevail. An understanding of these structures assists us in describing the behavior of the firm, pricing approaches, entry difficulties, and market performance. Market structure is also used in various competition disciplines, from business competition to competition law.

text: Unit, integration and system are the main levels of software testing used to guarantee correctness, reliability and quality of software applications at various stages of development. Unit testing seeks to ensure that this point of isolation is valid by testing the smallest testable parts of an application (typically individual function or method) in isolation from the remainder of the syste m. It is intended to catch bugs early by testing the internal logic of a component, using tools such as JUnit on Java or pytest on Python. Automated unit tests, which are small and high-level tests, are run with great regularity during development to assure the unit's expected behaviour. Integration testing verifies how various components or modules are seamlessly able to operate together as a group, interfaces between components are working properly, and data is being communicated between components in a consistent and efficient manner. This testing reveals interaction and data exchange issues that aren't exposed in unit tests in isolation. Methods are top-down, bottom-up, and sandwich integration testing. The last testing level, systems testing, tests the entire systems software package in an environment similar to that of production. It validates all aspects such as functional, performance, security, and usability of the system. The system test is done usually by another testing team, and different test cases are used to represent the full software behavior. All these 3 levels of testing put together make a testing strategy which assures that mistakes are noticed early, checks module cooperation, whether it is working with other, and that it does what you need it do – in general business as well as technical requirements – before you release anything which will improve the quality of software and cuts down the maintenance.

text: In object-oriented programming, constructors and destructors are special methods that are automatically invoked in the lifecycle of an object. Constructor is automatically called when a instance is created, its job is to initialize state of an object, i.e., assign some default or user provided values to the member variables. Constructors will often have the same name as the class, and will not have a return type. It can be default constructor (if there are no arguments), parameterized constructor (if there are arguments) or Copy Constructor (also used to create and initialize a new object from an existing one). If you contructor overload you can create objects with different initializations. For instance, in a Person class, a constructor might take a name and age and assign them to the object’s variables at the time when it is instantiated. In contrast, a destructor is a special method called automatically during the destruction or deallocation of an object, especially one of class type, in some languages such as C++ where destructors are used to prevent resource leaks and to release the resources held by the object. Since resources like memory or file handles need to be freed so that no resource leaks happen, destructors are used. In C++, destructors have the class name prefixed with a tilde (~) with no parameters or return type. In GC'd languages like Java and Python, destructors aren't as prominent and resource cleanup is done by finalizers/ context-managers. Constructors are very important for establishing an object, destructors for performing a cleanup job, particularly in systems that deal with hardware, files or dynamic memory. They are designed to automate the most significant set-up and tear-down activities, resulting in more cohesive, manageable, and readable tests, leading to proper and resource-friendly object management throughout a test run.

text: Gun violence impacts our experience of public spaces, including how we represent and memorialize mass shootings in public ways. Immediate memorials, complete with flowers and other ephemera, frequently appear at the sites of gun violence, at times to be followed by permanent memorials with contemplative spaces and names of victims etched in stone. Erika Doss (2006, p. 315) argues that the material abundance of immediate memorials at sites of collective trauma often remains “frozen in emotional catharsis” and disengaged from social and political action. Harriet Senie (2016) contends that permanent memorials like the one built at the site of the Columbine school shooting similarly engage in various denials. Designed often with the explicit input of grieving families, they evade any historical perspective or examination of critical issues in favor of producing what Senie calls “symbolic cemeteries”. Mirroring the stalemate in our political dialogue around guns and their proliferation, our dominant strategies of memorialization similarly offer little more than “thoughts and prayers”.

text: Salinity The condition where the solute composition of the soil or water is such that excessive amounts of soluble salts, usually sodium chloride, iron sulfide, and gypsum, impair the normal good growth of plants, soil characteristics, and general agricultural productivity. Soil salinization is a serious environmental problem in arid and semi-arid areas where strong evaporation (E a ) surpasses precipitation and its leaches, resulting in the accumulation of salts in the soil surface. These salts could be due to either natural sources, the use of saline water for irrigation, inadequate drainage, or encroachment of sea water. When the concentration of soluble salt in soil solutions becomes too high, it develops osmotic imbalance, water stress and limits water absorption in plants; hence plants are in physiological drought stress with available moisture. This crops poor germination, plant growth and nutrient uptake, as well as yield. Toxicity and other problems can also result from salinity by the accumulation of certain ions such as sodium and chloride to toxic concentrations. Symptoms of salinity stress manifest in the forms of leaf burn, reduced plant size, chlorosis, and wilting. Soil salinity is typically classified into salty, sodic, and salty-sodic groups depending on inherent salt composition and sodium level. Soil salinity management also includes actions designed to either increase the outflow (enhanced drainage, leaching with surplus irrigation water, application of gypsum to replace sodium ions in the cation exchange complex, use of salt-tolerant varieties, and correct irrigation scheduling). Routine monitoring of soil and water is necessary to monitor salinity levels and take appropriate management actions. Salinity is becoming an increasingly critical issue worldwide as a consequence of climate change, unsustainable irrigation, and land degradation, threatening food security and rural livelihoods. Scientists and extension workers are working on salt-tolerant crop varieties and sustainable land and water management in an effort to address some of the impacts of salinity. In short, salinity is the destructive accumulation of salts in soil or water that prevents plants from flourishing and undermines agricultural success if not controlled.

text: Secondary growth is the increasing in girth or thickness of a plant, a characteristic of dicots and gymnosperms. It is not identical with puckle, which makes the plant grow in length. Lateral meristems, particularly the vascular cambium, add content to stems and roots, while the secondary cambia (cork cambium) replace outer/older tissue in stems and roots. Vascular cambium, between the xylem and phloem, adds secondary xylem (wood) on the inside and secondary phloem on the outside. Each year the tree adds more and more secondary xylem, especially during good growing seasons, and this secondary xylem forms annual rings which can be counted to give the tree's age. Secondary phloem serves in translocation, but does not form as developed layers over time because leaves older phloem tissues outward. Cork cambium develops in the outer cortex or a phellem layer, sometimes with phelloderm produced inward; the latter is used to refer to the protective-dermal-tissue-replacing bark in the stem. But as it expands, the outer tissues can break and new layers of bark may grow every once in a while. This growth gives the plant its structural integrity and allows it to live a long time, evolving into branches and trunks. Secondary growth also involves the production of wood rays, which facilitate radial conduction and storage. Although a feature of many dicot trees (e.g. oak, mango), secondary growth is absent in most monocots themselves due to the absence of vascular cambium. However, anomalous secondary growth in some monocots occurs, such as in the palm family Arecaceae and the pandan family Pandanaceae. Secondary growth is used to produce wood, with economic importance, as well as providing a means of increasing resilience to environmental stress and pathogens. In summary, secondary growth is an important event for the longevity, strength and persistence of perennial plants.

text: Geological disposal refers to the permanent isolation of HLW and SNF deeply underground in geologically stable formations. This is seen as the most practicable long-term solution to avoid the release of such radioactivity to the environment. The idea is to dispose of waste in engineered containers in a repository from a few hundred meters to several kilometers underground, in rock materials, such as granite, clay, or salt formations. Those formations act as a geological barrier for the transport of radionuclides and are supplemented with engineered barriers including corrosion-resistant canisters and buffer materials that prevent radionuclide release by avoiding accumulation of around the canisters by ground water and corrosion. Geological disposal depends on the stability of the geology for hundreds of thousands to millions of years, to safeguard biospheres from radiation dose. This process and system are intended to safely isolate radioactive waste by not allowing human exposure and less release of radiation to the environment, while still not requiring active maintenance. Countries such as Finland, Sweden, and France are making progress with geological disposal research addressing site characterization, safety modeling, and public acceptance. Despite its technical and economic challenges, geological disposal is considered by many to be the safest way to deal with the long-lived radioactivity found in nuclear waste.

text: Copyright is a legal right that grants the creator of an original work exclusive control over the work, including its reproduction, distribution, performance, adaptations, and display. Information governance sets the legal framework for the collection, digitization, sharing and reuse of information. In the case of libraries, archives and digital repositories, adherence to copyright laws means avoiding a lawsuit and paying fines both domestically and abroad. Second, copyright plays a role in the development of digitization policies (e.g., what digitization can take place under “fair use” principles or certain licensing provisions), in interlibrary loan privileges, in user access rights, and in resource retention. It also facilitates licensing for electronic resources, including usage rights (e-book lending, database access), and budgetary decisions. When we speak of creators’ rights, there is an underlying layer of ethical considerations—such as the respect for the author to recognize and the safeguard of fair recompense. Copyright fosters creativity by enabling authors to profit from their work but over-restrictiveness may hinder knowledge diffusion. With services, information management must negotiate between legal protections and service mission --entailing exceptions such as fair use, creative commons licensing, and public domain. Libraries often provide copyright user education, take-down procedures and access management. Libraries and copyright in metadata and infrastructure Copyright can be easily added to metadata and digital library architecture so that libraries can manage rights and comply with licences. In an interconnected, digital world, where content is constantly on the move between borders and platforms, copyright underpins responsible stewardship of information—of protecting the rights of creators and accommodating the needs of users for access and innovation.
