text: Indexes are implemented in relational database management systems in order to speed up the process of retrieving records and there are two main types of indexes: clustered and non-clustered. A CINDEX impacts the physical order of data rows within a table. That is, the table is stored on disk and sorted based on the value of the clustered-indexed column(s). Since there can only be one actual order of data, a table can only have one clustered index. It is important to note, however, that the. The data rows themselves are included in the index so lookups, especially range queries, or ordering query results (ORDER BY) are extremely fast. For instance, it describes a rule by which if a table has a clustered index on an "ID" column the rows are stored in the way the ID values are sorted. A nonclustered index, on the hand, establishes another structure that points to the data rows in the table without specifying their physical order. Remember that non-clustered indexes are more flexible, we can have multiple non-clustered indexes per table that apply to different columns) e.g., if you do many searches on a "Name" column that is not your primary clustered index, a non-clustered index on "Name" will speed up these queries. Non-clustered indexes must also jump around based on pointers to find rows and as a result it can be a bit slower than clustered index for some operations. Both types of indexes allow queries to run faster, but are not free: you need extra storage to store the index data, and data modification operations (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) will become slower as well, because indexes need to be updated too. Whether to use clustered or non-clustered index is determined by the database schema as well as the querying behavior and performance requirement of the application.

text: In international relations, non-state actors such as IOs, NGOs, and social movements are significant, agenda-setting players (Gould, 1995; Hawkins et al. These actors include global non-governmental organizations (NGOs) such as the International Red Cross or Greenpeace, which generate and direct worldwide advocacy on humanitarian and environmental matters. Multinational companies (MNCs) – businesses like Apple, Shell or Toyota – are able to exert economic power that creates labor standards, regulation and other aspects of globalization through their supply chains and investment. Terrorist or extremist groups, like Al Qaeda or ISIS, challenge the sovereignty of states, and those states then react with security measures. Organized crime groups operate illegal commerce that presents law-enforcement issues and services cross-border risks. Epistemic communities — the social networks of experts in, say, climate science or public health — exert influence upon policy agendas and normative frameworks. Religious networks, diaspora groups, social movements (e.g. #MeToo, Extinction Rebellion) and digital communities also shape international public opinion and can exert pressure on states or organizations. Intergovernmental organisations and even global cities, or regions, on the other hand are ever more like semi-non-state actors carrying out global governance. They draw upon resources, moral authorization, modes of information, and strategic alliances to shape economic governance, human rights dialogue, conflict resolution, and environmental norms. Their worldwide infrastructure allows them totranscend national borders and classical power hierarchies – turning IR into a multi-actor system instead of a state-centric one.

text: There are two primary ways to connect compartments and assemblies between two points: series and parallel. In a series loop, the segments are connected in a row; one after the other, directly linking to one channel. In other words, each part is being traveled by the same amount of current in due order. This addition of all resistances in a string connection = a must be met in a string. The most obvious case of this is when Christmas lights are strung in a row. The string is broken if one goes out,* causing the entire circuit to go out. A parallel circuit connects the same two places, but it has more than one route for electricity to move along. All the resistors in parallel have the same voltage across them, however the current which flows into all of the parallel containing these branches divides into those branches. 1/R_eq = 1/R1 + 1/R2 +... This tells you that the equivalent resistance will always be lower than the lowest resistance. Parallel circuits are what you most often find in house wiring, because it is easier for the devices they power to work separately, and if one goes out, it doesn’t affect the others. Knowing the difference allows you to design circuits that comply with the voltage, current and reliability specifications.

text: Database concurrency control is about the techniques which try to prevent simultaneous operations from interfering with each other where it would lead to data inconsistencies in multiuser scenarios. If several users or programs are accessing and updating the same data at the same time, issues such as lost updates, which are dirty reads, non-repeatable reads and phantom reads could happen. Concurrency control mechanisms mitigate these issues by employing methods such as locking (shared and exclusive), timestamps, and multiversion concurrency control (MVCC). Lock-based schemes allow only a single transaction to modify a data element at any given moment, while all the rest are delayed. By using timestamp ordering, the transactions go through in the order in which they were submitted. That is, MVCC lets you have multiple versions of data and reader can run without bothering writer and writer can also continue without disturbing reader. Databases use isolation levels such as Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, and Serializable, which allow you to trade off between concurrency and consistency. Concurrency control is a crucial issue as far as the consistency and reliability of transactions are concerned, particularly in a more complex system that has intensive data fetching and concurrent processing.

text: The European Union (EU) is created out of the tragedy of broken dreams and the need for new ones The EU has 28 Member States (2014) who signed up “for peace, prosperity, democracy and fundamental citizen rights for all its people.” The idea of European integration emerged as part of a response to two calamitous world wars started in industrialised Europe. The European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC) was founded in 1951 by six countries — France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg — that wanted to entwine their economies so closely that it would be “not merely unthinkable, but materially impossible” to ever go to war against one another again. It was an obvious stepping stone to greater interaction. The EEC originated in 1957 as a way of promoting economic cooperation among six European countries, including a common market for goods, services, labor, and capital all among the entire European continent by eliminating tariffs and trade barriers. In the decades that followed, the forum expanded as political agreements proved the definition of the region to cover a greater number of Central and Eastern European nations. The E.U. was formed in 1993, when the Maastricht Treaty was signed, designing new forms of political integration and eventually leading to the euro, a single currency that is now used by 19 of its member nations. The EU established common policies in agriculture, trade, regional development and, in some areas, even criminal justice, as well as enabling people, goods, services and capital to move freely within national barriers. Of particular note in the 2004 expansion was that for the first time since the Eastern Expansion of the EU came about, countries that were once members of the Warsaw Pact dropped their socialist pasts and entered into a political union with the EU (the fact that former Yugoslav countries and the Soviet Union were never admitted to the EU was seen as a possibility if they became members of the EU). The EU has been popular but dogged by economic downturns (and especially in the aftermath of the European sovereign debt crisis), waning internationalism, the push of rising nationalism, influxes of immigration and schisms over governance. Brexit, the United Kingdom’s decision to leave the European Union, marked a turning point, as the case also exposed long-simmering frustrations over sovereignty and integration. But the EU remains one of the boldest political experiments in history, one that demonstrated that regional cooperation might be the best approach to peace, democracy and economic cooperation in a continent plagued by diversity and historical division.

text: Urbanization- the process of city growth and expansion has tremendous spillover on social change in Bangladesh. As an increasing number of people migrate from villages to cities for employment, education and standard of living, cities such as Dhaka, Chittagong and Khulna grew quite quickly. With the family migrating, family structures have altered and joint families have become nuclear due to the paucity of houses and economic requirements. text: Reporting and editing are separate yet mutually reliant processes in journalism--each serving a significant function in bringing news to readers. Reporting is the very activity that forms the front-line, where journlists reporr, gather and write the news. Reporters speak to sources, interview people, go to events and collect the facts to write their own pieces. Their job isn’t to endorse candidates or persuade you to vote for them, but to find the truth, to add meaning, to tell you what is important in terms you can understand and believe. Reporters are the narrators who transform raw data received in the field into news in the newsroom. And then there’s the edit: The work that comes after the reporting, and that’s done by assigning editors themselves — the winnowing and refining and shaping that goes into making raw material into what’s publishable or what’s on the air. Editors review the work of the reporter to ensure it is accurate, coherent, grammatically correct, is in the proper style and meets ethical standards. They make sure the story is consistent with the media outlet’s practices and policies. Editors may rearrange material, change headlines and leads, and excise irrelevant or potentially harmful material. Where reporters are concerned with getting and writing down facts, editors are concentrating on making facts available and guiding them into a package that has meaning for readers. Reporting is about investigation and creativity and editing about analysis and correction. Editors and news reporters have to collaborate and communicate together, after all, as editors need to work through with reporters their reactions to a story to make the final story better. Reporting and editing, the two are provocatively twinned, are the practice by which news is not just true and current but also clear, balanced and responsible.

In broad strokes, farming mechanization is a revolutionary force of improved productivity, labor saving and sustainable agriculture, which cannot be ignored in feeding the world's expending population.

text: Resonance is a strong physical process that takes place when an oscillatory system is driven by an external force at the same, or close to the same, frequency that the system itself prefers to oscillate at. Any oscillating system (like a pendulum, a bridge, even a musical instrument or an electrical circut) has one or more natural frequencies at which it likes to oscillate if slightly disturbed. The system will oscillate around this natural frequency, and any external force with the same frequency as the natural frequency, will create resonance -a large increase in the amplitude of the system's oscillations. This occurs because the system more effectively draws energy from the external force – each successive push provides just the right amount of energy in time with the system’s motion. For small concentrations of energy loss, one can very quickly achieve a very large amplitude, which can sometime result in structural damage. One of the most well-known incidents in history was the collapse in 1940 of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge, which led to self-excited vibrations that destroyed it at its own natural frequency. Resonance has its uses, though; it is used in musical instruments to make sound louder, in radio receivers to pick out one frequency from among the others, as well as in medical devices such as MRI machines that excite atomic nuclei at resonance frequencies. Engineers design systems carefully so as to prevent resonances or to damp them out. The analysis of resonance deals with forced oscillation, resonance curves, and Q-factors, which tell us how “sharp or broad” the resonance peak is. Resonance is an important phenomenon in mechanics and civil engineering, and in the study of acoustics, electronics and even quantum physics, where resonant absorption of energy is a key process involved in atomic and molecular transition.

text: Transparency and accountability are two fundamental principles of democratic governance and good public administration, due to which the activities of the government are open, comprehensible and accountable to the public. Transparency describes all government decisions, actions, policies, processes, and spending for the access and use by the people that government serves. It encompasses the freedom of information, access to public records, open meetings and the transparency of laws and regulations. Transparency empowers citizens to understand what their government is doing, why it is doing it, and how it impacts them. This transparency builds confidence, disincentivizes corruption, and allows citizens to engage in the process of governance. Responsibility, for its part, implies that officials and institutions are held responsible for their action and are required to account for their decisions to the public or other supervisory agencies. Mechanisms of accountability cover audits, anti-corruption bodies, judiciaries, legislative analysis, media scrutiny, and civil society activism. Public office-holders not only should be held to account by laws and ethics, but must experience consequences for their failure, abuse of power, or neglectfulness. Transparency and accountability In combination, the two elements form a culture of "integrity and response" [15] incentivising better behaviour and efficient use of public resources. Technology in the digital realm has a critical role in improving transparency through open data portals, e-governance and monitoring systems, among others. Yet for these principles to have meaning they require strong institutions, legal protections, an informed citizenry and political leadership. Without openness and oversight, governments can slip into waste, oppression, and public alienation. Accordingly, these principles are not mere administrative instruments but salutory principles that serve public administration on the path toward democracy, support citizens’ rights and lead to sustainable development.

text: Balance of trade (BOT or Net exports) is the difference between the value of a country's exports and the value of its exports over a specific period.A positive balance is known as a trade surplus if it consists of exporting more than is imported; a negative balance is referred to as a trade deficit or, informally, a trade gap. It is the biggest and most visible element of a country’s balance of payments, which covers all economic transactions with everyone else in the world. When exports of a country exceed its imports, the country has a trade surplus, which indicates that it is selling more goods and services to foreign nations than it is purchasing from them. On the contrary, when imports outnumber exports, the country is at a trade deficit, indicating that it spends more on foreign goods than it earns from its own exports. Trade, in the sense of exchange of goods and services, the economy, can be favorable or "unfavorable". A trade surplus is usually a sign of economic of strength and indicates production and competitiveness, whereas a trade deficit could be a consequence of a lack of competitiveness, use of excessive foreign inputs to production, or excessive consumer demand. But sustained surpluses or deficits can be both good and bad. A surplus of trade leads to currency appreciation which makes exports less competitive in the future, and a trade deficit results in currency depreciation and higher foreign debt. The trade balance is affected by factors such as exchange rates, production capacity in the domestic country, demand in foreign countries, trade policies, economic conditions, and inflation. Policymakers use the BOT to determine how well the economy is doing and to develop fiscal and trade policies. While a neutral trade balance is desirable, surpluses and deficits can be sustainable if underpinned by sound economic policy and management.

text: Fossils are so vital to interpreting evolution because they offer a literal, physical record of ancient life and transformation spanning millions of years, enabling scientists to piece together the history of life on this planet and track species as they changed over time on a geological time scale. Fossils — the preserved remains, impressions, or other traces of ancient organisms — enable paleontologists to document how life has evolved in structure, form, diversity, and complexity, as well as how creatures themselves have evolved, showing patterns of evolutionary descent with modification consistent with the theory of evolution. By establishing the chronological course of life fossils reveal the transitianl forms that connect one important group to another and provide ethological evidence of adaptations, variantion, speciation and extinction. For instance, fossil evidence of early amphibians illustrate the move from aquatic to land living, and of Archaeopteryx show a connection between dinosaurs and contemporary birds. The fossil record demonstrates how alterations in the environment and mass extinctions have influenced the direction that evolution has taken, determining which species and ecosystems would rise or fall. Scientists are able to compare fossilized anatomical structures to those of living organisms to make inferences about evolutionary relatedness, to develop phylogenetic trees, to trace how traits evolved. In addition, fossils contribute to molecular sequence analyses by offering a chronology to relate molecular phylogeny and allowing their calibration and the estimation of divergence times among species. Fossils also illustrate ancient biodiversity and the former geographic distribution of life, as well as illuminate biogeography and why certain groups of species are so diverse today. There are still holes in the fossil record, this is due to both preservation bias and geological processes, but new discoveries are enhancing evolutionary timelines and theories. Findings are augmented by methods like radiometric dating, stratigraphy, and paleogenetics, which allow for determining exact ages and genetic compositions of ancient fossils. In short, fossils are an essential time capsule for life’s history, letting scientists witness evolution in real time through the lens of deep time, and understand the forces that may have been shaping biological change, adaptation, and survival. Their research not only contributes to our understanding of how life originated and evolved but also helps conservation biology by placing extant biodiversity within the history of Earth's long-term evolutionary trajectory.

text: Within-group variability and between-group variability are a key idea in analysis of variance that account for the sources of variation in data when there are 3 or more groups to compare. The within-group variance refers to how the individual observations within each group are spread out around their group mean: It is random variation or variation in members of a population that is not due to a treatment or factor of interest. For example, when performing a drug comparison clinical trial, without-group variance would reflect natural differences among patients in the same treatment group owing to factors such as genetics, environment, or measurement error. The smaller within group variance bring the groups closer together in property space and makes it more likely that differences between groups can be detected. Between group variance, however, describes the spread among means of separate groups. It compares the influence of the factor or predictor and the extent to which the group means deviate from the mean of all observations. If the factor under investigation is very significant, then the group means will be spread out (a big between-group variance). F-ratio: The F-ratio, or F-statistic, is the value obtained when the ratio of between-group variance to within-group variance is computed. If the ratio is large, group differences are not likely to have resulted from chance and the factor is considered to have a large effect. Both kinds of variance are computed as sums of squares, and are fundamental in the total variance breakdown of the data. Understanding within-subject and between-subject variance allows researchers into how to interpret ANOVA results and determine if differences in group means are because of true differences, or if they are due to chance. They essentially quantify the degree to which data points within groups and group means between groups deviate from the grand mean.

text: Cluster analysis is a method used to treat exploratory data analysis which involves partitioning a set of objects or observations into groups or clusters such that items in a cluster share more similarities (according to a similarity or distance measure) with one another than with items in other clusters. It is an unsupervised learning method as there are no pre-defined labels and it uses the natural structure of the data to classify it. There are many examples of cluster analysis applications in marketing (for example, for customer segmentation), biology (for example, in taxonomy, gene expression analysis, DNA pattern matching), etc. One first define a similarity measurement (Euclidean distance for continuous data or Jaccard’s similarity for binary data) and then applies clustering methods such as k-means, hierarchical clustering, DBSCAN, or GMM. K-means clustering divides the data into a predetermined number of clusters by iteratively minimizing the variance within the cluster, whereas hierarchical clustering creates a sequence of nested clusters in a bottom-up or top-down fashion and forms a dendrogram for visualization. The selection of number of clusters is non-trivial (and challenging) and measuring cluster quality via, say, silhouette score or the Davies–Bouldin index. By organizing the data, patterns, relationships and structures in the data set can be discovered that may not previously have been apparent, assisting in direct marketing campaigns, anomaly-detection etc or to reduce a complex data-structure in preparation for other processes such as regression or PCA. Given its flexibility and applicability walking analysis is an essential tool for data-driven discovery in a number of fields.

text: Learning assessment plays an essential role in the learning processes of students. In educational settings, learning assessment is generally divided into three types: assessment for learning, assessment of learning, and assessment as learning (Earl & Katz, 2006). Assessment for learning or called as formative assessment involves continuous assessment and feedback given by teacher or real-time learning process analysis to understand students’ learning progress and outcomes during learning processes (Chen, Chen, & Horng, 2019; Nicol & Macfarlane-Dick, 2006). Assessment of learning or called as summative assessment refers to the assessment of learning progress and outcomes of students within a definite time as well as it consists of testing or accumulating evidence regarding to each student’s learning outcomes over time at the end phase of a learning process (Knight, 2002). Assessment as learning or called self-assessment involves critical analysis of oneself to identify the strength and weaknesses and thereby strive for achieving learning progress and goal (Earl, 2003). From the perspective of assisting students’ learning, each type of learning assessment has its values and meanings.

text: Mass communications feedback Feedback in mass communication is the return of part of the output from an initial event or phenomenon (such as a speech or publication) as input, especially as when this return acts to control the output (that is, when a response exert a control action back on the process that generated it). Compared to face-to-face communication, feedback in mass communication is often not directly or immediately accessible and may be delayed, indirect (through letters to the editor, calls to audience participation programs or talk shows, or displays of opinion polls) and/or mediated (by letters, phone calls, social media comments, or audience measurement or market research). Feedback is important because it provides media and other content producers with the information they need to understand what audiences like, what they are interested in, and how they are interpreting messages, in turn allowing them to adjust the way they produce content, organize programming, and communicate accordingly. It promotes an active dialogue between producers and audiences, rendering communication more interactive and adjustable rather than the one-way traffic in mass media. In this digital era, feedback is now also increasingly instant, and dynamic, via social media, where the audience can like, share, and crit process. This change has turned mass communication from a unidirectional into a multi-directional conversation, and it has affected editorial processes, advertising style, and political rhetoric. Feedback is also a crucial part in democratic society to make media responsible, to stimulate media literacy and promote transparency. In general, feedback serves as a vital link between mass communicators and mass audiences, encouraging understanding and enhancing the effectiveness of communication in an era of ever more complex media.

text: Acute stress response is initiated as the individual perceives the situation as challenging or threatening (Lazarus, 1966; Lazarus & Launier, 1978). This autonomic nervous system's (ANS) rapid response to perceived stressors is also known as the fight-or-flight response (Cannon, 1932). Both the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis of the parasympathetic branch and the sympathetic-adrenomedullary (SAM) axis of the sympathetic branch are activated (Charmandari, Tsigos, & Chrousos, 2005). The sympathetic nervous system primarily stimulates the body's stress response, while the parasympathetic system both assists and antagonizes sympathetic functions by withdrawing or increasing its activity, respectively (Gunnar & Quevedo, 2007). As a consequence, the individual is in a state of increased arousal, alertness, and vigilance. Heart rate and blood flow are increased, glucose is liberated to circulation, and vegetative functions such as appetite, feeding, and reproduction are inhibited. Core temperature is typically elevated and sweating increased in extremities such as in the palms (Gunnar & Quevedo, 2007). Though the response of the ANS to a stressor is essentially adaptive, the physiological changes associated with the acute stress response can result in alterations of cognitive and motor capabilities, as well as unwanted health outcomes such as life-threatening cardiovascular events. The effects of acute stress on cognition and performance follow roughly an inverted U-shaped function (Apoorvagiri & Nagananda, 2013; Lupien, Maheu, Tu, Fiocco, & Schramek, 2007). Low to moderate amounts of stress may improve performance, while high stress typically has an impairing effect. Moreover, the optimal level of stress is inversely related to the complexity of the task; that is, higher levels of arousal are optimal for simple tasks, whereas lower levels of arousal are optimal with complex tasks (Diamond, Campbell, Park, Halonen, & Zoladz, 2007). Hence, increased stress tends to impair performance more in complex tasks than in simple tasks.

text: Enduring theories of moral development ponder how we recognize right from wrong and apply reason to virtue. One of the most popular is a six-stage model developed by Lawrence Kohlberg: preconventional, conventional, and postconventional morality. As kids, we make moral decisions at the preconventional level in terms of not getting punished, or wanting a reward. (The latter stage typical in young adults and even in adolescence, emphasizes physical rules of social laws and social approval. Even fewer reach the postconventional stage, with abstract and hypothetical reasoning on universal morals based on personal reflection. Even more influential is Carol Gilligan’s addendum to Kohlberg; she has noted that moral development is also about care ethics and relationships that tend to emphasize things like compassion and responsibility instead of abstract justice. The Swiss developmental psychologist J. text: Time complexity (how fast is program or algorithm ) and Space complexity(how much memory space an algorithms use) both are measures in computer science that show how the resources of the system are utilized by an algorithm while solving a problem. Time complexity describes how the running time of an algorithm grows as a function of its input size, and it is frequently expressed in Big O notation, which is an estimate for the upper limit growth. For example, a simple loop over an array with n elements has O(n) time complexity because the running time increases linearly with the input size. More complex algorithms like BubbleSort will be O(n²) because they contain nested loops, comparing every element to every other element. Space complexity, on the other hand is directly proportional to the size of memory used during accessing a large input. For instance, you might say if an algorithm initializes / allocates and stores n new values in one of them, it has space complexity O(n), while an algorithm that uses the same fixed amount of memory (regardless of input size) would be considered to require O(1) space as it is also often called constant space. Recursive algorithms usually occupy more and store excess space on the call stack (of size proportional to the depth of recursion calls) — that is to say, a recursive Fibonacci implementation has a time and space complexity O(n). Once aware of these subtleties, programmers may choose the most suitable algorithms under certain constraints (opting for speed and/or using memory). An example of this would be mergesort, O(n log n) runtime and O(n) space because it needs extra space (divide-and-conquer), vs quicksort, O(n log n) time but O(log n) space b/c in-place and is running recursively. Long short: time complexity is about how fast an algorithm is in running, space complexity about memory usage, both of which matters when you profile/optimise your code.

text: Stratified sampling Stratified sampling is a kind of probability sampling in which the population is divided into a number of distinct, non-overlapping subgroups or strata with characteristics such as age, sex, income or education level among others. Once the homogeneous strata are defined, samples can be selected separately from each stratum typically in proportion to the size of the stratum in relation to the population. It makes it possible to enhance the representativeness and precision of entire sample through representation good coverage of crucial sub-groups, especially in cases where the strata there is high variability among. For instance, in a survey of political attitudes across the country, one might stratify by region or by ethnicity so that the sample will more closely reflect the demographics of the population. An advantage of stratified sampling over simple random sampling is that the standard error (SE) and variance are smaller under stratified sampling because it eliminates or reduces variability among units for which no extraneous factors apply within strata, while reducing variation in survey estimates by increasing precision. It also allows researchers to do subgroup analysis which can help uncover potential differences in subgroups. Stratified sampling is particularly beneficial if some strata are very rare in the population and yet precision on these is important to inform the research question. Generally this involves nominating strata, estimating the number in each stratum and then randomly or systematically selecting from each one. Two of the most often used stratified sampling methods are as follows -The first, is proportional stratified sampling (where sample size for a particular stratum is proportional to the population size of such a stratum).- Second, is disproportional sampling (more units are drawn from specific strata due to over representation following weighting in analysis). This approach improves the precision and efficiency of the estimate of treatment effect without increasing total sample size, as it is less expensive (in most instances) than measuring a new control group. It is also useful in solving the issue of coverage and sampling biases in divergent populations. Lastly, we wish to stress the need for using stratified sampling as a powerful surveying and research method, which has effects on how representative, reliable and detailed results would be analyzed or inferred from such study sets — systematic accounting for diversity within knitting sections of the public at large.

text: Corruption has detrimental effects on economic growth through its influence on market distortions, its impact on the cost of conducting business and prospects for the future, as well as on public trust in public institutions. It can be characterized as misuse of authority for personal or political gains, and is found in the shapes of bribery, embezzlement, favoritism, and nepotism. In a corrupt setting, resources are commonly allocated for projects that benefit patrons above and beyond society at large, and the outcome is inefficiency and inadequate infrastructure. For example, officials may promote certain companies in return for bribes, resulting in excessive prices and poor-quality services. Similarly, corruption deters domestic and foreign investment; investors dread ambiguous rules, rigged competition, and unaccounted for expansion. Businesses in countries with high levels of corruption — where it takes a lot of time and money to deal with red tape and to pay off officials to get things done — spend less time and money trying to innovate and to produce effectively. There’s also less money for government coffers and that has an impact on essential services such as education, healthcare, and poverty reduction, because corruption facilitates tax evasion and customs fraud … and so much more! That not only slows human capital formation, but it increases inequality as the poor are most affected by broken public systems and rising costs. At the level of the macro economy, corruption subverts the rule of law, diminishes good governance, and fuels political instability: none of these bodes well for sustained growth. In democratic societies corruption can eat away at public trust in leaders and institutions and can lead to voter apathy or even unrest. In authoritarian systems, it can consolidate elite power and block reforms. Combatting corruption needs sound laws, transparent institutions, an independent judiciary, watchful civil society, and free media. The bottom line however is this: Corruption, indeed, is not just a moral issue, it is a serious economic impediment for nations to achieve their full development potential and inclusive prosperity.

text: When leaves are healthy, they are a rich, deep green color, indicating that a large amount of chlorophyll, the primary pigment responsible for photosynthesis, is present. Chlorophyll absorbs most light in the blue and red regions of the spectrum and reflects the green light, which is why leaves appear green. This deep color is a visual indicator that the plant is photosynthesizing and in good health. The shade of green is strongly associated with the plant's nitrogen status since nitrogen is a primary constituent of cholorophyll molecules and proteins, and enzymes that are critical for growth. In addition to having plenty of nitrogen and other nutrients, plants with lush, dark green leaves are also very healthy, meaning they are functioning at their highest metabolic level and are able to take up nutrients at a steady rate. The exception to the rule is that leaves that are pale-green or yellowish can represent a lack of nutrients, usually nitrogen but sometimes magnesium or iron as well. Environmental stresses may cause brown or spotted leaves to be further indicative of plant damage or stress, such as drought, infestations of pests or diseases, or soil toxicity. Crops Monitoring and Crop Health Diagnosis Farmers and agronomists often use the colour of leaves as a cheap and efficient diagnosis tool to decide when a crop needs watering, how much fertilization it requires, or when the crop is being attacked by a pest. This capability has been further accelerated by technological developments in the form of handheld chlorophyll meters, drone-based multispectral imaging and satellite remote sensing that permit plants at scale to be closely monitored in terms of their health. The key reason is that maximal photosynthesis, biomass productivity and crop performance are all s ympathetically related to retaining healthy green coded leaves. Strong, healthy leaves allow the plant to most effectively convert sunlight into energy that will help power both root and shoot growth. Thus, tracking and controlling crop foliar color is a basic requirement in modern agriculture for sustainable production and global food security. It is a precursor of potential loss, as farmers and ranchers can take earlier action to stave off yield loss and preserve plant growth potential throughout the season.

text: Tourism and hospitality liabilities are clients’ or guests’ statutory obligations to service providers to financially compensate service providers for injury, loss, damage, or of their contractual obligations, such as airlines, hotels, travel agencies, tour operators, or transport. Liability may be based on negligence, failure to provide promised services, dangerous conditions on the property, careless food preparation, miscommunication, or violations of statutory obligations. For example, a hotel that has not properly maintained a stairway may be held accountable for injuries to a guest under premises liability laws. Likewise, tour companies could potentially be at fault if you are injured while on a guided tour, especially if you were not given proper safety gear or if the equipment supplied was defective. It's reasonable to expect tourism operators to take care of guests even though there are some inherent risks that come with travel. Contorts will often try to limit liability by the insertion of disclaimers and waivers, though such limitations would have to be reasonable, enforceable by law, and may not exempt liability for gross negligence or fraud. In international travel, international agreements define legal obligations including liability, compensation and treatment of the works of art that is transported across global borders. Insurance is a key instrument of management of liability, with most businesses holding public liability insurance and often product liability; it’s no different with trust. However, in some jurisdictions (in principle) the operation of the business (not the owner) may be held liable if the restaurant, hotel, or bar staff is at fault, for example due to food poisoning or unsafe accommodations. For the tourism sector, risk reduction in terms of easing liability hinges on clear communication, safety training, risk assessment and emergency planning. Proper management of liabilities is vital for the financial soundness of the tourism businesses but it also helps to ensure the confidence and sense of security of tourists.

text: Human perception is subject to certain speed limits, but some are less severe than others. We can perceive stimuli that last only a single millisecond and detect oscillating light at rates of up to 60 cycles per second (Hecht & Verrijp, 1933). But, to accurately judge the duration of a stimulus, we need considerably more time—just below a tenth of a second, an interval that has been referred to as a single “perceptual moment” (Allport, 1968; Efron, 1967). And within an interval of up to a quarter of a second, successive stimuli within still tend to be perceived as though they were part of a single episode or event (Akyürek & Wolff, 2016; Eriksen & Collins, 1967; Hogben & Di Lollo, 1974; Tervaniemi, Saarinen, Paavilainen, Danilova, & Näätänen, 1994), a phenomenon known as temporal integration (Dixon & Di Lollo, 1994; Di Lollo, 1980). Perceptual as well as cognitive processes may contribute to these varying limits (Loftus & Irwin, 1998), and the relevant temporal limit is also largely set by the perceptual task we are trying to accomplish. Simpler tasks, such as flicker detection, require less time than more cognitively complex tasks, such as full stimulus identification. The properties of the stimuli, as well as the context of the perceptual task, also influence the temporal resolution of perception. However, task context is likely only a factor when the task is sufficiently complex. The switching frequency at which a flickering light looks like a continuous light (known as the critical fusion frequency), for instance, is probably not influenced by expectations about its location or even the flicker speed. In more demanding stimulus identification tasks, such task expectations do modulate temporal integration (Akyürek, Toffanin, & Hommel, 2008).

text: The contributions of Latin and Greek to the English language, including English academic terminology, have been significant and most of the technical vocabulary that is used in specific sections of English like law, science, and engineering have transmitted the contemporary technical terms from Latin and Greek. English might be a Germanic language at heart, but more than 60% of its words are borrowed from Latin or Greek. This influence was established during the period of Roman occupation of Britain (43–410 AD), but it was most definitively strengthened by the Norman Conquest of 1066, which brought a Latinate vocabulary of over 10,000 words along with it.The inclusion of so many finished?masters of the French highlights the fact that it was not the linguistic accent of a crude conqueror which forced its way into the language and life of the people, but rather a civilizing, cultural influence which affected the counsels of the English king and modified the entire history of the English people. The Renaissance greatly heightened this exposure, as contemporaneous versions of ancient works reasserted their native languages, often through a liberal use of terms borrowed from the Latin or Greek languages to describe a new idea in science or art. Many abstract and technical nouns arose from Latin in the manuscripts, as: justice, liberty, temperature, and circumference. Greek, on the other hand, has given us a lot of science and medcine related words like biology (bios = life + logos = study), psychology, photography, and geography. Prefixes and suffixes from each — anti-, auto-, -logy, -phobia, -ist, for example — are frequently attached to new English words. The classical influence is one reason English is so vast and so able to expand itself: You can invent words with relative ease, and an enormous number of the English lexicon comprising more or less one big flux of words and meanings has been some form of egso perch. It also can assist learners in guessing the meaning of unfamiliar words by separating words into recognizable segments. For instance, knowing that tele- means “distance” and -graph means “to write” reveals the meaning of words like telegraph, television, or telecommunication. The influence of Latin and Greek is therefore more than just historical; it is practical, having formed the language we now know as English into one fit for precision and invention.

text: An orchard is a plant area of land dedicated to the cultivation of fruit or nut trees. It is a perennial-based farming system where trees and shrubs producing fruits (and oils, and medicinal or aromatic products) are grown. Types of trees grown in an orchard include those that produce nuts, such as walnuts, pistachios, and almonds; or fruits, such as apples, pears, apricots, plums, cherries, and citrus, which are among the most popular orchard trees. Apple trees are planted with specific spacings and arrangements and irrigated and maintained to achieve high productivity and health for many years to come. Orchard management includes pruning, fertilization, disease management and harvest methods, including post-harvest handling to ensure good fruit quality. orchards are substantial components of urban agriculture that provide food, jobs, and income, particularly in areas conducive to horticultural production. They take a while to grow and to start producing significant fruit while well nurtured trees will produce fruit for many years. They also support environmental sustainability by enhancing biodiversity, soil structure, erosion control and acting as carbon sinks. Orchards can be either a monoculture, where fruit is produced on a single variety of tree, or a mixed forest, where several varieties are grown in the same location to improve cross pollination and reduce the risk of a single crop failure. In the modern orchard, optimal efficiency is sought, and this has led to more and more use of such specialised bays, which have been introduced to make the best of drip and fertigation to maximise yields while cycling resources. Recreational and educational use Orchards may have recreational and educational value – for example, in the open space of public parks and city parks. In general, an orchard is an important agricultural enterprise involving sustainable fruit production, ecological security, and rural advancement.

text: Metabolism encompasses all the chemical reactions occurring in the body to sustain life. These reactions provide cells with the energy necessary to take up nutrients, to build biomolecules essential for their function, to excrete waste products and to adapt to environmental signals. Metabolism can be either catabolic or anabolic. Catabolism refers to the breaking of complex materials (such as complex carbohydrates, fats, and proteins) into simpler substances that can be used for energy, growth, and repair. For example, glucose is oxidized in cellular respiration to generate ATP, carbon dioxide, and water. An anabolic process is one that uses energy to build complex molecules from simpler ones, for example, amino acids into proteins, nucleotides into DNA, and (excitingly for all of us dieting this January) lipids into cell membranes. It is an essential component for growth, repair and storage. The pace of these reactions — the so-called metabolic rate — varies with a person’s age, body composition and health. A large variety of enzymes control metabolic reactions that occur with great efficiency and specificity. Other hormones (insulin, glucagon, the thyroid hormones) influence metabolic pathways. Metabolic disorders can result in illnesses like diabetes, the metabolic syndrome or even thyroid malfunction. In summary, life-sustaining chemical processes metabolism, are categorised as catabolism, the process of energy creation, and anabolism, the process of building compounds necessary for cellular function, and are dependent on energy, growth and the health of cells.

text: The Rule of Thirds is a rule of thumb in visual composition that is widely used for photographs, fims and paintings but is also applicable in design. It’s about halving a picture with two lines that are the same distance apart, resuling in squares. The fundamental idea is to position the focal point or main aspects of the scene along these lines or at their intersections, instead of in the center, for a more natural and dynamic composition. I find this to be a good technique, one that can lead the viewer to look at the picture in the right order of how you intend to be looked at and also brings a visual harmony and balance to the image without sacrificing the dynamism inherent to it. For example, with a landscape photo, set the horizon along the top or bottom horizontal line rather than in the middle to add perspective and visual interest. Also, for a more eye catching photo, try placing your subjects’ eyes or focal point near one of the 4 intersecting points. The rule of thirds also promotes the concept of negative space, which can be used to highlight the subject and remind the viewer of an emotion or a part of the story. Though the rule of thirds is a common and effective tool (it is so useful precisely because it is so simple and effective) and in this way it is a type of idea or rule of thumb, it is both not really a rule so much as a guideline (and skilled artists, photographers and so forth routinely break the rule on purpose, to produce compositions that are striking or unusual seeming to us)ConfigureAwaitment 1! And while it won’t — and shouldn’t — be followed to the letter by everyone, it will work as a solid guide for both new and experienced photographers in how to compose the elements in their frames to keep from jumbling or stacking their visuals. All in all The rule of thirds, when applied, increases an image's aesthetic appeal by adding balance, enabling your viewer to be directed around the image to create more captivating and more visually interesting art or photography.

text: The testing of hypotheses in time series is the use of statistical methods to compare time-dependent data to a set of models or hypotheses, in the presence of temporal dependence or autocorrelation. A challenge for time series hypothesis testing not present in standard tests for independent observations is the correlation between the measurements at different time points, and possibly the non-stationarity of the underlying process, that is, changing statistical properties like the mean or variance over time. Frequent hypothesis are checking whether a time series is stationary—has no unit root—what has implications for the adequate forecasting model. Stationarity such as with the Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test and the Phillips-Perron test is tested by comparing a null hypothesis of a unit root (non stationarity) with the alternative of stationarity. The Ljung-Box test simply tests if the residuals from a fitted model are uncorrelated, and therefore, it helps to determine model adequacy. Hypothesis testing is also able to test the importance of interventions or non-stationarities on the data, compare models, or test seasonality. These tests yield estimates of p values; the probability that observed patterns could be seen given the null hypothesis, which help researchers to decide on models and make inference. Appropriate conduct of hypothesis tests in time series is important, because ignoring temporal dependence may lead to biased estimates, underestimated standard errors and invalid conclusions of hypothesis tests. Therefore, HsT combines rigorously statistical treatment with the knowledge of the domain to support correct interpretation of dynamics related phenomena.

text: Exception Handling in java is one of the powerful mechanism to handle the runtime errors so that normal flow of the application can be maintained. That way is better than doing traditional error-handling via status codes. An exception is an error condition or error that occurs in code and are out of your control i.e., trying to divide a number by zero, accessing an object that has not been created etc. Java has a type structure for classes with Throwable at the top, and these fall into two groups: Checked exceptions which are enforced by the compile-time check and must either be caught (within a try-catch block) or declared on 'htrows'; Unchecked exceptions, which are ones that extend can RuntimeException that aren't forces to catch or declare. 5 keywords are used to handle Java exception, these are: try, catch, finally, throw and throws. You put code in your try block that you know might cause an exception and then compare if the catch block is what caused it. It is not necessary to have a finally-block, but if there is one, it may contain cleanup code that will be executed before the method exits. throw keyword is used to throw an exception actually and throws is the one that?s trying to announce an exception and a method would possibly throw. For example, if you read a file in Java, the java runtime might throw an IOException and handle it so that your program doesn't exit, but instead your code walks down its stack of execution and prints a message or recovers. In Java, exception handling pushes you towards writing code that is robust and fault-tolerant by separating your error-handling code from your regular business logic. And you would be able to do it just like Ben Nadel does it (for example) by extending the Exception class and handle any app specific exception that way. text: Sensor noise is defined as any random or corrupt variation or fluctuation in the data acquired from sensors that veils or corrupts the real signal which is the object of measurement. Such noise may arise from a variety of sources, including electrical interference, sources such as temperature and vibration, inherent limitations of the sensor, quantization error contributed by a digital sensor, or aging and wear of various components of a sensor. For robots, sensing noise is critical as it degrades the quality of information which robots use for perception, navigation and control. For instance, an image sensor of a camera may generate noisy images due to low lighting conditions or imperfection of the sensor, or a gyroscope may be suffered from drift and random noises that disturb orientation estimates. To account for such noise, robots use filters such as Kalman filters or particle filters and smoothing algorithms, which leverage probabilistic models and take multiple sensor readings over time to factor the true signal and the noise apart. Attenuation or control of sensor noise allows the robot to better understand the world around it, improves performance in changing environments, and also allows the robot to perform tasks better. Knowledge of the nature and source of sensor noise is critical to the development of sensor fusion techniques and to advancing better sensor hardware and software that lead to reliable robot operation.

text: A construction due to Arratia [1,2] shows that it is possible to make rigorous sense of the informal notion of starting an independent Brownian motion at each point of the real line and letting particles coalesce when they collide. Arratia proved that the set of particles remaining at any positive time is locally finite almost surely. Arratia’s argument is based on the simple observation that at the time two particles collide, one or the other must have already collided with each particle that was initially between them. The same argument shows that if we start an independent circular Brownian motion at each point of the circle and let particles coalesce when they collide, then, almost surely, there are only finitely many particles remaining at any positive time.

text: Interest groups (including advocacy groups, pressure groups, lobby groups, and some factions) use various forms of advocacy to influence public opinion and/or policy; they have played and continue to play an important part in the development of political and social systems. Unlike political parties, interest groups are not after political office, instead they aim to influence policy making, legislation, and public opinion. They come from various sectors, business, labor, environment, civil rights, religion, professional. When most people think of interest groups they think of them serving three crucial roles: as sources of specialized information and knowledge to policy makers, as mobilizers for public support, and as avenues for citizens to be involved in politics that are not limited to casting a ballot. Interest groups seek to influence government policies in a variety of different ways, using methods such as lobbying lawmakers, suing the government, staging demonstrations, or launching public relations campaigns. They also function as watchdogs, overseeing government behavior and revealing malfeasance or policy failures. Lobbying can also have a positive role as representing the voices of the minority groups,which could get overshadowed. Yet they can be controversial if powerful economic or corporate groups overwhelmingly have a say in policy-making, with critics voicing fears about inequality and corruption. Interest group effectiveness is conditional on the capacity that interest groups possess, including available resources, size of membership, organizational form, and access to policy makers. In pluralist democracies, they are seen as essential parts of a healthy political debate and a bulwark against an overly centralised state. Critics contend that rampant interest group activity could lead to balkanized politics or the focus on parochial interests at the expense of the common good. However, interest groups are still de rigeur in democratic governance, serving as potential conduits of organized collective action and political participation and influencing policy processes in highly variegated, pluralistic, and contentious societies.

text: Protestant Reformation The Protestant Reformation, sparked by Martin Luther's 1517 Ninety-Five Theses, according to traditional historiography, stands as the most significant European fermentation of all centuries, from those of the first millennium to the fifty of the second. Responding to issues such as the swindling of the faithful (the “sale of indulgences”) by clerics and critique of papal power, Luther and his successors, including John Calvin and Huldrych Zwingli, emphasized direct access to scriptures, salvation though faith alone, and the value of individual conscience. They translated the Bible into vernacular languages, challenging the Church’s monopoly on religion interpretation and enfranchising common people. This religious revolution divided Western Christianity and spawned Protestant denominations — Lutheran, Calvinist, Anglican — that rejected papal authority. A Reformation erupted in wars and conflicts—including the German Peasants’ War, the French Wars of Religion, and the Thirty Years’ War—that redrew Europe’s political map and would later help give birth to religious toleration and the separation of church and state. It also diminished the Holy Roman Empire and papal authority, and empowered secular rulers to control religious affairs. Protestant areas also tended to enjoy social and economic success, as reformers emphasized reading and hard work. Culturally, Reformation led to the development of a highly educated class of print readers which facilitated the spread of new ideas such as evangelicalism and resulted in the infrastructure of Protestant schooling, schools and universities. It also left its mark on art, music and ethics, establishing moral and ethical paradigms that have helped shape Western ideals and identity. Theologically, the Reformation spearheaded later religious movements, and reached even further forward into Enlightenment thought and liberal democratic individualism. It questioned the absolute authority of religion, advanced religious conscience and spread modernity. As such, it was the Protestant Reformation that effectively turned European society on its head; freeing the masses to think and believe what they wish and, it freed the state to rule as it desired.. For after the state, followed literacy, and then, the foundation stones for knowledge required to create modern civilization.

text: Renewable resources are energy sources that are naturally replenished on a human timescale; they include sunlight, wind, tides, waves, water, and various forms of biomass. Not like fossil fuels, renewable energy does not exhaust scarce resources or corrupt the atmosphere. Types: Overview Renewable resources from which energy can be obtained include sunlight (solar energy), wind, water (hydropower), land (geothermal), and power (biomass). These sources are clean, limitless, and becoming cheaper as technology continues to develop. Renewable energy is essential to fighting climate change because it decreases carbon footprints and reduces reliance on dirty fuels. Solar panels directly convert sunlight to electricity — and wind turbines take advantage of kinetic energy from the wind — while we harness the flow of water in hydroelectric plants to do the same. Biomass can be burned or processed into biofuels, and geothermal plants take heat from underground pools. Integration of renewables includes energy storage, smart grids, and hybrid systems for stable supply despite natural variations. Governments are advancing renewable through incentives, policies, and research in all over the world. In the end, renewable energy provides us with an ecologically sustainable solution to increasing energy needs without destroying the earth for future generations.

text: Mass society theory and Cultural theory provide two contrary views of the effects of mass media and mass communication on society. Mass-society theory, which flourished in the first half of the 20th century, tends to be negative: it views the mass media as producing a Homogenous, high-stakes culture that rips apart the delicate fabrics of traditional societies, local communities and unique selves. That it produces of a passive and ineffectual audience that can be easily shaped to the objectives of propaganda and social control. This, in itself, alienates people and calls into doubt democratic ideals. Such a theory was developed during very rapid industrial and urban development, and reflected a fear of the society fragmenting and culture collapsing. Cultural theory on the other hand has approached the issue with a more positive and nuanced view, concentrating instead on 'the active viewing, interpreting and negotiating of media texts by audiences in their cultural and social context. For cultural theorists, media serve as the sites of cultural battles, where meaning is fought out and identity constructed more than imposed technically. They emphasize the poser of media in culture diversity, resistance and empowerment, while at the same time recognizing that response of audience may be of different in various group of viewers. Mass society theory highlights the dangers of mass media can do cultural theory analyses the process of the media and the society either connected or reflected each other or constructed each other, humanity has to accept media as the space for refracting, testing and crystallising the redemptive spectrum of social complexity. Together, these viewpoints provide valuable constructs for interpreting social components of the mass media.

text: Microscopy is an important method in coyology which provides new insight to the complex structures of animal cells, tissues, and microorganisms, which is not visible to the naked aye, thus to reveal more about animal biology, development, and disease. The types of microscopes used by zoologists include light microscopes, electron microscopes (both scanning and transmission), and fluorescence microscopes, which provide detailed images of morphology, anatomy, and ultrastructure that are essential for identifying cell types, organelles, and cytological details necessary for physiological functions. Light microscopy is widely used to examine stained tissue sections and living cells, allowing researchers to visualize processes such as cell division, muscle fiber direction, and nervous system organization. The electron microscopy yields much better resolution and hence cellular membranes, mitochondria, synapses, and pathogen structures – which are necessary for explaining cellular mechanisms and interactions – are resolved in sufficient details. Although typically used in combination with a set of dyes or antibodies tagged with a fluorescent label, fluorescence microscopy enables proteins, nucleic acids, and other molecules in the cell to be examined and provides information of molecular pathways and cellular responses. Microscopy plays a pivotal role in developmental zoology where embryonic phases, cell differentiation and tissue generation are observed to ascertain how single cells gather into complex organisms. It is also important in the field of parasitology, where it can help identify parasites, learn about their life cycle, and diagnose infections in animals. Microscopy also assists taxonomy, by providing morphological information on the organisms and on details about the structure of individuals – especially of the less obvious or obvious to the naked eye (the so-called micro-invertebrates and the protozoa). In ecological research, microscopy is utilized to study gut contents or other environmental samples to infer about animal diets and relationships with microorganisms. New imaging findings, eg confocal microscopy, electron tomography, have also expanded the potential of 3D-imaging of tissues and cells, resulting in far more realistic image of biological structures. In general, through microscopy zoologists can explore the world of tiny animals in amazing detail, connecting molecular biology with whole-animal studies. This in depth knowledge is crucial for studies in physiology, pathology, genetics and evolution, and also has relevance for conservation, veterinary medicine, and the physiology of life processes in the animal kingdom.

text: Political systems are the formal and informal architecture and institutions by which a society organizes and governs itself, and by which power is distributed and exercised. All political systems are defined by three roles: head of state, head of government, and government manifesting the regime type. Some of the most well known include democracy, dictatorships, monarchies, and hybrid regimes. Democracy, which is supposed to be the most participatory and inclusive form of government. enables citizens to elect their leaders, guide laws and possess civil liberties, including freedom of expression and suffrage. This can then be broken down into democracy by distribution (or junta), in which the majority of positions in an institution are controlled by the majority, and democracy by aggregation, in which propositions are determined using either majority consent (for an IC), or some similar system. On the converse, authoritarianism is associated with centralized power and restricted political liberties. Power in such systems is commonly held by a single leader, beside military faction or party, and opposition is usually not tolerated. The Soviet Union was a totalitarian regime, the most severe form of authoritarianism, which sought to regulate all aspects of public and private life. Monarchies are forms of government where ultimate power is vested in a king or queen, either absolutely or constitutionally - and usually in both absolute and constitutional monarchy has the monarch's powers limited by law, a popularly elected legislatures, or a combination of the two. Hybrid, mixed systems that borrow from several models; for example, other countries may have elected governments, but with limited, somewhat common media and a weaker judiciary. (These are among the roughly 60 nations with federal systems, spreading power out between a central government and individual regions or states, as in the United States or India; conversely, some 140 others count as unitary, concentrating power at the country level.) Political systems are not without their merits and flaws, with everything they offer being influenced by various historical, social and economic reasons. The effectiveness of any political structure is measured by how well it reflects the desires of the citizen, respects rights, provides justice and meets changing social needs. Learning about these systems enables the people to positively participate in the political process and to rise up to demand for better leadership.

text: The Organization of African Unity (OAU) was established in 1963 to foster pan-Africanism, promote peace and security on the continent, and protect the independence of its member states. The AU aims to fast-track development, and to support peace and security on the continent with respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity. is administered by several bodies including the Assembly of the Heads of State, the Pan African Parliament and the African Court of Justice. The AU has become particularly instrumental in mediation and conflict resolution, sending peacekeeping missions and mediating disputes all across the continent, including civil wars, coups, and humanitarian crises. It also promotes initiatives to fight terrorism, encourage democracy, and strengthen human rights and the equality of the sexes. Economically, the AU seeks to, among other things, promote continental integration through proposals such as the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), which is expected to increase intra-African trade and economic growth. The AU also cooperates with ACP and other african international organisations in issues of a shared interest like the economy, migration and the rights of migrants and terrorism. Its achievements notwithstanding, the AU confronts problems such as lack of finances, varying political systems and external interference. Yet it is an important move toward Africa determining its destiny, becoming one, and solving problems as a collective and a region, with implications for regional and global relations by representing the interest of Africa at international level.

text: Booean Algebra is the section of algebra which uses two values (binary) and logical operators, it is used in digital electronics and logic design. It is named for the mathematician George Boole, and it operates on just two values: 0 (falsity) and 1 (truth). Even Boolean algebra itself treats three fundamental operations; one is NOT(_), two is OR (+), three is AND (·). AND outputs 1 for inputs 1 and 1, OR outputs 1 for inputs 1 and 1, or inputs 1 and 0, and NOT outputs the negation of its input (so that 0 becomes 0 and 0 becomes 1). Gates with other types of triggering are constructed from a combination of NAND, NOR, XOR and XNOR gates, and form the basic building blocks of digital integrated circuits. Such circuits are analyzed and minimized using Boolean expressions which aid in the development of well balanced and power-efficient hardware. Some of the laws of boolean logic are: Identity Law, Null Law, Idempotent Law, Distributive Law, Associative Law, DeMorgan’s Theorems, Absorption Law etc. These reduce or modify logical expressions and thereby engineers can reduce the number of gates in a digital circuit and hence save cost, space and power. You must have a pretty good knowledge of Boolean Algebra to be able to design combinational circuit ( adder, multiplexer, encoder ) and sequential circuits (flip-flop,counter and register). It also has applications to software development, database query logic and AI decision trees. Overall, we can conclude that boolean algebra is fundamental to all digital electronics, whether it be the memory we implement or the most advanced microprocessors and embedded systems we are using today.

text: Hydroponics is a plant-growing technique that brings plants without soil, feeding them the nutrients they need to grow from a perfectly balanced, pH neutral, oxygen and nutrient rich water-and-water only solution. The soilless growth module provides direct and exact control over the environment of the plant, such as nutrient concentration, pH, oxygen, and moisture. With the plants getting only what they need, hydroponics produces faster grow rates, greater yields, and effective use of water and nutrients than traditional soil-based growing. There are a few different methods of hydroponic gardening that focus on maximizing how nutrients and oxygen are provided to the root systems of the plants including: nutrient film technique (NFT), deep water culture (DWC), aeroponics, drip system hydroponics and ebb-and-flow hydroponics. NFT is nutrient solution that flows over roots in a thin film, DWC is roots are suspended in nutrient water that is oxygenated, and aeroponics are roots are misted with nutrient solution while being hung in air. Hydroponics is especially useful in urban agriculture, greenhouses, and areas where soil is poor or limited. Water usage is reduced through the recycling of nutrient solutions and c o n t r o l ove r the environment means pesticides and herbicides are no longer used on a mass scale. Examples of popular hydroponically-grown crops are leafy greens (e.g., lettuces and spinach), herbs (e.g., basil), and fruiting plants (e.g., tomatoes and strawberries). Hydroponics According to everyone, hydroponics has plenty of advantages, but it also requires technical expertise, round the clock monitoring of nutrients and pH, as well as capital expenditure on some infrastructure. An imbalance of nutrients can rapidly lead to deficiencies or toxicities which jeopardize the health of the plant. But automation, sensors and information technology are making hydroponic systems more accessible and scalable. With an expanding urban populace and decreasing arable land, hydroponics is a carbon-neutral and resource-efficient alternative to many traditional farming methods - and can help meet soaring demand for fresh, locally-grown produce both domestic and abroad with a smaller environmental impact.

text: The advantage of the dynamical system approach, in which partial differential equations of the dynamics are reduced to a small set of ordinary differential equations, lies not only in its mathematical simplicity. The approach allows the isolation and investigation of specific physical effects using concepts and techniques developed in the theory of dynamical systems. This approach allows circumnavigating the sea of possible solutions initiated by the sea of possible initial conditions in the following general way. Instead of searching for solutions it identifies critical sets of points in the phase space, which attract the solutions, and the probability for a solution to be in the attractor basins. The use of dynamical systems in atmospheric studies is not new. Besides the well-known Lorenz system, a series of dynamical models has been suggested (Charney and deVore, 1979) that stimulated the search for preferred regimes (basins of attractors) in atmospheric circulation. Such regimes in the Northern Hemisphere winter circulation have been indicated by various data analyses (Kimoto and Ghil, 1993, Pierce and Fairlie, 1993, Pawson and Kubitz, 1996, Christiansen, 2002, Monahan et al., 2003) but their causes were not examined. The dynamical system approach, of course, is limited already because it does not include many other physical effects that may be of importance. The comparison with observations is useful for validating the approach.

text: Vermicomposting is a form of composting in which certain species of earthworms, such as red wigglers, worms, and red worms, to create a heterogeneous mixture of decomposing vegetable or food waste, bedding materials, and vermicast. In this type of composting, worms feed on biodegradable organic material, such as kitchen scraps, agricultural byproducts, manure, and other organic residues, converting the waste into a dark, nutrient rich, "humus" material composed of a rich ecosystem of worms and micro-organisms. Aside from the convenience of vermiculturing as compared to hot composting, the product fertilizer is quicker to manufacture, eliminates odors, and contains far more soil fertility, aeration, and water retention -- all desired characteristics for the garden. The compost is rich in naturally occurring nutrients that plants need such as nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium and magnesium, along with beneficial microbes that help suppress soil-borne diseases and enhance nutrient uptake by plants. Moisture, temperature (about 20-30°C), aeration, and feedstock type need to be properly managed to have an optimal vermicomposting. Vermicomposting is employed in homes, farms, businesses, institutions, and communities because, as a natural process, it recycles all types of organic mater including food waste so reduces the amount of refuse that would otherwise end up in landfill adding mass and gases. By minimizing the use of chemical fertilizers, vermicomposting promotes sustainable agriculture, and reduces problems associated with environmental pollution. Moreover, the resulting vermicompost enhances the health of the soil, stimulates vigorous growth of the plants and thereby increases crop yields, which makes it an important product for organic farming systems and to preserve the environment all over the world.

text: In a play, character development is represented by a character changing, or learning new facts about a character. The change is a crucial component of compelling storytelling because it adds fillings and substance, and it’s also what draws us emotionally to the story and invites us to empathize with the characters, understand their struggles and their motives and their desires. Good characters have flaws and strengths and fears and goals that make them more like real people. Character development usually takes place in weaving together a character’s choices and responses to other characters and the events and challenges of the play. An author arc may be that of a character which can involve character development and growth, but isn't necessarily tied to the plot of the story.A character arc is a way to examine a character's internal journey. Dialogue, action and stage directions are some of the primary means playwrights utilize to bring these changes to light, frequently featuring characters either in crisis, reflection or epiphany. The constantly changing development of character seems to suck the audience in as they watch this organism struggling with issues and problems. Then there are static or flat characters, who never change and instead serve a more functional or symbolic purpose, offering little of the emotional engagement richer characters can provide. The thematic core of the as development also serves the thematic core of the play, with developments in a character often mirroring exploration of ideas such as redemption, identity, power, or morality. In a few plays, the character development is non-linear: fragments of the character's experience are shuffles, rather than presented in a chronological form (in a poetic log, for example—in many cases these are presented as poetic.) After all, character development is a crucial part that informs how the audience can read and interpret the story and adds more drama and theatrical value.
