text: Essential or volatile oils are odorous oily liquids in plants parts such as leaves, flowers, bark, seed and root. These oils are very concentrated and include volatile substances which can easily evaporate in room temperature and provide fragrance. Steam distillation is the most popular process utilized to isolate the volatile oils. In this method, the plant substance is introduced into a “still” and steamed. The plant cells burst under the heat, emitting the volatile compounds which then evaporate with the steam. This mixture of steam and essential oil vapor is condensed to liquid and recovered. And, because oil and water don’t mix, the essential oil can be isolated from the liquid distillate, which is usually referred to as floral water or hydrosol. Another one is cold pressing, which is primarily used for citrus oils such as lemon and orange. The skins (or rind) of the fruits are mechanically pressed in this process to get the oil. Solvent extraction is employed even for fragile flowers such as jasmine or rose which are too weak for steam distillation. Aromatics are also extracted from a solvent such as hexane, which is then removed to produce a concrete, a mixture of essential oil, waxes, resins, etc; from the concrete, an absolute can be obtained. SC-CO? extraction is a modern, environmentally friendly method that results in superior-quality oils with virtually no residual solvents. Essential oils are commonly used in aromatherapy, fragrance, cosmetics, food flavoring, and as antiseptics, analgesics, and anti-inflammatory agents in medicine. Depending on the plant species, geographical location and extraction method, the composition and quality of each oil will differ. In conclusion, steam distillation persists to be the commonest and successful method for extracting volatile oils while other methods are used depending on the nature of the plant material.

LIDAR is also less susceptible to the ambient illumination and non-scaffolding depth measurement so it should continue to work well in darkness and smoke, in contrast to vision based systems. It is commonly employed in the context of outdoor, dynamic environments, for which the precise understanding of the scenario is a key factor to allow a robot to properly perform its own tasks, while being safe. text: Static members in Java (static variables and methods) are class members, not instance members - there is one for an entire class rather than one per object. Use static variables when you want to define global constants or counters that are applied to all instances. Static methods can similarly be invoked without an object (the class itself does have to be defined though), class-name and move class-name.MethodName not necesary to methodName()). Because the static methods belong to the class— and not objects of sometime they cannot operate on the object's instance methods or instance variables directly. Notex: Static methods should not accessing instance attributes, only static members and other static methods. Static methods are commonly used for utility or helper functions that do not depend on an object state, e.g. Math. max() or Collections. sort(). The important aspect of static members, is their lifetime - they are loaded once the class is loaded into memory and stay there till the program completes. Static members allow us to share data or behavior at the class level and are very important in certain design patterns such as the Singleton pattern. But being heavy consumers of static variables or methods will make your code quite tight-coupled and testing it will be painful - they introduce global state. So, to summarize, static variables and methods are a way of defining state and behavior, that is common across all instances of the class, and is not specific to any given instance, which is what shared data and utility functions are in Java.

text: Globalisation has had a profound impact on political economy, reshaping the connection between governments, economies and societies beyond national borders. text: Abstracting is the process of producing a short description of a document, often an article in a scholarly journal, a report, or a document such as a book, video, or audiovisual, in order to convey the most important and relevant information to the user in the least amount of text, and to reflect its primary content and intent. Unlike indexing, which is based on a fixed vocabulary of subject terms, abstracts are written in natural language and may range in length from 100 to 300 words, summarizing elements such as research questions, approach/method, results, and implications. Abstracts may be descriptive, indicating the type of the work, the overall scope, the methodology, and the general results without any detail; informative, indicating the type of the work, the scope, the main results, and the conclusions; or: critical, describing the type of the work, the scope, the main findings, conclusions, and evaluations of the relevance, accuracy, or quality of the work. Abstracting helps users quickly form an idea of the document and decide whether to read the full document. Abstracts are present in bibliographic databases, journals and conference proceedings and function as the main access points for scholars to search huge data repositories. ABSTRACTORS need to be brief, clear and accurate without biasing the interpretation. In the case of digital publication, abstracts may help the performance of search engines because an abstract that gives context is used by many search engines to rank and filter search results. They are also a tool to improve the metadata accuracy and facilitate cross-disciplinary research and information exchange. In general, abstracting reduces bulky documents full of concepts and factual details into succinct and accessible summaries, which helps users to make relevance judgments and to move through information that is dense.

text: Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) and User Datagram Protocol (UDP) are two of the core transport layer protocols for pushing data around the Internet, and they're very different. The TCP is a so-called connection-oriented protocol that provides the sender and receiver to set up a reliable communication channel with a three-way handshake prior to data transmission. It provides reliable, ordered, error-checked delivery of a stream of packets to other hosts on an IP network, packets that might arrive out of order, missing, or duplicated.It adds nothing to the functionality of IP, only to the quality of service i.e., TCP guarantees that packets arrive in the same order in which they were sent and that duplicate packets are detected.TCP is very well suited for applications that require high reliability, and transmission time is relatively less critical. Due to its mechanisms of reliability, The TCP introduces unnecessary overhead that may lead to precise latency. On the other hand, UDP is connectionless and does not pre-allocate a dedicated path prior to data transmission. It provides full-duplex, connectionless, and unreliable communication but packets, datagrams, are transmitted over the network without the means to guarantee delivery, order, or verify that once datagram received it is error-free beyond a 16-bit checksum with the headers. This low-overhead protocol produces less a latency, serving applications such as video streaming, VoIP, online gaming, and broadcasting in which Realtime systems can benefit more from interactivity and low latency than from full reliability. UDP lets apps deal with the lost packets if necessary (and frequently, with some data loss). If TCP provides reliable and ordered communication with reliability and overhead multiplexing traffic, reliability and overhead then indeed, UDP lets go of the reliability for speed, and a more efficient stream of UDP packets arrives. TCP vs UDP should be decided based on what does matter for your specific application about reliability, performance and latency.

text: Kirchhoff’s second law (denoted by KVL or Kirchhoff’s voltage law) is a consequence of fundamentals of electrical circuit theory, which says that the net sum of emfs and potential differences around any closed loop in a circuit equals zero. This one says that if you add up all the voltage around a closed circuit It will always equal zero. I.e., for every one round around a circuit you take the total voltage that charges gain (typically from some power source such as battery or generator) exactly equals the total voltage they lose going over various circuit elements, such as resistors, capacitors, and inductors. This complies with the fundamentally sound principle that energy cannot be ceated or destroyed, only change forms and therefore overall it must be true that the energy coming from sources is equal to energy going into or out of components at a loop. Right polarity of voltage increases and decreases must be included if the voltage is in that direction. Kirchhoff’s voltage law is crucial in the analysis of electrical circuits — especially in more complex ones, those with multiple loops and junctions. That's because it’s necessary for writing equations to solve for unknown voltages and currents. For DC circuits, and for AC circuits using components only (no transmit/receive lines) with phase shifts in the voltage and current could impose even more complexity. Together with Kirchhoff’s current law for charge conservation, KVL is one of the cornerstones of methods for analyzing circuits (such as mesh and nodal analysis) that engineers, physicists use to design, optimize, debug both electronic and electrical systems. From residential house wiring to the newest laser technology, Kirchhoff's second law will help keep a design safe and functioning with known results from electrical current capabilities to voltage fields and magnetic interference. To break it would be like having energy spontaneously poof into or out of existence, which we know the first law of thermodynamics forbids. So KVL isn't just a mathematical trick at all, it's actually a law of nature that we need to be able to use electrical principles everywhere else in science and engineering.

text: Kepler's third law of planetary motion, also known as the Law of Harmonies, describes a mathematical relationship between the average distance of planets from the Sun and their orbital periods. It is the proposition that the square of the orbital period (T) of a planet is directly proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis (R) of its orbit. In formula form, T² ? R³. In other words, the farther a planet is from the Sun, the more time it takes to complete one orbit than its closer counterparts, and so on, in a known and predictable sequence. For example, Earth travels around the Sun in one year at a certain average distance, and Jupiter being farther away takes about twelve years. Kepler’s law was empirically formulated by Kepler himself, then theoretically explained by the law of universal gravitation in the Newtonian theory of gravitation. The proportionality constant is identical for all Planets of one and the same star, this implies a universal harmony with in Planetary systems. This law also enables astronomers and scientists to determine the period of any planet or moon if its distance from the central body is known, and vice versa. And as it turns out, it applies to moons around planets and man-made satellites around Earth, too. A cornerstone of astrophysics, planetary science, and space mission design, Kepler’s third law serves as the bridge between time and distance in orbital mechanics. It uncovers the beautiful mathematical structure of the motion of planets and is still considered the foundation of modern astronomy.

text: Kant and deontology Deontology is primarily an alternative to a consequentialist account of morality, according to which what we ought to is a function not of what individuals believe to be there duty, but rather what the consequences of their action may have succeeded in bringing about. Contrary to the consequentialist theories like utilitarianism, deontology believes that there are some acts, which are intrinsically right or wrong irrespective of their outcomes. At the center of Kantian deontology is the notion of the categorical imperative, or, the supreme principle of morality which dictates that each person ought to act only in a way that is logically consistent as a universal law and applied equally to all rational beings. Deontology's focus on treating humans as individuals who are ends in themselves, supporting human dignity and autonomy. This view grounds morality in an abstractly defined deontological framework centered on intentions and moral duties, to coerce people to act from duty and not from inclination or feeling. deontological ethics is associated with contemporary accounts of human rights, the pursuit of justice, and professional ethical codes as they emphasize the significance of concepts like honesty, fairness, and respect. Nevertheless, this ethical standard is being criticized for leading to conflicting obligations and also morally troubling consequences when principles contradict each other, as the model is not addition tell us how to weigh moral duties that come into conflict with one another. Nevertheless, deontology continues to be of central importance in moral philosophy, constituting a principled account of ethics that values as inviolate the rights and dignity of individuals, no matter what the potential social benefits.

text: The MRS is a key concept in consumer theory, and it gives how fast a consumer can be willing to trade between two goods towards keeping the same level of utility or satisfaction. Assuming the level of utility remains constant, opportunity cost is the quantity of a good that is to be forgone to allow an increase of one unit of another good. On an indifference curve, the value of MRS is given by the slope of the curve at that point. For instance, if your MRS to coffee is 2, you're willing to give up 2 cups of coffee for 1 cup of tea, and every single tradeoff, you're equally happy. The MRS generally declines, the farther one travels along an indifference curve (the law of diminishing MRS). That is, the more consumers replace one good with another, the less they are willing to do so, because of the declining marginal utility of the good. MRS can explain about the slope as well as the convexity of indifference curves. It also has that crucial aspect of consumer equilibrium, where the MRS equals the price ratio of the two goods (MRS = P?/P?). At this stage the consumer has no reason to adjust their consumption combination since, subject to their bags of money, they are at an optimum. MRS, fundamentally, is the link between what preference and market counter-factuals, ensuring its centrality in both theoretical and empirical/microeconomic concepts.

text: Mass media, including both radio and television, has always influenced society, via the shaping of opinion, customs, political behavior, and stock market trends. It's inherent scope is mass communication that can be delivered to mass audiences all at once, to form educated citizens and shared social experiences. In democracies, the broadcast media has an essential role of backing transparency, accountability, and the culture of citizen participation with their coverage of government actions, as well as their election reporting, and public debates. It is also a watchdog, bringing to light corruption, inequity, or other societal issues that might otherwise slide under the radar. Culturally, broadcasting satisfies the need of the society to preserve and promote its culture through archiving them as programs and inform all productions part of the cultural heritage of the world. This twin mission — protecting local identity while promoting global understanding — has helped civilizations grow and change. Furthermore, in economic terms, the broadcast media has made an increasingly consumer culture, where brands and lifestyles are promoted in ads or endorsements, to ensure that people spend their money in the way that they did. It also generates jobs in journalism, production (in various technical roles), advertising and other related services. Yet critics fear media consolidation, distorted coverage, sensationalism and disinformation. Used irresponsibly, broadcast media can distort public opinion, stoke dissension and even provoke violence. There are rules in place to protect against these abuses, but enforcement is a mixed bag. Yet the power of the broadcast media to assist in education, public health, disaster communication and social cohesion is evident. And Its capacity to influence millions live and in real time means it continues to be a potent force shaping the contemporary world, even as it continues to change to meet the various permutations of digital and social media around the globe.

text: Gendered workplace policies aim to avoid discrimination, foster equality and develop an inclusive environment which is based on the the rights and concerns of all staff irrespective of gender. These are policies to ensure both men, women, and gender diverse individuals have the same opportunities when it comes to recruitment, promotion, pay, benefits, training and making decisions. They usually include equal pay initiatives, flexible work arrangements, and parental leave; anti-discrimination, anti-harassment and complaint/reporting mechanisms are also part of such policies and programs. Such policies, by proactively removing gender bias from job descriptions, evaluation criteria and pipelines to leadership, are meant to narrow the gender gap and create a more balanced workplace. Further, some companies conduct diversity and inclusion (D&I) training to enlighten employees about unconscious bias and respectful conduct. Moreover, gender-specific policies can also deal with real needs – like safe and clean facilities, maternity support, and health services – as well as promote women's access to industries that have historically been male-dominated, through sponsorship and development schemes. Many countries have black letter laws obliging companies to meet gender equality standards and report data related to gender in the workplace – effectively it’s about having accountability and transparency. What’s more, can positively affect both the bottom line for companies and their workers’ happiness, innovation and performance. As such, gender equity as part of a company’s culture and policy, helps tear down obstacles that are structured and help pave the way for individuals of any gender identity or expression to succeed professionally and help the company thrive. The upshot is that gender-responsive workplace policies are a critical way to create equitable, effective and forward-thinking workplaces.

text: Biodiversity, which is the diversity of all living organisms on the planet (including the broad array of plants, animals, fungi and micro-organisms and the ecosystems they form), is essential for the health, stability and resilience of natural environments and human societies. It serves as the basis of ecosystem services that support and sustain life by regulating climate, cleansing air and water, decomposing waste, pollinating crops, controlling pests, and recycling nutrients, required in agriculture, medicine and industry. A high level of biodiversity makes ecosystems more productive, healthier and sustainable, with the capacity to resist future shocks, such as disease, extreme events and climate shocks, among others. In addition, climatic stability has driven genetic diversity within species, in order to adapt to new regions and to combat newly introduced diseases. It adds cultural, aesthetic and recreational value, enhancing the human-naturec experience, eco-tourism and traditional knowledge. But the loss of diversity compromises the services provided by ecosystems, which may ultimately result in lower food security, more susceptibility to natural disasters, and less potential to find new medicines or materials. Human activities including habitat destruction, pollution, overexploitation and climate change are driving the loss of biodiversity at an unprecedented rate - leading to imbalances that are problematic for both wildlife and human well-being. Maintainig biodiversity is crucial to maintain ecosystems, safegurding genetic resources as well as source of livelihood particularly for the communities that primarily depend on natural resources. By conserving habitats and protecting and restoring species, and using resources in a sustainable manner to keep biodiversity. - Biodiversity is also a global responsibility because ecosystems and species do not observe national borders, and thus demands international cooperation and policies. Through scientific research and environmental education, their value place is increased and encourage behavior to be sustainable. In the end, biodiversity is the infrastructure of life on Earth, inextricably linked to ecological functions and human existence, so its conservation is essential to preserving the equilibrium, health, and quality of life of the planet’s inhabitants both now and in the future.

text: The OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) was developed as a reference model to create a common understanding of how different protocols should communicate within a layered system, with the goal of supporting interoperable systems. It organizes network communication into seven different layers, each of which is responsible for specific tasks. The Physical layer (Layer 1) is responsible for sending the bits themselves over a physical medium – whether wires, air, or glass – and it defines the electrical conditions, connectors and speed (rate). Data Link layer: It deals with node to node data transfer, frames packets and performs error detection and correction using MAC addresses of devices on the same network. The Network layer (Layer 3) provides logical addressing and routing, it determines the best path for packets through networks with the help of IP addresses, and it also deals with congestion and packet forwarding. The Transport layer (Layer 4) is responsible for reliable data delivery from end-to-end, including flow control, segmentation, error correction, and retransmission using protocol standards like TCP (reliable) or UDP (unreliable). Session Layer (Layer 5) It creates, maintains, and terminates communication sessions between applications, manages dialogs and synchronization. The Presentation layer (Layer 6) is responsible for formatting the data to be presented to the user, interprets data and encrypts/decrypts and/or compresses data in a form that is understood by the application. The Application layer (Layer 7), end to end communication between two parties for applications is supported on this layer and this layer interacts with user applications directly, for example HTTP, SMTP, FTP, DNS, providing services like file transfer, email, and web surfing. The function of each layer is such that it serves the one above it and is used by the one below, in a way favourizing modularity, compatibility and debug. A solid grasp of the OSI model allows network engineers and developers to troubleshoot and debug complex networks because they know isolating the problem to a specific layer helps them rig up the fixes.

text: There is a well known efficient algorithm to compute the shortest path from a single source vertex to all other vertices of a weighted graph in which edges have no negative weights which goes under the name Dijkstra's algorithm. It maintains a set of all the vertices for which it knows the minimum distance from the source to the vertex, and keeps selecting which vertex to expand by taking away vertex with a minimum tentative value that is reachable from existing nodes. Denote the distance to the source by 0, and the distance to all other pixels by a big number?. At each iteration of the algorithm, it selects in turn the vertex with the smallest distance from the source using a priority queue (or heap). This reassigns the other vertices if through this chosen vertex lies a shorter path. This is iterated until all the nodes of the graph are known, or until shortest-path to available nodes is computed. Dijkstra’s algorithm calculates shortest distance to all nodes from one node, it works with the graph having no negative weight edges and runs with O((V + E) log V) time using priority queue, where V is number of vertices and E is number of edges. Owing to their efficiently and effectiveness, these algorithms have been widely used in the areas of network routing, GIS and decision-making optimization. While this is the case for graphs with non-negative edge weights, it is not true in general, as in the presence of negative edge weights algorithms such as Belman-Ford are faster. By successively expanding the frontier of known shortest paths and refining (decreasing) distances, Dijkstra’s algorithm is an example of a clear and structured path to reach a decision about the minimum cost (or distance) from the source to any other node in a graph.
